questions.q: Given a dictionary containing nested tuple elements, group the data based on specific index values within the tuples.
questions.a:
# Input data: Dict mapping category keys to lists of tuples (ID, Category, Value)
data = {
    "batch_1": [(101, "A", 45), (102, "B", 30), (103, "A", 80)],
    "batch_2": [(104, "B", 15), (105, "A", 60), (106, "C", 95)]
}

# Goal: Group all tuples across batches by their Category element (index 1)
grouped_data = {}

for batch in data.values():
    for item in batch:
        category = item[1]
        if category not in grouped_data:
            grouped_data[category] = []
        grouped_data[category].append(item)

print(grouped_data)

Output:

{
  'A': [(101, 'A', 45), (103, 'A', 80), (105, 'A', 60)],
  'B': [(102, 'B', 30), (104, 'B', 15)],
  'C': [(106, 'C', 95)]
}

questions.q: Walk through the exact execution sequence when an AI Agent receives a user query in an enterprise agentic chatbot system.
questions.a:
1. User Query & Context Orchestration: The user query hits the agent framework (e.g., LangGraph, CrewAI). The system retrieves short-term conversation memory and relevant state history.
  2. ReAct Reasoning (Thought Phase): The LLM evaluates the user intent against available tool descriptions (defined via JSON Schemas) and decides whether to output a direct response or execute a tool call.
  3. Tool Execution (Action Phase): The framework invokes external functions (e.g., vector database retrieval, enterprise search, code interpreter, or external REST API).
  4. Observation & Reflection (Evaluation Phase): The tool returns structured output back to the agent loop. The LLM verifies if the observation satisfies the goal. If error/incomplete, it retries or adjusts tool inputs.
  5. Final Output Streaming: Once all sub-tasks complete, the final response is generated, passed through moderation/safety guardrails, and streamed back to the client.

questions.q: In an enterprise Text-to-SQL agent, how do you prevent the LLM from executing destructive or hallucinated SQL queries?
questions.a:
• Approach 1: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)

  • Interrupt the agent execution prior to database call. Present the generated SQL query to an authorized human operator via an interface/prompt for manual verification and approval.

  • Approach 2: Parameterized Template Search (Deterministic Pre-Approved SQL)

  • Rather than permitting the LLM to generate raw arbitrary SQL strings, write pre-validated, parameterized SQL query templates stored inside a vector database.
  • The agent uses semantic search to locate the correct query template and uses the LLM only to extract and populate entity parameters (e.g., date_range, user_id).

questions.q: How does Deloitte handle framework selection for Agentic AI projects across different client engagements?
questions.a:
• Client-Led Engagements: When a client arrives with a mandatory pre-existing tech stack (e.g., Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, LangChain, or Semantic Kernel), the consultancy builds custom agentic pipelines bound strictly within those enterprise constraints.
  • Consultant-Led Engagements: When Deloitte retains full architectural ownership, the team selects the framework and stack based on project demands (e.g., choosing LangGraph for stateful multi-agent systems, AutoGen/CrewAI for collaborative agent roles, or custom Python orchestration using native APIs for low latency).

questions.q: How do you handle a project scenario where your delivery team is lagging behind and risking an upcoming deadline?
questions.a:
1. Identify the Bottleneck: Audit the sprint board to distinguish between technical blockers, scope creep, or missing external dependencies.
  2. Re-Prioritize & De-Scope: Conduct a backlog grooming session with stakeholders to freeze non-essential feature additions and focus resources strictly on the Minimum Viable Product (MVP).
  3. Resource Re-Allocation & Swarming: Pair senior developers with junior teammates on critical-path blocking tasks to clear execution hurdles quickly without introducing technical debt.
  4. Transparent Stakeholder Communication: Proactively inform project managers and client leads with an updated burn-down chart, adjusted risk matrix, and clear mitigation timeline.

questions.q: Tell me about a Generative AI project that you have worked on recently.
questions.a:
• Core Application: Built an enterprise document chatbot utilizing a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture.
  • Pipeline Components: Document ingestion, chunking, embedding generation using standard transformer models, vector database indexing, dynamic similarity search, and prompt synthesis powered by an LLM backend.

questions.q: If ChatGPT / frontier LLMs are so powerful and have huge context windows, why don't we just send the entire PDF directly to the model instead of using RAG?
questions.a:
1. Context Window Limitations & Cost: Sending full multi-page PDFs repeatedly quickly exceeds or bloats token limits, driving up API costs exponentially with every user query.
  2. Retrieval Efficiency & Latency: Large context payloads significantly increase Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and processing latency.
  3. Information Needle-in-a-Haystack Problem: LLMs tend to perform worse at retrieving precise facts buried deep in massive prompt contexts ("lost in the middle" phenomenon) compared to focused, relevant context chunks provided by RAG.

questions.q: What chunk size do you usually use, and why add overlap between chunks?
questions.a:
• Chunk Size: Typically between 500 to 1,000 tokens, dynamically adjusted depending on document density and structural complexity.
  • Why Add Overlap (e.g., 10–20% / 50–100 tokens):
  • Prevents critical semantic context from being sliced across boundary splits.
  • Preserves continuity of ideas, entities, and relationships between adjacent text segments so key details are not lost during vector retrieval.

questions.q: Explain embeddings without using the word "vector."
questions.a: • An embedding converts human text into a mathematical or numerical representation so that words, sentences, or concepts with similar meanings can be identified, grouped, and compared efficiently based on their semantic relationships.

questions.q: Imagine your chatbot is giving wrong answers to users. What would be your debugging approach?
questions.a:
Instead of immediately changing or blaming the underlying LLM, systematically isolate components across the pipeline:

  1. Verify Document Ranking & Retrieval Quality: Inspect if the vector store actually fetched the correct candidate chunks for the query.
  2. Assess Source Relevance: Check whether the source documents in the knowledge base contain accurate, up-to-date information.
  3. Evaluate Prompt Construction: Ensure system instructions and retrieved context are clearly structured without conflicting guidelines.
  4. Inspect LLM Generation Parameters: Check settings like temperature or top-p if output formatting or reasoning is drifting.

questions.q: Can hallucinations be completely removed from a Generative AI application?
questions.a:
• No. Hallucinations cannot be 100% eliminated because LLMs are fundamentally probabilistic next-token prediction engines rather than deterministic fact lookup tables.
  • Mitigation Strategy: Hallucinations can be significantly reduced using strict RAG grounding, lower temperature settings, refusal constraints ("I don't know"), prompt guardrails, and automated groundedness validation steps before outputs reach the end user.

questions.q: Walk through everything that happens behind the scenes when a user submits a query in your RAG application, and identify where maximum latency occurs.
questions.a:
• Behind-the-Scenes Pipeline Flow: 1. User submits natural language query. 2. Query is converted into an embedding representation via an embedding API/model. 3. Similarity search runs against the vector database (e.g., ANN search via HNSW index). 4. Top-\(K\) relevant context chunks are retrieved. 5. Context chunks + system prompt + user query are assembled. 6. Assembled prompt payload is sent to the LLM. 7. LLM processes context and generates the completion response.

  • Maximum Latency Bottleneck: The LLM generation stage (specifically generation time and Time-To-First-Token) introduces the vast majority of latency in the pipeline, followed by embedding generation and network I/O. Vector database retrieval is typically the fastest phase when indexed properly.

questions.q: What happens when temperature is set to 0, and what if it is increased to 1.2?
questions.a:
• Temperature = 0: The model becomes deterministic and focused, picking the highest-probability token at each step. This yields consistent, highly repeatable outputs ideal for factual extraction and structured tasks.
  • Temperature = 1.2: Introduces high randomness into the token probability distribution. Creativity and variety increase significantly, but reliability, factual adherence, and consistency decrease, raising the risk of nonsensical outputs or hallucinations.

questions.q: Scenario: A client states that their company data must never leave their enterprise environment. What Generative AI solution architecture would you propose?
questions.a:
• Enterprise Cloud Private Deployments: Deploy dedicated, isolated model instances (e.g., Azure OpenAI Service with private endpoints) where data is not logged, retained, or used for model training.
  • Self-Hosted Open-Source Models: Host open-weights models (e.g., Llama 3, Mistral) on self-managed infrastructure within the client's private cloud (VPC) or on-premise servers.
  • Enterprise Security Measures:
  • Strict Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and identity provider integration (e.g., Azure AD / Okta).
  • Data encryption at rest and in transit.
  • Private VPC peering to ensure zero data egress to public internet endpoints.

questions.q: System Design: Design a corporate document chatbot that serves 10,000 employees and answers questions from internal company files. How would you scale this system if usage suddenly increases 10x?
questions.a:
[ 10,000+ Corporate Employees ]
                                 │
                                 ▼
                     [ API Gateway & Auth ]
                                 │
                     [ Async Load Balancer ]
                                 │
                 ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
                 ▼                               ▼
       [ Semantic Redis Cache ]        [ FastAPI Services ]
          (Cached Answers)                       │
                                                 ├──> [ Async Vector DB Cluster ]
                                                 │    (Sharded Index + Metadata Filters)
                                                 │
                                                 └──> [ Managed / Self-Hosted LLM Pool ]
                                                      (Token Rate Limit Queues)

  1. Core Architecture Layers: * Ingestion Layer: Document parsing, semantic chunking, embedding worker pools, delta indexing. * Retrieval Layer: Distributed vector database with metadata filtering scoped to employee authorization groups. * LLM & API Layer: Async API services (FastAPI) backed by load-balanced LLM endpoints. * Security & Observability Layer: Single Sign-On (SSO/OAuth2), RBAC access control, trace monitoring, audit logging.

  2. Scaling 10x Strategy (System Design): * Semantic Caching: Deploy a distributed cache (e.g., Redis) using vector similarity to serve repeated corporate queries instantly, bypassing vector search and LLM invocation. * Vector Database Sharding & Indexing: Distribute vector indices across multi-node clusters, utilize HNSW indexing, and pre-filter searches using metadata tags to keep query latencies low. * Async Request Queues: Implement worker queues (e.g., Celery/Redis) with auto-scaling API containers to absorb query spikes. * Model Provisioning & Fallbacks: Provision dedicated throughput/capacity (e.g., Provisioned Throughput Units on Azure OpenAI) with fallback routes to secondary model regions to prevent hitting rate limits during peak usage hours.

questions.q: How would you manage incident data efficiently in a database to support fast execution and low-latency RAG retrieval?
questions.a:
• Database Partitioning: Partition incident tables by Time Window (e.g., monthly/weekly) and Severity (e.g., Critical, High, Low) to isolate heavy read/write volumes and avoid full-table scans.
  • Indexing Strategy: Create composite B-Tree indexes on heavily queried filtering columns, specifically (incident_id, timestamp, severity).
  • Hybrid RAG Storage:
  • Keep structured operational data (status, assigned team, timestamps) in a relational store (PostgreSQL) or document store with partitioning.
  • Offload raw, unstructured incident logs and post-mortems to a vector database (or pgvector) with metadata payload filters (incident_id, created_at) to enable fast, targeted semantic retrieval during automated RAG incident analysis.

questions.q: How would you execute three independent AI Agents in parallel, and how do you isolate failures so one agent's crash does not affect the others?
questions.a:
[ User Request / Event ]
                           │
                           ▼
              [ async Task Orchestrator ]
                (asyncio.gather / TaskGroup)
                           │
 ┌─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
 ▼                         ▼                         ▼


[ Agent A Task ]          [ Agent B Task ]          [ Agent C Task ]
(Wrapped in try/except)   (Wrapped in try/except)   (Wrapped in try/except)
│                         │                         │
▼                         ▼                         ▼
[ Success / Error ]       [ Success / Error ]       [ Success / Error ]
│                         │                         │
└─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┘
│
▼
[ Aggregate Results & Fallbacks ]

Answer: * Asynchronous Execution: Use Python's asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True) or asyncio.TaskGroup() to spawn and run the agents concurrently on an async event loop, significantly reducing overall execution time compared to sequential calls. * Fault Isolation: Wrap each agent's execution logic in an isolated try...except block or execute them via safe worker tasks. * Handling return_exceptions=True: Setting return_exceptions=True ensures that if Agent B throws an unhandled exception or API timeout, asyncio.gather does not cancel Agent A and Agent C. Instead, it captures the Exception object for Agent B while returning valid outputs for Agents A and C.

import asyncio
import logging
from typing import Dict, Any, List, Union

async def run_agent_a() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    # Simulating LLM call / Tool execution
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    return {"agent": "Agent_A", "status": "success", "data": "Analysis complete"}

async def run_agent_b() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
    # Simulating a failure (e.g., API Rate Limit / Timeout)
    raise TimeoutError("LLM Provider timed out during agent processing")

async def run_agent_c() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.4)
    return {"agent": "Agent_C", "status": "success", "data": "Routing verified"}

async def orchestrate_parallel_agents() -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Executes multiple agents concurrently while isolating individual failures.
    """
    tasks = [
        run_agent_a(),
        run_agent_b(),
        run_agent_c()
    ]

    # return_exceptions=True prevents one failing task from cancelling others
    results: List[Union[Dict[str, Any], Exception]] = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)

    processed_responses = []
    for idx, result in enumerate(results):
        if isinstance(result, Exception):
            logging.error(f"Task {idx} failed with error: {result}")
            processed_responses.append({
                "agent_index": idx,
                "status": "failed",
                "error": str(result),
                "fallback_data": None
            })
        else:
            processed_responses.append(result)

    return processed_responses

# Run event loop
if __name__ == "__main__":
    output = asyncio.run(orchestrate_parallel_agents())
    print(output)

questions.q: How do you design an automated retry mechanism with backoff for Agent execution?
questions.a:
• Use an explicit Retry Counter alongside Exponential Backoff with Jitter to prevent overwhelming downstream LLM providers or external API tools during rate limiting (\(429\)) or server errors (\(5xx\)).
  • Stop retrying once max_retries is reached, and return a structured fallback response or route to an error state.
import asyncio
import random
from typing import Callable, Any

async def execute_with_retry(
    agent_func: Callable[[], Any], 
    max_retries: int = 3, 
    initial_delay: float = 1.0
) -> Any:
    """
    Executes an async agent function with exponential backoff and jitter.
    """
    delay = initial_delay
    for attempt in range(1, max_retries + 1):
        try:
            return await agent_func()
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries:
                print(f"[FINAL FAILURE] Max retries ({max_retries}) reached. Error: {e}")
                return {"status": "failed", "reason": str(e)}

            # Exponential delay calculation + random jitter
            jitter = random.uniform(0, 0.5)
            sleep_time = delay + jitter
            print(f"[RETRY {attempt}/{max_retries}] Sleeping for {sleep_time:.2f}s due to: {e}")
            await asyncio.sleep(sleep_time)
            delay *= 2  # Double the backoff interval

questions.q: What is the primary difference between a Chain and an Agent?
questions.a:
• Chain (e.g., LCEL / Sequential Pipeline): A hardcoded, deterministic execution graph where step sequence is predefined (Step A -> Step B -> Step C). The LLM is used strictly for data transformation or extraction at specific nodes.
  • Agent: An autonomous control loop driven dynamically by an LLM acting as a reasoning engine. The agent evaluates the user input, decides which tools to call, inspects tool outputs, and dynamically determines the next step until the objective is satisfied.

questions.q: How is State managed in LangGraph?
questions.a:
• State Schema via TypedDict or Pydantic: LangGraph manages state by defining a centralized schema (a Python TypedDict or BaseModel) that represents the memory payload accessible by all graph nodes.
  • Node Updates & Reducers: Each node in a LangGraph graph receives the current state, executes its processing logic, and returns a dictionary with updated fields.
  • State Progression: Channels within the state can use reducer functions (e.g., operator.add for appending messages to a list) to update state deterministically as execution transitions between nodes.
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
import operator

# Defining LangGraph State using TypedDict and Reducers
class AgentGraphState(TypedDict):
    # 'operator.add' ensures new messages are appended rather than overwritten
    messages: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]
    current_agent: str
    is_complete: bool
    retry_count: int

questions.q: Why is Fast-API preferred for Gen AI agent backends, and how does Pydantic fit in?
questions.a:
• Fast-API: Provides high-throughput, native asynchronous (async/await) HTTP support built on Starlette and Pydantic. It enables non-blocking I/O operations necessary when streaming tokens or handling long-running LLM tool calls.
  • Pydantic Validation: Fast-API uses Pydantic models to automatically validate incoming JSON request payloads and enforce typed response schemas. For LLM backends, Pydantic is used to enforce Structured Outputs (e.g., tool schemas, function calling signatures) directly from the model.

questions.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol), and how does its integration work?
questions.a:
• Model Context Protocol (MCP): An open standard designed by Anthropic that standardizes how LLM clients securely connect to local or remote context providers (databases, search tools, enterprise applications).
  • Integration Mechanics: Operates via a Client-Server Architecture. An MCP Server exposes capability definitions (tools, prompts, resources) using a standardized JSON-RPC protocol over standard I/O (stdio) or Server-Sent Events (SSE). The LLM Client (e.g., Claude Desktop, custom agent) connects to the server, discovers exposed capabilities, and invokes them cleanly without requiring custom custom API wrappers for every separate data source.

questions.q: Explain the differences between Temperature, Top-P, and Top-K.
questions.a:
• Temperature: Scales the unnormalized logit values before applying the Softmax function.
  • \(T \to 0\) (Greedy Decoding): Makes the model output deterministic by always choosing the highest-probability token.

  • High \(T\): Flattens the probability distribution, encouraging variety and creativity.

  • Top-K: Constrains selection strictly to the top \(K\) most probable next tokens, zeroing out probabilities for all tokens ranked outside \(K\).

  • Top-P (Nucleus Sampling): Selects tokens dynamically from the top candidate pool whose cumulative probability sum reaches or exceeds threshold \(P\) (e.g., \(P = 0.90\)). The candidate set expands or contracts based on the model's confidence across different context points.

questions.q: How do LLMs understand words with multiple meanings (e.g., "bank" of a river vs. financial "bank")?
questions.a:
• Self-Attention Mechanism: The Transformer's self-attention mechanism evaluates pairwise relationships between every token in the input sequence simultaneously.
  • Contextual Vector Representation: Rather than using static word lookup embeddings (like Word2Vec), the self-attention heads compute dynamic Query (\(Q\)), Key (\(K\)), and Value (\(V\)) transformations. The representation of the word "bank" changes dynamically based on attention weights assigned to surrounding context tokens (e.g., "river", "water", "mud" vs. "money", "deposit", "interest").

questions.q: How do you detect and handle hallucinations in an Agentic system?
questions.a:
1. Context Grounding Audit: Verify generated claims directly against retrieved source documents using an entailment classifier or automated evaluation suite (RAGAS / DeepEval).
  2. ReAct Reflection & Verification Loops: Program an explicitly defined "Verification Node" in LangGraph that evaluates tool outputs against generated text before finalizing output execution.
  3. Strict System Constraints: Use deterministic system prompts mandating refusal ("I do not know") if facts are absent from the context.
  4. Self-Correction Retry: If a hallucination is detected at an intermediary step, trigger a retry loop passing the error state back to the agent to regenerate the response with strict constraints.

questions.q: Walk me through the Transformer architecture. Why does self-attention work better than RNNs?
questions.a:
• Input: tokens are turned into embeddings, and positional encodings are added because attention alone has no sense of order.
  • Self-attention: each token creates a Query, Key and Value. Attention weights are softmax(QKᵀ/√d) and are applied to V, so every token can look at every other token in one step.
  • Multi-head: several attention heads run in parallel, each learning a different relationship (syntax, coreference, and so on). Their outputs are concatenated and projected.
  • Each block: attention → add & layer-norm → feed-forward network → add & layer-norm. Encoders (BERT) see the whole sentence; decoders (GPT) use a causal mask.
  • Why it beats RNNs: there is no step-by-step recurrence, so training is fully parallel on GPUs. Long-range dependencies are one hop away instead of N hops, which avoids vanishing gradients. It also scales cleanly with data and compute.

questions.q: How have you used LangChain in a project? What are its core building blocks?
questions.a:
• Building blocks:
  • Models: chat-model wrappers such as ChatOpenAI or Azure OpenAI.
  • Prompts: ChatPromptTemplate with variables.
  • Output parsers / structured output: Pydantic schemas.
  • Retrievers: a vector store via .as_retriever().
  • Tools: decorated Python functions.
  • LCEL: chains such as prompt | llm | parser with invoke, batch and stream.
  • A typical project answer: "I built a RAG assistant over policy PDFs. A loader feeds a recursive splitter (800 tokens, 100 overlap), then embeddings go into FAISS or Chroma. A retriever with k=4 feeds a prompt that tells the model to answer only from the context and cite sources. Streaming responses are served through FastAPI. For agent steps I moved to LangGraph, because it gives explicit state, loops and human approval."
  • Always say why you chose it (speed of integration, swapping providers) and what you would change, such as fewer abstraction layers for latency-critical paths.

questions.q: How did you deploy your model or GenAI application to production?
questions.a:
• Packaging: wrap the model or chain in a FastAPI service with /health and /predict (or /chat) endpoints and Pydantic request/response models, then build a Docker image.
  • Hosting: use a managed endpoint (Azure ML, SageMaker or Vertex AI), or Kubernetes / AKS for scale, behind an API gateway that handles authentication and rate limits.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps runs tests and an evaluation suite (a golden question set for LLM apps), builds the image, and deploys blue-green or canary.
  • Operations:
  • Structured logs with request ID, latency and token count.
  • Tracing with LangSmith or OpenTelemetry.
  • Dashboards for p95 latency, error rate and cost.
  • Alerts on drift or a drop in quality.
  • Secrets live in Key Vault or Secrets Manager, never in code.

questions.q: Explain an AI agent you have built. What tools and memory did it use?
questions.a:
• The loop: the LLM is the reasoning engine. It reads the goal, chooses a tool, reads the tool result and repeats until it is done (the ReAct pattern).
  • Tools: typed functions such as search_kb(query), get_order(id) or create_ticket(...). Each has a clear description and a JSON schema, and only what the role needs is exposed.
  • Memory:
  • Short-term: the conversation state in the graph or checkpointer.
  • Long-term: a vector store or database of user facts and past resolutions.
  • Summary memory: compresses long chats into a summary.
  • Safety: a maximum number of iterations, timeouts, human approval for write actions, and validation of tool arguments.
  • Example: "A support agent in LangGraph. It classifies the intent, retrieves policy, calls the order API, drafts a reply, and escalates to a human when confidence is low or a refund exceeds ₹5,000."

questions.q: How do you scale RAG while keeping hallucinations and latency low?
questions.a:
• Retrieval quality:
  • Use semantic or structure-aware chunking with metadata.
  • Use hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) and a cross-encoder re-ranker.
  • Filter on metadata (department, date).
  • Grounding:
  • Instruct the model to answer only from the context, and to say "I don't know" when it can't.
  • Require citations.
  • Run a faithfulness check (RAGAS or an LLM judge) on samples.
  • Latency:
  • Cache embeddings and answers (including a semantic cache).
  • Use ANN indexes such as HNSW.
  • Retrieve a small top-k after re-ranking.
  • Stream tokens.
  • Route easy questions to smaller models.
  • Run async parallel retrieval.
  • Scale: shard or partition the index by tenant, update it incrementally, and monitor recall@k and p95 latency.

questions.q: How is an agentic system different from a traditional GenAI (prompt or RAG) system?
questions.a:
• Traditional: a single pass of input → (retrieve) → generate. The flow is fixed by the developer and easy to test, cheap and predictable.
  • Agentic: the model plans and chooses actions. It calls tools, loops, reflects and may coordinate several agents. It handles open-ended, multi-step tasks.
  • Trade-offs: agents cost more and are slower and less predictable, so they need guardrails, step limits, tracing and evaluation of whole trajectories.
  • Rule of thumb: use a deterministic workflow when the steps are known, and an agent only when the path truly depends on intermediate results.

questions.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and why does it help?
questions.a:
• What it is: MCP is an open protocol for connecting LLM applications to tools and data in a standard way. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts, and any MCP-capable client (an IDE, a chat app or an agent) can use them.
  • Why it helps:
  • Write an integration once and reuse it across many models and apps, instead of writing custom function-calling glue for each one.
  • It has clear capability discovery and keeps permissions and transport separate (stdio or HTTP).
  • Enterprise view: put authentication, least-privilege scopes and audit logs on the server side, and treat tool output as untrusted input.

questions.q: How do you defend an enterprise LLM app against prompt injection and data leakage?
questions.a:
• Separate instructions from data: retrieved documents and tool outputs are untrusted. Wrap them in delimiters and tell the model never to follow instructions found inside them.
  • Least privilege:
  • Tools get only the permissions they need.
  • Document-level access control is applied before retrieval, so users only retrieve what they are allowed to see.
  • Filters:
  • On input, detect jailbreaks and injections.
  • On output, mask PII and secrets and enforce policy (for example Azure AI Content Safety or Guardrails).
  • Human approval for sensitive actions (payments, emails, deletes).
  • Testing: red-team prompt sets in CI, plus logging and monitoring for anomalies.

questions.q: How do you make an LLM return valid structured JSON every time?
questions.a:
• Use the provider's structured output or JSON schema mode, or function calling, with a Pydantic model.
  • Validate the response. If validation fails, send the validation error back for a single retry. If it still fails, fall back to a safe default.
  • Keep the schema small and give field descriptions and enums, with temperature at 0 to 0.2.
  • In LangChain use llm.with_structured_output(Model); parsers such as PydanticOutputParser work with any model.

questions.q: Describe a production AI failure you debugged.
questions.a:
Answer (STAR structure):

  • Situation: "Our RAG bot's answer accuracy dropped from about 85% to 60% after a document refresh."
  • Task: find the root cause within a day.
  • Action: "I checked traces in LangSmith and saw that the new PDFs were scanned images, so the extracted text was empty and retrieval was returning irrelevant chunks. I added OCR, a check that rejects documents with too little text, and an alert on mean retrieval score."
  • Result: accuracy came back to 86%, and the evaluation set now runs on every ingestion.
  • Interviewers want to see observability, root-cause analysis and prevention, not just the fix.

questions.q: In 30 minutes, build an image classifier (PyTorch). What's your minimal, correct approach?
questions.a:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torchvision as tv
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

tf = tv.transforms.Compose([tv.transforms.Resize((64, 64)), tv.transforms.ToTensor(),
                            tv.transforms.Normalize([.5] * 3, [.5] * 3)])
train = tv.datasets.ImageFolder("data/train", tf); val = tv.datasets.ImageFolder("data/val", tf)
dl, vl = DataLoader(train, 64, shuffle=True), DataLoader(val, 128)
model = tv.models.resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1"); model.fc = nn.Linear(512, len(train.classes))   # transfer learning
opt, lossf = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), 1e-3), nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
for epoch in range(3):
    model.train()
    for x, y in dl:
        opt.zero_grad(); lossf(model(x), y).backward(); opt.step()
    model.eval(); correct = total = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for x, y in vl: correct += (model(x).argmax(1) == y).sum().item(); total += len(y)
    print(epoch, correct / total)
  • Transfer learning from a pre-trained backbone is the fastest route to good accuracy. Mention augmentation, a learning-rate schedule and class imbalance if you have time.

questions.q: Build a phrase (text) classifier quickly. What would you do?
questions.a:
• Baseline (2 minutes): TF-IDF + logistic regression. It is often strong.
  • DNN: an embedding layer → mean pool (or a BiLSTM/CNN) → dense → softmax. Or fine-tune DistilBERT if a GPU and time allow.
import torch.nn as nn
class TextClf(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab, n_cls, d=128):
        super().__init__(); self.emb = nn.EmbeddingBag(vocab, d, mode="mean"); self.fc = nn.Linear(d, n_cls)
    def forward(self, ids, offsets): return self.fc(self.emb(ids, offsets))
  • Report macro-F1 for imbalanced classes and show a confusion matrix.

questions.q: Implement KNN from scratch (by hand, no IDE).
questions.a:
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

def knn(Xtr, ytr, Xte, k=3):
    out = []
    for x in Xte:
        d = np.linalg.norm(Xtr - x, axis=1)
        nn_idx = np.argsort(d)[:k]
        out.append(Counter(ytr[nn_idx]).most_common(1)[0][0])
    return np.array(out)
  • State the complexity (O(n·d) per query), the need to scale features, choosing k, ties, and faster search (KD-tree, FAISS).

questions.q: How does Adobe-style generative AI (e.g. Firefly) differ from generic image generation? What would you consider as an MLE?
questions.a:
• Commercially safe training data (licensed or owned content) and content credentials (C2PA provenance) are key differentiators.
  • Controllability: inpainting, outpainting, style and structure reference, editing that fits creative workflows (Photoshop's Generative Fill).
  • MLE concerns:
  • Latency and cost of diffusion inference: fewer sampling steps, distillation (LCM, consistency models), batching, GPU scheduling.
  • Safety filters.
  • Evaluation (FID/CLIP score plus human creative ratings).
  • Personalisation without leaking IP.

questions.q: Why might pure LeetCode prep be insufficient for an ML engineer role, and what is "domain judgement"?
questions.a:
• Real ML work depends on choosing the right problem framing, data, metrics and trade-offs: knowing when a simple model wins, spotting leakage, defining the evaluation and planning deployment.
  • Domain judgement means connecting the ML to the product (for creative tools: user intent, quality perception, latency tolerance), and debugging models (error analysis, data issues).
  • Prepare ML case discussions and past-project trade-offs, not just algorithms.

questions.q: Behavioural: what did you do in your previous role, and where do you want to be in 3 years?
questions.a:
• Past: a concise impact story with metrics (2–3 minutes). Highlight a decision you owned.
  • Future: "Grow into an ML engineer who owns end-to-end features: model, serving and evaluation. I'm especially interested in generative imaging and the inference efficiency that makes it usable inside creative apps."
  • Tie your goals to Adobe's products (Firefly, Express, Document Cloud AI Assistant).

questions.q: Airbnb: should we fine-tune an LLM or use RAG for an internal employee chatbot?
questions.a:
• RAG first: internal knowledge changes often (policies, docs), needs citations and access control, and RAG is cheaper and faster to iterate.
  • Fine-tune when: you need a consistent style or format, domain jargon the base model handles poorly, lower latency or cost at high volume (a smaller fine-tuned model), or tool-use patterns specific to your systems.
  • Often both: RAG for knowledge plus a light LoRA fine-tune for tone and format.
  • Decide with an evaluation set: accuracy, faithfulness, latency, cost and maintenance burden.

questions.q: Model debugging: offline AUC is 0.90, but online the model hurts bookings. What do you check?
questions.a:
1. Training/serving skew: feature values computed differently online, stale features, missing defaults. Compare feature distributions online vs offline.
  2. Leakage offline: a feature that wasn't available at prediction time.
  3. Objective mismatch: optimised clicks, not bookings; position bias in the training data.
  4. Distribution shift: seasonality, new markets, or a new UI.
  5. Experiment issues: sample-ratio mismatch, a bug in the treatment, interference. - Fix the root cause, then add parity tests and online monitoring.

questions.q: Design an unsafe-content detector for listings and messages.
questions.a:
• Policies first: define the categories (scams, discrimination, explicit content, off-platform payment requests) with examples.
  • Models: multimodal classifiers (text + images); LLM-based classification for nuanced cases; rules for known patterns (phone numbers, payment links).
  • Thresholds by severity: auto-block high-confidence severe cases, send ambiguous ones to human review, warn on low-severity issues.
  • Feedback loop: reviewer labels → retraining; adversarial evolution (scammers adapt), so monitor new patterns.
  • Metrics: precision and recall per category, review-queue load, time to action, false-positive appeals.

questions.q: When would an SVM beat deep learning?
questions.a:
• Small to medium tabular or text datasets with good features (TF-IDF): SVMs (linear or kernel) are strong, fast to train and less prone to overfitting than large neural networks.
  • High-dimensional sparse data with clear margins (text classification).
  • Need for convex optimisation, few hyperparameters, or limited compute.
  • Deep learning wins with large data, raw inputs (images, audio) and when representation learning is needed.

questions.q: TikTok: generate all valid combinations of n pairs of parentheses.
questions.a:
def gen(n):
    out = []
    def bt(s, o, c):
        if len(s) == 2 * n: out.append(s); return
        if o < n: bt(s + "(", o + 1, c)
        if c < o: bt(s + ")", o, c + 1)
    bt("", 0, 0); return out
print(gen(3))   # ['((()))','(()())','(())()','()(())','()()()']
  • Backtracking with the counts of open and close brackets. The number of results is the n-th Catalan number.

questions.q: Search in a rotated sorted array.
questions.a:
def search(a, t):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[m] == t: return m
        if a[lo] <= a[m]:                     # left half sorted
            if a[lo] <= t < a[m]: hi = m - 1
            else: lo = m + 1
        else:                                 # right half sorted
            if a[m] < t <= a[hi]: lo = m + 1
            else: hi = m - 1
    return -1
  • O(log n): one half is always sorted, so decide which side the target lies on.

questions.q: Implement logistic regression from scratch (no ML libraries).
questions.a:
import numpy as np

class LogReg:
    def __init__(self, lr=0.1, epochs=1000, l2=0.0):
        self.lr, self.epochs, self.l2 = lr, epochs, l2
    def fit(self, X, y):
        n, d = X.shape
        self.w, self.b = np.zeros(d), 0.0
        for _ in range(self.epochs):
            p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ self.w + self.b)))
            gw = X.T @ (p - y) / n + self.l2 * self.w
            gb = np.mean(p - y)
            self.w -= self.lr * gw; self.b -= self.lr * gb
        return self
    def predict_proba(self, X):
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ self.w + self.b)))
    def predict(self, X, t=0.5):
        return (self.predict_proba(X) >= t).astype(int)
  • Explain the log-loss gradient Xᵀ(p − y)/n, why features should be standardised, L2 regularisation, and numerical stability (clip the logits).

questions.q: Find the median of a stream of numbers.
questions.a:
import heapq

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo, self.hi = [], []          # max-heap (negated), min-heap
    def add(self, x):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -x)
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, -heapq.heappop(self.lo))
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -heapq.heappop(self.hi))
    def median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi): return -self.lo[0]
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2
  • Two heaps keep the lower half and the upper half: insert is O(log n) and reading the median is O(1).
  • Follow-ups: a fixed window means lazy deletion; a bounded integer range means a counting array.

questions.q: Science Application: design a system that summarises product reviews into key concepts.
questions.a:
• Goal: a short "customers say..." summary plus pros and cons per product, kept fresh as reviews arrive.
  • Pipeline: 1. Filter spam and very short reviews. 2. Aspect extraction: an LLM or fine-tuned model tags aspects (battery, fit, delivery) with sentiment. 3. Aggregate: count aspects, weighted by helpfulness and recency. 4. Summarise: an LLM writes a grounded summary from the top aspects and representative quotes.
  • Scale: batch processing for millions of products; incremental updates when there are more than N new reviews; a smaller model for extraction and a larger one for the final text.
  • Evaluation:
  • Faithfulness: every claim must be supported by reviews.
  • Coverage of the top aspects.
  • Human ratings.
  • Online A/B on conversion and returns.
  • Risks: hallucination, fake-review manipulation, and bias towards early reviews. Use guardrails and periodic audits.

questions.q: Science Breadth: explain the bias-variance trade-off with examples.
questions.a:
• Bias: error from wrong assumptions. The model is too simple (linear on non-linear data) and underfits.
  • Variance: error from sensitivity to the training sample. The model is too complex (a deep tree) and overfits.
  • Expected error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise.
  • Levers:
  • More data reduces variance.
  • Regularisation and bagging (random forests) reduce variance.
  • Boosting and richer features reduce bias.
  • Diagnose with learning curves: if both errors are high, it's bias; if the gap is large, it's variance.

questions.q: Science Depth (LLMs): explain how an LLM is pre-trained and then aligned.
questions.a:
• Pre-training: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of web, code and book text.
  • Decoder-only Transformer with AdamW and warm-up plus cosine schedule.
  • Mixed precision (bf16).
  • Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism.
  • Scaling laws (Chinchilla) guide the balance of model size and tokens.
  • Mid-training / continued pre-training on domain or long-context data.
  • Post-training:
  • SFT on instruction data.
  • Preference optimisation (RLHF with PPO, or DPO).
  • RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning (maths and code).
  • Safety tuning.
  • Evaluation across benchmarks plus red-teaming. Watch for contamination and reward hacking.

questions.q: Leadership Principles: tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager (Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit).
questions.a:
Answer (STAR, about 2 minutes):

  • Situation: "My manager wanted to launch the LLM classifier to all customers within two weeks."
  • Task: I believed precision on minority categories was too low.
  • Action: "I shared an error analysis: 18% false positives on refund requests. I proposed a two-week staged launch to 10% of traffic with human review. We agreed on the metrics up front."
  • Result: "The staged launch caught a labelling bug. The full launch went a week later with 94% precision. My manager adopted staged launches as the default."
  • Use data, keep it respectful, and show that you committed once the decision was made.

questions.q: Leadership Principles: tell me about a time you had to dive deep to find a root cause (Dive Deep).
questions.a:
• Pick a story where you went beyond the dashboards. Example: "The model's AUC dropped 4 points in one region. I traced it to a change in an upstream feature pipeline: a currency field switched from INR to USD without notice."
  • Explain the mechanisms you added: a data contract, a schema check, alerts on shifts in feature distributions.
  • Quantify the impact: "We prevented about ₹X of mis-scored applications."

questions.q: Tech talk: how should you structure the 45-minute presentation?
questions.a:
1. Problem and why it matters (3 minutes): business impact.
  2. Your approach (15 minutes): data, model choices and why, the alternatives you rejected.
  3. Results (7 minutes): offline and online metrics, ablations, failure cases.
  4. What you would do next (3 minutes), then questions. - Be precise about your own contribution. Expect "why not X?" probes, and prepare backup slides with maths details.

questions.q: What is overfitting, and how do you detect and prevent it?
questions.a:
• Overfitting: low training error but high validation or test error, because the model memorised noise.
  • Detect: train-vs-validation gap, learning curves, cross-validation variance.
  • Prevent:
  • More data or augmentation.
  • Regularisation (L1/L2, dropout).
  • Simpler models.
  • Early stopping.
  • Feature selection.
  • Ensembling.
  • Proper validation (no leakage).

questions.q: Optimisation: why does Adam often converge faster than SGD, and when might SGD generalise better?
questions.a:
• Adam adapts the per-parameter learning rate using first and second moment estimates. It is fast on sparse or noisy gradients and needs little tuning.
  • SGD with momentum often generalises better in vision models, because it finds flatter minima. Adam can overfit or converge to sharper solutions.
  • AdamW (decoupled weight decay) plus warm-up and cosine decay is the standard for Transformers.
  • Tune the learning rate first; it matters more than the optimiser choice.

questions.q: State the linear regression assumptions and the closed-form solution.
questions.a:
• Model: y = Xw + ε. The OLS solution is ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, or the pseudo-inverse or QR decomposition for numerical stability.
  • Assumptions:
  • Linearity.
  • Independent errors.
  • Homoscedasticity (constant variance).
  • Normally distributed errors (for inference).
  • No perfect multicollinearity.
  • Diagnostics: residual plots, Q-Q plot, VIF. Use Ridge when XᵀX is ill-conditioned.

questions.q: Transformers: why is attention scaled by √dₖ?
questions.a:
• For random vectors with unit-variance components, the dot product q·k has variance dₖ. Large values push the softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients.
  • Dividing by √dₖ keeps the scores at unit variance, so the softmax stays in a well-behaved range and training is stable.

questions.q: Statistics: what is a p-value, and what is a common misinterpretation?
questions.a:
• p-value: the probability of observing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.
  • It is NOT the probability that the null is true, nor the size of the effect.
  • Small p-values with huge samples can come from trivial effects, so report effect sizes and confidence intervals.
  • Correct for multiple testing (Bonferroni, Benjamini–Hochberg) and avoid peeking (sequential testing needs special methods).

questions.q: Apple hard coding: return the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m, n))).
questions.a:
def find_median(a, b):
    if len(a) > len(b): a, b = b, a
    m, n = len(a), len(b); lo, hi = 0, m
    while lo <= hi:
        i = (lo + hi) // 2; j = (m + n + 1) // 2 - i
        aL = a[i-1] if i else float("-inf"); aR = a[i] if i < m else float("inf")
        bL = b[j-1] if j else float("-inf"); bR = b[j] if j < n else float("inf")
        if aL <= bR and bL <= aR:
            return max(aL, bL) if (m + n) % 2 else (max(aL, bL) + min(aR, bR)) / 2
        if aL > bR: hi = i - 1
        else: lo = i + 1
  • Binary-search the partition of the smaller array so that the left halves hold half of all the elements. Talk through the invariants and edge cases. Even if you don't finish, a clear approach earns credit.

questions.q: Design a system that recommends Confluence articles to users.
questions.a:
• Contexts: the home feed ("for you"), "related pages" on a page, and search-adjacent suggestions.
  • Signals: the user's space and team membership, recently viewed or edited pages, Jira issues they work on, collaborators, page popularity and freshness, permissions (never recommend pages the user can't see).
  • Candidates: co-view graph (item-to-item), content embeddings (title + body), pages from the user's team and spaces, trending pages.
  • Ranker: GBM or a two-tower model predicting P(click) and P(dwell longer than 30 s); diversity and freshness re-ranking.
  • Cold start: new users get team and space popular pages; new pages get content similarity plus exploration.
  • Evaluation: offline recall@k / NDCG on held-out views; online CTR, dwell time and return visits; guardrails on latency and permission leaks (zero tolerance).

questions.q: Data structure: track stock prices with updates and corrections; support current, max and min price.
questions.a:
import heapq
class StockPrice:
    def __init__(self):
        self.p, self.latest = {}, 0
        self.maxh, self.minh = [], []
    def update(self, t, price):
        self.p[t] = price; self.latest = max(self.latest, t)
        heapq.heappush(self.maxh, (-price, t)); heapq.heappush(self.minh, (price, t))
    def current(self): return self.p[self.latest]
    def maximum(self):
        while -self.maxh[0][0] != self.p[self.maxh[0][1]]: heapq.heappop(self.maxh)   # lazy delete stale
        return -self.maxh[0][0]
    def minimum(self):
        while self.minh[0][0] != self.p[self.minh[0][1]]: heapq.heappop(self.minh)
        return self.minh[0][0]
  • Two heaps with lazy deletion: O(log n) amortised. Add unit tests for corrections at the same timestamp.

questions.q: Code design: can a new movie fit into a day's schedule (open 10:00, last end 23:00, setup and cleanup inside the duration)?
questions.a:
from dataclasses import dataclass
OPEN, CLOSE = 10 * 60, 23 * 60
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Show: start: int; duration: int          # minutes since midnight
def can_schedule(shows: list[Show], duration: int) -> int | None:
    """Return the earliest start minute that fits, or None."""
    slots = sorted(shows, key=lambda s: s.start); t = OPEN
    for s in slots:
        if s.start - t >= duration: return t
        t = max(t, s.start + s.duration)
    return t if CLOSE - t >= duration else None

assert can_schedule([Show(600, 120), Show(780, 90)], 60) == 720
assert can_schedule([Show(600, 780)], 30) is None
  • Discuss: validation (overlapping existing shows), multiple screens (a list per screen), time zones, extensibility (a pluggable rule set), and tests for boundary cases (exactly fits at 23:00).

questions.q: Tell me about challenges in a past ML project and how you handled them.
questions.a:
Answer (a structure that works):

  • Challenge 1 (data): "Labels were noisy. 15% disagreement found by an audit." Action: relabelling guidelines plus confident learning to flag likely errors. Result: +4 F1.
  • Challenge 2 (serving): "p95 latency was 400 ms." Action: distilled the model and cached embeddings. Result: 80 ms.
  • Keep each one to challenge → decision → measurable result, and be ready for "why not X?" follow-ups.

questions.q: Intuit: how would you build an ML model to categorise financial transactions for small businesses?
questions.a:
• Inputs: merchant name and description text, amount, MCC code, date, the user's past categorisations, the business type.
  • Model: text embeddings + tabular features → a classifier; personalisation from user corrections (a per-user override memory or fine-tuning).
  • Cold start: global model priors by merchant; active learning that asks users about low-confidence items.
  • Metrics: accuracy and macro-F1 by category, correction rate, time saved.
  • Trust: explanations ("categorised as Travel because of the merchant 'IndiGo'"), easy undo, privacy controls.

questions.q: SQL: explain RANK(), DENSE_RANK() and ROW_NUMBER().
questions.a:
SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,     -- 1,2,3,4 (unique)
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk,     -- 1,2,2,4 (gaps after ties)
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drk     -- 1,2,2,3 (no gaps)
FROM employees;
  • Add PARTITION BY dept for per-group rankings, e.g. the top 3 salaries per department.

questions.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
questions.a:
• UNION combines results and removes duplicates, which needs a sort or hash, so it is slower.
  • UNION ALL keeps all rows, including duplicates, and is faster.
  • Both require the same number of columns with compatible types. Use UNION ALL unless you truly need deduplication.

questions.q: pandas: merge two tables and plot the result.
questions.a:
import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"); customers = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
df = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
monthly = (df.assign(month=pd.to_datetime(df.order_date).dt.to_period("M").astype(str))
             .groupby(["month", "segment"]).amount.sum().unstack(fill_value=0))
monthly.plot(kind="line", marker="o", figsize=(8, 4), title="Revenue by segment"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
  • Mention how= options, validate= to catch duplicate keys, and checking for unmatched rows (indicator=True).

questions.q: Count the frequency of each character, and check whether a string is a palindrome.
questions.a:
from collections import Counter
s = "Madam, I'm Adam"
clean = "".join(ch.lower() for ch in s if ch.isalnum())
print(Counter(clean))                 # character frequencies
print(clean == clean[::-1])           # palindrome check -> True
def reverse_sub(s, i, j): return s[:i] + s[i:j+1][::-1] + s[j+1:]   # reverse s[i..j]

questions.q: Barclays: what is MCP, and how does it relate to agentic AI in a bank?
questions.a:
• MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard for exposing tools, resources and prompts to LLM apps through servers, so any compatible agent can discover and call them.
  • In a bank:
  • Wrap internal systems (customer lookup, transaction history, policy search) as MCP servers with strict authentication, scopes and audit.
  • Agents compose them for tasks such as complaint triage or KYC refresh.
  • Controls:
  • Read-only by default.
  • Human approval for any action that changes money or records.
  • PII minimisation.
  • Logging of every tool call.
  • Treat tool outputs as untrusted (prompt-injection risk).

questions.q: How do you prioritise several urgent tasks at once?
questions.a:
• Clarify impact and deadlines with stakeholders. Use an impact × urgency matrix.
  • Communicate trade-offs early: "I can deliver A today and B tomorrow. Is that acceptable?"
  • Unblock others first, time-box investigations, and automate repeated work.
  • Example: "During quarter-end, I triaged three data requests by regulatory deadline, delivered the regulator's one first, and agreed new dates for the others. All three landed on time."

questions.q: Flatten a nested JSON object into a single-level dictionary.
questions.a:
def flatten(obj, parent="", sep="."):
    out = {}
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        for k, v in obj.items():
            out.update(flatten(v, f"{parent}{sep}{k}" if parent else k, sep))
    elif isinstance(obj, list):
        for i, v in enumerate(obj):
            out.update(flatten(v, f"{parent}{sep}{i}" if parent else str(i), sep))
    else:
        out[parent] = obj
    return out

print(flatten({"a": 1, "b": {"c": 2, "d": [3, 4]}}))  # {'a':1,'b.c':2,'b.d.0':3,'b.d.1':4}

questions.q: Compute the average of a column in a CSV that is too large for memory.
questions.a:
import pandas as pd

total, count = 0.0, 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv("big.csv", usecols=["amount"], chunksize=1_000_000):
    s = chunk["amount"].dropna()
    total += s.sum(); count += len(s)
print(total / count)
  • Stream in chunks, keeping a running sum and count. Alternatives: DuckDB (SELECT avg(amount) FROM 'big.csv'), Polars lazy scan, or Spark for distributed data. For a running variance, use Welford's algorithm.

questions.q: Design a pipeline that makes unstructured client documents (contracts, scanned reports) searchable.
questions.a:
• Ingest: connectors (SharePoint, S3) → file-type detection → OCR for scans (Azure Document Intelligence or Textract) → layout-aware parsing (tables, clauses).
  • Enrich: extract metadata (parties, dates, contract type) with an LLM using structured output; detect and redact PII.
  • Index: chunks by clause or section → embeddings + BM25 → a hybrid index with metadata filters and document-level ACLs.
  • Serve: search UI + RAG Q&A with citations; a re-ranker; "find all contracts with auto-renewal clauses" via metadata plus semantic search.
  • Govern: audit logs, retention policy, an evaluation set built with client SMEs; measure time saved per review.
questions.page: BCG X: AI/ML Engineer & Forward-Deployed DS

questions.q: Design a bank fraud-detection system that alerts customers by text message.
questions.a:
• Real-time scoring at authorisation: features (velocity, merchant risk, geo-distance, device) from an online feature store, a GBM model, a latency budget under 100 ms.
  • Decision tiers: approve / SMS confirmation ("Reply YES if this ₹24,999 purchase was you") / decline.
  • SMS flow: send through a gateway, hold the transaction for N minutes; YES approves, NO blocks the card and opens a case; no reply follows the default policy.
  • Feedback loop: customer replies and chargebacks become labels; retrain regularly; monitor false-positive rates by segment.
  • Risks: SMS phishing (never include links), delivery delays, fairness across customer groups.

questions.q: Case: a retailer wants AI to reduce churn in its subscription business. How do you approach it as a consultant?
questions.a:
1. Frame the value: churn rate, revenue at risk, the cost of retention offers. "A 1-point churn reduction ≈ ₹X crore a year."
  2. Hypotheses: price sensitivity, poor onboarding, delivery issues, competitor offers.
  3. Data: subscriptions, usage, support tickets, NPS, delivery performance.
  4. Approach: a churn-risk + uplift model → segment-specific actions (onboarding fixes, targeted offers, service recovery).
  5. Metrics: retained revenue, offer ROI, and a controlled pilot in 2 regions.
  6. Adoption: who uses the scores (the CRM team), workflow integration, a dashboard, training, and governance for model refresh. - Keep the technical detail light and tie every step to client value.

questions.q: Why BCG X, and why a client-facing, forward-deployed role?
questions.a:
• "I enjoy turning ambiguous business problems into shipped AI products. A forward-deployed role puts me close to the client's real constraints and users, where impact is measured, not assumed."
  • Show evidence: a time you handled ambiguity, brought stakeholders along, and drove adoption (not just model accuracy).
  • Ask good questions back: how teams split between BCG X engineers and consultants, and how success is measured after go-live.
