questions.q: ANN vs CNN: what's the difference, and when do you use each?
questions.a:
• ANN/MLP: fully connected layers, where every input connects to every neuron. Good for tabular or flat feature vectors. For images it means a huge number of parameters and no spatial awareness.
  • CNN: convolutional filters with local connectivity + weight sharing, plus pooling. They capture spatial hierarchies, are translation-equivariant and need far fewer parameters.
  • Use CNNs for images, video frames, spectrograms and some time series (1D conv); MLPs for tabular data or as heads on top of embeddings.

questions.q: How does gradient descent work? Explain it as if to a junior engineer.
questions.a:
• "Imagine standing on a hill in fog, trying to reach the valley. You feel the slope under your feet (the gradient) and take a step downhill (opposite to the gradient). The step size is the learning rate."
  • Formally, θ ← θ − η ∇L(θ). Mini-batches estimate the gradient cheaply (SGD); momentum and Adam smooth and adapt the steps.
  • Too big a step overshoots or diverges; too small is slow. Use learning-rate schedules and monitor the loss curves.

questions.q: How do you adapt an already-trained model to a new task (transfer learning)?
questions.a:
• Feature extraction: freeze the backbone and train a new head. Use with small data and a similar domain.
  • Fine-tuning: unfreeze the top layers (or all) with a low learning rate and discriminative learning rates; augment data.
  • For LLMs: prompting / few-shot → RAG for knowledge → LoRA fine-tuning for behaviour or format.
  • Domain shift (e.g. factory images vs ImageNet): more unfrozen layers, domain-specific augmentation, possibly self-supervised pre-training on unlabelled factory images.

questions.q: Honeywell online assessment: train a random forest on a dataset. What does a clean solution include?
questions.a:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv"); y = df.pop("target"); X = pd.get_dummies(df, drop_first=True).fillna(df.median(numeric_only=True))
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=None, min_samples_leaf=2, class_weight="balanced", n_jobs=-1, random_state=42)
print(cross_val_score(rf, Xtr, ytr, cv=5, scoring="f1_macro").mean())
rf.fit(Xtr, ytr); print(classification_report(yte, rf.predict(Xte)))
  • Mention feature importance, tuning (max_features, depth) and avoiding leakage (fit encoders and imputers on the training data only, ideally in a Pipeline).

questions.q: Which loss function do you use for which task?
questions.a:
Task Loss
Regression MSE (penalises large errors), MAE (robust), Huber (both)
Binary classification Binary cross-entropy (log loss); focal loss for imbalance
Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy (softmax); label smoothing
Ranking / embeddings Contrastive, triplet, InfoNCE
Segmentation Dice / IoU loss + cross-entropy
Quantiles / intervals Pinball (quantile) loss

questions.q: Design a predictive-maintenance system for factory motors.
questions.a:
• Data: vibration, temperature, current (IoT sensors at high frequency), maintenance logs (failures as labels), operating context.
  • Features: rolling statistics, FFT spectral bands, trends; handle sensor drift and missing data.
  • Models: anomaly detection (autoencoders, Isolation Forest) where there are few failures; remaining-useful-life regression or survival models once labels exist.
  • Edge + cloud: lightweight scoring at the edge for alerts; cloud training and fleet dashboards.
  • Value: downtime avoided against false-alarm cost; a technician feedback loop.

questions.q: Explain ANN, RNN and LSTM. Why did Transformers replace LSTMs?
questions.a:
• ANN (MLP): layers of neurons with non-linear activations, trained by backpropagation. They have no memory of sequence order.
  • RNN: reuses one cell across time steps with a hidden state hₜ = f(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁). It suffers from vanishing or exploding gradients on long sequences.
  • LSTM: adds a cell state plus forget, input and output gates that control what to keep, so it remembers longer. GRU is a lighter version.
  • Why Transformers won:
  • Self-attention links any two tokens directly.
  • Training is fully parallel rather than step by step.
  • They scale far better, which made pre-trained LLMs possible.

questions.q: What prompting techniques do you use?
questions.a:
• Zero-shot: a clear instruction with a role, the task, constraints and the output format.
  • Few-shot: 2 to 5 examples that show the exact pattern, which is great for classification or extraction.
  • Chain-of-thought: ask the model to reason step by step. Use it for maths and logic, and hide the reasoning from end users if needed.
  • Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths and take a majority vote.
  • ReAct: reasoning plus tool calls, which is the basis of agents.
  • Structured output: a JSON schema, delimiters around the context, and "answer only from the context, else say I don't know".
  • Always evaluate prompts against a small labelled set rather than judging by eye.

questions.q: Which LLMs have you worked with, and how do you choose between them?
questions.a:
• Hosted: GPT-4o / 4.1 / o-series, Claude, Gemini.
  • Open-weight: Llama 3.x, Mistral/Mixtral, Qwen, Phi and Gemma.
  • Selection criteria:
  • Task quality on your evaluation set
  • Context length
  • Latency and cost per 1k tokens
  • Data privacy (on-premises vs API)
  • Licensing
  • Tool-calling and JSON support
  • Language support (Hindi or other regional languages)
  • Common pattern: a big model for complex reasoning, a small or cheap model for classification and routing, and an open model self-hosted when data cannot leave the network.

questions.q: What is a vector database and how does it work?
questions.a:
• What it stores: embeddings (dense vectors) together with metadata, and it returns the nearest neighbours for a query vector.
  • Similarity: usually cosine or dot product (L2 is also used).
  • ANN indexes make search fast at scale:
  • HNSW: a graph index with high recall that uses a lot of memory.
  • IVF: clustering; it searches only the nearest clusters.
  • PQ: product quantization, which compresses vectors.
  • Examples:
  • Libraries: FAISS.
  • Databases: Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus.
  • Extensions: pgvector, Azure AI Search.
  • Features to mention: metadata filtering, hybrid (keyword + vector) search, multi-tenancy, incremental upserts.

questions.q: How do you run an LLM locally with Ollama, and why would you?
questions.a:
• ollama pull llama3.1:8b, then ollama run llama3.1. It serves a local REST API on port 11434, which LangChain uses through ChatOllama.
  • Why:
  • Data privacy: nothing leaves the machine.
  • No API cost.
  • Offline development.
  • Quick testing of open models.
  • Limits: quality is below frontier models, it is bound by your hardware, and it is not built for high-concurrency serving. For production throughput use vLLM or TGI.

questions.q: What is quantization and how does it affect an LLM?
questions.a:
• Definition: storing weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits, such as FP16 → INT8 → 4-bit.
  • Gains: about 2 to 4 times less memory, faster inference, and larger models fit on smaller GPUs or even laptops.
  • Methods:
  • Post-training quantization: GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes NF4, and GGUF (llama.cpp / Ollama).
  • QLoRA: fine-tuning adapters on top of a 4-bit base model.
  • Cost: a small loss of accuracy, larger at 3 bits or fewer and on reasoning-heavy tasks. Always re-run your evaluation set after quantizing.

questions.q: Explain RAG end to end.
questions.a:
• Ingestion: load documents → clean them → chunk them (for example 500 to 1,000 tokens with overlap) → embed → store in the vector DB with metadata.
  • Query:
  • Embed the question and retrieve the top-k chunks (hybrid search plus a re-ranker for quality).
  • Build the prompt with the context, then generate a cited answer.
  • Evaluation:
  • Retrieval: recall@k and MRR.
  • Generation: faithfulness, answer relevance and context precision (RAGAS).
  • Why RAG rather than fine-tuning for knowledge: the data stays fresh, answers cite sources, it is cheaper, and access control can be applied per document.

questions.q: What is agentic AI? Give an example.
questions.a:
• Definition: systems where an LLM decides the next step. It plans, calls tools or APIs, observes the result and iterates, often with memory and several specialised agents.
  • Example: an invoice-processing agent. 1. Extract the fields with a vision LLM. 2. Validate them against the ERP API. 3. Flag a mismatch to a human. 4. Post the entry.
  • Frameworks: LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel, OpenAI Agents SDK.
  • Must-haves: step limits, typed tools, approval for actions with side effects, and tracing.

questions.q: You haven't deployed a model. How would you take your RAG app to production?
questions.a:
• FastAPI service → Docker image → Azure Container Apps, AKS or ECS.
  • Keep secrets in Key Vault.
  • Use a managed vector store and async endpoints with streaming.
  • Ingestion pipeline as a scheduled job.
  • CI/CD with tests plus an evaluation gate.
  • Monitoring: latency, tokens, cost, user feedback and traces.
  • Release: canary, with a rollback plan.
  • Tip: deploy even a hobby project (Azure free tier, Render or Hugging Face Spaces) so you can say "I deployed it" truthfully. This is exactly what one rejected candidate was missing.

questions.q: Python: reverse each word in a sentence but keep the word order.
questions.a:
def reverse_words(s: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(w[::-1] for w in s.split())

print(reverse_words("gen ai engineer"))  # neg ia reeenigne
  • split() with no argument handles multiple spaces. The function is O(n) in time and space.
  • Explain edge cases aloud (empty string, punctuation). Interviewers at this level care about clarity, not tricks.

questions.q: Given an agent-framework repository, how do you find where the reward is calculated?
questions.a:
1. Search first: grep -rn "reward" --include=*.py, plus terms like score, return, advantage.
  2. Start from the entry point (training script or main) and follow the loop: environment step() → reward, or trajectory → reward model / verifier call.
  3. Check configs (YAML) for reward function names, then jump to their definitions in the IDE.
  4. Confirm by running a small test with logging or a breakpoint to watch where the reward value is created. - Explain your systematic navigation; interviewers care about the method as much as finding the line.

questions.q: How would you make a small language model (SLM) better at reasoning?
questions.a:
• Distillation: fine-tune on reasoning traces (chain of thought) from a larger teacher model; filter for correct answers (rejection sampling).
  • RL with verifiable rewards: maths and code tasks with automatic checkers (GRPO/PPO), plus format rewards. Watch for reward hacking.
  • Data quality: curriculum (easy → hard), deduplication, decontamination.
  • Inference-time: self-consistency (majority vote), verifier re-ranking, tool use (a calculator or code interpreter), extra "thinking" tokens.
  • Evaluate on GSM8K, MATH and held-out domain tasks; check the calibration of the final answers.

questions.q: How does reward modelling work in RLHF, and what are its pitfalls?
questions.a:
• Train a model to score responses so that r(chosen) > r(rejected) (Bradley–Terry loss) on human preference pairs; then optimise the policy against it with a KL penalty.
  • Pitfalls:
  • Reward hacking: exploiting quirks such as length or flattery.
  • Distribution shift as the policy improves.
  • Noisy or biased preference labels.
  • Overoptimisation (Goodhart's law).
  • Mitigations: ensembles, regular reward-model refreshes, length normalisation, human audits.

questions.q: Feature importance: how do you determine which features matter most?
questions.a:
• Model-based: tree gain or split counts (biased towards high-cardinality features), coefficients for scaled linear models.
  • Permutation importance: the drop in the validation metric when a feature is shuffled. Model-agnostic, but correlated features split the importance.
  • SHAP: consistent per-prediction attributions; global importance is the mean |SHAP|.
  • Caveat: importance is not causality. Check stability across folds and deal with correlated groups.

questions.q: Where can ML help in chip design (EDA)?
questions.a:
• Design-space exploration: RL or Bayesian optimisation to tune synthesis and place-and-route parameters for power, performance and area.
  • Prediction: estimate timing, congestion and power early, from netlist and graph features (GNNs), to avoid slow full runs.
  • Verification: prioritise test cases, cluster failures, analyse logs with LLMs.
  • GenAI copilots: RTL code assistants, documentation Q&A, script generation for EDA tools.

questions.q: DSA: find the k-th largest element in an array.
questions.a:
import heapq
def kth_largest(nums, k):
    h = nums[:k]; heapq.heapify(h)
    for x in nums[k:]:
        if x > h[0]: heapq.heapreplace(h, x)
    return h[0]
  • A min-heap of size k gives O(n log k). Quickselect averages O(n).

questions.q: How does a decision tree decide where to split? How do you stop it overfitting?
questions.a:
• Classification: choose the feature and threshold that maximise impurity reduction.
  • Gini = 1 − Σpᵢ², or entropy = −Σpᵢ log pᵢ, weighted by child sizes (information gain).
  • Regression: minimise the variance (MSE) of the children.
  • Greedy and recursive: it continues until a stopping criterion is met.
  • Control overfitting:
  • max_depth, min_samples_leaf, min_samples_split.
  • Cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha).
  • Or ensembles: random forests (bagging) and gradient boosting.
  • In banking: shallow trees and scorecards are favoured for explainability to regulators.

questions.q: Design a RAG system for internal banking policies and procedures.
questions.a:
• Ingestion: policy PDFs and SOPs → layout-aware parsing → clause-level chunks with metadata (policy ID, version, effective date, business unit, classification) → embeddings → vector DB, plus BM25.
  • Access control: entitlement filters at retrieval (users see only the policies for their business unit and classification).
  • Query: rewrite → hybrid search → cross-encoder re-rank → latest effective version only → grounded answer with clause citations.
  • Guardrails:
  • No financial advice to customers.
  • PII redaction.
  • "Not found" when retrieval confidence is low.
  • Prompt-injection filtering.
  • Governance:
  • A model inventory entry and validation (model risk management).
  • An evaluation set signed off by compliance.
  • Audit logs, periodic review, and data residency on a private model endpoint.

questions.q: What is a vector database and how would you choose one for a bank?
questions.a:
• What it does: stores embeddings with ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF-PQ) for fast similarity search, plus metadata filtering.
  • Bank criteria:
  • On-premises or private-cloud deployment.
  • Encryption at rest and in transit.
  • RBAC and attribute filters.
  • Audit logs.
  • High availability and backups.
  • Scale (millions of chunks).
  • Hybrid search.
  • Vendor approval.
  • Options: pgvector (inside an approved Postgres), Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (often already approved), Milvus, Qdrant (self-hosted), Azure AI Search with private endpoints.

questions.q: Explain batch normalisation and why it helps.
questions.a:
• For each mini-batch, normalise the activations to mean 0 and variance 1, then apply a learned scale γ and shift β.
  • Benefits:
  • Stabilises the distribution of layer inputs.
  • Allows higher learning rates and faster convergence.
  • Reduces sensitivity to initialisation.
  • Has a mild regularising effect.
  • Inference: uses running averages of the mean and variance.
  • Limitations: depends on batch size (small batches hurt), so Transformers use LayerNorm.

questions.q: How would you optimise a reinforcement-learning algorithm that trains slowly or unstably?
questions.a:
• Stability:
  • Target networks and experience replay (DQN).
  • Clipped objectives (PPO).
  • Gradient clipping.
  • Normalised observations and rewards.
  • Entropy bonus for exploration.
  • Sample efficiency:
  • Prioritised replay.
  • Off-policy algorithms (SAC, TD3).
  • Reward shaping (carefully).
  • Imitation learning or pre-training on logged data.
  • Speed: vectorised and parallel environments, a smaller network, tuned hyperparameters (learning rate, γ, batch size), and tracking learning curves over several seeds.
  • Banking use cases: dynamic pricing, collections strategy, trade execution. Mention offline RL and the need for safe policy evaluation.

questions.q: Case-study presentation: how do you structure a 15-minute data-science case presentation for senior stakeholders?
questions.a:
1. Executive summary first (1 slide): the problem, the recommendation, the impact.
  2. Context and data (2 slides).
  3. Approach (2–3 slides): keep it simple, explain why.
  4. Results (2 slides): metrics and business impact in money terms.
  5. Risks and next steps (1 slide): limitations, monitoring, governance. - Leave time for questions. Executives probe assumptions and risk, not hyperparameters.

questions.q: Which chunking strategies do you know, and when do you use each?
questions.a:
• Fixed-size + overlap (e.g. 512 tokens, 10–15% overlap): simple and a good baseline.
  • Recursive character / structure-aware: split on headings → paragraphs → sentences, keeping sections whole. Best for documentation and policies.
  • Semantic chunking: split where adjacent-sentence embedding similarity drops. Gives cleaner topics, at extra cost.
  • Document-specific: keep tables and code blocks whole; slide-level or page-level for PDFs.
  • Parent–child / small-to-big: retrieve small chunks, send the parent section to the LLM.
  • Pick by evaluation: measure recall@k and faithfulness for 2–3 strategies on your own Q&A set.

questions.q: What is hybrid search and why does it beat pure vector search?
questions.a:
• Hybrid = sparse (BM25 keywords) + dense (embeddings), with results fused using Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = Σ 1/(k + rank).
  • Dense search catches meaning and synonyms. Sparse search catches exact terms: product codes, names, error IDs, acronyms. Embeddings often miss these.
  • Add a cross-encoder re-ranker on the fused top 50 for the best precision.
  • Available in Azure AI Search, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant and Pinecone (sparse-dense).

questions.q: Explain self-attention step by step.
questions.a:
1. For each token embedding x, compute Q = xW_Q, K = xW_K, V = xW_V.
  2. Scores: QKᵀ, the similarity of each query with every key.
  3. Scale by √d_k so the softmax doesn't saturate, then apply a mask (causal or padding).
  4. Softmax turns the scores into attention weights that sum to 1.
  5. Output = weights × V: each token's new representation mixes information from the relevant tokens. - Cost is O(n²·d) in sequence length, which is why long context is expensive. FlashAttention and sparse or linear attention help.

questions.q: Coforge panel: how do you use GenAI in your day-to-day work and frameworks?
questions.a:
Answer (practical and specific):

  • Engineering productivity: Copilot-style code assistants for tests and boilerplate, always reviewed; LLMs for test-case generation from requirements in QA.
  • Frameworks: LangChain/LangGraph for RAG and agents, LlamaIndex for ingestion, RAGAS for evaluation, LangSmith for tracing.
  • What I built: "A RAG assistant over 2,000 test-strategy documents. Hybrid search plus a re-ranker; it cut test-planning time by about 30%."
  • If challenged: "There are several valid designs. I chose X because of constraints A and B; I'd switch to Y if latency or cost mattered more." Stay calm and evidence-based.

questions.q: Python: group words that are anagrams of each other.
questions.a:
from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        g["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)
    return list(g.values())

print(group_anagrams(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]))
  • O(n · k log k) for k-length words. Using a 26-letter count tuple as the key gives O(n·k).

questions.q: What is agentic AI, and how would you make an agent reliable?
questions.a:
• Agentic AI: an LLM that plans, calls tools, observes the results and iterates towards a goal, often with memory and several cooperating agents.
  • Reliability checklist:
  • Few, well-described tools with strict schemas.
  • A step and time limit.
  • Retries with validation.
  • A deterministic workflow where the path is known.
  • Human approval for side effects.
  • Tracing of every step.
  • A trajectory evaluation set.
  • Fallback to a human when unsure.

questions.q: Write a function that checks whether a number is prime.
questions.a:
def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2: return False
    if n % 2 == 0: return n == 2
    i = 3
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0: return False
        i += 2
    return True
  • Checking divisors only up to √n gives O(√n). For many numbers at once, mention the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which is O(n log log n).

questions.q: Implement merge sort and give its complexity.
questions.a:
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a
    m = len(a) // 2
    L, R = merge_sort(a[:m]), merge_sort(a[m:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(L) and j < len(R):
        if L[i] <= R[j]: out.append(L[i]); i += 1
        else: out.append(R[j]); j += 1
    return out + L[i:] + R[j:]
  • O(n log n) in every case, O(n) extra space, and stable (equal items keep their order). Quicksort averages O(n log n) and sorts in place, but its worst case is O(n²).

questions.q: Explain the four pillars of OOP, and what a wrapper class is.
questions.a:
• Encapsulation: bundle data with the methods that use it, and hide the internals behind a clear interface.
  • Abstraction: expose what an object does, not how (abstract classes and interfaces).
  • Inheritance: a child class reuses and extends a parent class.
  • Polymorphism: one interface, many implementations (method overriding, duck typing in Python).
  • Wrapper class (Java): an object version of a primitive (int → Integer) so it can be used in collections; autoboxing converts between them. In Python the general idea is a class that wraps another object to add behaviour, such as a decorator or adapter.

questions.q: What are SQL joins? Write a query for employees without a department.
questions.a:
• INNER JOIN returns matching rows only. LEFT JOIN returns all left rows plus matches (NULL where there is none). RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both sides.
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE d.dept_id IS NULL;
  • This is the "anti-join" pattern. NOT EXISTS is an alternative that handles NULLs more safely than NOT IN.

questions.q: Explain your AI/ML project in depth.
questions.a:
Answer (a 3-minute structure):

  1. Problem and data: "Predict loan default from 50k applications with 30 features."
  2. Approach: cleaning (missing values, outliers), features, a baseline logistic regression, then XGBoost, with stratified cross-validation.
  3. Result: "AUC 0.84 against a 0.76 baseline; recall of 0.71 at 0.8 precision."
  4. Your part: "I built the feature pipeline and the Streamlit demo."
  5. What you'd improve: "Calibration, SHAP explanations and deployment with FastAPI." - Expect follow-ups such as "why XGBoost?", "how did you handle imbalance?" and "what is AUC?". Know every line of your resume.

questions.q: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning? Give examples.
questions.a:
• Supervised: you learn from labelled examples (X → y).
  • Classification: spam detection, churn.
  • Regression: price prediction.
  • Algorithms: linear and logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, SVM, neural networks.
  • Unsupervised: there are no labels; you find structure in the data.
  • Clustering: customer segments with k-means.
  • Dimensionality reduction: PCA.
  • Anomaly detection.
  • Also mention: semi-supervised learning, self-supervised learning (how LLMs are pre-trained), and reinforcement learning (rewards).

questions.q: In NumPy, implement softmax cross-entropy with a numerically stable gradient.
questions.a:
import numpy as np
def softmax_xent(logits, y):            # logits (N, C), y (N,) int labels
    z = logits - logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)          # stability
    p = np.exp(z); p /= p.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    N = len(y)
    loss = -np.log(p[np.arange(N), y] + 1e-12).mean()
    grad = p.copy(); grad[np.arange(N), y] -= 1; grad /= N  # dL/dlogits = p - onehot
    return loss, grad
  • Mention log-sum-exp, why subtracting the maximum doesn't change the softmax, and checking the gradient numerically.

questions.q: Explain post-training: SFT → preference optimisation → RL. What can go wrong?
questions.a:
• SFT: curated instruction–response data teaches format and helpfulness. Data quality beats quantity.
  • Preference optimisation: RLHF (reward model + PPO with KL) or DPO/IPO/KTO on chosen-vs-rejected pairs, aligning tone, safety and helpfulness.
  • RL with verifiable rewards: maths and code unit tests (GRPO-style) improve reasoning.
  • Failure modes:
  • Reward hacking.
  • Verbosity bias.
  • Over-refusal.
  • Mode collapse (lost diversity).
  • Catastrophic forgetting.
  • Benchmark contamination.
  • Mitigations: KL regularisation, length-controlled evaluation, diverse preference data, held-out human evaluations.

questions.q: Perplexity screen: why do Transformers need positional encoding, and how does RoPE work?
questions.a:
• Attention is permutation-invariant, so without position information token order is lost.
  • RoPE: rotate each 2-D pair of Q/K dimensions by an angle θ·position, so the dot product q_m · k_n depends on (m − n): relative position comes for free and extends to longer contexts (with NTK/YaRN scaling).
  • Alternatives: sinusoidal (fixed, added), learned absolute (bounded length), ALiBi (a linear bias by distance).

questions.q: Glean ML design: design permission-aware enterprise search across Slack, Drive, Jira and email.
questions.a:
• Connectors ingest content and ACLs incrementally (webhooks plus crawls); normalise into a unified document schema with metadata (owner, time, source, people graph).
  • Index: BM25 plus dense embeddings; a knowledge graph of people, documents and activity. Permission filtering at query time using ACL sets (pre-filtered search).
  • Ranking:
  • A learning-to-rank model with text relevance, freshness, personal signals (my team's docs), popularity, authority.
  • A cross-encoder for the top results.
  • Assistant: RAG over the permitted results with citations.
  • Evaluation: click models, NDCG on judged queries, answer faithfulness; strict tests that ACL leaks never occur.

questions.q: Research presentation: how should you present your work to an LLM research team?
questions.a:
• Contribution first: "We improved X by Y% at Z cost."
  • Setup: data, model size, baselines. Be precise about compute.
  • Results with ablations and error bars; failure cases.
  • Why it works (hypothesis plus evidence) and its limits.
  • Next steps and how it would scale.
  • Expect hard questions on confounders and evaluation validity. Welcome them.

questions.q: AI take-home: build a small RAG evaluation harness. What would you include?
questions.a:
• A dataset of about 50–100 questions with reference answers and gold document IDs.
  • Retrieval metrics: recall@k, MRR against the gold documents.
  • Generation metrics: faithfulness (an LLM judge plus claim-level checks), correctness against the reference, citation accuracy.
  • Reports: per-question failures grouped by type (retrieval miss vs generation error), latency and cost.
  • Engineering: a config-driven CLI, caching of LLM calls, deterministic seeds, a clear README with results and next steps.

questions.q: SQL: monthly active users, transaction count and total order amount for 2025.
questions.a:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', t.created_at) AS month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT t.user_id)          AS active_users,
       COUNT(*)                           AS transactions,
       SUM(t.quantity * p.price)          AS order_amount
FROM transactions t
JOIN products p ON p.id = t.product_id
WHERE t.created_at >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND t.created_at < DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
  • A sargable date range (no function on the column in WHERE) lets the engine prune partitions.

questions.q: How would you build a production RAG app on a lakehouse platform?
questions.a:
• Data: documents in Delta tables governed by a catalog (lineage, ACLs); an incremental pipeline for parse → chunk → embed.
  • Vector index: synced from the Delta table (it updates automatically as data changes), filtered by permissions.
  • App: chain/agent code logged as a model (MLflow), served behind an endpoint with guardrails and an AI gateway (rate limits, usage tracking).
  • Evaluation: MLflow LLM evaluation / an LLM judge on a curated set; tracing in production; feedback tables.
  • Governance: one permission model for data and AI assets; PII tagging; cost monitoring.

questions.q: How do you optimise a slow SQL query on a large table?
questions.a:
1. Read the query plan: full scans? Shuffles? Skew?
  2. Prune data: partition/clustering keys, date filters, select only the needed columns (columnar formats).
  3. Joins: broadcast small tables, filter before joining, avoid exploding many-to-many joins, handle skewed keys (salting).
  4. Aggregations: pre-aggregate or materialise; avoid SELECT DISTINCT on huge sets when not needed.
  5. Caching / Z-ordering / clustering; check file sizes (compact small files).

questions.q: Take-home: what makes a strong AI engineering submission?
questions.a:
• Working end to end: a clear entry point, reproducible environment (requirements file and a Makefile), sample run.
  • Correctness and tests: unit tests on key functions, an evaluation script with metrics.
  • Clean code: modules, typed functions, configuration over hard-coding, logging.
  • README: the problem, the approach and its trade-offs, results, limitations, "what I'd do with more time".
  • Respect the time box. Polish matters more than extra features.

questions.q: Forward-deployed: a customer wants a "chat with our data" assistant. How do you scope it?
questions.a:
1. Users and questions: collect 30 real questions; split them into document Q&A (RAG) and analytics questions (text-to-SQL).
  2. Data readiness: where the data lives, quality, permissions, semantic definitions (metrics layer).
  3. Approach: RAG for documents; text-to-SQL with a curated semantic layer, few-shot examples, query validation and row-level security for tables.
  4. Success metrics: answer accuracy on the question set, time saved, adoption.
  5. Plan: a 2-week proof of concept → pilot with one team → production hardening (monitoring, evaluation, governance).

questions.q: Snowflake: how would you use the warehouse's own tools for ML?
questions.a:
• Feature engineering in SQL / Snowpark (Python DataFrames) inside the warehouse, so data never moves.
  • Training: Snowpark ML or a model registry; UDFs or containers for inference.
  • LLM functions (Cortex-style) for summarisation and classification over tables; vector search for RAG.
  • Governance: role-based access, masking policies on PII, cost control via warehouse sizing.

questions.q: How does a RAG system work, and how does an agent-based LLM system work?
questions.a:
• RAG: retrieve relevant chunks from a knowledge base and put them in the prompt, so the LLM answers from your data with citations. The flow is fixed: retrieve → augment → generate.
  • Agent: the LLM runs a loop: think → pick a tool → observe the result → repeat, until the goal is met. Retrieval can be one of its tools, alongside APIs, calculators, SQL and so on.

questions.q: What is the difference between RAG and agents? When would you pick each?
questions.a:
RAG Agent
Control flow Fixed pipeline The model decides the steps
Best for Q&A over documents Multi-step tasks that need actions
Cost / latency Low, predictable Higher, variable
Testing Easy Needs trajectory evaluation
  • Choose RAG for "answer questions from our policies".
  • Choose an agent for "check the order status, apply the refund rule, email the customer".
  • Many production systems are agentic RAG: an agent that decides when and where to retrieve.

questions.q: How do multiple agents share memory?
questions.a:
• Shared state object: in LangGraph, a typed state (messages, plan, findings) is passed between nodes and persisted by a checkpointer, so every agent reads and writes the same state.
  • Blackboard / shared store: agents write findings to a shared database, cache or vector store that others query.
  • Message passing: a supervisor routes messages and each agent receives only what it needs, which saves tokens.
  • Design concerns:
  • Scope memory per user or session.
  • Summarise to control context size.
  • Prevent conflicting writes (one owner per field).
  • Never put secrets in shared memory.

questions.q: Scenario: design an agent for a business process. Walk me through it.
questions.a:
Answer (example: an expense-claim agent):

  1. Goal and scope: validate claims against policy and approve small ones automatically.
  2. Tools: - read_receipt (OCR or a vision LLM) - get_policy (RAG) - get_employee_grade (HR API) - submit_decision
  3. Flow (LangGraph): extract → validate → decide. If the amount exceeds the limit or confidence is low, route to human approval.
  4. Guardrails: typed tool arguments, read-only permissions except for submit_decision, a maximum of 8 steps, and an audit log.
  5. Evaluation: 200 historical claims as a test set; measure decision accuracy, false approvals and time saved.
  6. Rollout: run in shadow mode first, then auto-approve claims under ₹2,000.

questions.q: How do you choose an embedding model?
questions.a:
• Check MTEB leaderboard scores for retrieval, then test on your own documents: build 50 to 100 question→document pairs and measure recall@5.
  • Consider:
  • Language support (multilingual for Hindi or other Indian languages)
  • Domain (legal or medical text)
  • Dimension size (cost and memory)
  • Maximum input tokens
  • Hosted API vs self-hosted (privacy)
  • Examples: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small/large, Cohere embed-v3, BGE / E5 / GTE (open models), and all-MiniLM for quick prototypes.
  • Re-embed everything if you switch models, because vectors from different models are not comparable.

questions.q: The knowledge base is huge, with millions of documents. How do you retrieve from it efficiently?
questions.a:
• Index design: ANN (HNSW or IVF-PQ), with the index sharded or partitioned by business unit or tenant.
  • Pre-filter with metadata (department, year, document type) so search runs only over a small slice.
  • Two-stage retrieval: a fast hybrid search returns the top 100, then a cross-encoder re-ranks them to the top 5.
  • Hierarchical retrieval: search document summaries first, then the chunks inside the best documents.
  • Operations: incremental indexing, caching of frequent queries, and monitoring of recall and latency. Use a managed service (Azure AI Search, Pinecone, Elasticsearch) for scale.

questions.q: Python: count the frequency of each word in a text.
questions.a:
from collections import Counter
import re

def word_freq(text):
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9']+", text.lower())
    return Counter(words).most_common()

print(word_freq("RAG or agents? RAG first."))
  • Counter is O(n). Mention normalising case and punctuation, and most_common(k) for the top k.

questions.q: Client round: explain to a non-technical client why your GenAI assistant can be trusted.
questions.a:
Answer (keep it plain):

  • "It only answers from your approved documents, and every answer shows the source so your team can check it."
  • "If it isn't sure, it says so and hands over to a person. It doesn't guess."
  • "We tested it on 300 real questions from your team before launch. It was right 92% of the time, and every miss was logged and fixed."
  • "Your data stays in your cloud tenant, access follows your existing permissions, and we monitor it every week."
  • Finish with the business value: hours saved, faster responses, and a clear next step such as a pilot with one team.

questions.q: Explain entropy, with examples. Where is it used in ML?
questions.a:
• Entropy H(X) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x) measures uncertainty.
  • A fair coin has H = 1 bit; a biased (0.9/0.1) coin has H ≈ 0.47; a certain outcome has H = 0.
  • Uses:
  • Decision-tree splits (information gain = parent entropy − weighted child entropy).
  • Cross-entropy loss for classification.
  • KL divergence (distillation, VAEs, RLHF penalties).
  • Uncertainty sampling in active learning.
  • Perplexity = 2^H for language models.

questions.q: Design a system that predicts prices for digital art (NFT-style marketplace).
questions.a:
• Target: the expected sale price (or price range) for a listing. The heavy-tailed distribution calls for log-price regression or quantiles.
  • Features:
  • Artist: past sales, followers, volume.
  • Collection: floor price, rarity traits, trend.
  • Item: image embeddings (CLIP), trait rarity scores.
  • Market: overall volume, crypto price, time.
  • Model: gradient boosting on tabular features plus image embeddings; quantile regression (P10/P50/P90) to show the uncertainty.
  • Pitfalls: wash trading (filter suspicious sales), very little data for new artists (use hierarchical priors by collection), market regime shifts (time-based validation, frequent retraining).
  • Evaluation: MAPE on log price, interval coverage; product impact on listing success and time to sale.

questions.q: Design an A/B test for a new recommendation algorithm on a travel app.
questions.a:
• Unit: the user, split 50/50. The primary metric is booking conversion (sessions → bookings) or revenue per user; guardrails are cancellations, latency and complaints.
  • Duration: at least 2 full weeks to cover weekday and weekend patterns (travel intent varies); compute the sample size from the baseline conversion and the minimum detectable effect.
  • Pitfalls:
  • Novelty effects.
  • Seasonality (holidays).
  • Long consideration windows (users browse for days), so attribute bookings within N days.
  • Analysis: conversion lift with confidence intervals; segment by new vs returning users and by domestic vs international.

questions.q: Intuition behind gradient boosting.
questions.a:
• Build an additive model F(x) = Σ ηₘ hₘ(x) of shallow trees. Each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss (the residuals for MSE) of the current model, so every step corrects the remaining error.
  • The learning rate η shrinks each step: a smaller η with more trees generalises better.
  • Regularisation: tree depth, subsampling (stochastic GB), column sampling, L1/L2 on leaf weights (XGBoost), early stopping.

questions.q: Which metrics evaluate a ranking model, and when do you use each?
questions.a:
• Precision@k / Recall@k: binary relevance with a fixed list length.
  • MRR: where the first relevant item appears (search with one right answer).
  • NDCG@k: graded relevance with position discounting (hotel lists, feeds).
  • MAP: averages precision over all relevant items.
  • Online: CTR, conversion, revenue per search, and time to first click.

questions.q: Coding: implement a stack using queues.
questions.a:
from collections import deque
class Stack:
    def __init__(self): self.q = deque()
    def push(self, x):
        self.q.append(x)
        for _ in range(len(self.q) - 1): self.q.append(self.q.popleft())   # rotate so x is at the front
    def pop(self): return self.q.popleft()
    def top(self): return self.q[0]
    def empty(self): return not self.q
  • Push is O(n) and pop is O(1). The alternative makes push O(1) and pop O(n).

questions.q: You used an LSTM in your project. Explain how it works and why you chose it.
questions.a:
• LSTM cell: a cell state (long-term memory) plus three gates:
  • Forget gate: what to drop.
  • Input gate: what new information to add.
  • Output gate: what to expose as the hidden state.
  • Why it helps: the additive cell-state updates let gradients flow over long sequences, which avoids the vanishing gradients of plain RNNs.
  • Why I chose it: "Network KPI time series with daily and weekly patterns; the LSTM beat ARIMA by 12% MAPE." Also mention that Temporal CNNs or Transformers are alternatives, and why you didn't use them (data size, latency).

questions.q: How would you detect anomalies in network KPIs (latency, packet loss, throughput)?
questions.a:
• Baselines: seasonal decomposition (STL) and residual z-scores per cell or site; EWMA control charts.
  • ML: Isolation Forest on multivariate KPIs; LSTM/Transformer forecasters, flagging large residuals; autoencoders on KPI vectors.
  • Practicalities: a different seasonality per site, alert fatigue (aggregate and correlate alarms), root-cause hints (neighbouring cells, config changes).
  • Evaluate with labelled incidents (precision and recall of alerts, time to detect).

questions.q: You used Docker. What problem does it solve, and how is it different from a VM?
questions.a:
• Docker packages an app with its dependencies into an image; containers run it consistently anywhere ("works on my machine" solved).
  • vs VM: containers share the host OS kernel, so they are lightweight and start in seconds. VMs virtualise the hardware with a full guest OS, giving stronger isolation but at a heavier cost.
  • In ML: reproducible training and serving environments, easy deployment to Kubernetes.

questions.q: How can GenAI help telecom network operations?
questions.a:
• NOC copilot: summarise alarms and incidents, suggest likely root causes from past tickets (RAG), draft change plans.
  • Natural-language intent → configuration: translate operator intents into validated configuration templates (with human approval and simulation).
  • Knowledge assistants over 3GPP standards and vendor documents.
  • Guardrails: never push config changes without validation; audit trails; strict access control.

questions.q: How do you explain your project clearly in an interview?
questions.a:
Answer (3-minute template):

  1. One sentence: "I built an LSTM model that forecasts cell-tower traffic 24 hours ahead to save energy."
  2. Data: source, size, preprocessing (two sentences).
  3. Model: why LSTM, its key parameters, the baseline comparison.
  4. Result: "MAPE 8.4% against 9.6% for ARIMA, enabling sleep mode at off-peak sites."
  5. Your role and learnings. - Rehearse aloud and record yourself. Clarity was the deciding factor in this report.

questions.q: What is 5G network slicing, and where might ML help?
questions.a:
• Slicing: logically separate virtual networks on shared infrastructure, each with guaranteed characteristics (e.g. low-latency for industrial IoT, high-bandwidth for video).
  • ML uses: forecasting slice demand, dynamic resource allocation (RL), SLA violation prediction, anomaly detection per slice.

questions.q: Derive the logistic regression loss from first principles.
questions.a:
• Model y ∈ {0,1} as Bernoulli with p = σ(wᵀx) = 1 / (1 + e^(−wᵀx)).
  • Likelihood: L = ∏ pᵢ^yᵢ (1 − pᵢ)^(1 − yᵢ). Taking the negative log gives the binary cross-entropy: −Σ [yᵢ log pᵢ + (1 − yᵢ) log(1 − pᵢ)].
  • Gradient: ∂/∂w = Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢ. The loss is convex, so there is a unique optimum, found by gradient descent or Newton/IRLS.
  • L2 regularisation = a Gaussian prior on w (MAP estimate): add λ‖w‖².
  • Bayes link: the log-odds of the posterior, log P(y=1|x)/P(y=0|x), is linear in x when the class-conditional distributions are Gaussian with shared covariance (or from the exponential family).

questions.q: How does CLIP work? What is the contrastive loss, and what does BLIP's Q-Former add?
questions.a:
• CLIP: an image encoder (ViT) and a text encoder map into a shared embedding space.
  • For a batch of N pairs (say 32), compute the N×N cosine-similarity matrix scaled by a learned temperature.
  • The InfoNCE loss treats the diagonal as positives and the other N − 1 entries as negatives, symmetric over image→text and text→image.
  • A bigger batch means more negatives, which gives better representations.
  • Weaknesses:
  • Bag-of-words behaviour: weak on compositional understanding (word order, counting, relations).
  • Biases inherited from web data.
  • BLIP-2 Q-Former: a small Transformer with learned query tokens that cross-attend to a frozen image encoder. It extracts a fixed number of visual tokens that are fed to a frozen LLM, bridging vision and language cheaply.
  • Hard negatives (similar but wrong captions) improve fine-grained discrimination.

questions.q: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC: when do you use each? What is calibration?
questions.a:
• ROC-AUC: the probability that a random positive ranks above a random negative. It is insensitive to class balance, so it can look great under heavy imbalance.
  • PR-AUC: focuses on the positive class (precision vs recall). Prefer it for fraud, credit default and other rare events.
  • Calibration: predicted probabilities should match observed frequencies (of loans scored 0.2, about 20% should default). Check with reliability curves or the Brier score; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression.
  • It matters for pricing, credit limits and expected loss, where the probability value itself is used, not just the ranking.

questions.q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you avoid it when fine-tuning?
questions.a:
• What it is: fine-tuning on a new task overwrites the general abilities the model had (for example, after domain fine-tuning the LLM loses general reasoning or safety).
  • Mitigations:
  • PEFT (LoRA): the base weights stay frozen.
  • Lower learning rate and fewer epochs.
  • Replay: mix in 5–20% general or original data.
  • Regularisation towards the original weights (EWC, or a KL penalty).
  • Model merging.
  • Always evaluate on general benchmarks as well as the target task, before and after.

questions.q: Design a credit-risk model to approve users for a new EMI feature with no history and no bank data (cold start).
questions.a:
• Target and constraints: P(default or 90+ DPD within 6–12 months). Regulatory explainability and fairness apply.
  • Signals available without bank data (with consent and policy):
  • Platform behaviour: account age, order frequency, return and cancellation rates, payment-method history (COD vs prepaid), address stability.
  • Device and KYC signals.
  • Bureau score, if permitted.
  • Cold-start strategy: 1. Start with rules + a conservative limit for a test cohort. 2. Use proxy labels from related products (pay-later or COD-refusal behaviour). 3. Transfer a model from a similar portfolio. 4. Grow limits gradually as repayment data arrives (explore/exploit).
  • Model: a gradient-boosted tree with monotonic constraints, plus a scorecard for explainability (SHAP or reason codes); calibrated probability → expected-loss-based limit.
  • Evaluation: a time-split, out-of-time test; KS and AUC; reject inference for unapproved applicants; fairness checks; monitoring of vintage curves.
  • Why not X? Deep models are hard to explain to regulators, and pure rules leave money on the table. Be ready to defend every choice.

questions.q: Coding (2 h): build an end-to-end fraud detection pipeline. What would a clean solution look like?
questions.a:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, classification_report
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

df = pd.read_csv("transactions.csv", parse_dates=["ts"]).sort_values("ts")
df["hour"] = df.ts.dt.hour
df["amt_log"] = np.log1p(df.amount)
df["user_txn_24h"] = (df.groupby("user_id").rolling("24h", on="ts").amount.count()
                        .reset_index(level=0, drop=True).values)
num, cat = ["amt_log", "hour", "user_txn_24h"], ["merchant_cat", "device_type"]
cut = int(len(df) * 0.8)                       # time-based split, no leakage
tr, te = df.iloc[:cut], df.iloc[cut:]
pre = ColumnTransformer([("n", StandardScaler(), num),
                         ("c", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])
model = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(class_weight="balanced"))])
model.fit(tr[num + cat], tr.is_fraud)
p = model.predict_proba(te[num + cat])[:, 1]
print("PR-AUC", average_precision_score(te.is_fraud, p))
  • Talk through: a time-based split, velocity features, class imbalance, choosing the threshold on cost, and a predict(txn) function for inference. Code quality (functions, naming, comments) was explicitly assessed.

questions.q: Compare PPO-based RLHF and DPO for aligning an LLM or VLM.
questions.a:
• PPO (RLHF): train a reward model on preferences, then do on-policy RL with a clipped objective and a KL penalty to the reference model.
  • Powerful, but complex: 4 models in memory (policy, reference, reward, value), unstable, and expensive.
  • DPO: a closed-form re-parametrisation. Optimise the log-ratio of chosen vs rejected responses relative to the reference model, directly with a cross-entropy-style loss.
  • No reward model, no sampling loop, and stable.
  • Choose:
  • DPO (or ORPO, KTO) for most preference tuning on fixed datasets.
  • PPO or GRPO when you have a live reward signal (verifiable maths or code, or a learned reward) and want online exploration.

questions.q: Case: set discounts across several shoe brands, given competitors, to maximise revenue.
questions.a:
• Model demand per product: q = f(own price, competitor price, brand, seasonality, inventory, traffic). Estimate price elasticity, ideally with past experiments or with instruments or DML to handle the fact that prices are endogenous.
  • Optimise: maximise Σ (price × q(price)), or margin, subject to inventory, brand MAP rules, minimum margin and cannibalisation between brands (cross-elasticities).
  • Solve: a price grid plus constrained optimisation (or a contextual bandit for online learning).
  • Test: A/B or switchback experiments by region and time; guardrails on margin and returns.
  • Always ask: "revenue or profit?" Revenue-only optimisation can destroy margin.

questions.q: Explain the gradient descent optimisers: SGD, Momentum, RMSProp and Adam.
questions.a:
• Batch GD uses the whole dataset per step. SGD / mini-batch uses small batches, which is noisier but faster and generalises well.
  • Momentum: keeps a moving average of gradients (v = βv + g) to speed through ravines and damp oscillation.
  • RMSProp: scales the learning rate per parameter by a running average of squared gradients, which suits non-stationary problems.
  • Adam: Momentum + RMSProp (first and second moments) with bias correction; the default for deep learning. AdamW decouples weight decay and is the standard for Transformers.
  • Learning-rate schedule: warm-up then cosine decay for LLM training or fine-tuning.

questions.q: How do you preprocess data and evaluate an ML model properly?
questions.a:
• Preprocessing:
  • Handle missing values (impute plus a missing-indicator flag) and outliers.
  • Encode categoricals (one-hot, target encoding inside the CV folds).
  • Scale numeric features for distance-based or linear models.
  • Engineer features from domain knowledge.
  • Avoid leakage: fit transformers only on the training fold, and use Pipeline + ColumnTransformer. For time-based data, use a time-based split.
  • Evaluation: stratified k-fold, a metric that matches the business (F1 or PR-AUC for imbalance, RMSE or MAPE for forecasting), a baseline to compare against, and error analysis by segment.

questions.q: What are sentence transformers and where do you use them?
questions.a:
• What they are: BERT-style encoders fine-tuned (often in a Siamese setup with contrastive or MultipleNegativesRanking loss) so that one vector represents a whole sentence, with cosine similarity reflecting meaning. Examples: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge, e5.
  • Uses:
  • Semantic search and RAG retrieval
  • Clustering and topic discovery
  • Deduplication
  • Semantic textual similarity
  • Zero-shot classification by similarity to label descriptions
  • Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder: a bi-encoder embeds the query and document separately (fast, indexable); a cross-encoder reads the pair together (slower, more accurate), so it is used for re-ranking.

questions.q: How are word embeddings trained, and how do contextual embeddings differ?
questions.a:
• Word2Vec:
  • Skip-gram predicts the context words from the centre word; CBOW predicts the centre word from its context.
  • It is trained with negative sampling.
  • Words that appear in similar contexts end up close together.
  • GloVe: factorises global co-occurrence statistics. FastText: adds sub-word n-grams, so it handles rare and misspelt words.
  • Limitation: one vector per word, so "bank" (river) = "bank" (money).
  • Contextual (ELMo, BERT, GPT): the vector for a token depends on the whole sentence, produced by deep bidirectional or causal Transformers, so different senses get different vectors.

questions.q: Explain positional encoding. Why is it needed, and what variants exist?
questions.a:
• Why: self-attention is permutation-invariant, so without position information, "dog bites man" = "man bites dog".
  • Sinusoidal (original Transformer): fixed sin and cos at different frequencies, added to the embeddings. It can extrapolate somewhat.
  • Learned absolute: a trainable vector per position (BERT, GPT-2), limited to the maximum length seen in training.
  • Relative / rotary (RoPE): rotates Q and K by position so attention depends on relative distance. Used in Llama, Mistral and Qwen, and extendable with scaling (NTK, YaRN) for long context.
  • ALiBi: adds a distance-based bias to the attention scores.

questions.q: Design the RAG architecture you would build at Fractal for a client.
questions.a:
• Ingestion: document parsing that keeps layout and tables → semantic or heading-based chunks with metadata → embeddings → vector DB, refreshed incrementally.
  • Retrieval:
  • Query rewriting or multi-query
  • Hybrid BM25 + dense search
  • Metadata filters for access control
  • Cross-encoder re-rank to the top 5
  • Generation: a grounded prompt with citations and an "insufficient context" fallback. JSON output if a downstream system consumes it.
  • Evaluation and operations:
  • A RAGAS evaluation set
  • Tracing and logging
  • Feedback loop
  • Cost and latency dashboards
  • Guardrails for PII

questions.q: How do RAGAS and DSPy help? What do they measure or do?
questions.a:
• RAGAS evaluates RAG systems, mostly using an LLM as the judge:
  • Faithfulness: are the claims supported by the context?
  • Answer relevancy
  • Context precision / recall: did retrieval bring the right chunks?
  • Answer correctness against ground truth.
  • It can also generate synthetic test sets.
  • DSPy programs LLM pipelines instead of hand-writing prompts:
  • You declare signatures (input → output) and modules such as ChainOfThought or Retrieve.
  • An optimiser (BootstrapFewShot, MIPRO) automatically tunes prompts and few-shot examples against your metric.
  • Together: DSPy optimises the pipeline, and RAGAS-style metrics act as the objective and the regression tests.

questions.q: How do you benchmark one LLM or embedding model against another?
questions.a:
• Public benchmarks for shortlisting:
  • MMLU and GPQA (knowledge)
  • GSM8K and MATH (reasoning)
  • HumanEval (code)
  • MTEB (embeddings)
  • LMSYS Arena (preference)
  • Decide on your own benchmark:
  • 200+ in-domain examples
  • Fixed prompts
  • Temperature 0
  • Several runs
  • Metrics: accuracy / F1, faithfulness, latency, cost per 1k requests
  • Control variables: same context and same prompt format; watch for contamination. Report confidence intervals, and do a blind human review of a sample.

questions.q: How does an LLM generate text? Explain tokens, logits and decoding.
questions.a:
• The steps: 1. Text is tokenised (BPE / SentencePiece) into IDs, then embedded. 2. Decoder blocks with causal self-attention produce logits over the vocabulary for the next token. 3. Softmax turns the logits into probabilities. 4. Decoding picks a token: greedy, beam search, or sampling with temperature, top-k and top-p. 5. The new token is appended and the process repeats until a stop token or the maximum length.
  • A KV cache stores past keys and values so each new token costs O(n) attention rather than recomputing everything.

questions.q: What NLP techniques would you use to extract information from insurance claim documents?
questions.a:
• OCR + layout parsing for scanned forms (Document Intelligence, Textract).
  • Named-entity recognition for policy number, dates, amounts, diagnosis codes: spaCy or a fine-tuned BERT, or an LLM with a JSON schema (zero- or few-shot).
  • Classification of claim type and fraud flags; summarisation of adjuster notes.
  • Validation: regex and checksum rules, cross-checks against the policy database, and human review when confidence is low.
  • Metrics: field-level precision and recall, straight-through-processing rate, handling-time saved.

questions.q: Explain dropout and batch normalisation.
questions.a:
• Dropout: during training, randomly zero a fraction p of activations, so the network can't rely on specific neurons. It acts as an ensemble of sub-networks and reduces overfitting. At inference it is off (activations are scaled accordingly).
  • Batch Norm: normalises a layer's inputs per mini-batch (mean 0, variance 1), then applies a learned scale and shift. It stabilises and speeds up training and allows higher learning rates.
  • Transformers use LayerNorm instead (per token, independent of batch size), usually as pre-norm in modern LLMs.

questions.q: Python: remove duplicates from a list while preserving order.
questions.a:
def dedupe(xs):
    seen = set()
    return [x for x in xs if not (x in seen or seen.add(x))]

print(dedupe([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]))   # [3, 1, 2]
# or: list(dict.fromkeys(xs))   # dicts keep insertion order (Python 3.7+)

questions.q: Print the boundary (outer layer) of a binary tree anticlockwise.
questions.a:
def boundary(root):
    if not root: return []
    is_leaf = lambda n: not n.left and not n.right
    res = [root.val] if not is_leaf(root) else []
    n = root.left                                   # left boundary (top-down, no leaves)
    while n:
        if not is_leaf(n): res.append(n.val)
        n = n.left or n.right
    def leaves(n):
        if not n: return
        if is_leaf(n): res.append(n.val); return
        leaves(n.left); leaves(n.right)
    leaves(root)
    right, n = [], root.right                       # right boundary (bottom-up, no leaves)
    while n:
        if not is_leaf(n): right.append(n.val)
        n = n.right or n.left
    return res + right[::-1]

questions.q: Insert a value into a binary search tree.
questions.a:
def insert(root, val):
    if not root: return Node(val)
    if val < root.val: root.left = insert(root.left, val)
    else: root.right = insert(root.right, val)
    return root
  • O(h) time: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed. Mention self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black).

questions.q: Quicksort: what is its time complexity, and how do you avoid the worst case?
questions.a:
• Average O(n log n), worst case O(n²) when the pivots are consistently the smallest or largest (for example, sorted input with a first-element pivot).
  • Avoid it: random pivot, median-of-three, introsort (switch to heapsort at a recursion-depth limit), and three-way partitioning for many duplicates.
  • It sorts in place (O(log n) stack) and is not stable.

questions.q: ML terminology quick-fire: precision, recall, AUC, regularisation, cross-validation, feature leakage.
questions.a:
• Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Recall = TP/(TP+FN).
  • AUC = the probability that a random positive ranks above a random negative.
  • Regularisation penalises complexity (L1/L2) to reduce overfitting.
  • Cross-validation rotates validation folds for a robust estimate.
  • Leakage means a feature contains information unavailable at prediction time, which inflates offline scores.
  • Give one-line definitions plus an example each; quick-fire rounds reward crispness.

questions.q: Precision vs recall: which matters more for fraud detection?
questions.a:
• Recall (the share of frauds caught) usually matters more, because a missed fraud costs real money and trust.
  • But precision can't collapse: false alarms block genuine customers, overload investigators and hurt the customer experience.
  • Correct answer: it depends on cost.
  • Estimate the cost of a false negative (the fraud amount) and of a false positive (review cost plus customer friction).
  • Choose the threshold that minimises expected cost.
  • Often use tiers: auto-block when the score is very high, step-up authentication (OTP) in the middle, and allow when low.
  • Report PR-AUC and recall at a fixed precision (for example, recall @ 90% precision), because fraud data is highly imbalanced.

questions.q: System design: design an app that helps blind people navigate an indoor space.

  • Responsible AI: fail-safe behaviour on low confidence, battery use, and on-device privacy.

questions.q: Coding (DP): what is the minimum number of coins that makes up an amount?
questions.a:
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = amount + 1
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return -1 if dp[amount] == INF else dp[amount]
  • Bottom-up DP is O(amount × coins).
  • How to talk through it: define the state (dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a), the transition, the base case and the order of filling. Start from the recursive brute force, add memoisation, then convert to a table.
  • Leave 10 minutes for edge cases and complexity. This is where one candidate ran out of time.

questions.q: Coding: find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
questions.a:
def longest_unique(s):
    last, start, best = {}, 0, 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= start:
            start = last[ch] + 1
        last[ch] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best
  • A sliding window with the last-seen index of each character: O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

questions.q: How do you handle highly imbalanced data, such as 0.1% fraud?

  • Undersampling the majority class.
  • SMOTE, carefully and only on the training fold.
  • Anomaly-detection features.
  • Models: gradient boosting (XGBoost or LightGBM) with scale_pos_weight, plus graph features (shared device or IP).

questions.q: SQL: find the second-highest salary in each department.

SELECT department_id, salary
FROM (

         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk

questions.q: DSA: return the indices of the two numbers that add up to a target.
questions.a:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []
  • One pass with a hash map: O(n) time and O(n) space, compared with O(n²) for brute force. State the brute force first, then optimise.

questions.q: How did you use RAG in your project, and what problems did you face?
questions.a:
Answer (a structure to follow):

  1. The problem: "Analysts spent hours searching 3,000 policy PDFs."
  2. The architecture: loader → chunker (800 tokens, 120 overlap) → embeddings → vector DB → retriever (hybrid + re-rank) → LLM with a citation prompt → FastAPI + UI.
  3. Problems and fixes: - Tables were split badly, so I switched to layout-aware parsing. - Wrong chunks were retrieved, so I added a re-ranker and metadata filters. - The model hallucinated, so I made the prompt strict and showed "no answer" when the retrieval score was low.
  4. Metrics: recall@5 went from 0.71 to 0.89, faithfulness reached 0.93, and p95 latency was 2.1 seconds.

questions.q: Which metrics do you use for classification models, and when?
questions.a:
• Accuracy: only when classes are balanced.
  • Precision: of the items predicted positive, how many really are positive. Use it when false positives are costly, such as spam filters.
  • Recall: of the actual positives, how many were caught. Use it when misses are costly, such as fraud or disease detection.
  • F1: the harmonic mean of precision and recall, for imbalanced data.
  • ROC-AUC: ranking quality across thresholds. PR-AUC is better under heavy imbalance.
  • Confusion matrix: the full picture. Pick the decision threshold based on the business cost of each error type.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an LLM application?
questions.a:
• Offline:
  • A golden set of 100 to 500 questions with expected answers.
  • Retrieval metrics: recall@k and MRR.
  • Generation metrics (RAGAS / DeepEval): faithfulness, answer relevance, correctness.
  • Task-specific checks such as exact match for extraction or JSON validity.
  • LLM-as-judge with a clear rubric, calibrated against human labels.
  • Online: thumbs up/down, escalation rate, resolution rate, latency and cost per query, plus A/B tests for prompt or model changes.
  • Safety: toxicity, PII leakage, jailbreak test sets.

questions.q: Explain overfitting and the ways to reduce it.
questions.a:
• Overfitting: the model learns the noise in the training data, so it scores high on training and low on validation.
  • Fixes:
  • More or augmented data
  • A simpler model
  • Regularisation (L1/L2, dropout, weight decay)
  • Early stopping
  • Cross-validation
  • Feature selection
  • Ensembles (bagging)
  • For LLM fine-tuning: a lower learning rate, fewer epochs, LoRA instead of a full fine-tune, and a held-out evaluation set.

questions.q: Python: what is the difference between a list and a tuple, and between deep copy and shallow copy?
questions.a:
• List vs tuple: a list is mutable; a tuple is immutable, hashable (if its elements are), slightly faster, and can be used as a dict key.
  • Shallow copy (copy.copy, list[:]): a new outer object whose nested objects are shared.
  • Deep copy (copy.deepcopy): recursively copies everything, so changing a nested item does not affect the original.

questions.q: Final round: how would you approach a new AI use case from a business team?
questions.a:
1. Clarify: what problem, who the users are, what success looks like (a metric), and the constraints (data, privacy, budget).
  2. Check feasibility: what data exists and its quality, whether a simple rule or classic ML would do before reaching for an LLM, and the risks.
  3. Build a quick proof of concept on a small evaluation set and show it to users early.
  4. Plan production: security, monitoring, cost and a human fallback.
  5. Measure and iterate against the agreed metric. - Managers listen for business thinking + pragmatism, not just model names.

questions.q: Range XOR queries on an array with updates. Which data structure?
questions.a:
• Static array: a prefix XOR, px[i] = a[0]^…^a[i−1], so XOR(l..r) = px[r+1] ^ px[l]. O(1) per query.
  • With updates: a Fenwick tree or segment tree storing XOR. O(log n) per update and query.
class BIT:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n, self.t = n, [0] * (n + 1)
    def upd(self, i, v):          # xor v at index i (0-based)
        i += 1
        while i <= self.n: self.t[i] ^= v; i += i & -i
    def pre(self, i):             # xor of [0, i)
        r = 0
        while i: r ^= self.t[i]; i -= i & -i
        return r
    def query(self, l, r): return self.pre(r + 1) ^ self.pre(l)
  • To set a value instead of XOR-ing it in, apply upd(i, old ^ new).

questions.q: Minimum insertions to make string A follow a target order, solved with LCS.
questions.a:
• If the goal is to turn A into a supersequence of the alphabet order (or of string B) with the fewest insertions: answer = len(B) − LCS(A, B), since the characters in the LCS already line up and the others must be inserted.
def lcs(a, b):
    dp = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
    for x in a:
        prev = 0
        for j, y in enumerate(b, 1):
            cur = dp[j]
            dp[j] = prev + 1 if x == y else max(dp[j], dp[j - 1])
            prev = cur
    return dp[-1]
  • O(|A|·|B|) time with O(|B|) space.

  • Ad: creative, advertiser, format.

questions.q: Your project used LLMs. Explain how the Transformer decoder generates text, and its main costs.
questions.a:
• The flow: tokens → embeddings + positions → N decoder blocks (causal self-attention + MLP) → logits → sampling → append → repeat.
  • Costs:
  • Prefill (processing the prompt) is compute-bound.
  • Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and proportional to the number of output tokens.
  • The KV cache grows with batch × sequence × layers.
  • Optimisations: batching (continuous), quantization, FlashAttention, GQA, speculative decoding, shorter prompts.

questions.q: Probability: two cards are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are aces?
questions.a:
• (4/52) × (3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221 ≈ 0.0045.
  • General approach: the multiplication rule for dependent events, or combinations: C(4,2)/C(52,2) = 6/1326 = 1/221.

questions.q: How would you rank posts in a regional-language social feed (ShareChat-style)?

  • Language: Indic multilingual models (IndicBERT, MuRIL) for text; video and audio embeddings.

questions.q: How do you optimise a deep-learning model to run fast on a CPU or NPU (e.g. an AI PC)?
questions.a:
• Convert and compile: export to ONNX, then use a vendor runtime/compiler (OpenVINO for Intel CPUs, GPUs and NPUs; ONNX Runtime with an execution provider). These fuse operators and choose optimised kernels.
  • Quantize: INT8 post-training quantization with calibration data (or quantization-aware training if accuracy drops); INT4 weight-only for LLMs.
  • Model choices: a smaller or distilled model, pruning, static shapes, batch size tuned to the latency target.
  • Measure: latency (p50/p95), throughput and power on the target device, plus the change in accuracy against FP32.

questions.q: What is ROCm, and how does it compare to CUDA for ML engineers?
questions.a:
• ROCm is AMD's open GPU compute stack (HIP programming model, libraries such as rocBLAS and MIOpen) with PyTorch and JAX support. CUDA is NVIDIA's proprietary equivalent, with the most mature ecosystem.
  • For ML engineers: most PyTorch code runs on both, since PyTorch builds for ROCm. Custom CUDA kernels can be ported with HIPify. Performance depends on library maturity for specific operators.
  • Inference stacks (vLLM, ONNX Runtime) support both. Benchmark your model, because results vary.

questions.q: LeetCode medium: merge overlapping intervals.
questions.a:
def merge(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]); out = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]: out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else: out.append([s, e])
    return out
  • Sort by start, then sweep: O(n log n).

questions.q: Explain INT8 quantization: how it works and how you keep accuracy.
questions.a:
• Map floats to 8-bit integers: q = round(x / scale) + zero_point. Use per-channel scales for weights and per-tensor scales for activations.
  • Calibration: run representative data to choose activation ranges (min-max, percentile, entropy/KL).
  • Keep accuracy: leave sensitive layers (first and last, attention softmax) in FP16, use SmoothQuant for LLM activations with outliers, or use quantization-aware training.
  • Validate on the full evaluation set. A typical drop is under 1% for CNNs and varies for LLMs.

questions.q: Jio: you listed "CNN-based classifier" on your resume. Explain convolution, pooling and why CNNs work for images.
questions.a:
• Convolution: learned filters slide over the image computing local weighted sums, detecting edges, textures and parts. Weight sharing cuts parameters, and the operation is translation-equivariant.
  • Pooling: downsampling (max/avg) adds some translation invariance and grows the receptive field.
  • Depth: early layers learn edges, middle layers motifs, deep layers object parts. Residual connections (ResNet) allow very deep networks.
  • Be precise about your project: input size, architecture, augmentation, metrics, what failed. The interviewer will probe exactly those claims.

questions.q: Airtel: implement a RAG pipeline with LangGraph that decides whether to retrieve.
questions.a:
from typing import TypedDict, List
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END

class S(TypedDict): question: str; docs: List[str]; answer: str; route: str

def router(s):   s["route"] = "retrieve" if needs_kb(s["question"]) else "direct"; return s
def retrieve(s): s["docs"] = retriever.invoke(s["question"]); return s
def generate(s): s["answer"] = llm_answer(s["question"], s.get("docs", [])); return s

g = StateGraph(S)
g.add_node("router", router); g.add_node("retrieve", retrieve); g.add_node("generate", generate)
g.set_entry_point("router")
g.add_conditional_edges("router", lambda s: s["route"], {"retrieve": "retrieve", "direct": "generate"})
g.add_edge("retrieve", "generate"); g.add_edge("generate", END)
app = g.compile()
  • Explain: typed state, conditional routing, adding a grader node (is the context relevant? if not, rewrite the query and retry), checkpointing for memory, and tracing.

questions.q: Full-stack: how do you stream LLM tokens from a Node.js backend to a React UI?
questions.a:
// Node (Express) — Server-Sent Events
app.post("/chat", async (req, res) => {
  res.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/event-stream");
  res.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-cache");
  for await (const chunk of llm.stream(req.body.messages)) res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify(chunk)}\n\n`);
  res.end();
});

// React — read the stream and append tokens to state
const [text, setText] = useState("");
async function send(messages) {
  const r = await fetch("/chat", { method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"}, body: JSON.stringify({ messages }) });
  const reader = r.body.getReader(); const dec = new TextDecoder();
  for (;;) { const { value, done } = await reader.read(); if (done) break;
    dec.decode(value).split("\n\n").filter(Boolean).forEach(l => setText(t => t + JSON.parse(l.slice(6)).delta)); }
}
  • Mention abort controllers (stop generation), back-pressure, and error states in the UI.

questions.a:

questions.q: Basic DSA: check whether parentheses are balanced.
questions.a:
def balanced(s):
    pairs, st = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}, []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{": st.append(ch)
        elif ch in pairs:
            if not st or st.pop() != pairs[ch]: return False
    return not st
