questions.q: JPMC: perform EDA on a dataset and handle the outliers. Walk through your code.
questions.a:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("transactions.csv")
print(df.shape, df.dtypes, df.isna().mean().round(3), sep="\n")
print(df.describe(percentiles=[.01, .25, .5, .75, .99]).T)

col = "amount"
q1, q3 = df[col].quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
out = (df[col] < lo) | (df[col] > hi)
print(f"outliers: {out.mean():.2%}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
ax[0].boxplot(df[col].dropna()); ax[0].set_title("Amount (raw)")
ax[1].hist(np.log1p(df[col].clip(lower=0)), bins=50); ax[1].set_title("log(1+amount)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

df["amount_capped"] = df[col].clip(lo, df[col].quantile(.995))   # winsorise, keep the rows
df["is_outlier"] = out.astype(int)                              # keep the signal for fraud models
  • Say why: in banking, outliers are often the signal (fraud), so flag them rather than deleting them. Cap them for linear models, and log-transform skewed money amounts.
  • Also mention z-scores vs IQR (IQR is robust to skew), and Isolation Forest for multivariate outliers.

questions.q: How do you choose a method to handle outliers?
questions.a:
• First ask whether the outlier is an error or a real rare event. Data-entry errors get fixed or removed; real extremes (large transactions) are kept.
  • Options:
  • Winsorise or cap.
  • Log or Box-Cox transform.
  • Robust scaling (median/IQR).
  • Tree models, which are insensitive to outliers.
  • Robust losses (Huber).
  • A separate model for the extreme segment.
  • Multivariate outliers: Isolation Forest, LOF, Mahalanobis distance.
  • Document the decision and its effect on model metrics; regulators may ask.

questions.q: How would you build a credit-card fraud detection system at a bank?
questions.a:
• Real-time scoring within about 100 ms at authorisation.
  • Features:
  • Velocity (transactions in 1 h / 24 h).
  • Amount vs the user's typical spend.
  • Merchant risk, geography and travel distance.
  • Device and channel.
  • Time of day.
  • Graph links (shared cards, devices, merchants).
  • Model: gradient boosting for tabular data plus rules for known patterns; consider a sequence model for transaction history.
  • Imbalance: class weights; PR-AUC; recall at a fixed false-positive rate.
  • Decision layer: approve / step-up (OTP) / decline, with thresholds tuned on fraud loss vs customer friction.
  • Operations:
  • Labels arrive with a delay (chargebacks), so handle that.
  • Monitor drift, retrain weekly or monthly.
  • Model risk management (SR 11-7 style validation) and explainability via reason codes.

questions.q: How do GenAI use cases in banking differ from other industries?
questions.a:
• Common use cases:
  • Internal knowledge assistants (policies, procedures).
  • Document extraction (KYC, trade documents).
  • Call summarisation.
  • Code assistants.
  • Research summarisation for analysts.
  • Extra constraints:
  • Data residency.
  • No customer PII leaving the bank's boundary (private endpoints or self-hosted models).
  • Explainability and audit trails.
  • Model risk governance.
  • Strict accuracy on numbers.
  • Patterns: RAG with citations, a human in the loop for any customer-facing or decision output, deterministic tools for calculations (never let the LLM do the arithmetic), and red-teaming for prompt injection.

questions.q: Amex: guesstimate how many transactions per second your fraud model must handle.
questions.a:
Answer (show the structure, not the exact number):

  • Assume about 100 million active cards, with about 1.5 transactions per card per day → about 150 million transactions per day.
  • 150M / 86,400 s ≈ 1,700 TPS on average. Peak (festive sales, evenings) is roughly 3–5× → design for about 8,000 TPS.
  • At a p99 latency budget of about 50 ms per score, with each instance handling about 500 requests per second → about 16 instances, plus headroom across 2 regions.
  • State your assumptions clearly, sanity-check them, and tie them to the design (caching features in Redis, horizontal scaling).

questions.q: Explain the vanishing gradient problem and how modern networks avoid it.
questions.a:
• The problem: in backpropagation through many layers, gradients are products of derivatives. With sigmoid or tanh (derivatives below 1), they shrink exponentially, so early layers barely learn. RNNs suffer this over time steps.
  • Fixes:
  • ReLU / GELU activations.
  • Residual connections (ResNets, Transformers).
  • Normalisation (Batch / Layer Norm).
  • Careful initialisation (He / Xavier).
  • LSTM / GRU gates for sequences.
  • Gradient clipping, for exploding gradients.

questions.q: Behavioural (JPMC VP): how do you lead a data science team through a model that fails validation?
questions.a:
• Own it: "Our credit model failed independent validation on stability (PSI 0.3 in one segment)."
  • Act: 1. Run a root-cause review with the team, without blame. 2. Find the issue: a feature driven by a policy change. 3. Rebuild with stable features and add segment-level monitoring. 4. Communicate the timeline to the business and risk teams every week.
  • Result: "It passed revalidation in five weeks. We added stability tests to our standard development checklist, and the next two models passed on the first submission."
  • A VP-level answer shows governance, communication, coaching and process improvement.

questions.q: How would you approach price and cost optimisation for a client? What data do you need?
questions.a:
• Clarify the objective: maximise margin or revenue, or hit a volume target? What constraints apply (minimum margin, competitor parity, contracts)?
  • Data:
  • Transaction history (price, quantity, discounts).
  • Product attributes and cost (COGS).
  • Competitor prices.
  • Seasonality, promotions and channel.
  • Customer segments.
  • Inventory.
  • Method: 1. Estimate price elasticity per product or segment (log-log regression, or hierarchical Bayesian for sparse products). 2. Model demand = f(price, competitor price, season...). 3. Optimise price within the constraints (grid search or linear/non-linear programming). 4. Validate with A/B or regional tests.
  • Cost side: analyse spend by supplier and category, find outliers, and compare against should-cost models.
  • Deliver: a pricing recommendation dashboard with the expected impact and its risks.

questions.q: How do you handle imbalanced data?
questions.a:
• Metrics first: PR-AUC, F1, recall at a fixed precision. Never accuracy.
  • Data level: undersample the majority class, oversample (SMOTE) only on the training folds, collect more minority data.
  • Algorithm level: class weights (class_weight="balanced", scale_pos_weight), focal loss, anomaly detection for extreme rarity.
  • Decision level: tune the threshold on business costs, and calibrate probabilities.

questions.q: How do you evaluate a predictive model properly?
questions.a:
• A split that matches reality: time-based for forecasting and fraud; grouped by customer to avoid leakage.
  • A metric tied to the decision: RMSE or MAPE (forecasting), AUC/PR-AUC/F1 (classification), plus calibration.
  • Compare against a baseline (naïve forecast, a rule, last-period value).
  • Error analysis by segment, stability over time, and an explainability check.
  • Business evaluation: expected savings or revenue at the chosen threshold.

questions.q: How do you approach a time-series forecasting problem?
questions.a:
• Explore: trend, seasonality (daily, weekly, annual), holidays, structural breaks, missing data.
  • Baselines: naïve, seasonal naïve, moving average.
  • Models:
  • Statistical: ETS, ARIMA/SARIMA, Prophet.
  • ML: LightGBM with lag, rolling and calendar features, which works across many series.
  • Deep learning: N-BEATS or TFT for large panels.
  • Validation: rolling-origin (walk-forward) backtesting. Never shuffle.
  • Metrics: MAPE/sMAPE, WAPE, MASE; prediction intervals for planning.

questions.q: When would you use Bayesian methods in a business problem?
questions.a:
• Small or sparse data, where priors stabilise the estimates: hierarchical models for many stores or products sharing information.
  • When you need uncertainty: credible intervals for decisions (inventory, pricing risk).
  • Bayesian A/B testing: "the probability that B beats A is 96%", which is easier for business teams to read; it also allows continuous monitoring.
  • Tools: PyMC, Stan, NumPyro. Mention the trade-off: more compute, and you must justify the priors.

questions.q: Why KPMG, and how would you apply GenAI for KPMG clients?
questions.a:
• Why: "I want to solve varied, high-impact client problems in regulated industries, where trust and governance matter. KPMG's audit, tax and advisory work is exactly where responsible GenAI adds value."
  • Use cases to mention:
  • Contract and policy review with RAG and citations.
  • Audit-evidence summarisation.
  • Tax-query assistants.
  • Risk and compliance monitoring.
  • Finance-close automation with agents and human approval.
  • Emphasise governance: data privacy, explainability, human review and audit trails.

questions.q: Why do Indic languages need special handling in LLMs?
questions.a:
• Tokenisation: English-centric BPE splits Devanagari and Tamil text into many tokens, which raises cost and latency and lowers quality. Indic-aware tokenisers (larger vocabularies, script-specific merges) cut the token count 2–4×.
  • Data scarcity and quality: less web text, so use translation-augmented, synthetic and curated data, and careful deduplication.
  • Code-mixing and transliteration: Hinglish in Latin script ("kal milte hain"). Train on romanised text too.
  • Evaluation: benchmarks such as IndicGLUE, IndicXTREME, FLORES for translation, and human evaluation by native speakers.

questions.q: How would you evaluate a speech-to-speech dubbing pipeline (ASR → translation → TTS)?
questions.a:
• Per component:
  • ASR: WER/CER.
  • Translation: BLEU/chrF/COMET plus human adequacy and fluency.
  • TTS: MOS, intelligibility (ASR on the TTS output), speaker-similarity cosine of voice embeddings.
  • End to end:
  • Lip-sync and timing alignment.
  • Preservation of emotion and prosody.
  • Naturalness ratings.
  • Error propagation analysis.
  • Non-determinism: fix seeds, sample several outputs, report distributions; use A/B preference tests against global baselines.

questions.q: How do you optimise LLM inference on GPUs?
questions.a:
• Serving engine: vLLM / TensorRT-LLM / SGLang with continuous batching, a paged KV cache, prefix caching.
  • Model: FP8/INT8/INT4 quantization (AWQ, GPTQ), GQA, speculative decoding (a small draft model), distillation.
  • Kernels: FlashAttention, fused ops, CUDA graphs.
  • Measure: time to first token, tokens per second per GPU, p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens; profile with Nsight. Tune batch size against latency targets.

questions.q: Clean this DataFrame in Python. What steps and syntax would you use?
questions.a:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("campaign.csv")
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "_")     # tidy names
df = df.drop_duplicates()
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce", dayfirst=True)   # fix types
df["spend"] = pd.to_numeric(df["spend"].astype(str).str.replace(r"[₹,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
df["channel"] = df["channel"].str.strip().str.title().replace({"Fb": "Facebook"})
df["spend_missing"] = df["spend"].isna().astype(int); df["spend"] = df["spend"].fillna(df.groupby("channel")["spend"].transform("median"))
q1, q3 = df["spend"].quantile([.25, .75]); df["spend"] = df["spend"].clip(upper=q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1))
df = df.dropna(subset=["date", "campaign_id"])
  • Explain each step: names, duplicates, types, standardised categories, missing values (with a flag), outliers, required keys. Then validate with df.info() and describe().

questions.q: SQL: rank departments by the share of employees earning more than ₹20 LPA.
questions.a:
SELECT department,
       AVG(CASE WHEN salary > 2000000 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS high_earner_share,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(CASE WHEN salary > 2000000 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) DESC) AS rk
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10;          -- avoid tiny departments dominating

questions.q: How would you measure the ROI of a marketing campaign?
questions.a:
• Incrementality first: use a holdout or geo test, or a matched control, to estimate the incremental conversions and revenue caused by the campaign.
  • ROI = (incremental gross margin − campaign cost) / campaign cost.
  • Attribution for always-on channels: marketing-mix modelling (MMM) with adstock and saturation, or data-driven multi-touch attribution where tracking allows.
  • Report confidence intervals and cost per incremental acquisition, and recommend a budget reallocation.

questions.q: Is data separable? How would you check whether two classes are linearly separable?
questions.a:
• Visual: pair plots or PCA/t-SNE for intuition.
  • Formal: fit a linear SVM with a very large C (a hard margin) or a perceptron. Zero training error means linearly separable. Linear programming feasibility is the exact test.
  • If not separable: kernels (RBF), feature crosses, trees or neural networks.

questions.q: As an assistant manager, how do you manage a client analytics project with a tight deadline?
questions.a:
• Scope tightly: agree the 2–3 key questions and the deliverable format on day 1.
  • Plan: a work breakdown with owners, daily stand-ups, risks (data access) escalated early.
  • Quality: peer reviews of SQL and logic, sanity checks against known totals.
  • Communicate: a mid-point preview to the client; then the final story with insight, recommendation and impact.
  • Show delivery + people management + client handling.

questions.q: A/B test: how do you decide whether a result is significant and worth shipping?
questions.a:
• Pre-register the metric, the minimum detectable effect, α and power, and the duration.
  • Check for sample-ratio mismatch; compute the lift with a confidence interval (z-test or bootstrap).
  • Significant and practically meaningful (above the MDE) and guardrails intact → ship. Otherwise iterate.
  • Watch for peeking, novelty effects, and multiple comparisons.

questions.q: What is data leakage and how do you prevent it?
questions.a:
• Definition: information from outside the training data, often the target or the future, gets into training. Validation scores then look great while production performs badly.
  • Common causes:
  • Scaling or imputing on the full dataset before the split.
  • Target encoding without folds.
  • Random splits on time-series data.
  • Duplicate rows that fall into both train and test.
  • Features that are only known after the outcome.
  • Prevention:
  • Split first.
  • Fit preprocessing inside a Pipeline per CV fold.
  • Use time-based or group-based splits.
  • Deduplicate.
  • Review every feature for "would I know this at prediction time?"

questions.q: What is the difference between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RLHF? Where does DPO fit?
questions.a:
• SFT: train on (prompt → ideal response) pairs with next-token loss. It teaches format, style and how to follow instructions.
  • RLHF: 1. Collect human preferences (response A is better than B). 2. Train a reward model on them. 3. Optimise the policy with PPO to maximise reward, with a KL penalty to stay close to the SFT model.
  • It aligns the model to helpfulness and harmlessness.
  • DPO: optimises directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss, with no reward model and no RL loop. It is simpler and more stable, and widely used now.
  • Typical pipeline: pre-training → SFT → preference tuning (RLHF, DPO or ORPO).

questions.q: How do you evaluate generative models beyond perplexity?
questions.a:
• Perplexity only measures how well the model predicts text. It doesn't tell you whether the answer is correct, helpful or safe.
  • Reference-based:
  • Exact match or F1 for QA
  • BLEU or ROUGE for translation and summaries (limited)
  • BERTScore (semantic)
  • Reference-free: LLM-as-judge with a rubric, pairwise preference (win rate), faithfulness to the context, and RAGAS for RAG.
  • Task benchmarks: MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, plus a domain-specific test set.
  • Human evaluation on a sample, plus safety and toxicity tests, latency and cost.

questions.q: How do you reduce LLM inference latency?
questions.a:
• Model side:
  • Use a smaller or distilled model.
  • Quantize (INT8 / 4-bit).
  • Speculative decoding.
  • Serving:
  • vLLM or TGI with continuous batching and PagedAttention for the KV cache.
  • Tensor parallelism.
  • Optimised kernels (FlashAttention).
  • Application:
  • Stream tokens.
  • Cache responses.
  • Shorten prompts and outputs.
  • Use prompt or prefix caching.
  • Run retrieval and tools in parallel.
  • Route simple queries to small models.
  • Measure time to first token and tokens per second separately; they have different fixes.

questions.q: How do you handle model versioning and drift for an LLM application?
questions.a:
• Version everything:
  • Model name and version
  • Prompt templates (in git)
  • Embedding model
  • Index snapshot
  • Evaluation set
  • Record them all in each trace.
  • Kinds of drift:
  • Data/query drift: users ask new things. Monitor the embedding distribution and topic clusters.
  • Knowledge drift: documents go out of date. Use a refresh pipeline and freshness metadata.
  • Provider drift: the hosted model is updated. Pin versions and re-run the evaluation before upgrading.
  • Respond: run the evaluation set nightly or weekly, alert on drops in quality or feedback, and roll back via a model or prompt registry.

questions.q: How do you protect sensitive data when fine-tuning?
questions.a:
• Minimise: use only the fields you need, and detect and mask PII (Presidio, regex + NER) before training.
  • Environment: train in a private VPC or VNet, keep encryption at rest and in transit, and enforce strict IAM. Use a cloud provider's no-retention fine-tuning or self-host.
  • Memorisation risk: deduplicate, train for fewer epochs, consider differential privacy for highly sensitive data, and test for regurgitation of training records.
  • Governance: data-use approval, lineage, model cards, and access control on the resulting model.

questions.q: What is LoRA/PEFT and why use it?
questions.a:
• LoRA: freeze the base weights W and learn a low-rank update ΔW = B·A (rank r = 4 to 64) only on selected layers, usually the attention projections.
  • Benefits:
  • Trains under 1% of the parameters.
  • Needs far less GPU memory.
  • Produces small adapter files, one per task, that can be swapped.
  • Avoids catastrophic forgetting better than a full fine-tune.
  • QLoRA: LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base, so a 7B to 13B model can be fine-tuned on one GPU.
  • Other PEFT methods: prefix or prompt tuning, IA³, adapters.

questions.q: What does CI/CD look like for an LLM application?
questions.a:
• CI (on each pull request):
  • Unit tests
  • Linting
  • Prompt and chain tests with mocked LLMs
  • An evaluation gate: run the golden set and fail if faithfulness or accuracy drops more than X%
  • Security scans
  • CD:
  • Build the container.
  • Deploy to staging.
  • Run smoke and evaluation tests.
  • Canary or blue-green release to production.
  • Automatic rollback on alerts.
  • Artefacts: prompts, configs and model versions in a registry; infrastructure as code (Terraform or Bicep).

questions.q: HCLTech: which NLP libraries would you use for a text classification task, and how?
questions.a:
• Quick baseline: scikit-learn TfidfVectorizer + LogisticRegression in a Pipeline, evaluated with stratified CV.
  • Preprocessing:
  • spaCy for tokenisation, lemmas and NER.
  • NLTK for stop words and stemming in classic pipelines.
  • re for cleaning.
  • Better accuracy: Hugging Face transformers, fine-tuning DistilBERT or RoBERTa with Trainer, or sentence-transformer embeddings with a classifier.
  • LLM option: zero- or few-shot classification with structured output, useful when labels are scarce.
  • Explain why: start simple, measure, then increase complexity only if needed.

questions.q: HCLTech scenario: the chatbot gives correct answers in testing but users complain in production. What do you do?
questions.a:
1. Collect evidence: pull production traces and look for negative-feedback clusters. Are failures tied to a topic, a language or long chats?
  2. Compare distributions: production questions are often messier than the test set (typos, Hinglish, multi-part questions).
  3. Find the root cause: - Retrieval misses (low scores)? - Stale documents? - Lost context in long chats? - Latency timeouts?
  4. Fix and prevent: - Add real queries to the evaluation set. - Query rewriting. - Better chunking. - Memory summarisation. - Monitor feedback by topic.
  5. Communicate progress to stakeholders with metrics.

questions.q: How do precision and recall change as you move the classification threshold?
questions.a:
• Raise the threshold: fewer positives are predicted, so precision usually rises and recall falls.
  • Lower it: more positives, so recall rises and precision falls.
  • The PR curve traces this trade-off. Choose the threshold by business cost (fraud loss vs declined good transactions) or by a target (e.g. recall ≥ 80% at the highest precision).

questions.q: Why do we use log loss for classification instead of MSE?
questions.a:
• Log loss = the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model. It is the principled maximum-likelihood objective for probabilities.
  • With a sigmoid output it is convex in the weights (MSE + sigmoid is not), and its gradients don't vanish when the model is confidently wrong. Gradient (p − y)·x gives strong corrections.
  • It heavily penalises confident mistakes and encourages calibrated probabilities.

questions.q: Derive the gradient-descent update for logistic regression.
questions.a:
• Loss: L = −(1/n) Σ [y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)], with p = σ(wᵀx).
  • Using dσ/dz = σ(1−σ): ∂L/∂w = (1/n) Σ (p − y) x.
  • Update: w ← w − η · (1/n) Xᵀ(p − y). Add λw for L2.
  • Shortcomings to mention: sensitivity to the learning rate, feature scaling, and slow convergence on ill-conditioned data. Second-order methods (Newton/IRLS, L-BFGS) converge faster for small d.

questions.q: Explain a customer-segmentation project end to end.
questions.a:
• Goal: segment cardholders for targeted offers.
  • Features: RFM, category mix (travel, dining, groceries), channel (online/POS), cross-border share, tenure. Log-transform skewed spend, then standardise.
  • Method: k-means (choose k with the elbow, silhouette and business interpretability) or a GMM; PCA for visualisation.
  • Personas: "frequent travellers", "online shoppers", "essentials-only", "dormant".
  • Validation: stability across months; uplift from a targeted campaign A/B test (e.g. +12% activation in the travel segment).

questions.q: Which unsupervised methods have you used, and for what?
questions.a:
• Clustering: k-means (segments), DBSCAN (density-based, finds outliers), hierarchical (taxonomies).
  • Dimensionality reduction: PCA (compression, denoising), t-SNE/UMAP (visualisation).
  • Anomaly detection: Isolation Forest, autoencoders (reconstruction error for fraud).
  • Topic modelling / embeddings: LDA, or embeddings + clustering on complaint text.
  • Association rules: market-basket analysis.
  • For each, say why it fits and how you validated it without labels.

questions.q: Design a fraud-detection model for card-not-present (online) transactions.
questions.a:
• Signals: device fingerprint, IP/geo mismatch, email age, velocity per card/device/merchant, basket and amount anomalies, merchant risk, 3-D Secure result.
  • Model: gradient boosting plus graph features (shared devices/cards), with a real-time feature store; a latency budget under 50 ms.
  • Labels: chargebacks (delayed) and confirmed fraud; handle label delay and class imbalance.
  • Decision: approve / step-up (3DS/OTP) / decline, with thresholds by merchant risk.
  • Monitoring: fraud basis points, false-decline rate, drift; weekly retraining; explainability reason codes.

questions.q: Scenario: design a CNN to classify road signs from dash-cam images.
questions.a:
• Data: cropped sign images across lighting, weather and occlusion; class balance; augmentation (brightness, blur, small rotations, no horizontal flips for asymmetric signs).
  • Model: a pre-trained lightweight backbone (MobileNet/EfficientNet) for edge deployment; replace the head with N classes; fine-tune with AdamW and cosine learning-rate decay.
  • Evaluation: per-class recall (safety-critical classes such as STOP are weighted), a confusion matrix, robustness tests (night, rain), latency on the target hardware.
  • Deployment: quantize to INT8 and validate; monitor field data for drift (new sign designs).
questions.page: Mercedes-Benz R&D India & Philips: AI / Data Scientist

questions.q: How do you choose the batch size?
questions.a:
• Memory: the largest batch that fits on the GPU (activations scale with batch × resolution); gradient accumulation can simulate bigger batches.
  • Optimisation: large batches give smoother gradients and better throughput, but may generalise worse and need learning-rate scaling (the linear scaling rule plus warm-up). Small batches add noise that can help generalisation but train more slowly.
  • BatchNorm needs reasonably large batches (or use Group/LayerNorm).
  • In practice: tune the batch size together with the learning rate; common choices are 32–256 for vision fine-tuning.

questions.q: Philips: how do you check whether data is normally distributed?
questions.a:
• Visual: a histogram/KDE and a Q-Q plot (points on the line suggest normality).
  • Tests: Shapiro–Wilk (small n), D'Agostino K², Anderson–Darling. With large samples, tiny deviations become "significant", so rely more on plots and effect size.
  • If not normal: transform (log, Box-Cox), use non-parametric tests (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon) or bootstrap.
questions.page: Mercedes-Benz R&D India & Philips: AI / Data Scientist

questions.q: How do you interpret logistic regression coefficients for a categorical variable?
questions.a:
• One-hot encode with a reference category. Each coefficient β is the change in log-odds relative to the reference, holding other variables constant.
  • exp(β) is the odds ratio. For example, β = 0.69 for "smoker" vs "non-smoker" means about 2× the odds of the outcome.
  • Check the confidence intervals; changing the reference category changes the coefficients, but not the model's predictions.
questions.page: Mercedes-Benz R&D India & Philips: AI / Data Scientist

questions.q: How do you handle longitudinal (repeated-measures) patient data?
questions.a:
• Don't treat visits as independent (that underestimates the variance and leaks across splits). Split by patient.
  • Models:
  • Mixed-effects models (random intercepts and slopes per patient).
  • GEE.
  • Survival models for time-to-event.
  • Sequence models (RNN/Transformer) for event histories.
  • Missing visits: distinguish missing-at-random from dropout due to health status; use multiple imputation or models that handle irregular time.
questions.page: Mercedes-Benz R&D India & Philips: AI / Data Scientist

questions.q: What does a confusion matrix tell you, and which metrics come from it?
questions.a:
• A table of actual vs predicted classes: TP, FP, FN, TN (N×N for multi-class).
  • Metrics:
  • Accuracy.
  • Precision.
  • Recall / sensitivity.
  • Specificity (TN/(TN+FP)), which is important in medicine.
  • F1.
  • Positive and negative predictive values, which depend on prevalence.
  • Use it to spot which classes get confused and to set thresholds based on clinical cost.

questions.q: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put.
questions.a:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap, self.d = capacity, OrderedDict()
    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.d: return -1
        self.d.move_to_end(key); return self.d[key]
    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.d: self.d.move_to_end(key)
        self.d[key] = value
        if len(self.d) > self.cap: self.d.popitem(last=False)
  • Mention the classic version: a hash map + doubly-linked list (move a node to the head on access, evict the tail), which interviewers may ask you to write without OrderedDict.

questions.q: Design a ranking system for a news feed.
questions.a:
• Goal: maximise long-term meaningful engagement (not just clicks), with integrity constraints.
  • Stages: 1. Candidate generation: recent posts from friends, groups and pages plus recommended content (two-tower embeddings, ANN), giving thousands of candidates. 2. Light ranker: a cheap model trims to hundreds. 3. Heavy ranker: a multi-task deep model (DLRM-style) predicts P(like), P(comment), P(share), P(hide/report) and dwell time, combined with a value function of weighted predictions. 4. Re-ranking: diversity, freshness, creator fairness, integrity filters, ad insertion.
  • Features: user–author affinity, content embeddings, recency, engagement velocity, context (device, time).
  • Training: logged impressions; handle position bias; daily or online updates.
  • Evaluation: offline NDCG and AUC per task → online A/B on engagement and guardrails (reports, time well spent).
  • Serving and scale: feature store, caching, under 200 ms end to end; monitor drift and feedback loops.

questions.q: Have you maintained an end-to-end ML pipeline in production? What did "maintaining" involve?
questions.a:
Answer (show operational ownership):

  • Data: scheduled ingestion with data-quality checks (schema, nulls, distributions) and alerts.
  • Training: automated weekly retraining, experiment tracking, and an evaluation gate against the current model.
  • Deployment: model registry, canary release, rollback.
  • Monitoring: feature drift (PSI), prediction drift, latency, business KPIs, and label-delayed performance tracking.
  • Incidents: "An upstream logging change broke a feature. Our drift alert fired, we rolled back within an hour, and we added a data contract."
  • Interviewers want evidence that you owned it after launch, not just trained a notebook model.

questions.q: Coding: find the k most frequent elements.
questions.a:
from collections import Counter
import heapq

def top_k(nums, k):
    return [x for x, _ in heapq.nlargest(k, Counter(nums).items(), key=lambda t: t[1])]
  • O(n log k) with a heap. Bucket sort by frequency gives O(n). Discuss ties and streaming variants (Count-Min Sketch).

questions.q: How do you handle position bias in ranking training data?
questions.a:
• Users click higher positions more regardless of relevance, so naïve training learns "position = relevance".
  • Fixes:
  • Add position as a feature during training, and set it to a constant at serving.
  • Inverse propensity weighting using estimated examination probabilities (from randomisation or result swaps).
  • Click models such as cascade or DBN.
  • Small exploration traffic to collect less-biased data.

questions.q: Behavioural: tell me about a time you took ownership beyond your role.
questions.a:
Answer (STAR):

  • Situation: "Our model's online gains disappeared after launch; nobody owned the logging pipeline."
  • Action: "I traced it to a mismatch between training and serving features, wrote a parity test, and set up a weekly cross-team review with the data platform team."
  • Result: "We recovered the +2.1% engagement lift, and the parity test caught two later issues before launch."
  • Meta values move fast with ownership and impact backed by metrics.

questions.q: Design a RAG system that generates a slide deck from a user's prompt.
questions.a:
• Clarify: the input (topic plus optional documents), the output (PPTX/JSON slides with title, bullets, images, notes), enterprise data access, latency budget (under 30 s), and brand templates.
  • Pipeline: 1. Intent and outline: the LLM produces a structured outline (sections, slide count) as JSON. 2. Retrieval per section: hybrid search over the user's permitted documents (SharePoint/Graph) → re-rank → top passages. 3. Slide generation: the LLM fills a slide schema (title, 3–5 bullets, speaker notes, citation IDs, a suggested visual) per section, with sections run in parallel. 4. Rendering: map the JSON to the template (python-pptx / Office.js), insert charts or images, keep the brand theme. 5. Review loop: the user edits, and "regenerate slide 4" re-runs only that slide.
  • Quality:
  • Faithfulness: every bullet must cite a source.
  • No overflow (bullet length limits).
  • Human ratings.
  • A rubric for an LLM judge.
  • Safety and scale: access control respected at retrieval, PII filters, caching of document embeddings, cost control (a smaller model for the outline, a larger one for content).

questions.q: Prove that binary cross-entropy is convex in the logistic-regression weights.
questions.a:
• The loss for one example is ℓ(w) = −y log σ(z) − (1−y) log(1−σ(z)), with z = wᵀx.
  • Gradient: ∇ℓ = (σ(z) − y) x.
  • Hessian: ∇²ℓ = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) x xᵀ.
  • σ(z)(1−σ(z)) ≥ 0 and x xᵀ is positive semi-definite, since vᵀ(x xᵀ)v = (xᵀv)² ≥ 0. So the Hessian is PSD.
  • The sum over examples (plus an optional L2 term λ‖w‖², whose Hessian is 2λI) stays PSD, so the loss is convex, and with L2 strictly convex. Any local minimum is global.

questions.q: Compute and plot a precision-recall curve from scratch.
questions.a:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def pr_curve(y, s):
    order = np.argsort(-s); y = np.asarray(y)[order]
    tp = np.cumsum(y); fp = np.cumsum(1 - y)
    precision = tp / (tp + fp); recall = tp / y.sum()
    return np.r_[1, precision], np.r_[0, recall]

y = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]); s = np.array([.9, .8, .7, .6, .55, .4, .35, .1])
p, r = pr_curve(y, s)
ap = np.sum((r[1:] - r[:-1]) * p[1:])          # average precision (step-wise)
plt.step(r, p, where="post"); plt.xlabel("Recall"); plt.ylabel("Precision"); plt.title(f"AP={ap:.2f}"); plt.show()
  • Sort by score descending and use the cumulative TP/FP counts. AP is the area under the step curve. Mention sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_curve for checking.

questions.q: Explain KNN and PCA. What are their trade-offs?
questions.a:
• KNN: non-parametric; predicts from the k nearest neighbours.
  • Simple, no training, handles multi-class.
  • But: slow at prediction (O(n·d)), sensitive to scale and irrelevant features, suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Choose k by cross-validation.
  • PCA: linear projection onto the directions of maximum variance.
  • Reduces noise and dimensionality, speeds up models, aids visualisation.
  • But: linear only, the components are hard to interpret, it is scale-sensitive, and it ignores labels.
  • Together: PCA before KNN often helps, because distances become more meaningful in fewer dimensions.

questions.q: Rapid-fire LLM fundamentals: what is the context window, the KV cache and temperature, and why do models hallucinate?
questions.a:
• Context window: the maximum number of tokens the model attends to (prompt + output). Longer windows are costlier and can suffer "lost in the middle".
  • KV cache: stores past attention keys and values during generation, so each new token needs only incremental compute. Memory grows with sequence length × layers × heads.
  • Temperature: scales the logits. Lower is more deterministic; higher is more diverse.
  • Hallucination: the model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not verified facts, and gaps in its knowledge or ambiguous prompts lead to confident errors. Mitigate with grounding (RAG), tools and verification.
  • Fine-tuning vs RAG: fine-tuning teaches behaviour and format; RAG supplies fresh, citable knowledge.

questions.q: Behavioural: tell me about a conflict with a teammate and how you resolved it.
questions.a:
Answer (STAR):

  • Situation: "My teammate wanted to fine-tune a model; I believed RAG would meet the deadline and keep the data fresh."
  • Action: "I suggested we each prototype for two days on the same 50-question evaluation set, and we agreed on the metrics in advance."
  • Result: "RAG scored 0.86 against 0.81 for fine-tuning, at a fifth of the cost. We shipped RAG and used his fine-tuning work later for a classification step."
  • Microsoft values a growth mindset and collaboration. Show that you listened, used data and kept the relationship strong.

questions.q: Compare GANs, VAEs and diffusion models.
questions.a:
GAN VAE Diffusion
Idea Generator vs discriminator game Encode to a latent distribution, then decode Learn to reverse gradual noising
Quality Sharp Blurrier State of the art (Stable Diffusion, Imagen)
Training Unstable, prone to mode collapse Stable (ELBO loss) Stable but slow to sample (many steps)
Latent space Implicit Smooth, interpretable Noise space; latent diffusion uses a VAE latent
  • Uses: GANs for super-resolution and style transfer; VAEs for anomaly detection and representation learning; diffusion for text-to-image, image editing and audio.

questions.q: How do you evaluate a generative model?
questions.a:
• Images:
  • FID: the distance between real and generated feature distributions. Lower is better.
  • Inception Score, precision/recall for generative models, and CLIP score for text-image alignment.
  • Text: task metrics (exact match, ROUGE), LLM-as-judge, human preference, and faithfulness for RAG.
  • Always include human evaluation on a sample, plus safety checks (toxicity, bias) and diversity versus quality trade-offs.

questions.q: Scenario: your model performs well offline but underperforms in production. What do you do?
questions.a:
1. Check the data first: a feature pipeline mismatch between training and serving (training-serving skew), missing features, or schema changes.
  2. Drift: compare production input distributions with training (PSI, KS test). Concept drift means the label relationship has changed.
  3. Evaluation flaws: leakage in the offline set, or a random split when it should have been time-based.
  4. Fix: retrain on recent data, add monitoring and alerts, run a shadow model, and roll back if needed.
  5. Prevent: a feature store, data contracts, and a scheduled re-evaluation.

questions.q: Design a system that generates personalised content (for example, marketing emails) for users.
questions.a:
• Inputs: a user profile and segment, recent behaviour, product catalogue and brand guidelines.
  • Pipeline: 1. A candidate generator: rules plus a recommender picks products and offers. 2. An LLM writes copy from a template prompt (tone, length, compliance rules), with structured output. 3. Guardrails: banned claims, PII, brand checks. 4. Human approval for new templates.
  • Scale: batch generation overnight and caching by segment; real-time generation only for high-value triggers.
  • Measure: an A/B test on open rate, click-through and conversion, plus unsubscribe rate as a guardrail.

questions.q: What architecture would you use for a real-time AI application?
questions.a:
• Event stream (Kafka or Kinesis) → stream processor (Flink or Spark Streaming) that computes features → online feature store (Redis) → model service (low-latency REST or gRPC, autoscaled) → decision / action.
  • Keep offline training consistent with the same feature definitions.
  • Latency budget: under 100 ms, using lightweight models, cached features and async logging.
  • Reliability: fallback rules if the model times out, canary deploys, and monitoring of latency and drift.

questions.q: Write a function that generates synthetic data from a given distribution.
questions.a:
import numpy as np

def synth(n, dist="normal", seed=42, **p):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if dist == "normal":  return rng.normal(p.get("mu", 0), p.get("sigma", 1), n)
    if dist == "poisson": return rng.poisson(p.get("lam", 3), n)
    if dist == "categorical":
        cats, probs = zip(*p["probs"].items()); return rng.choice(cats, size=n, p=probs)
    raise ValueError(dist)

print(synth(5, "categorical", probs={"A": .5, "B": .3, "C": .2}))
  • For realistic tabular synthetic data, mention SDV (CTGAN or Gaussian copula), keeping correlations, and privacy checks.

questions.q: Puzzle: measure exactly 4 litres using only a 3 L jug and a 5 L jug.
questions.a:
1. Fill the 5 L jug (5, 0).
  2. Pour into the 3 L jug until it is full → (2, 3).
  3. Empty the 3 L jug → (2, 0).
  4. Pour the 2 L into the 3 L jug → (0, 2).
  5. Fill the 5 L jug again → (5, 2).
  6. Pour from the 5 L into the 3 L until it is full (1 L moves) → (4, 3). Done: the 5 L jug holds 4 L. - Explain your reasoning out loud. Interviewers grade the process (states, constraints), not just the answer. Since gcd(3, 5) = 1, any whole number of litres up to 5 is reachable.

questions.q: Explain a CNN in the context of machine learning.
questions.a:
• Convolutional layers apply small learned filters across the image, detecting local patterns (edges → textures → parts → objects). Weight sharing means few parameters and translation equivariance.
  • Pooling downsamples for robustness; fully connected or global-pooling heads produce class scores.
  • Training: backprop with cross-entropy; data augmentation; transfer learning from pre-trained models (ResNet, EfficientNet).
  • Business use: shelf-image product recognition, defect detection, document classification.

questions.q: Scenario: a retail client's sales dropped in one region. How would you approach it?
questions.a:
• Clarify: which metric (revenue, units), which time frame, compared against what (last year, plan).
  • Break it down: stores (same-store vs new or closed), categories, traffic × conversion × basket size, channels.
  • Hypotheses: competitor opening, stock-outs, price changes, local events or weather, marketing changes.
  • Data and tests: compare with control regions (difference-in-differences), check inventory logs, analyse promotion calendars.
  • Recommend actions with the expected impact, and a monitoring plan.

questions.q: Tell me about the challenges in a past project.
questions.a:
Answer (STAR, 90 seconds):

  • "In my churn project, the challenge was that 40% of the usage data was missing for older customers."
  • "I investigated and found it was a logging change in 2023, so I created a flag feature and imputed using similar segments."
  • "Result: AUC improved from 0.71 to 0.78, and the client used the top-decile list for a retention campaign that reduced churn by 6% in that group."

questions.q: SQL: find the second-highest-selling product in each category.
questions.a:
SELECT category, product, units
FROM (
  SELECT category, product, SUM(units) AS units,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY SUM(units) DESC) AS rk
  FROM sales GROUP BY category, product
) t
WHERE rk = 2;

questions.q: Guesstimate: how many cups of tea are sold in Bengaluru per day?
questions.a:
Answer (structure):

  • Population about 1.4 crore; about 60% drink tea or coffee outside the home on a given day; about 50% of those choose tea, so about 42 lakh tea drinkers outside the home.
  • About 1.5 cups each → about 63 lakh cups a day (plus office pantries). Sanity-check: about 50,000 tea stalls × about 120 cups ≈ 60 lakh cups. That matches.
  • Clearly state the assumptions and adjust if the interviewer pushes back.

questions.q: Meesho DS2 case: design a product recommendation system for a value-commerce app.
questions.a:
• Users: many are first-time internet shoppers with sparse histories, so handle cold start with popularity by region and category, plus onboarding preferences.
  • Pipeline: 1. Candidate generation: item-to-item co-view/co-buy, two-tower embeddings, trending in the user's region and price band. 2. Ranking: a GBM or DNN predicts P(click), P(order) and P(return); combine into expected value = P(order) × margin × (1 − P(return)). 3. Re-ranking: diversity, seller fairness, price band, out-of-stock filtering.
  • Evaluation: offline recall@k and NDCG; online A/B on orders per user, GMV and return rate (a guardrail).
  • Serving: precompute candidates, run real-time ranking under 100 ms, refresh features hourly.

questions.q: What is the difference between LoRA and QLoRA?
questions.a:
• LoRA: freeze the base model and train low-rank adapters (ΔW = BA) on chosen layers. The base runs in FP16/BF16.
  • QLoRA: the same adapters, but the frozen base is quantized to 4-bit (NF4) with double quantization and paged optimisers. A 7–70B model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.
  • Trade-off: QLoRA uses far less memory and is slightly slower; quality is usually close to LoRA.

questions.q: PySpark: what is lazy evaluation, and what are left semi and left anti joins?
questions.a:
• Lazy evaluation: transformations (filter, select, join) build a logical plan. Nothing runs until an action (count, collect, write). That lets the Catalyst optimiser push down filters and combine stages.
  • Left semi join: returns the left rows that have a match (columns from the left only), like EXISTS.
  • Left anti join: returns the left rows with no match, like NOT EXISTS. Example: users who never ordered.
active = users.join(orders, "user_id", "left_semi")
never_ordered = users.join(orders, "user_id", "left_anti")

questions.q: Type I vs Type II error, and how power relates to the p-value threshold.
questions.a:
• Type I (α): a false positive, rejecting a true null hypothesis (shipping a feature that does nothing).
  • Type II (β): a false negative, missing a real effect. Power = 1 − β.
  • A lower α (stricter p-value threshold) lowers power, unless you increase the sample size. Power also rises with the effect size and lower variance.
  • Plan the sample size before the test, with α = 0.05 and power 0.8 as typical values.

questions.q: Myntra SQL: find the top 3 brands by revenue in each category, excluding returned orders.
questions.a:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.brand, SUM(oi.price * oi.qty) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id
  WHERE r.order_item_id IS NULL
  GROUP BY p.category, p.brand
)
SELECT category, brand, revenue
FROM (SELECT rev.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rk FROM rev) t
WHERE rk <= 3;

questions.q: Coding: the asteroid collision problem.
questions.a:
def asteroid_collision(a):
    st = []
    for x in a:
        while st and x < 0 < st[-1]:
            if st[-1] < -x: st.pop(); continue
            if st[-1] == -x: st.pop()
            break
        else:
            st.append(x)
    return st
print(asteroid_collision([5, 10, -5]))   # [5, 10]
  • Use a stack for asteroids moving right. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so it is O(n).

questions.q: How do you evaluate performance on each class in a multi-class problem?
questions.a:
• Confusion matrix (N×N), then per-class precision, recall, F1 (one-vs-rest).
  • Aggregate: macro-average (each class counts equally, which matters for rare diseases), weighted (by support), micro (overall, equal to accuracy for single-label problems).
  • Per-class ROC-AUC / PR-AUC, plus calibration per class.
  • In medical imaging, report sensitivity and specificity per condition with confidence intervals; clinically important misses get extra weight.

questions.q: Explain backpropagation.
questions.a:
• Forward pass: compute the activations layer by layer and the loss.
  • Backward pass: apply the chain rule from the loss backwards. For each layer, ∂L/∂W = (∂L/∂output) × (∂output/∂W), and the gradient passes to the previous layer via ∂L/∂input.
  • Frameworks build a computation graph and do this automatically (autograd). The optimiser then updates the weights.
  • Issues: vanishing or exploding gradients, solved with good initialisation, ReLU-family activations, normalisation, residual connections and gradient clipping.
questions.page: Novartis, GE HealthCare, Optum & IQVIA: Data Science

questions.q: How did you design your training dataset (GE HealthCare)?
questions.a:
• Representativeness: patients from several sites, scanners and vendors, demographics, disease severities. Avoid single-hospital bias.
  • Splits by patient (never by image) to prevent leakage; an external site as the test set.
  • Labels: expert annotation with an inter-rater agreement check (Cohen's κ); adjudicate disagreements.
  • Imbalance: stratify; oversample rare findings carefully; augmentation that is realistic for the modality.
  • Documentation: a datasheet covering source, inclusion criteria and known gaps, needed for regulatory submission.
questions.page: Novartis, GE HealthCare, Optum & IQVIA: Data Science

questions.q: IQVIA guesstimate: average daily income of an 8-lane toll plaza.
questions.a:
Answer (structure):

  • 8 lanes, so about 4 per direction. Peak throughput with FASTag is about 300 vehicles per lane per hour; the average over 24 hours is about 40% of peak, giving about 120 vehicles per lane per hour.
  • 8 × 120 × 24 ≈ 23,000 vehicles a day.
  • Mix: 70% cars at ₹100, 20% buses and trucks at ₹300, 10% heavy multi-axle at ₹500 → average ≈ 70 + 60 + 50 = ₹180.
  • Daily income ≈ 23,000 × ₹180 ≈ ₹41 lakh. Sanity-check against highway traffic and state your assumptions.

questions.q: Explain SQL join types with a healthcare example.
questions.a:
• patients(patient_id), claims(patient_id, amount):
  • INNER JOIN: patients with at least one claim.
  • LEFT JOIN: all patients, with NULL claim fields for those without claims (to find patients with no claims, add WHERE c.patient_id IS NULL).
  • RIGHT JOIN: all claims, even orphan ones (a data-quality check).
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: everything from both tables, for reconciliation.

questions.q: Novartis: how would you plan a data-science project from scratch?
questions.a:
1. Define: the business or clinical question, the stakeholders, the success metric, the constraints (privacy, timeline).
  2. Data: sources, access approvals, a quality assessment.
  3. Approach: baseline → model plan, with an evaluation design (including bias and fairness checks).
  4. Milestones: discovery (2 weeks), proof of concept (4 weeks), validation, deployment and monitoring. Assign owners and risks.
  5. Governance: documentation, review gates, reproducibility. - Use a simple plan (timeline + RACI) and agree checkpoints with stakeholders.
questions.page: Novartis, GE HealthCare, Optum & IQVIA: Data Science

questions.q: How would you deploy an AI agent using an MVC architecture?
questions.a:
• Model layer: domain data and state, meaning conversation and session state, a tool registry, and the persistence behind them (DB, vector store, checkpointer).
  • Controller: the API layer (FastAPI). It receives requests, authenticates, loads state, invokes the agent runtime (LangGraph or an agent executor), streams the result, and saves state.
  • View: the UI (React chat, Teams or Slack bot) rendering streamed tokens, tool-progress events and citations.
  • Agent runtime as a service: keep it stateless behind the controller. Tools call downstream APIs through adapters.
  • Deploy: containers on Kubernetes or Container Apps, autoscaled. Use Redis for session cache, queues for long tasks, and observability (traces per step).

questions.q: How does an agent connect to other components, and how do you manage caching?
questions.a:
• Connections: tools wrap internal APIs and databases (with typed schemas); MCP servers expose tools in a standard way; message queues hand off long-running work; webhooks deliver callbacks.
  • Caching layers:
  • LLM response / semantic cache: a hash or embedding of (prompt + context) → answer, with a TTL.
  • Tool-result cache: e.g. order status for 60 s.
  • Retrieval cache for frequent queries.
  • Provider prompt caching for long static system prompts.
  • Invalidation: TTLs plus event-based busting when the source data changes. Never cache per-user sensitive data across users.

questions.q: How do you choose an ML algorithm, and when should you avoid it?
questions.a:
Algorithm Use when Avoid when
Linear / logistic regression Need interpretability, linear-ish signal, a baseline Strong non-linear interactions
Decision tree / random forest Tabular data, mixed types, quick strong baseline Need smooth extrapolation; very high-dimensional sparse text
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) Best for tabular data Tiny data (overfits), strict latency on huge ensembles
KNN Small data, simple similarity Large n or high dimensions (slow, curse of dimensionality)
SVM Medium data, clear margins, text Very large datasets
Neural nets / Transformers Text, images, audio, lots of data Small tabular datasets, need full explainability
  • Always start with a simple baseline and let cross-validated metrics decide.

questions.q: Write a function to check for an Armstrong number.
questions.a:
def is_armstrong(n: int) -> bool:
    digits = str(n)
    k = len(digits)
    return n == sum(int(d) ** k for d in digits)

print([x for x in range(1, 1000) if is_armstrong(x)])  # 1..9, 153, 370, 371, 407
  • An Armstrong (narcissistic) number equals the sum of its digits, each raised to the power of the number of digits.

questions.q: How do you deploy an LLM application on AWS?
questions.a:
• Model: Amazon Bedrock (Claude, Llama, Titan) with IAM-scoped access, or SageMaker endpoints for self-hosted models.
  • Retrieval: Bedrock Knowledge Bases or OpenSearch Serverless (vector), with documents in S3.
  • App: FastAPI on ECS Fargate or Lambda behind API Gateway; Cognito for authentication.
  • Security and ops: Secrets Manager, a VPC with PrivateLink, Bedrock Guardrails, CloudWatch logs and metrics, cost alarms.
  • CI/CD: CodePipeline or GitHub Actions, with an evaluation gate before deploy.

questions.q: Which chunk size would you choose, and how do you decide?
questions.a:
• Typical range: 300–1,000 tokens with 10–20% overlap. Smaller chunks give precise retrieval but may lose context; larger chunks carry more context, add noise and cost more.
  • Decide with data: test 256 / 512 / 1,024 chunks on your evaluation set and compare recall@k, faithfulness and latency. Respect document structure (sections, tables).
  • Combine with metadata, re-ranking or parent-document retrieval to get both precision and context.

questions.q: Implement multi-head self-attention from scratch (PyTorch).
questions.a:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, math

class MHSA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, causal=False):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.h, self.dk, self.causal = n_heads, d_model // n_heads, causal
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model); self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
    def forward(self, x):                       # x: (B, T, C)
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=-1)
        q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v))   # (B,h,T,dk)
        att = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(self.dk)
        if self.causal:
            mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device), 1)
            att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        y = att.softmax(-1) @ v                 # (B,h,T,dk)
        return self.out(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C))
  • Discuss the O(T²) memory, FlashAttention (tiled, IO-aware, no T×T matrix in HBM), F.scaled_dot_product_attention, and GQA/MQA for a smaller KV cache.

questions.q: What is tensor parallelism, and how does it differ from data and pipeline parallelism?
questions.a:
• Data parallelism (DDP): each GPU holds a full model copy and processes a different batch; gradients are all-reduced. FSDP/ZeRO also shards the parameters, gradients and optimiser states.
  • Tensor parallelism (Megatron-LM): split individual weight matrices across GPUs.
  • For an MLP, split the first linear layer column-wise and the second row-wise, so only one all-reduce is needed per block.
  • Attention heads are split across GPUs.
  • It needs fast interconnect (NVLink), so it is usually used within a node.
  • Pipeline parallelism: split layers into stages across GPUs, with micro-batches to reduce "bubbles" (GPipe, 1F1B).
  • Sequence / context parallelism splits long sequences. Large LLM training combines all of these (3D/4D parallelism).

questions.q: Why do we need activation functions? Compare the common ones.
questions.a:
• Without non-linearity, stacked layers collapse into a single linear map, so activations give networks their expressive power.
  • Sigmoid/tanh: saturate and cause vanishing gradients; sigmoid is now mostly used for gates and outputs.
  • ReLU: cheap and non-saturating for x > 0, but can produce dead units.
  • GELU / SiLU (Swish): smooth, used in Transformers.
  • SwiGLU (gated) is used in modern LLMs (Llama) for better quality per FLOP.

questions.q: Which regularisation methods do you know for deep networks?
questions.a:
• Weight decay (L2; decoupled in AdamW), dropout, data augmentation (mixup, cutmix, random erasing), label smoothing, early stopping, stochastic depth.
  • Normalisation (batch/layer norm) has a regularising side effect.
  • For LLM fine-tuning: a low learning rate, LoRA, fewer epochs, mixing in general data.

questions.q: How do mixed precision (FP16/BF16/FP8) and gradient checkpointing help training?
questions.a:
• Mixed precision: compute in FP16/BF16 on Tensor Cores (2–4× faster, half the memory) with FP32 master weights.
  • FP16 needs loss scaling to avoid underflow.
  • BF16 has the FP32 exponent range, so it is more stable.
  • FP8 (Hopper/Blackwell, Transformer Engine) adds per-tensor scaling for further speed.
  • Gradient (activation) checkpointing: don't store all activations; recompute them in the backward pass. This trades about 30% extra compute for large memory savings, so you can use bigger batches or models.

questions.q: Recent Transformer advances: what changed after the original 2017 design?
questions.a:
• Pre-norm and RMSNorm for stability; RoPE positional encoding; SwiGLU feed-forward layers.
  • GQA/MQA for an efficient KV cache; FlashAttention kernels; sliding-window or sparse attention for long context.
  • Mixture-of-Experts (Mixtral, DeepSeek) for more parameters at a similar compute per token.
  • Inference: speculative decoding, paged KV cache (vLLM), quantization (FP8/INT4).
  • Training: scaling laws, better data mixtures, RLHF, DPO and RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning.

questions.q: Linear regression: define the cost function and derive the gradient-descent update.
questions.a:
• Model: ŷ = Xw + b. Cost (MSE): J(w, b) = (1/2n) Σ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)².
  • Gradients: ∂J/∂w = (1/n) Xᵀ(ŷ − y), ∂J/∂b = (1/n) Σ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ).
  • Update: w ← w − α ∂J/∂w; b ← b − α ∂J/∂b. Scale the features for faster convergence. The closed form is w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.

questions.q: CRED SQL (hard): find the top 5 product pairs most often bought together by the same user.
questions.a:
WITH up AS (                                   -- distinct user-product purchases
  SELECT DISTINCT p.user_id, pr.name
  FROM purchases p JOIN products pr ON pr.id = p.product_id
)
SELECT a.name AS product_1, b.name AS product_2, COUNT(*) AS together
FROM up a JOIN up b
  ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.name < b.name   -- each unordered pair once, alphabetical
GROUP BY a.name, b.name
ORDER BY together DESC, product_1, product_2
LIMIT 5;
  • At scale: the self-join explodes for heavy users, so cap the products per user, pre-aggregate, or approximate with sampling or MinHash. State the ordering convention the question asks for (this one wants the alphabetically first item listed second, so swap the output columns if needed).

questions.q: Product sense: how would you measure the success of CRED's rewards programme?
questions.a:
• North star: monthly active payers paying bills on time through CRED (core behaviour), plus retention.
  • Supporting metrics:
  • Reward redemption rate.
  • Repeat payments.
  • Payment value share.
  • Engagement with new features.
  • Referral rate.
  • Economics: reward cost per incremental active payer, LTV/CAC, and the margin from partners.
  • Guardrails: fraud and abuse rates, user complaints, payment failure rates.
  • Causality: holdout groups for reward changes; cohort analysis.

questions.q: How does Ola's surge pricing work conceptually, and how would you model it?
questions.a:
• Idea: when demand exceeds supply in a zone and time window, raise the price multiplier to reduce demand and attract drivers, restoring wait times.
  • Model: 1. Forecast demand and supply per zone for the next 15–30 minutes (gradient boosting or spatio-temporal models using events, weather, time). 2. Estimate demand elasticity to price. 3. Choose a multiplier that meets a target ETA or fulfilment rate, with caps and smoothing (no sudden jumps) and fairness constraints.
  • Evaluate: completed rides, ETA, cancellations, driver earnings, rider complaints; switchback experiments.

questions.q: Explain a tree-based algorithm you used: why random forest or XGBoost over logistic regression?
questions.a:
• Trees capture non-linearities and interactions automatically, handle mixed feature types and missing values (XGBoost), and need no scaling.
  • Logistic regression is more interpretable and well calibrated, and better with sparse high-dimensional text or very little data.
  • Choice: cross-validated performance plus the need for explainability. Use SHAP to explain the tree models.

questions.q: Describe hurdles you faced in a data project and how you overcame them.
questions.a:
• Data access delays: "I built the pipeline against a sample schema while approvals were pending, so I was ready on day 1 of access."
  • Unclear metric definitions: "I aligned with the PM on a written definition doc."
  • Model–business mismatch: "High AUC, but ops couldn't act on 30% of the flags. I retuned the threshold to the ops team's capacity."
  • Each hurdle should show proactiveness and measurable impact.

questions.q: Multi-part coding: simulate disease spread on a grid (an infected cell infects its neighbours each day). How long until everyone is infected?
questions.a:
from collections import deque
def days_to_infect(grid):          # 1 = infected, 0 = healthy, -1 = empty
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0]); q = deque(); healthy = 0
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            if grid[r][c] == 1: q.append((r, c, 0))
            elif grid[r][c] == 0: healthy += 1
    days = 0
    while q:
        r, c, d = q.popleft(); days = max(days, d)
        for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and grid[nr][nc] == 0:
                grid[nr][nc] = 1; healthy -= 1; q.append((nr, nc, d + 1))
    return days if healthy == 0 else -1
  • Multi-source BFS, O(R·C).
  • Typical follow-up parts: recovery after k days, immunity, probabilistic infection, very large sparse grids (use a hash set), tracking the per-day count. Write modular code so each new part is a small change.

questions.q: Longest substring without repeating characters.
questions.a:
def length_of_longest(s):
    pos, start, best = {}, 0, 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if pos.get(ch, -1) >= start: start = pos[ch] + 1
        pos[ch] = i; best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best
  • A sliding window, O(n). Explain it before coding, then test edge cases ("", "aaaa", "abba").

questions.q: Design Slack (real-time team messaging).
questions.a:
• Requirements: channels and DMs, message ordering, presence, notifications, search, files; millions of concurrent connections.
  • Architecture:
  • Clients ↔ WebSocket gateway fleet (connection state in Redis).
  • The message service writes to a partitioned store keyed by channel_id (Cassandra/Scylla, or sharded Postgres), with ordering by per-channel sequence IDs.
  • Fan-out through a pub/sub layer (Kafka plus in-memory channel subscriptions) to the gateways holding channel members.
  • Offline users: push notifications; unread counts per user per channel.
  • Search: async indexing into Elasticsearch with ACL filtering.
  • Scale and reliability: hot-channel handling (sharded fan-out), idempotent message IDs from clients, backpressure, multi-region with channel home regions.

questions.q: How would you design the serving layer for a large LLM API?
questions.a:
• The front door: API gateway → auth and rate limiting per organisation and tier (token buckets on requests and tokens).
  • Router: choose the model or deployment by capacity, region and priority; queue with fair scheduling.
  • Inference servers: continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching for shared system prompts, streaming via SSE.
  • Reliability: autoscaling on GPU queue depth, failover across clusters, graceful degradation (shed low-priority traffic).
  • Observability and billing: token metering, per-request traces, abuse and safety monitoring.

questions.q: Project deep dive: what do interviewers look for?
questions.a:
• Ownership: what you designed and decided, not the team.
  • Technical depth: why this architecture? What broke at scale? How did you measure it?
  • Trade-offs and mistakes: what you'd change now.
  • Impact: users, latency, cost, reliability numbers.
  • Prepare one project you can discuss for 45 minutes without running out of depth.

questions.q: Behavioural: tell me about a time you moved fast without breaking things.
questions.a:
Answer (STAR):

  • "We had to ship a streaming API in two weeks. I cut scope to the core path, wrote contract tests first, used a feature flag, and ran a 1% canary with automatic rollback on error-rate alerts. We launched on time with no incidents, then iterated on the deferred features."
  • OpenAI values speed with safety, clear communication and mission alignment.

questions.q: Check whether one string is a rotation of another.
questions.a:
def is_rotation(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    return len(a) == len(b) and b in (a + a)

print(is_rotation("waterbottle", "erbottlewat"))  # True
  • Every rotation of a is a substring of a + a. That is O(n) with KMP, and Python's in is efficient in practice.

questions.q: Check whether two binary trees are structurally identical (same shape and values).
questions.a:
def same_tree(p, q):
    if not p or not q: return p is q
    return p.val == q.val and same_tree(p.left, q.left) and same_tree(p.right, q.right)
  • O(n) time, O(h) recursion depth. For "structure only", drop the value comparison.

questions.q: SQL self-join: list employees alongside their manager's name.
questions.a:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id;
  • A self-join joins a table to itself with aliases. Use LEFT JOIN so the CEO (no manager) still appears. A follow-up asks for employees who earn more than their manager: add WHERE e.salary > m.salary.

questions.q: Salesforce: explain RAG and where it fits in a CRM.
questions.a:
• RAG grounds LLM answers in retrieved enterprise data, which reduces hallucination and keeps answers current.
  • CRM uses:
  • A service agent answers cases from knowledge articles and past resolutions.
  • Sales gets account summaries from opportunities, emails and calls.
  • Field-service troubleshooting.
  • Trust layer: respect record-level sharing rules at retrieval, mask PII before the LLM, apply zero-data-retention with the model provider, log audits, and filter toxicity. Cite the source records.

questions.q: How do you evaluate and monitor ML or LLM models in production?
questions.a:
• Online metrics: business KPIs (case deflection, conversion), user feedback, latency and error rates, cost per request.
  • Model health: input and output drift, prediction-distribution shifts, data-quality checks, performance on delayed labels.
  • LLM-specific: sampled LLM-judge scores (faithfulness, helpfulness), refusal and toxicity rates, prompt-injection attempts, retrieval hit rate.
  • Process: dashboards, alerts against SLOs, shadow and canary releases, periodic re-evaluation on a golden set, rollback plans.

questions.q: Oracle managerial: why do you want to switch companies?
questions.a:
• Stay positive and forward-looking: "I've built strong foundations in X at my current company. I'm looking for larger-scale AI problems, like the OCI GenAI services and AI features in Oracle Database (vector search, Select AI), where I can work closer to the platform."
  • Avoid criticising your current employer. Connect your skills to the team's work.
  • Have a clear expected salary range, based on research, ready.

questions.q: Build a regression model from raw data. Walk through the cleaning and modelling.
questions.a:
1. Understand the target and the grain (e.g. predict monthly merchant volume). Check duplicates, the date range and leakage.
  2. Clean: - Fix data types. - Handle missing values (median + indicator) and outliers (cap or log). - Encode categoricals. - Use time-aware splits.
  3. Baseline: last value or mean; then linear/Ridge regression; then gradient boosting.
  4. Evaluate: RMSE/MAE (and MAPE if the scale varies); residual plots; error by segment.
  5. Explain: coefficients or SHAP; document the assumptions.

questions.q: Design and analyse an A/B test for a new checkout flow.
questions.a:
• Hypothesis and metric: the primary metric is payment success rate; guardrails are latency, refunds and support tickets.
  • Sample size: from the baseline rate, the minimum detectable effect, α = 0.05 and power 0.8. Randomise by user (not session), run full weeks, and avoid peeking (or use sequential testing).
  • Analysis:
  • Two-proportion z-test or a bootstrap confidence interval.
  • Check for sample-ratio mismatch.
  • Segment checks (device, bank).
  • CUPED for variance reduction.
  • Decide: ship if the lift is significant and the guardrails hold. Report the effect size with its confidence interval.

questions.q: What does the Central Limit Theorem say, and why does it matter?
questions.a:
• For independent, identically distributed samples with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution N(μ, σ²/n) as n grows, regardless of the underlying distribution.
  • Why it matters: it justifies z/t tests and confidence intervals for means and proportions in A/B tests, even for skewed metrics such as revenue, given enough samples.
  • Caveats: heavy tails need larger n (or bootstrap / log transforms), and dependent samples break the assumption.

questions.q: z-test vs t-test: when do you use each?
questions.a:
• z-test: the population variance is known, or the sample is large (n > ~30, by the CLT). Proportions in large A/B tests use z-tests.
  • t-test: the variance is unknown and estimated from a small sample, using the t distribution with heavier tails. Use Welch's t-test when variances are unequal; use a paired t-test for before/after on the same units.

questions.q: SQL: compute monthly cohort retention for merchants.
questions.a:
WITH first_month AS (
  SELECT merchant_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(txn_date)) AS cohort
  FROM transactions GROUP BY merchant_id
), activity AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT merchant_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', txn_date) AS active_month FROM transactions
)
SELECT f.cohort,
       (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM a.active_month) - EXTRACT(YEAR FROM f.cohort)) * 12
         + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM a.active_month) - EXTRACT(MONTH FROM f.cohort) AS month_n,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.merchant_id) AS active
FROM first_month f JOIN activity a USING (merchant_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
  • Divide by the cohort size at month 0 to get retention percentages, and plot them as a heatmap.

questions.q: PayPal: how would you use RAG to help fraud investigators?
questions.a:
• Corpus: fraud playbooks, past case notes, policy rules, typology write-ups.
  • Assistant flow: 1. The investigator opens a case. 2. The system retrieves similar past cases (embedding similarity over case summaries) and the relevant playbook steps. 3. The LLM drafts a case summary, a suggested next action and the evidence checklist, with citations.
  • Controls:
  • The LLM never decides alone; the human investigator approves.
  • PII is minimised; access is role-based.
  • Audit logs.
  • An evaluation of summary faithfulness and time-to-resolution.

questions.q: What is a genetic algorithm? Where might it be used?
questions.a:
• An evolutionary optimisation method: 1. Keep a population of candidate solutions. 2. Evaluate their fitness. 3. Select the best, apply crossover (combine parents) and mutation (random changes). 4. Repeat for many generations.
  • Good for non-differentiable, combinatorial search: feature selection, hyperparameter search, scheduling, routing.
  • Trade-offs: no gradient needed, but slow and stochastic. Alternatives are Bayesian optimisation or simulated annealing.

questions.q: RCA: UPI payment success rate dropped from 97% to 94% yesterday. How do you investigate?
questions.a:
1. Validate: a logging or definition change? A partial-day effect? Compare with the same weekday last week.
  2. Segment the drop: - Bank (issuer or remitter): one bank's server down? - PSP/app version, OS, merchant category, transaction type (P2P vs P2M), amount band, geography, hour.
  3. Error codes: timeouts vs declines vs "insufficient funds" (user behaviour) vs technical failures.
  4. External events: NPCI incidents, bank maintenance windows, festivals with traffic spikes.
  5. Quantify each contributor (contribution to the delta), then recommend: route around a failing bank, alert the partner, add retries, fix the app bug.
  6. Prevent: anomaly alerts by bank and error code.

users(user_id PK, name, phone UNIQUE, email, city, created_at)

questions.q: SQL: find users whose number of transactions dropped more than 50% month over month.
questions.a:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', txn_time) AS mon, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM txns GROUP BY 1, 2
), w AS (
  SELECT user_id, mon, n, LAG(n) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY mon) AS prev_n FROM m
)
SELECT user_id, mon, prev_n, n
FROM w WHERE prev_n IS NOT NULL AND n < 0.5 * prev_n;
  • Note that users with zero transactions in a month have no row, so join to a calendar (or user × month grid) to catch full drop-offs.

questions.q: Case: how would you measure the success of a new cashback campaign?
questions.a:
• Goal: incremental transactions or users, not just total redemptions.
  • Design: a randomised holdout (or geo test); a primary metric (incremental transacting users, GMV); guardrails (cost per incremental user, fraud/abuse, post-campaign retention).
  • Analysis: lift vs holdout with confidence intervals; ROI = incremental margin − cashback cost; check cannibalisation and pull-forward effects; segment by new vs existing users.
  • Recommendation: continue for the segments with positive ROI and stop elsewhere.

questions.q: How would you detect fraud or abuse in a cashback or referral programme?
questions.a:
• Signals:
  • Many accounts on one device.
  • Shared bank accounts or UPI handles.
  • Rapid sign-up → redeem → dormant patterns.
  • Circular P2P transfers.
  • Emulator or rooted-device flags.
  • Methods: rules for known patterns, a graph (connected components on device/bank/phone links), anomaly scores, and a supervised model once labels exist.
  • Actions: hold rewards for review, set velocity limits, require KYC for higher tiers. Track the false-positive impact on genuine users.

questions.q: Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and between INNER and LEFT JOIN with a filter.
questions.a:
• WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).
  • Pitfall: LEFT JOIN b ... WHERE b.col = 'x' turns it into an inner join (rows with NULLs are dropped). Put the condition in the ON clause to keep the unmatched left rows.

questions.q: Case study: build an AI app on open-source LLM endpoints. How would you structure it?
questions.a:
• Scope: for example, "a product-FAQ assistant for a retail client". Define 20 test questions first.
  • Stack:
  • An open model through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, TGI or a provider).
  • bge-small embeddings and FAISS/Chroma.
  • LangChain LCEL.
  • FastAPI + a simple Streamlit/Gradio UI.
from openai import OpenAI          # works with OpenAI-compatible open-model servers
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="not-needed")
def answer(q, ctx):
    msg = [{"role": "system", "content": "Answer only from the context; cite [n]."},
           {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{ctx}\n\nQuestion: {q}"}]
    return client.chat.completions.create(model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", messages=msg, temperature=0).choices[0].message.content
  • Deliverables: a README (architecture, how to run), an evaluation table (accuracy or faithfulness on the 20 questions), the known limitations, and next steps (re-ranker, guardrails).

questions.q: Why use open-source LLM endpoints instead of a proprietary API?
questions.a:
• For: data control and on-premises deployment, no per-token vendor lock-in, fine-tuning freedom, predictable cost at scale, and region or regulatory compliance.
  • Against: lower quality on hard reasoning tasks, ops burden (GPUs, scaling, updates), and safety tuning is your responsibility.
  • Pattern: prototype on both, compare on your evaluation set, and choose by quality, cost and latency. A router can mix them: open models for simple queries, a frontier API for hard ones.

questions.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off and how you tune it.
questions.a:
• High bias (underfit): the model is too simple. Add features, use a more flexible model, reduce regularisation.
  • High variance (overfit): the model is too complex for the data. Get more data, add regularisation or dropout, simplify, use bagging or early stopping.
  • Tune with validation curves (vary complexity) and learning curves (vary data size), using cross-validation.

from collections import Counter

def first_unique(s):
    c = Counter(s)
    return next((ch for ch in s if c[ch] == 1), None)

print(first_unique("swiss"))  # w

questions.a:
• Start with the decision and the impact: "The model flags 8% of orders as high-risk and catches 70% of fraud, saving about ₹40 lakh a month."

questions.q: Derive the gradient descent update rule, including the learning rate.
questions.a:
• Minimise the loss L(θ). A first-order Taylor expansion gives L(θ + Δ) ≈ L(θ) + ∇L(θ)ᵀΔ.
  • To decrease L fastest for a small step of fixed size, choose Δ in the direction opposite to the gradient: Δ = −η ∇L(θ).
  • Update: θₜ₊₁ = θₜ − η ∇L(θₜ), where the learning rate η controls the step size. Too large and it diverges or oscillates; too small and it is slow.
  • Example (MSE linear regression): L = (1/n)‖Xw − y‖² gives ∇L = (2/n)Xᵀ(Xw − y), so w ← w − η (2/n)Xᵀ(Xw − y).
  • Convergence: for an L-smooth convex function, η ≤ 1/L guarantees a decrease.
