questions.q: Implement PCA without libraries (NumPy only).
questions.a:
import numpy as np

def pca(X, k):
    Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)                     # 1. centre
    C = Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - 1)                # 2. covariance (d x d)
    vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)              # 3. eigen-decomposition (symmetric)
    order = np.argsort(vals)[::-1][:k]          # 4. top-k by variance
    W = vecs[:, order]
    return Xc @ W, vals[order] / vals.sum()     # projected data, explained-variance ratio
  • By hand: centre → covariance → eigenvalues and eigenvectors → sort → project. Using the SVD of Xc is numerically more stable.

questions.q: Why normalise inputs, and which activation functions would you use where?
questions.a:
• Normalisation (standardise or min-max): puts features on similar scales, so gradient descent converges faster (a rounder loss surface), distance-based models work, and regularisation treats features fairly. Inside networks, Batch or Layer Norm stabilise training.
  • Activations:
  • ReLU: simple, no saturation for positive values, but can produce "dead" neurons.
  • Leaky ReLU / GELU / SiLU: smooth, standard in Transformers.
  • Sigmoid: binary output probabilities.
  • Softmax: multi-class output.
  • tanh: zero-centred, used in older RNNs.

questions.q: Probability: two dice are rolled. What is P(sum = 7 | at least one die shows 3)?
questions.a:
• Outcomes with at least one 3: 6 + 6 − 1 = 11.
  • Of those, the sum is 7 for (3,4) and (4,3): 2.
  • P = 2/11 ≈ 0.18.
  • Method: count the conditioning event first, then the favourable outcomes inside it. Bayes' rule P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = (2/36)/(11/36).

questions.q: What are multiple attention heads and why use them?
questions.a:
• Split d_model into h heads of size d_k = d_model/h. Each head has its own W_Q, W_K, W_V and computes attention in parallel. The outputs are concatenated and projected with W_O.
  • Why: different heads learn different relationships (syntax, coreference, position, delimiters) at the same compute cost as a single full-width head.
  • Variants: Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention (MQA / GQA) share K and V across heads, which shrinks the KV cache and speeds up inference (used in Llama 2/3 and Mistral).

questions.q: What are the main limitations of LLMs, and how do you reduce hallucination?

  • Knowledge cutoff.

questions.q: Token limits: a document is longer than the context window. What chunking and retrieval strategies would you use?
questions.a:
• Chunking:
  • Recursive or structure-aware (headings, sections) at 300–1,000 tokens with 10–20% overlap.
  • Semantic chunking: split where embedding similarity drops.
  • Keep tables intact.
  • Hierarchical / parent-child: retrieve small chunks for precision, but send the parent section to the LLM for context.
  • Summaries: map-reduce or refine summarisation for "summarise the whole document"; a RAPTOR-style tree of summaries.
  • Long-context models: even with 128k–1M tokens, retrieval is cheaper and often more accurate. Put key context at the start or end of the prompt.

questions.q: Multithreading vs multiprocessing in Python: which would you use for an LLM pipeline?
questions.a:
• GIL: in CPython only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time.
  • I/O-bound work (calling LLM APIs, vector-DB queries, HTTP): use threads or better asyncio (asyncio.gather), which releases the GIL while waiting. This gives large speedups for parallel API calls.
  • CPU-bound work (parsing PDFs, tokenising, local embeddings on CPU): use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor, which bypasses the GIL across processes.
  • Example: embed 10k documents through an API with asyncio, a semaphore (rate limit) and retries; parse PDFs with a process pool.

questions.q: DL system design: how would you deploy a deep-learning model at scale?

  • Reliability: canary releases, health checks, timeouts, fallback to a smaller model.
  • Monitoring: latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput, GPU memory, drift in inputs and outputs, and cost per 1,000 requests.

questions.q: What is the difference between k-fold and stratified k-fold cross-validation?
questions.a:
• K-fold: split the data into k equal folds; train on k−1 and validate on the remaining one, rotating through all k.
  • Stratified k-fold: each fold keeps the same class proportions as the full dataset. This is essential for imbalanced classification, otherwise some folds may have very few positives.
  • Others: GroupKFold (no leakage across users or patients) and TimeSeriesSplit (forward-chaining) for temporal data.

questions.q: Bagging vs boosting: how do they differ?
questions.a:
• Bagging (random forest): trains many models in parallel on bootstrap samples (plus feature subsampling) and averages them. It reduces variance and is robust and hard to overfit.
  • Boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost): trains models sequentially, each fixing the previous errors (fitting gradients of the loss). It reduces bias, is often more accurate on tabular data, but needs tuning (learning rate, depth, early stopping) and can overfit noise.

questions.q: Case: how would you predict customer churn from a dataset? Walk through end to end.
questions.a:
1. Frame it: what counts as churn (no purchase in 60 days? contract cancelled?), the prediction horizon, the intervention budget, and the success metric (retained revenue).
  2. EDA: churn rate, cohorts, tenure curves, usage trends, complaints, price changes. Check for leakage (cancellation-request fields).
  3. Features: recency/frequency/monetary (RFM), usage deltas, support tickets, plan changes, payment failures.
  4. Model: logistic baseline → gradient boosting; time-based validation; PR-AUC and lift@top-10%; calibrate.
  5. Interpret: SHAP drivers; segment personas.
  6. Act: target by uplift (who will respond to an offer), not just risk; run a controlled experiment; monitor.

questions.q: Average comments per user dropped 10% last month. How would you investigate?
questions.a:
• Is it real? Check logging and instrumentation changes, bots or spam filters, and the definition (active users vs all users).
  • Decompose: comments per user = (comments / active commenters) × (commenters / users). Which part dropped?
  • Segment: platform (iOS/Android/web), region, new vs existing users, content type, app version.
  • Look for causes: a product change (comment-box UI, ranking), seasonality, an influx of new users (mix shift), an outage, competitor events.
  • Confirm with an experiment or a natural comparison, quantify the impact, and recommend a fix.

questions.q: How would you troubleshoot an API that returns HTTP 500 errors?
questions.a:
• A 500 is a server-side error. Read the server logs and stack traces for the failing requests and correlate them with timestamps and request IDs.
  • Reproduce with the same payload (curl/Postman), then check recent deploys, config or secret changes, and dependency health (DB, downstream APIs, model endpoint: timeouts, OOM).
  • Check inputs: unexpected nulls or types that crash the handler. Add validation that returns a 4xx instead.
  • Mitigate (roll back, or scale up if the cause is resource exhaustion), fix the root cause, and add alerts and tests.

questions.q: How do you handle multicollinearity in regression?
questions.a:
• Detect: a correlation matrix, VIF above 5–10, and unstable coefficients that flip sign.
  • Effects: inflated variances, so the coefficients become uninterpretable. Predictions may still be fine.
  • Fix:
  • Drop or combine correlated features.
  • Use domain-driven feature selection.
  • Ridge regularisation.
  • PCA (at the cost of interpretability).
  • Centre interaction terms.

questions.q: Samsung-style DP: what is the minimum cost path in a grid (moves right or down)?
questions.a:
def min_path(grid):
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0]); dp = [0] * C
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            if r == 0 and c == 0: dp[c] = grid[0][0]
            elif r == 0: dp[c] = dp[c-1] + grid[r][c]
            elif c == 0: dp[c] = dp[c] + grid[r][c]
            else: dp[c] = min(dp[c], dp[c-1]) + grid[r][c]
    return dp[-1]
  • O(R·C) time and O(C) space with a rolling array. For four-direction moves with non-negative weights, switch to Dijkstra.

questions.q: Graph: count the number of islands (connected components) in a grid.
questions.a:
def islands(g):
    R, C = len(g), len(g[0]); seen = set(); n = 0
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            if g[r][c] == 1 and (r, c) not in seen:
                n += 1; stack = [(r, c)]; seen.add((r, c))
                while stack:
                    x, y = stack.pop()
                    for dx, dy in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
                        a, b = x + dx, y + dy
                        if 0 <= a < R and 0 <= b < C and g[a][b] == 1 and (a, b) not in seen:
                            seen.add((a, b)); stack.append((a, b))
    return n

questions.q: Micron networking: what happens when you type a URL into the browser?
questions.a:
1. DNS resolution (browser cache → OS → resolver → root/TLD/authoritative servers) gives the IP address.
  2. TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), then the TLS handshake for HTTPS (certificate check, key exchange).
  3. HTTP request → server (load balancer → web server/app) → response.
  4. The browser parses HTML, fetches CSS/JS/images (more requests, often HTTP/2 multiplexed), and renders. - Know the OSI/TCP-IP layers, TCP vs UDP, ports, and what a subnet mask is.

questions.q: TCP vs UDP: when would an ML system use each?
questions.a:
• TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-based (handshake, retransmission, congestion control). Used for APIs, model serving (HTTP/gRPC) and database connections.
  • UDP: connectionless with no delivery guarantee, lower latency. Used for real-time video and audio, telemetry streams, DNS, QUIC (HTTP/3 builds reliability on top of UDP).
  • Example: factory sensor telemetry might use UDP or MQTT for speed; model inference APIs use TCP.

questions.q: ServiceNow coding: choose stocks to maximise profit within a budget (each stock has a cost and an expected profit).
questions.a:
def max_profit(costs, profits, budget):          # 0/1 knapsack
    dp = [0] * (budget + 1)
    for c, p in zip(costs, profits):
        for b in range(budget, c - 1, -1):
            dp[b] = max(dp[b], dp[b - c] + p)
    return dp[budget]
print(max_profit([5, 4, 6, 3], [10, 40, 30, 50], 10))   # 90
  • This is 0/1 knapsack: O(n·B) time, O(B) space. If the problem is instead "buy and sell one stock over time", it is a single pass tracking the minimum price.
  • Clarify assumptions first (integer costs? one share each?). The candidate's frustration came from mismatched assumptions.

questions.q: Explain XGBoost and how it works.
questions.a:
• Gradient-boosted decision trees: add trees sequentially, each fitting the gradient (and Hessian) of the loss with respect to the current predictions, using a second-order Taylor approximation.
  • Regularised objective: loss + γ·(number of leaves) + ½λ‖leaf weights‖², giving the optimal leaf weight −G/(H + λ) and a split gain formula.
  • Engineering: histogram/approximate split finding, sparsity-aware missing-value handling (a learned default direction), column and row subsampling, shrinkage (η), parallel tree building, early stopping.
  • Key hyperparameters: max_depth, eta, n_estimators, subsample, colsample_bytree, min_child_weight, lambda/alpha, scale_pos_weight.

HAVING SUM(sales) > 1000000;            -- filters groups after aggregation

questions.q: Recommend exactly one song per user per day. How would you design it?
questions.a:
• One slot means very high precision. Optimise for P(listen > 30 s) × P(save/like), with diversity across days.
  • Candidates: collaborative filtering (user–track embeddings), content audio embeddings, the user's recent genres, new releases from followed artists, and exploration.
  • Ranker: a multi-objective model with features such as user taste vectors, time of day, context (workout, commute), track freshness and popularity.
  • Exploration: a bandit (Thompson sampling) to learn from feedback and avoid repetitive picks; never repeat a recently skipped track.
  • Evaluation: offline replay on logged data (counterfactual); online A/B on listen-through, saves and long-term retention.

questions.q: Build a data pipeline that ranks the most popular artists in each country daily.
questions.a:
• Ingest: stream events (play, skip, duration, country, artist_id) → Kafka → a raw table partitioned by date.
  • Daily batch (Spark or SQL):
WITH plays AS (
  SELECT country, artist_id, COUNT(*) AS streams, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS listeners
  FROM play_events
  WHERE event_date = DATE '2025-04-01' AND ms_played >= 30000      -- count qualified streams
  GROUP BY country, artist_id
)
SELECT country, artist_id, streams, listeners,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY listeners DESC, streams DESC) AS rk
FROM plays QUALIFY rk <= 50;
  • Quality: deduplicate events, filter bots and fraud (stream farming), handle late data, data quality checks (volume anomalies).
  • Serve: write to a table and a cache for the "Top Artists" API; backfill and an idempotent rerun strategy.

questions.q: Forecast monthly active users (MAU).
questions.a:
• Decompose: MAU = retained users + new users + resurrected users, and forecast each with cohort retention curves and acquisition drivers (marketing spend, seasonality, market launches).
  • Models: cohort-based survival curves plus a time-series model (Prophet or ARIMA) for new users; scenario inputs for planned launches.
  • Validate: backtest; provide intervals; explain the drivers to finance and product.

questions.q: Design the backend that serves an ML recommendation model.
questions.a:
• Offline: train embeddings and candidate indexes daily; push to a model registry and an ANN index (e.g. ScaNN/FAISS).
  • Online request: API → fetch user features (feature store) → candidate retrieval (ANN) → ranking model service (batching, GPU or CPU) → business rules → response, all under 100 ms.
  • Caching: precompute recommendations for most users, compute in real time only on context change.
  • Reliability: fallbacks (popular items), timeouts, canaries; logging impressions for training and evaluation.

questions.q: Netflix: how do you evaluate a recommender beyond accuracy?
questions.a:
• Online: long-term engagement (hours viewed, retention, churn reduction), not just clicks.
  • Offline: NDCG and recall, plus diversity, novelty, coverage (long-tail exposure) and calibration to the user's taste mix.
  • Interleaving experiments are more sensitive than A/B for ranking comparisons.
  • Guardrails: no over-concentration on a few titles, fairness to new content.

questions.q: Coding (medium): design a hit counter for the last 5 minutes.
questions.a:
from collections import deque
class HitCounter:
    def __init__(self, window=300): self.q, self.w = deque(), window
    def hit(self, t): self.q.append(t)
    def get_hits(self, t):
        while self.q and self.q[0] <= t - self.w: self.q.popleft()
        return len(self.q)
  • For high volume, use 300 buckets of (timestamp, count) in a circular array, which needs O(1) memory per second.

questions.q: Design an autocomplete for Swiggy search (restaurants and dishes).
questions.a:
• Data structure: a trie of normalised queries, where each node stores the top-k completions by popularity. Lookup is O(prefix length).
  • Ranking signals: global popularity, location (only serviceable restaurants nearby), time of day, the user's history, open/closed status, freshness of trends.
  • Robustness: typo tolerance (edit distance or n-gram index), transliteration ("paneer" vs "panir"), synonyms ("biryani" ≈ "biriyani").
  • Serving: precomputed top-k per prefix per city in Redis; a latency budget under 50 ms; update the counts in near real time from logs.
  • Evaluation: keystrokes saved, CTR on suggestions, search-to-order conversion; A/B test ranking changes.

questions.q: Explain L1 vs L2 regularisation and when to use each.
questions.a:
• L2 (Ridge): penalty λΣw². Shrinks weights smoothly and handles correlated features. The usual default.
  • L1 (Lasso): penalty λΣ|w|. Produces sparse weights (feature selection), good with many irrelevant features.
  • Elastic Net mixes both. In neural networks, weight decay (L2) plus dropout.
  • Tune λ by cross-validation and standardise features first.

questions.q: How would you predict food delivery time (ETA)?
questions.a:
• Decompose: preparation time + rider assignment wait + rider to restaurant + restaurant to customer.
  • Features:
  • Restaurant prep history by dish and time of day.
  • Current kitchen load.
  • Rider availability.
  • Distance and road-graph ETA.
  • Traffic, weather, rain flags.
  • Festival days.
  • Model: gradient boosting per component, or one model with quantile loss. Predict P50 and P90 so you can promise conservatively.
  • Metrics: MAE, plus the share of orders delivered later than promised (customer trust). Monitor by city and zone; retrain often.

questions.q: SQL: find each customer's most frequently ordered cuisine.

WITH c AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, r.cuisine, COUNT(*) AS n,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rk
  FROM orders o JOIN restaurants r ON r.restaurant_id = o.restaurant_id
  GROUP BY o.customer_id, r.cuisine
)
SELECT customer_id, cuisine, n FROM c WHERE rk = 1;
  • A window function over an aggregate works in a single CTE. RANK keeps ties; use ROW_NUMBER to pick exactly one.

questions.q: How would you identify genuine customers vs fake or abusive accounts on a dine-in offer?

• Signals: device and payment reuse across accounts, new accounts that redeem immediately, mismatches between location and restaurant, repeated maximum-discount bills, reviews posted only by linked accounts.
  • Methods: velocity rules, a graph of shared identifiers (connected components), an anomaly score, then a supervised model once labels exist.
  • Action: limit offers for risky clusters and require verification. Measure the false-positive impact on genuine users.

def top_dishes(orders, k=3):

questions.q: How would you forecast weekly demand for thousands of SKUs across stores?
questions.a:
• Hierarchy: SKU × store × week, with reconciliation across levels (store → region; SKU → category).
  • Features: lags, rolling means, seasonality, holidays and events, price and promotions, weather, stock-outs (to correct censored demand), new-store flags.
  • Models: a global LightGBM across series (scales well), or deep models (TFT) for rich covariates; baselines are seasonal naïve and ETS.
  • Validation: rolling-origin backtests; metrics WAPE and bias; error by velocity segment (fast vs slow movers).
  • Ops: weekly retraining, monitoring, and planner overrides with a feedback loop.

questions.q: MLOps: how do you take a model from notebook to production reliably?
questions.a:
• Code: modular packages, config files, unit tests; data validation (Great Expectations / pandera).
  • Tracking and registry: MLflow for experiments; a model registry with stages and approvals.
  • Pipelines: orchestrated training and batch scoring (Airflow, Kubeflow, Databricks Jobs); a feature store for consistency.
  • Deployment: batch (scheduled) or real-time (a container + autoscaling); CI/CD with an evaluation gate.
  • Monitoring: data and prediction drift, performance on delayed labels, latency and cost; automatic alerts and retraining triggers.

questions.q: Spark architecture: driver, executors, and what happens on a shuffle?
questions.a:
• Driver: builds the DAG from transformations, the Catalyst optimiser plans stages, and the scheduler assigns tasks to executors (JVMs on worker nodes) that process partitions in parallel.
  • Narrow transformations (map, filter) stay within a partition; wide ones (groupBy, join) trigger a shuffle: data is redistributed across the network by key, which is expensive.
  • Optimise: broadcast small tables, filter early, choose partition counts sensibly, handle skew (salting, AQE skew-join), cache reused DataFrames.

questions.q: Data lake vs data warehouse vs lakehouse.
questions.a:
• Data lake: cheap object storage of raw files in any format (schema-on-read). Flexible, but it can become a "swamp" without governance.
  • Warehouse: structured, schema-on-write, fast SQL, strong governance; more costly and less flexible for ML.
  • Lakehouse: open table formats (Delta / Iceberg / Hudi) on a lake add ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel and fast SQL, so BI and ML work on one copy of the data.

questions.q: Explain join types on a sample table, and a common pitfall.
questions.a:
• orders(customer_id) vs customers(customer_id): INNER (customers with orders), LEFT (all orders, plus customer info where it exists), RIGHT, FULL OUTER (reconciliation).
  • Pitfall: duplicate keys on both sides multiply rows (a many-to-many explosion). Check key uniqueness before joining, and deduplicate or aggregate first.

questions.q: Python: flatten a nested list and remove duplicates while keeping order.
questions.a:
def flatten(xs):
    for x in xs:
        if isinstance(x, list): yield from flatten(x)
        else: yield x
print(list(dict.fromkeys(flatten([1, [2, [3, 1]], 4, [2]]))))   # [1, 2, 3, 4]

questions.q: How did you implement AI in your project? Walk through the pipeline.
questions.a:
• Business problem → data → model → serving → monitoring.
  • Example: "An email-triage assistant for a telecom client.
  • Emails go through PII masking and are then classified into 12 intents by a fine-tuned DistilBERT.
  • For complex cases, a GPT-4o-mini RAG step drafts a reply from the knowledge base.
  • The service runs on FastAPI in Azure App Service and is monitored with Application Insights.
  • Outcome: 38% fewer manual touches and 2 minutes saved per email."
  • Always say why each component was chosen and what you measured.

questions.q: Explain the Transformer architecture briefly.
questions.a:
• Embeddings: tokens become embeddings, and positional encodings are added.
  • N blocks, each containing multi-head self-attention (softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V) and a feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer norm around both.
  • Variants: encoders (BERT) understand text, decoders (GPT) generate it with a causal mask, and encoder-decoders (T5) translate or summarise.
  • Why it is powerful: parallel training, long-range context, and it scales to LLMs.

questions.q: Client round: which cloud services would you use to deploy a GenAI app on Azure?
questions.a:
• Models: Azure OpenAI (private endpoint) or Azure AI Foundry for open models.
  • Retrieval: Azure AI Search (hybrid + semantic ranker), with Blob Storage for documents.
  • Compute: Azure Container Apps, AKS or App Service running FastAPI; Functions for ingestion jobs.
  • Security: Entra ID authentication, Key Vault for secrets, VNet with private endpoints, and Content Safety filters.
  • Operations: Application Insights / Azure Monitor, plus a CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions.
  • On AWS: Bedrock, OpenSearch, ECS or Lambda, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch.

questions.q: Python: return all primes up to n.
questions.a:
def primes_upto(n):
    if n < 2: return []
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1); sieve[0] = sieve[1] = False
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i*i::i] = [False] * len(sieve[i*i::i])
    return [i for i, p in enumerate(sieve) if p]
  • The Sieve of Eratosthenes runs in O(n log log n). Return an empty list when n < 2.

questions.q: How would you predict customer churn for a telecom client?
questions.a:
• Label: the customer churned within the next 30 or 60 days.
  • Features: tenure, plan, ARPU trend, data usage drop, complaints and support calls, payment delays, network quality in the customer's area.
  • Model: a gradient-boosted tree with time-based validation, judged on PR-AUC, and lift in the top decile.
  • Action: give retention offers to the high-risk, high-value segment; measure uplift with a control group, not just accuracy.
  • Explain the drivers with SHAP for the business team.

questions.q: How do you clean missing values in a dataset?
questions.a:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
print(df.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False))            # missing ratio
df["income_missing"] = df["income"].isna().astype(int)          # keep the signal
df["income"] = df["income"].fillna(df["income"].median())
df["city"] = df["city"].fillna("Unknown")
df = df.dropna(subset=["customer_id"])                          # critical key
  • Strategy: understand why values are missing (completely at random, at random, or not at random). Drop a column if more than ~60% is missing and it isn't useful. Impute with median or mode, or use model-based imputation (KNN, iterative). Fit imputers on the training data only.

questions.q: What is the difference between top-k and top-p sampling? Where does temperature fit?
questions.a:
• Temperature scales the logits before softmax. Low values (0 to 0.3) make output deterministic and focused; high values (above 0.8) make it more creative and random.
  • Top-k: sample only from the k most likely tokens, for example k=40. It is a fixed-size cut regardless of how confident the model is.
  • Top-p (nucleus): sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, for example 0.9. The set adapts: small when the model is confident, large when it isn't.
  • In practice:
  • Extraction, SQL or JSON: temperature 0.
  • Chat: temperature around 0.7 with top-p 0.9.
  • Avoid tuning top-k and top-p heavily at the same time.

questions.q: How do you approach prompt design for an enterprise use case?
questions.a:
1. Define the task and success metric with the business, and collect 30 to 50 real examples.
  2. Structure the prompt: - A role - The task - The context in delimiters - Rules (cite sources, never invent numbers) - The output format, as a JSON schema - 2 or 3 few-shot examples
  3. Iterate against an evaluation set, not by eye. Version prompts in git.
  4. Add guardrails: PII masking, refusal rules, a check on maximum length.
  5. Optimise cost: a shorter system prompt, prompt caching, a smaller model where it is good enough.

questions.q: What are the components of a RAG system, including data ingestion?
questions.a:
• Ingestion:
  • Connectors (SharePoint, S3, databases)
  • Parsing (PDF, tables, OCR)
  • Cleaning and deduplication
  • Chunking with metadata
  • Embedding
  • Indexing
  • A scheduled or incremental refresh
  • Retrieval: query understanding or rewriting → hybrid search → filters → re-ranker.
  • Generation: prompt assembly, the LLM, citations, and output validation.
  • Platform: access control, caching, monitoring, an evaluation harness, and a feedback loop.

questions.q: What ethical risks do LLMs carry, and how would you test for bias?
questions.a:
• Risks:
  • Hallucination
  • Bias and unfair outcomes
  • Toxic content
  • Privacy leaks (PII in training data or prompts)
  • Copyright
  • Over-reliance by users
  • Prompt injection
  • Testing for bias:
  • Build counterfactual pairs: the same input with only a protected attribute changed (name, gender, region), then compare outputs and scores.
  • Measure differences in refusal or approval rates and in sentiment.
  • Use benchmarks such as BBQ or StereoSet for a general check.
  • Mitigations:
  • Remove protected attributes from decision prompts.
  • Add policy prompts and output filters.
  • Keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions.
  • Document everything in a model card, and audit regularly.

questions.q: Design a system that summarises thousands of call transcripts every day.
questions.a:
• Ingestion: audio → speech-to-text (Whisper or Azure Speech with speaker diarisation) → transcript stored with call metadata.
  • Processing: a queue (Kafka or Service Bus) feeding workers. Long calls use map-reduce: summarise chunks, then combine. A JSON schema captures the summary, intent, sentiment, action items and compliance flags.
  • Model choice: a small, cheap model for most calls; a large model for escalations. Use the batch API for overnight jobs, which costs about 50% less.
  • Quality: a sampled human review, LLM-judge faithfulness checks, and PII redaction before storage.
  • Output: written to a warehouse and dashboards; searchable through RAG for supervisors.

questions.q: Should we fine-tune an open-source model or use a hosted API?
questions.a:
Factor Hosted API (GPT, Claude, Gemini) Fine-tuned open model (Llama, Mistral)
Time to value Days Weeks
Quality on general tasks Highest Lower, unless the task is narrow
Data privacy Vendor terms / private endpoint Full control
Cost at high volume Grows per token Fixed GPU cost, cheaper at scale
Ops burden Low High (serving, scaling, updates)
  • Recommendation pattern: start with an API plus RAG. Fine-tune (LoRA) only when you need a specific style or format, low latency or cost at scale, or must run on-premises. Prove it with an evaluation set first.

questions.q: How do you keep an LLM application fast and highly available in production?
questions.a:
• Latency:
  • Streaming
  • Response and semantic caching
  • Smaller models for routing
  • Parallel tool and retrieval calls
  • Shorter prompts
  • Prompt caching
  • Region close to users
  • Availability:
  • Multiple deployments or providers with fallback
  • Retries with exponential backoff
  • Timeouts and circuit breakers
  • Rate-limit and quota management
  • Autoscaling stateless services
  • Health checks
  • Monitor p50/p95 latency, error rate, tokens and cost, with alerts against SLOs.

questions.q: pandas: filter and reshape a dataset of support tickets.
questions.a:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("tickets.csv", parse_dates=["created_at"])
recent = df[(df.created_at >= "2025-01-01") & (df.status != "spam")]
pivot = (recent.assign(month=recent.created_at.dt.to_period("M"))
               .pivot_table(index="month", columns="category",
                            values="ticket_id", aggfunc="count", fill_value=0))
long = pivot.reset_index().melt(id_vars="month", var_name="category", value_name="tickets")
  • Explain boolean masks, pivot_table vs groupby().unstack(), and melt to go back from wide to long format.

questions.q: Clean a noisy text corpus before feeding it to a Transformer.
questions.a:
import re, html, unicodedata

def clean(t: str) -> str:
    t = html.unescape(t)
    t = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", t)
    t = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", t)              # HTML tags
    t = re.sub(r"https?://\S+", "<URL>", t)      # URLs
    t = re.sub(r"\S+@\S+", "<EMAIL>", t)         # PII-ish
    t = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", t).strip()
    return t
  • For Transformers, don't stem, remove stop words or lowercase blindly, because the tokenizer and model rely on natural text. Do deduplicate, drop boilerplate, fix encoding and filter by language.

questions.q: How did you measure the business impact (ROI) of a GenAI solution?
questions.a:
• Baseline first: average handling time, cost per ticket, error rate, all measured before launch.
  • After launch: A/B or phased rollout, then compare. Example: "Agents using the assistant cut handling time from 9.5 to 6.8 minutes (−28%) across 40k tickets a month, about ₹38 lakh a year saved, against ₹6 lakh a year of LLM and infrastructure cost."
  • Include quality (CSAT and accuracy) and adoption (weekly active users), not just cost.

questions.q: SQL: create a table, insert rows and update values (DDL/DML basics).

CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region VARCHAR(20), amount DECIMAL(10,2), sale_date DATE);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'North',1200.50,'2025-07-01'), (2,'South',800.00,'2025-07-02');

ALTER TABLE sales ADD COLUMN channel VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'online';

questions.q: Find the majority element (more than n/2 occurrences) in an array.
questions.a:
def majority(nums):
    cand, cnt = None, 0
    for x in nums:                       # Boyer–Moore voting
        if cnt == 0: cand = x
        cnt += 1 if x == cand else -1
    return cand if nums.count(cand) > len(nums) // 2 else None
  • O(n) time, O(1) space. The final check verifies the candidate when a majority isn't guaranteed.

questions.q: Python vs SQL: when would you do a transformation in each?
questions.a:
• SQL: set-based work close to the data (filtering, joins, aggregations, window functions) on large tables in the warehouse. Pushing computation down avoids moving data.
  • Python (pandas/PySpark): complex logic, ML feature engineering, API calls, text processing, statistical modelling, plotting.
  • Rule of thumb: aggregate in SQL, then model in Python. Keep the logic in one tested place.

questions.q: Design a model to predict whether a driver will accept a ride request.
questions.a:
• Label: accept/decline (or timeout) per request. Mind the selection bias: only dispatched offers are logged.
  • Features:
  • Pickup distance and ETA; trip length and direction (towards home?).
  • Surge level; time and day.
  • The driver's acceptance history, hours online, earnings so far.
  • Rider rating; pickup area type (airport).
  • Model: gradient boosting (or a two-tower model for driver–request matching), calibrated probabilities.
  • Use: the dispatch optimiser maximises expected matches = Σ P(accept) × value; avoid over-offering to the same drivers.
  • Evaluation: log-loss and AUC offline; online A/B on match rate, pickup ETA, cancellation, driver earnings fairness.

questions.q: How do you monitor a newly deployed ETA model?
questions.a:
• Accuracy: MAE/MAPE against actual trip times (delayed labels arrive after the trip) by city, hour, distance band; the share of trips more than X minutes late.
  • Input drift: distributions of traffic, GPS quality, new road closures; prediction drift against the previous model.
  • System: p99 latency, error rate, fallback rate (to a heuristic), feature staleness.
  • Business: cancellations, rider complaints, driver idle time.
  • Alerts and rollback: shadow first, then canary; automatic rollback if MAE regresses by more than a threshold.

questions.q: Why can the same algorithm on the same dataset give different results?
questions.a:
• Randomness: weight initialisation, data shuffling, dropout, bagging/feature subsampling, train/test split seeds.
  • Non-determinism: GPU kernels (atomic adds), multithreading, floating-point order of operations.
  • Different hyperparameters or library versions; data-order effects with early stopping.
  • Fixes: set seeds, use deterministic flags, pin versions; report mean ± std over several seeds.

questions.q: Implement gradient descent from scratch to fit a line.
questions.a:
import numpy as np
def fit_line(x, y, lr=0.01, epochs=2000):
    w = b = 0.0; n = len(x)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        y_hat = w * x + b
        dw = (2 / n) * np.dot(y_hat - y, x); db = (2 / n) * np.sum(y_hat - y)
        w -= lr * dw; b -= lr * db
    return w, b
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4.]); y = np.array([3, 5, 7, 9.])
print(fit_line(x, y))   # ≈ (2, 1)
  • Discuss the learning rate choice, feature scaling and convergence checks (when the loss stops improving).

questions.q: Design an experimentation framework for a two-sided marketplace.
questions.a:
• The problem: interference. Treating some riders changes the drivers available to control riders, which biases user-level A/B tests.
  • Designs:
  • Switchback tests: randomise by city-region × time window.
  • Geo/cluster randomisation.
  • Driver-side vs rider-side randomisation depending on the feature.
  • Metrics: marketplace health (match rate, wait time, surge frequency, earnings per hour, cancellations) plus guardrails.
  • Analysis: account for carry-over between windows, use cluster-robust standard errors, run long enough to cover weekly cycles.

questions.q: Behavioural: describe a model that caused a production issue and how you handled it.
questions.a:
Answer (STAR):

  • Situation: "A new pricing model inflated fares in one city after a holiday-calendar bug."
  • Action: "I detected it from an alert on fare distribution, rolled back within 20 minutes, quantified the affected trips, worked with ops on refunds, and added a calendar unit test plus a canary gate."
  • Result: "There were no repeat incidents, and the postmortem became the team's release checklist."
  • Show speed, ownership, transparency and prevention.

questions.q: When does a complex neural network behave like a linear model?
questions.a:
• No non-linear activations (or identity or linear activations): stacking linear layers gives W₂(W₁x) = Wx, which is still linear.
  • Activations operating in their linear region: small pre-activations with tanh or sigmoid near 0, or ReLU units that are all active (always positive), behave linearly.
  • Very wide networks at initialisation (NTK regime): with a small learning rate, training behaves like a linear model in the parameters.
  • Heavy regularisation pushes weights towards 0, which keeps activations near their linear zone.
  • Takeaway: non-linearity comes from the activations; without it, depth adds nothing.

questions.q: How does regularisation help linear regression? Compare L1 and L2.
questions.a:
• Purpose: it adds a penalty on the size of the weights to reduce variance and overfitting, especially when features are many or correlated.
  • L2 (Ridge), λ‖w‖²: shrinks all weights smoothly, handles multicollinearity, and has a closed form (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy.
  • L1 (Lasso), λ‖w‖₁: pushes some weights to exactly 0, which performs feature selection.
  • Elastic Net: a mix of both, good when there are groups of correlated features.
  • Tune λ with cross-validation and always standardise features first.

questions.q: How do BERT (encoder), a Transformer decoder and GPT-3 work? What are their inputs and outputs?
questions.a:
• BERT (encoder-only, bidirectional):
  • Input: [CLS] tokens [SEP] with segment and position embeddings.
  • Trained by masked language modelling (plus NSP originally).
  • Output: contextual embeddings for every token. [CLS] is used for classification, and token vectors for NER or QA spans.
  • It does not generate free text.
  • Original Transformer decoder (in encoder-decoder models such as T5 or translation): uses masked self-attention over the output so far plus cross-attention to the encoder output, and generates the target sequence token by token.
  • GPT-3 (decoder-only, causal):
  • Input: a prompt. A causal mask means each token sees only earlier tokens.
  • Trained on next-token prediction.
  • Output: a probability distribution over the next token, sampled repeatedly (autoregressively).
  • Supports in-context learning (few-shot) and has 175B parameters.

questions.q: How do you evaluate LLM outputs when there is no ground truth?
questions.a:
• LLM-as-judge with a clear rubric (relevance, correctness, completeness, tone, scored 1–5) or pairwise comparison between two systems. Calibrate the judge on 50 to 100 human-labelled items.
  • Reference-free metrics:
  • Faithfulness or groundedness to the provided context (RAGAS).
  • Self-consistency across samples.
  • Uncertainty via log-probs.
  • Behavioural checks: format and JSON validity, policy and toxicity classifiers, length.
  • Human and online signals:
  • Expert review of a sample.
  • Thumbs up/down.
  • Edit distance (how much users change drafts).
  • Task success and escalation rate.
  • A/B tests.

questions.q: Explain PCA and LDA. How do they differ?
questions.a:
• PCA (unsupervised):
  • Finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or the SVD of the centred X.
  • Keep the top components that explain, say, 95% of the variance.
  • Uses: compression, denoising, visualisation.
  • LDA (supervised):
  • Finds directions that maximise between-class separation relative to within-class scatter.
  • At most (C − 1) components.
  • Uses: dimensionality reduction before classification.
  • Key difference: PCA ignores labels, so it may keep directions that are useless for classification; LDA uses labels but assumes Gaussian classes with shared covariance.

questions.q: Explain TF-IDF, then use it to find the document most similar to a query.
questions.a:
• TF is how often a term appears in a document. IDF = log(N / (1 + df)) down-weights common words. TF × IDF highlights words that are distinctive for a document.
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

docs = ["refund for damaged item", "track my order", "return policy for shoes"]
vec = TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), stop_words="english")
X = vec.fit_transform(docs)
q = vec.transform(["how to return shoes"])
best = cosine_similarity(q, X).argmax()
print(docs[best])   # return policy for shoes
  • Limitations: no semantics (synonyms are missed) and sparse, high-dimensional vectors. Dense embeddings or hybrid search fix this.

questions.q: Implement KNN classification from scratch.
questions.a:
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

def knn_predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k=5):
    preds = []
    for x in X_test:
        d = np.sqrt(((X_train - x) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
        idx = np.argpartition(d, k)[:k]
        preds.append(Counter(y_train[idx]).most_common(1)[0][0])
    return np.array(preds)
  • Prediction is O(n·d) per query, so use KD-trees, ball trees or ANN at scale. Scale features first. Choose k by cross-validation (odd k for binary problems). Distance-weighted voting is a common follow-up.

questions.q: SQL: find the top 3 products by revenue in each category for the last 30 days.
questions.a:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.product_id, SUM(o.qty * o.price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.product_id = o.product_id
  WHERE o.order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY
  GROUP BY p.category, p.product_id
)
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT rev.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn
  FROM rev
) t WHERE rn <= 3;
  • Mention ROW_NUMBER vs RANK for ties, and an index on (order_date, product_id).

questions.q: Case study: store sales of a product dropped 15% last month. How would you investigate and model it?
questions.a:
1. Clarify the data: which stores, whether the drop is real (data pipeline issues, a holiday calendar shift), and the comparison with last year.
  2. Decompose: traffic × conversion × basket size; by region, store and channel (online vs store).
  3. Hypotheses: stock-outs, price change or competitor promotion, a product-page or listing change, seasonality, weather.
  4. Quantify: a difference-in-differences against control stores, and an inventory join to detect lost sales.
  5. Model: a demand forecast (LightGBM with lag, price, promotion and holiday features) to estimate the expected baseline, then attribute the gap to drivers.
  6. Recommend actions with the expected impact, and monitor.

questions.q: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER() and ROWID in Oracle?
questions.a:
• ROWID: a physical address pseudocolumn identifying where a row is stored (data object, file, block, slot). It is fast for direct access, unique per row in a table, but can change after operations such as table moves or export/import. Not for business logic.
  • ROW_NUMBER(): an analytic function that assigns a sequential number to rows in a result set based on OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). Used for ranking, top-N per group and deduplication.
  • Also: ROWNUM is a pseudocolumn assigned before ORDER BY, a classic pitfall for top-N queries.

questions.q: How do you optimise a slow SQL query in a bank's reporting system?
questions.a:
• Read the execution plan: full scans, bad join orders, sorts spilling to disk.
  • Indexes on the join and filter columns (composite, in the right column order); avoid functions on indexed columns in WHERE.
  • Reduce data early: filter before joining, select only the needed columns, pre-aggregate.
  • Partition large fact tables by date; use materialised views for repeated reports; update statistics.
  • Measure before and after, and keep correctness checks (row counts, totals).

questions.q: Dijkstra's shortest path: implement it in Python.
questions.a:
import heapq
def dijkstra(graph, src):                 # graph: {u: [(v, w), ...]}
    dist = {src: 0}; pq = [(0, src)]
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist.get(u, float("inf")): continue
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist.get(v, float("inf")):
                dist[v] = nd; heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))
    return dist
  • O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap; it needs non-negative weights (otherwise use Bellman-Ford).

questions.q: What is the correlation coefficient? What are its limitations?
questions.a:
• Pearson r = cov(X, Y) / (σ_X σ_Y), ranging from −1 to 1. It measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship.
  • Limitations:
  • Misses non-linear relationships (use Spearman for monotonic ones, or mutual information).
  • Sensitive to outliers.
  • Correlation ≠ causation.
  • Can be distorted by confounders or by combining groups (Simpson's paradox).
  • In ML: high correlation between features means multicollinearity, so drop one or use regularisation or PCA.

questions.q: Live coding: detect whether a linked list has a cycle.
questions.a:
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
  • Floyd's tortoise and hare: O(n) time, O(1) space. A follow-up asks you to find the cycle's start: reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time until they meet.

questions.q: Zepto task: EDA on products (product ID, rating, brand, return rate), then build a model. What would you do?
questions.a:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
df = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
print(df.describe(), df.isna().mean(), df.brand.value_counts().head(10), sep="\n")
print(df.groupby("brand")["return_rate"].agg(["mean", "count"]).query("count >= 20").sort_values("mean").tail(10))
print(df[["rating", "return_rate"]].corr())
# model: predict return rate from rating + brand (target-encoded with smoothing) to flag risky listings
brand_stats = df.groupby("brand")["return_rate"].agg(["mean", "count"]); gm = df.return_rate.mean()
df["brand_te"] = df.brand.map((brand_stats["mean"] * brand_stats["count"] + gm * 20) / (brand_stats["count"] + 20))
X, y = df[["rating", "brand_te"]], df["return_rate"]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.2, random_state=0)
m = GradientBoostingRegressor().fit(Xtr, ytr); print("MAE", mean_absolute_error(yte, m.predict(Xte)))
  • Framing: predict the return rate (or a high-return flag) to act on: delist, fix product descriptions, renegotiate with brands.
  • Note: target encoding must be computed inside the CV folds to avoid leakage. The quick version above is for illustration; say so in the interview.
  • Insights to present: brands with high return rates and low ratings, the rating–return correlation, and recommended actions.

questions.q: Merge two sorted arrays in place (nums1 has room at the end).
questions.a:
def merge(nums1, m, nums2, n):
    i, j, k = m - 1, n - 1, m + n - 1
    while j >= 0:
        if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]: nums1[k] = nums1[i]; i -= 1
        else: nums1[k] = nums2[j]; j -= 1
        k -= 1
  • Fill from the back: O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space. That is the optimal answer the interviewer wanted.

questions.q: Top-k frequent elements, breaking ties by the smaller number.
questions.a:
from collections import Counter
def top_k(nums, k):
    c = Counter(nums)
    return [x for x, _ in sorted(c.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:k]]
print(top_k([4, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2))   # [1, 2]
  • A sort with the key (−frequency, value) is O(n log n). For large n and small k, use a heap with the same tuple ordering. State how ties are handled before you code.

questions.q: Zoho system design: railway booking with an RAC (Reservation Against Cancellation) waitlist.
questions.a:
• Entities: Train, Coach and Berth, Booking (CONFIRMED / RAC / WL), Passenger.
  • Logic:
  • Book: if a berth is free → CONFIRMED; else if RAC slots remain → RAC (two passengers share a side-lower berth); else → WL queue.
  • Cancel a confirmed ticket: the first RAC passenger is promoted to CONFIRMED (gets the berth), and the first WL passenger moves to RAC.
  • Cancel RAC: promote the first WL passenger to RAC.
from collections import deque
class Train:
    def __init__(self, berths, rac):
        self.free, self.rac_cap = list(range(berths)), rac
        self.conf, self.rac, self.wl = {}, deque(), deque()
    def book(self, pid):
        if self.free: self.conf[pid] = self.free.pop(); return "CNF"
        if len(self.rac) < self.rac_cap: self.rac.append(pid); return "RAC"
        self.wl.append(pid); return "WL"
    def cancel(self, pid):
        if pid in self.conf:
            berth = self.conf.pop(pid)
            if self.rac:
                self.conf[self.rac.popleft()] = berth
                if self.wl: self.rac.append(self.wl.popleft())
            else: self.free.append(berth)
        elif pid in self.rac:
            self.rac.remove(pid)
            if self.wl: self.rac.append(self.wl.popleft())
        elif pid in self.wl: self.wl.remove(pid)
  • Discuss: concurrency (locking per train and date), persistence, berth preferences, and charts.

questions.q: How do Transformer models work? Describe the architecture.
questions.a:
• Token + positional embeddings → N layers of multi-head self-attention (each token weighs all the others) + feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer norm.
  • Encoder-only (BERT) for understanding; decoder-only (GPT) for generation with a causal mask; encoder-decoder (T5) for sequence-to-sequence tasks.
  • Why it works: parallel training, long-range context, and scaling with data and compute (pre-training then fine-tuning).

questions.q: Postman: design a high-throughput, near-real-time event-processing service (e.g. API monitoring results).
questions.a:
• Ingest: a stateless HTTP/gRPC API → validate → write to a partitioned log (Kafka, keyed by workspace or monitor ID for ordering).
  • Process: a consumer group of stream processors (aggregations, alert rules) with exactly-once or idempotent writes; windowed metrics (p95 latency per monitor).
  • Store: a time-series DB for metrics, an OLAP store (ClickHouse) for analytics, Redis for the latest status.
  • Alerting: a rule engine + notification fan-out with deduplication and rate limits.
  • Scale and reliability: back-pressure, DLQs, autoscaling on consumer lag, multi-AZ deployment.

from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings, ChatOpenAI

    "Answer only from the context. If unsure, say you don't know.\n\nContext:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}")

chain = ({"context": retriever | fmt, "question": RunnablePassthrough()}
         | prompt | ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0) | StrOutputParser())
print(chain.invoke("What is the refund policy for late deliveries?"))

questions.q: How do BERT embeddings differ from Word2Vec?
questions.a:
• Word2Vec:
  • Static: one vector per word type, learned with a shallow skip-gram or CBOW network.
  • No context ("bank" always has the same vector), out-of-vocabulary words are a problem, and it is cheap.
  • BERT:
  • Contextual: the vector depends on the whole sentence through deep bidirectional self-attention.
  • Uses sub-word (WordPiece) tokens, so there is no OOV problem.
  • Captures syntax and senses, but costs more to compute.
  • For sentence-level similarity, plain BERT [CLS] vectors are weak; use sentence-transformers fine-tuned contrastively.

questions.q: How does excessive sub-word splitting by the tokenizer affect sentiment analysis or NER?
questions.a:
• Problems:
  • Words broken into many pieces ("un", "##believ", "##ably") dilute meaning across tokens and use up the context length.
  • Rare names, Hinglish ("bahut tasty") and dish names ("paneer-tikka") fragment badly.
  • NER: entity boundaries must be re-aligned from sub-words to words; labelling only the first sub-word, or aggregating, adds noise.
  • Sentiment: negations and intensifiers split oddly; more tokens means more sequence and a higher chance of truncation.
  • Fixes:
  • A domain or multilingual tokenizer (or extend the vocabulary with domain tokens and fine-tune).
  • Normalise text.
  • Use word-level aggregation (first or mean sub-word) for NER.
  • Choose models trained on Indic and code-mixed data.

questions.q: Learned positional embeddings from a patch/CNN stem vs the fixed sinusoidal encodings of the original Transformer: what is the trade-off?
questions.a:
• Sinusoidal (fixed): no parameters; it encodes relative offsets through sin/cos phase and can extrapolate somewhat to longer sequences.
  • Learned absolute (ViT patch positions, BERT): flexible and data-driven, but limited to the trained length or resolution. Changing image size requires interpolating the position grid.
  • Convolutional or patch stems bring implicit positional information (local inductive bias, zero-padding effects), which some models use instead of, or as well as, explicit embeddings, as in ConvNeXt-style or CvT designs.
  • Modern LLMs use RoPE or ALiBi (relative) for better length generalisation.

questions.q: How do you optimise speech-to-text and text-to-speech models for low-latency inference? How does quantization affect quality?
questions.a:
• Speech-to-text (Whisper, Conformer):
  • A smaller or distilled model (distil-whisper).
  • Streaming / chunked decoding with VAD to skip silence.
  • CTranslate2 or faster-whisper, batching, GPU FP16 or INT8.
  • Text-to-speech (FastSpeech, VITS):
  • Non-autoregressive models for speed.
  • A streaming vocoder.
  • Cache frequent phrases.
  • Quantization:
  • INT8 usually costs under 1% WER or MOS.
  • 4-bit can hurt accents, noisy audio and prosody noticeably.
  • Measure WER (speech-to-text) and MOS or MCD (text-to-speech) on your data (Hindi or Hinglish, noisy restaurant audio) before and after.
  • Use calibration data from the real domain.

questions.q: Design improvements to an existing agentic pipeline (for example, a customer-support agent).
questions.a:
1. Measure first: trace every step (LangSmith or Langfuse) and find where it fails. Common culprits are wrong tool choice, loops and slow steps.
  2. Routing: a cheap classifier or small LLM sends simple intents (order status) to deterministic flows. Only complex cases reach the full agent.
  3. Tools: tighter descriptions and schemas, fewer and more specific tools, validation of arguments, idempotent APIs.
  4. Memory and context: summarise long chats, retrieve only the relevant policy chunks, and cache user and order lookups.
  5. Reliability: a maximum number of steps, timeouts, retries with backoff, fallback models, and human handoff for refunds above a threshold.
  6. Evaluation: a trajectory test set; measure resolution rate, average steps, latency, cost per conversation and CSAT.

questions.q: What is the difference between linear and logistic regression?
questions.a:
Linear regression Logistic regression
Target Continuous Binary (or multi-class with softmax)
Output ŷ = wᵀx + b, unbounded p = σ(wᵀx + b) in (0, 1)
Loss MSE (least squares) Log-loss (cross-entropy)
Interpretation Coefficient = change in y Coefficient = change in log-odds (exp → odds ratio)
Assumptions Linearity, homoscedastic errors Linear in the log-odds; independent observations

questions.q: Why is ReLU preferred in neural networks?
questions.a:
• No saturation for positive inputs: the gradient is 1, which avoids the vanishing gradients of sigmoid and tanh, so deep networks train faster.
  • Cheap to compute (max(0, x)), and produces sparse activations.
  • Downside: "dying ReLU" (units stuck at 0). Fixes are Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU and GELU/SiLU (used in Transformers), plus a good initialisation (He) and learning rate.

questions.q: Precision vs recall: when do you prioritise each? (Give a pharma example.)
questions.a:
• Precision: when false positives are costly. For example, flagging physicians for an expensive field-sales visit means we want flagged doctors to really be high-potential.
  • Recall: when misses are costly. For example, detecting adverse-event mentions in medical text, where missing one is a compliance risk.
  • Balance with F1 or a cost-weighted threshold, and show the precision-recall curve to stakeholders so they can choose the operating point.

questions.q: How do you evaluate a RAG application?
questions.a:
• Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, context precision (are the retrieved chunks relevant?).
  • Generation: faithfulness (claims supported by the context), answer relevance, correctness against ground truth.
  • Tools: RAGAS, DeepEval, TruLens, LangSmith evaluations; a golden set of 100+ questions written with domain experts.
  • Online: user feedback, citation click-through, escalation rate, latency and cost.
  • Regression testing: re-run the suite on every prompt, model or index change.

questions.q: What is MLflow and how do you use it?
questions.a:
• An open-source platform for the ML lifecycle:
  • Tracking: log parameters, metrics and artefacts per run, and compare experiments.
  • Projects: reproducible runs.
  • Models: a standard packaging format, served via REST.
  • Model Registry: versions plus stages (staging/production), approvals and lineage.
  • Usage: mlflow.autolog() in training, register the best model, and deploy from the registry in CI/CD. Newer versions also trace and evaluate LLM apps.

questions.q: How do you treat outliers in a modelling dataset?
questions.a:
• Investigate first: an error (fix or remove) or a real extreme (keep it; it may be important).
  • Detect: IQR rule, z-score (on roughly normal data), visual checks, Isolation Forest for multivariate outliers.
  • Treat: cap/winsorise, log transform, robust scalers or losses (Huber), tree-based models.
  • Document the impact on metrics, and never "clean away" the signal you're trying to predict.

questions.q: Guesstimate: how many diabetes patients visit endocrinologists in Bengaluru each month?
questions.a:
Answer (show your structure):

  • Bengaluru population about 1.4 crore → adults about 70% ≈ 98 lakh.
  • Diabetes prevalence in urban adults about 12% → about 11.8 lakh diabetics; about 60% diagnosed ≈ 7 lakh.
  • Share seeing an endocrinologist (rather than a GP) about 20% ≈ 1.4 lakh patients; visits every 3 months → about 47,000 visits a month.
  • State your assumptions and sanity-check them: about 300 endocrinologists × about 160 visits a month ≈ 48,000. That matches.

questions.q: Scenario: Your RAG-based chatbot for a client is confidently returning information that does not exist in the knowledge base (hallucination). The client is upset. How do you diagnose and fix this in production today?
questions.a:
1. Isolate Retrieval vs. Generation Failure: * Determine if the retrieval step failed to fetch the right context chunks, or if the LLM received the correct context but ignored/hallucinated beyond it. * Inspect retrieval similarity scores and log the raw context chunks passed to the LLM for failing queries.

  2. Mitigate LLM Hallucinations (Prompt Engineering & Grounding Constraints): * Tighten system prompts with explicit grounding instructions and strict refusal rules (e.g., "Answer ONLY using the provided context. If the answer is not present, state 'I do not have this information'").

  3. Implement Light Guardrails & Automated Checks: * Introduce a fast, cheap groundedness check (a lightweight classifier or small model evaluator) that compares the generated response against retrieved chunks before serving it to the user.

  4. Immediate Fallback Mechanism: * If the groundedness score falls below a set safety threshold, intercept the output and trigger a safe fallback message ("I cannot find this information in the official documents") rather than serving confident, false statements.

questions.q: Scenario: Your knowledge base expanded from 10,000 documents to 5 million documents. Latency has crashed, and API/infrastructure costs are spiking. How do you scale this architecture?
questions.a:
1. Vector Database Optimization & Indexing: * Migrate to a production-grade, distributed vector database (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, or tuned PGVector). * Tune Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index parameters (HNSW/IVF) to trade a negligible fraction of recall for massive speed gains.

  2. Pre-Filtering with Metadata: * Implement metadata pre-filtering so the vector search space is partitioned before dense similarity execution rather than filtered post-retrieval.

  3. Tiered / Hybrid Retrieval Architecture: * Implement a two-tiered retrieval pipeline: run a fast, low-cost sparse keyword search (BM25) first to narrow millions of docs down to candidate subsets, then apply dense vector search and cross-encoder reranking on top candidates.

  4. Caching Strategy: * Implement semantic caching (e.g., Redis) to serve repeated or semantically equivalent user queries directly from cache without hitting the vector database or LLM.

questions.q: Scenario: Your Gen AI feature was approved for a $2,000/month API budget, but costs hit $18,000/month and are rising. How do you analyze and optimize cost consumption?
questions.a:
1. Model Routing & Cascading: * Replace one-size-fits-all calls to expensive frontier models (e.g., GPT-4 class) with intelligent routing. Route simple extraction, classification, or summarization tasks to smaller, lower-cost models (e.g., GPT-4o-mini, Claude Haiku, or fine-tuned SLMs).

  2. Prompt Payload Reduction: * Inspect prompt sizes to ensure full, un-chunked raw documents are not being injected into context when small, precise retrieved chunks suffice.

  3. Caching & Deduplication: * Enable prompt caching provided by LLM vendors and deploy semantic caching at the backend layer to eliminate duplicate LLM calls.

  4. Batch Processing: * Offload non-real-time asynchronous tasks (e.g., nightly report generation, data indexing summary jobs) to batch processing APIs, which typically offer 50% cost discounts.

questions.q: Case Study: Design an internal AI tool for employees to query 3,000 HR and policy PDF documents (updated weekly). Requirements: Strict multi-department access control (e.g., Legal can only view Legal policies, HR can only view HR policies; zero data leakage between departments). Walk through the end-to-end design.
questions.a:
[ Ingestion Pipeline ]
  PDF Documents (3,000) ──> Chunking ──> Tag Metadata (dept_id) ──> Delta Re-Embedding (Weekly Changes)

[ Query & Retrieval Pipeline ]
  User Query + User Identity (RBAC) ──> Pre-Retrieval Metadata Filter ──> Scoped Vector Search ──> Relevant Chunks

[ Generation & Guardrail Layer ]
  Scoped Chunks ──> System Prompt + Citation Instructions ──> Grounded Response with Citations

[ Continuous Evaluation ]
  Periodic Automated Test Suite ──> Check Answer Accuracy & Verify Access Control / Zero Leakage

  1. Ingestion Layer: * Chunk PDF documents and attach strict department access metadata tags (dept_id, access_level) to every vector chunk at ingestion time. * Implement delta/incremental re-indexing for weekly document updates, re-embedding only added or modified PDFs instead of re-processing the entire 3,000-document store.

  2. Pre-Retrieval Access Control (Critical): * Enforce pre-retrieval filtering: the vector database query must be scoped directly to match the requesting user's validated RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) permissions. * Never rely on the LLM prompt to restrict or hide sensitive data. Unfiltered context chunks must never enter the model prompt if the user lacks explicit permissions.

  3. Generation Layer: * Inject retrieved, permission-verified chunks into the prompt with strict formatting rules requiring explicit source document citations so users can verify outputs.

  4. Evaluation & Compliance Monitoring: * Run continuous test suites per department to systematically verify output accuracy and test against permission bypass/data leakage risks, treating access bugs as critical compliance violations.

questions.q: Follow-Up: How do you handle overlapping policies (e.g., a document relevant to both Legal and HR departments) without duplicating data?
questions.a:
• Multi-Tag Metadata Association: Tag overlapping document chunks with a multi-value array or list of authorized departments (departments: ["Legal", "HR"]) instead of duplicating storage entries.
  • Filter Operator Logic: Update the pre-retrieval vector search filter condition from an exact match (department == user_dept) to an inclusion match (user_dept IN metadata.departments).

questions.q: Client Scenario: A non-technical client insists their chatbot must be 100% accurate and "never make a mistake." How do you explain that this expectation is unrealistic without losing their confidence?
questions.a:
• Avoid Technical Jargon: Frame the explanation around risk management and operational guardrails rather than raw AI limitations or model mathematics.
  • Analogy & Reality Framing: Explain that no complex system—human or AI—is 100% error-free. Just as human specialists require review processes, AI systems require governance structures.
  • Focus on Containment & Guardrails: Shift the conversation to how the engineering team mitigates risks:
  • Automated groundedness filters.
  • Explicit fallback routines when confidence is low.
  • Human-in-the-Loop escalation paths for high-stakes decisions.

questions.q: Standard Behavioral Scenarios
questions.a:
• Scope Changes Mid-Project: Handled by prioritizing core deliverables, evaluating trade-offs with stakeholders, establishing clear change-control documentation, and re-baselining delivery timelines transparently.
  • Technical Disagreements with Teammates: Resolved through objective benchmarking, running isolated proof-of-concept (PoC) tests, comparing metric trade-offs (e.g., latency vs. accuracy vs. cost), and aligning on common enterprise goals.
  • Staying Up-to-Date with AI Advances: Continuously follow research papers, major open-source repository releases, hands-on prototyping, and industry-standard engineering benchmarks.

questions.q: Scenario 1: A production RAG chatbot is confidently hallucinating information that does not exist in the knowledge base. The client is escalatng. How do you diagnose and fix this in production today?
questions.a:
Diagnostic & Fix Workflow



           [ Production Incident: High Hallucination ]
                               │
                               ▼
                 [ Isolate Failure Point ]
                               │
    ┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┐
    ▼                                                     ▼


[ Retrieval Failure Check ]                           [ Generation Failure Check ]
(Query vector logs: Are valid                        (Are valid chunks present in prompt,
chunks retrieved in top-K?)                          but ignored by the model?)
│                                                     │
▼                                                     ▼
• Apply Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense)                  • Enforce Strict System Guardrails
• Adjust chunking parameters                          • Add Groundedness Evaluator
• Tune HNSW index recall                              • Trigger Fallback ("I don't know")

  1. Isolate Retrieval Failure vs. Generation Failure: * Query the production vector logs for the failing requests. * If the correct context chunks are not present in the top-\(K\) candidates, the issue is a retrieval failure (fix chunking, embeddings, or search scoring). * If correct chunks are present but the model invents external facts, the issue is a generation failure (model ungroundedness).

  2. Immediate Production Mitigation (Generation Failure): * Prompts & Boundaries: Tighten the system prompt with explicit constraints (e.g., "Answer ONLY using the provided <context> tags. If the exact answer is not contained within, respond with 'I do not have sufficient information to answer this question.'"). * Groundedness Guardrail (LLM-as-a-Judge / Light Classifier): Insert an inline check (e.g., automated entailment step or small classifier) between model output generation and user response delivery.

  3. Fallback Implementation: * If the calculated groundedness score falls below a safety threshold (e.g., \(<0.85\)), suppress the completion and return a safe fallback: "I am sorry, but I cannot find a verified reference in the knowledge base to answer this query."

Key Takeaway: It is significantly better for a client-facing consulting solution to under-perform visibly with a safe fallback than to deliver false information confidently.

questions.q: Scenario 2: The knowledge base grew from 10,000 documents to 5,000,000 documents. Retrieval latency crashed, and hosting costs spiked. How do you re-architect the system?
questions.a:
Architectural Interventions

  1. Metadata Pre-Filtering: Do not run raw vector similarity across the entire 5-million vector index. Apply structured metadata pre-filters (e.g., tenant_id, department, document_type, date_range) to shrink the search space before vector computation occurs.
  2. HNSW Index Parameter Tuning: * Adjust HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) parameters such as \(M\) (number of bi-directional links per node) and efSearch (size of the dynamic candidate list during search) to trade off fractional recall gains for massive speed improvements.
  3. Tiered / Two-Stage Retrieval: * Stage 1 (Coarse & Cheap): Execute BM25 / Sparse keyword search or inverted index lookup to trim the 5,000,000 document space down to top 500 candidate chunks. * Stage 2 (Fine & Semantic): Run dense vector similarity and cross-encoder reranking only over those top 500 candidate chunks.
  4. Vector Database Sharding & Semantic Caching: Migrate to scalable vector databases (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, or sharded pgvector) and implement a Semantic Cache (Redis) to serve frequent user queries instantly without hitting vector indices or LLM APIs.

questions.q: Scenario 3: A Gen AI feature was approved for a $2,000/month LLM API budget. Current spend is hitting $18,000/month and rising. How do you audit and optimize this?
questions.a:
Cost Audit & Optimization Strategy

  1. Model Tiering & Dynamic Query Routing: Stop using frontier models (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) for basic classification, summarization, or simple retrieval synthesis. Route requests dynamically based on query complexity: * Simple Queries: Route to smaller, distilled models (e.g., GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1 8B, Claude 3 Haiku). * Complex Queries: Route to high-reasoning frontier models.
  2. Context Window Optimization: Audit prompt construction logs. Ensure entire multi-page documents are not passed in every API payload when only 3 retrieved chunks (e.g., 1,200 tokens) are necessary.
  3. Eliminate Duplicate API Calls via Caching: Implement exact-match prompt caching and semantic response caching (e.g., Redis VL, GPTCache) to intercept identical or highly similar user queries.
  4. Batch Processing: For non-real-time workloads (such as nightly evaluation runs or document summarizations), utilize OpenAI / Anthropic Batch APIs to obtain a 50% cost discount.

questions.q: Case Study: Enterprise HR Chatbot System Design
questions.a:
Client Requirements

  • Scale: 3,000 internal HR PDF documents, updated weekly.
  • Security & Isolation: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)—Legal team must only access Legal documents; HR team must only access HR documents. Zero cross-department information leakage allowed.

Complete System Design



     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                     INGESTION PIPELINE                      │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Weekly Modified Document Loader ]
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Chunking & Department Metadata Tagging ]
                     (e.g., metadata={"dept": ["HR", "Legal"]})
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Embedded & Indexed Vector Store ]
                                    │
                                    │
     ┌──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
     │                     RETRIEVAL & SECURITY                    │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ User Authenticated JWT Input ]
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Pre-Retrieval Metadata Filter ]
                     (Query scope restricted BEFORE vector search)
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Scoped Vector Database Search ]
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Cross-Encoder Reranker ]
                                    │
                                    │
     ┌──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
     │                    SYNTHESIS & EVALUATION                   │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Grounded LLM Prompt Generation ]
                     (With document citations)
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   [ Offline Evaluation Suite (RAGAS) ]

Layer-by-Layer Breakdown

1. Ingestion Layer

  • Delta Processing: Instead of re-indexing 3,000 documents weekly, run a file hash comparison (SHA-256) during the weekly cron job to process and embed only newly added or updated files.
  • Metadata Attachment: Attach explicit access arrays during chunking: ```json { "chunk_id": "pdf_882_chunk_4", "text": "Medical leave rollover policies...", "allowed_departments": ["HR", "Legal"] }

#### 2. Retrieval & Security Layer (Pre-Retrieval RBAC)

* **Pre-Search Filtering:** Never rely on system prompts to enforce data access boundaries (e.g., *"Do not reveal legal docs to HR"*).
* **Scoped Execution:** Embed user identity assertions (JWT tokens) at the API Gateway level. Filter vector searches directly at the database query layer:
```python
# Scoped Vector Search Example
user_department = user_jwt.get("department")  # e.g., "HR"

vector_db.query(
    vector=query_embedding,
    top_k=5,
    filter={"allowed_departments": {"$in": [user_department]}}
)
  • Overlapping Policies Handling: If a document applies to both HR and Legal, tag allowed_departments with ["HR", "Legal"] and use $in operator matching instead of exact single-string equality.

3. Generation & Citation Layer

  • Enforce strict inline source citation mapping ([Doc Name, Page Number]) inside the prompt template so employees can independently verify retrieved policies against raw PDFs.

4. Evaluation & Compliance Layer

  • Construct a benchmark evaluation set across departments. Run automated nightly regression pipelines testing for both Answer Correctness (RAGAS) and Security Leakage (attempting cross-department unauthorized queries).

questions.q: Scenario 1: The client insists their chatbot must be 100% accurate and never make a mistake. How do you handle this without jargon?
questions.a:
Approach & Script

Avoid deep neural network theory, mathematical loss functions, or probability distribution jargon. Frame the conversation entirely around Risk Management and Containment:

"In enterprise software, no automated system—or human workforce—operates at 100% flawless accuracy. Generative models operate probabilistically, similar to hiring a highly capable analyst. Our engineering focus is not promising theoretical perfection; it is building Guardrails, Isolation Filters, and Monitoring Loops around the system. When the model encounters an ambiguous request or an out-of-scope query, our guardrails catch it, prevent raw guessing, and fail safely by routing the user to a human operator or returning a verified fallback response."
