Vector Database: Storing embeddings alongside document metadata (e.g., page number, file name, access permissions) in a vector store like Pinecone, Qdrant, or FAISS. 4. Retrieval Phase: Generating query embeddings, executing dense semantic retrieval (Top-K similarity search), and applying reranking (e.g., Cohere Rerank) to filter the top 3–5 chunks. 5. Generation Phase: Injecting retrieved context into a structured prompt, passing it to the generator LLM (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o), and enforcing response schemas or citations.

questions.q: Why did you choose RAG over using a standalone LLM or Fine-Tuning?
questions.a:
• Compared to Standalone LLM: Standalone base models lack access to private, real-time, or domain-specific company data and are prone to hallucinations when asked about internal documents.
  • Compared to Fine-Tuning:
  • Dynamic Knowledge Updating: RAG updates its knowledge base instantaneously whenever new files are uploaded, whereas Fine-Tuning requires costly and time-consuming GPU retraining runs.
  • Verifiability & Citations: RAG allows strict source attribution by citing chunk metadata; fine-tuned model weights store knowledge implicitly without verifiable source references.
  • Cost Efficiency & Access Control: Fine-tuning base weights cannot enforce user-level security permissions, while RAG can easily enforce Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) metadata filters during vector retrieval.

questions.q: What chunking strategy did you use, and why?
questions.a:
• Fixed-size Chunking (with overlap): e.g., 500-token chunks with a 50-token overlap. Simple, but can break semantic sentences across boundaries.
  • Recursive Character Text Chunking: Splits text hierarchically using double line breaks (\n\n), single line breaks (\n), spaces, and characters. This preserves logical paragraphs and complete thought structures.
  • Semantic Chunking: Calculates embedding distances between adjacent sentences and creates split boundaries when vector similarity drops below a predefined threshold, ensuring each chunk contains a single coherent concept.
  • Parent-Child / Hierarchical Chunking: Uses small child chunks (e.g., 100–150 tokens) for precise vector distance calculation during search, but returns the larger parent block (e.g., 1000 tokens) to the generator model to provide rich context.

questions.q: How do you evaluate retrieval quality? Explain Precision@K, Recall@K, and MRR.
questions.a:
• Precision@K: Measures the proportion of relevant chunks within the top \(K\) retrieved chunks: \[\text{Precision@K} = \frac{\text{Number of Relevant Chunks in Top } K}{K}\]
  • Recall@K: Measures the fraction of all truly relevant chunks in the database that were successfully retrieved in the top \(K\): \[\text{Recall@K} = \frac{\text{Number of Relevant Chunks in Top } K}{\text{Total Number of Relevant Chunks in Dataset}}\]
  • Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR): Evaluates the position of the first relevant result across multiple test queries: \[\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{\vert{}Q\vert{}} \sum_{i=1}^{\vert{}Q\vert{}} \frac{1}{\text{rank}_i}\] where \(\text{rank}_i\) is the 1-based position of the first relevant chunk returned for query \(i\).

questions.q: What is the difference between System Prompt and User Prompt?
questions.a:
• System Prompt: Sets the global behavior, role boundaries, tone, constraints, and safety guardrails for the model (e.g., "You are an internal corporate support assistant. Only answer queries using the provided context."). It carries higher structural priority in model instructions.
  • User Prompt: The dynamic, variable query or input provided by the end-user during a specific conversation turn (e.g., "What is our company's parental leave policy?").

questions.q: How do LLM parameters like Temperature, Top-P, and Top-K affect generation?
questions.a:
• Temperature: Controls output randomness by flattening or steepening the Softmax probability distribution over tokens.
  • Low Temperature (\(0.0 - 0.2\)): Makes outputs deterministic and factual (ideal for RAG/code).
  • High Temperature (\(0.7 - 1.0\)): Increases output creativity and variability.
  • Top-P (Nucleus Sampling): Selects tokens from the smallest cumulative probability set whose sum equals \(P\) (e.g., Top-P = \(0.9\) samples from tokens making up the top \(90\%\) probability mass).
  • Top-K Sampling: Restricts token choices strictly to the top \(K\) most probable next tokens, discarding all others.

questions.q: How do you detect and reduce LLM hallucinations in a production system?
questions.a:
1. RAG Grounding: Restrict the system prompt to explicitly state: "Answer strictly based on the context. If the answer is not contained within the context, state 'I do not have enough information to answer.'"
  2. Self-Correction & Reranking: Run a lightweight secondary LLM step or evaluator to verify if every assertion in the output is supported by the context before returning the response.
  3. Guardrails & Structured Outputs: Enforce Pydantic output parsing or frameworks like NeMo Guardrails to reject ungrounded generations.
  4. Lower Temperature: Set temperature to \(0.0\) to minimize creative divergence.

questions.q: What is Agentic AI, and how does it differ from standard Generative AI?
questions.a:
• Standard Generative AI: Single-turn input-to-output mapping (e.g., drafting an email or generating a single response from a prompt).
  • Agentic AI: Autonomous systems capable of multi-step planning, tool selection, environment interaction, and self-correction to achieve complex end goals without step-by-step human intervention.

questions.q: How would you design an AI Agent with external tools?
questions.a: • Uses the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) framework: 1. Thought: The agent breaks down the problem and determines which tool is needed. 2. Action: The agent outputs a structured tool invocation request (e.g., calling a REST API or executing an SQL query). 3. Observation: The environment runs the tool and returns the response back into the context window. 4. Iteration: The agent evaluates the output and decides the next action or presents the final answer.

questions.q: How do you prevent AI Agents from getting trapped in infinite execution loops?
questions.a:
1. Max Iteration Limits: Enforce strict execution step counters (max_iterations = 5).
  2. State & Duplicate Action Tracking: Maintain an action log; if the agent attempts the exact same tool call with identical parameters twice in a row, interrupt execution.
  3. Fallback & Graceful Timeout Handlers: Implement system timeouts that force the agent into a human-in-the-loop or default error message state if task completion takes too long.

questions.q: What is the difference between Multithreading and Multiprocessing in Python?
questions.a:
• Multithreading (threading module):
  • Multiple threads run within the same process memory space.
  • Subject to Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), meaning threads cannot run CPU-bound code in parallel across multiple CPU cores.
  • Best for: I/O-bound tasks (e.g., asynchronous API calls, fetching data from vector DBs).
  • Multiprocessing (multiprocessing module):
  • Creates separate process instances, each with its own memory space and Python interpreter instance.
  • Bypasses the GIL, enabling true parallel execution across multi-core CPUs.
  • Best for: CPU-bound tasks (e.g., tokenization, chunking, data processing, heavy local model inference).

questions.q: What is the Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)?
questions.a:
• The GIL is a mutex (mutual exclusion lock) used by the CPython interpreter to ensure that only one thread executes Python bytecode at any given moment.
  • It prevents race conditions and ensures memory safety in CPython's reference-counting garbage collection system, but limits Python multithreading from leveraging multi-core parallel computing for heavy mathematical or CPU computations.

questions.q: How do you debug high latency issues in a RAG pipeline?
questions.a:
1. Add End-to-End Tracing: Integrate observability platforms like LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, or OpenTelemetry to measure latency at each individual pipeline step: \[\text{Total Latency} = T_{\text{embedding}} + T_{\text{vector\_search}} + T_{\text{reranking}} + T_{\text{LLM\_TTFT}} + T_{\text{generation}}\]
  2. Identify the Bottleneck: * If Vector Retrieval is slow: Optimize database indexing (e.g., switch from exact search to approximate nearest neighbor HNSW), or cache frequent embedding results. * If Generation is slow: Enable streaming responses (Time to First Token - TTFT), use smaller/quantized LLMs, or adopt prompt caching strategies.

questions.q: What metrics should you continuously monitor for a production Gen AI application?
questions.a:
• System Metrics: Latency (TTFT, Total Response Time), API Error Rates, GPU Memory/Compute Utilization, Token Throughput (tokens/sec).
  • Quality & RAG Metrics: Context Relevance, Answer Groundedness (Faithfulness), User Feedback (Thumbs Up / Thumbs Down ratios).
  • Operational & Cost Metrics: Daily Token Consumption (Input vs. Output tokens), API Cost Per User Query, Guardrail Trigger Rates (blocked prompt injections / toxic inputs).

questions.q: What is the difference between Top-K and Top-P sampling? Where are they used, and what are their real-life use cases?
questions.a:
• Top-K Sampling: Filters the candidate token pool to strictly the top \(K\) most probable next tokens, redistributing probability among only those \(K\) options.

  • Use Case: Useful when you want tight boundaries over generation choices, but can produce repetitive output if \(K\) is too low or include low-quality tokens if \(K\) is static across varying probability distributions.

  • Top-P (Nucleus) Sampling: Dynamically selects the smallest set of top tokens whose cumulative probability mass equals or exceeds threshold \(P\) (e.g., \(0.90\)).

  • Use Case: Highly adaptive across varying contexts. In predictable contexts, the candidate pool shrinks automatically; in creative contexts, it expands naturally.

  • Real-World Application: Factual corporate extraction or code generation uses low \(P\) (\(0.1–0.3\)) or small \(K\), whereas creative copywriting or brainstorming tasks use higher \(P\) (\(0.8–0.95\)).

questions.q: What is the Transformer architecture, and why do LLMs rely on it instead of traditional RNNs?
questions.a:
• Transformer Architecture: Introduced in "Attention Is All You Need," transformers rely entirely on the Self-Attention Mechanism to model dependencies between tokens across an entire sequence simultaneously without sequential recurrence.
  • Why Transformers Replace RNNs:
  • Parallelization: RNNs process text sequentially (token-by-token), creating a severe hardware bottleneck during training. Transformers process full context sequences in parallel on modern GPUs.
  • Long-Range Dependencies: RNNs suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients over long contexts. Transformers compute direct pairwise attention weights between all tokens regardless of sequence distance.

questions.q: What is the difference between Decoder-Only models and Encoder-Decoder models?
questions.a:
• Decoder-Only Models (e.g., GPT-4, Llama):
  • Uses causal self-attention (tokens can only attend to previous tokens).

  • Best For: Autoregressive text generation, open-ended conversation, reasoning, and code completion.

  • Encoder-Decoder Models (e.g., T5, BART):

  • The encoder processes the full source sequence bidirectionally; the decoder generates the output autoregressively while cross-attending to the encoded representation.
  • Best For: Sequence-to-sequence transformation tasks like language translation, summarization, and conditional text generation.

questions.q: What is hallucination in LLMs? Why does it happen, and what parameters influence it?
questions.a:
• Definition: Hallucination occurs when an LLM generates plausible-sounding text that is factually incorrect, ungrounded, or completely fabricated relative to real-world knowledge or provided context.
  • Root Causes:
  • Probabilistic nature of next-token prediction without internal truth verification mechanisms.

  • Out-of-distribution prompts, noisy training data, or missing context in the prompt payload.

  • Influencing Parameters: High temperature, high Top-P, and long unstructured prompt sequences elevate hallucination risks.

questions.q: How do you evaluate hallucination? What metrics are used?
questions.a:
• Faithfulness / Groundedness Metric: Evaluates what fraction of claims made in the generated answer can be directly inferred from the retrieved reference context.
  • Context Recall & Precision: Measures whether the necessary source text was retrieved and if irrelevant noise was excluded.
  • Evaluation Frameworks: Frameworks like RAGAS or DeepEval utilize G-Eval (LLM-as-a-Judge) patterns alongside semantic entailment classifiers (NLI models) to systematically score hallucination severity before production release.

questions.q: Explain the end-to-end RAG system design and pipeline.
questions.a:
1. Ingestion: Document parsing, text extraction, semantic chunking, embedding generation via vector encoders.
  2. Indexing: Storing vector representations and metadata in a vector database (e.g., FAISS, Pinecone).
  3. Retrieval: User query embedding, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) vector search, metadata filtering, optional reranking.
  4. Synthesis: System prompt construction (injecting retrieved chunks), LLM inference, guardrail validation, and response streaming to the client.

questions.q: How do you handle unrestricted vs. restricted data during retrieval in RAG systems?
questions.a:
• Pre-Retrieval Metadata Filtering: Do not rely on prompt directives to restrict data access. Attach explicit security metadata tags (role, department_id, access_level) to vector chunks during ingestion.
  • RBAC Vector Scoping: Scope the vector search query execution directly to match the authenticated user's access rights. Unrestricted data is accessible globally; restricted data chunks are returned only if the user's validated token matches chunk security tags.

questions.q: What is FAISS, and what is PEFT?
questions.a:
• FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search): An open-source library optimized for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, offering GPU-accelerated Indexing (e.g., IVF-PQ, HNSW) for high-speed retrieval.
  • PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning): A set of techniques (e.g., LoRA, QLoRA) that fine-tunes large language models by updating only a small fraction of parameters (adapter matrices) while freezing base model weights, drastically reducing compute and VRAM requirements.

questions.q: How would you host your LLM for latency optimization when handling high traffic spikes?
questions.a:
1. Specialized Serving Frameworks: Deploy models using high-throughput inference engines like vLLM or TGI (Text Generation Inference) utilizing PagedAttention and continuous batching.
  2. Quantization: Load models in 4-bit or 8-bit precision (AWQ / GPTQ) to reduce memory bandwidth bottlenecks.
  3. Autoscaling & Replicas: Deploy model replicas behind an asynchronous load balancer with autoscaling triggered by GPU utilization and queue depth.
  4. Caching & Speculative Decoding: Implement semantic response caching (Redis) and speculative decoding (using a draft smaller model to speed up generation).

questions.q: What is the difference between Decorators and Generators in Python? How do Generators relate to streaming LLM responses?
questions.a:
• Decorator: A higher-order function that takes another function as an argument, extends its behavior without explicitly modifying it, and returns a new function (e.g., @app.get(), @time_it).
  • Generator: A function that produces a sequence of values over time using the yield keyword instead of return, maintaining its internal state between execution calls.
  • LLM Streaming Connection: When an LLM API streams tokens back chunk-by-chunk (Time-To-First-Token optimization), Python backend services use generators (or async generators) to yield server-sent events (SSE) continuously to the frontend interface without loading the entire response into memory at once.

questions.q: How do you handle and process large quantities of data in Python without encountering Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors?
questions.a:
1. Iterative Data Streaming: Use generators and file streaming streams (ijson, pandas chunking via chunksize) to process data sequentially line-by-line or batch-by-batch instead of loading entire datasets into memory.
  2. Memory-Efficient Data Structures: Utilize numpy arrays, Polars, or PyArrow backends instead of native high-overhead Python objects.
  3. Distributed Processing: Scale out large ETL tasks using distributed processing engines like PySpark or Dask when single-node memory capacity is exceeded.

questions.q: What are the different types of chunking strategies, and what parameters do you pass during chunking?
questions.a:
• Strategies:
  • Fixed-Size Chunking: Splits text by character/token count with a fixed overlap window.
  • Recursive Chunking: Splits hierarchy-wise by natural boundaries (paragraphs, sentences, punctuation) to keep semantic thoughts intact.

  • Semantic Chunking: Computes embedding distances between adjacent sentences and splits text when semantic divergence exceeds a set threshold.

  • Key Parameters: chunk_size (token/character limit), chunk_overlap (boundary continuity window), separators (delimiter priority order), and length_function (len vs. token counters).

questions.q: What is Function Calling in an LLM, and when does the model trigger it?
questions.a:
• Function Calling: An LLM capability where the model evaluates a user query against provided JSON schemas of external tools/functions, detects when external data or actions are required, and outputs structured JSON arguments matching the tool's parameter signature rather than plain text.
  • Triggering: Triggered automatically when the user prompt demands external information (e.g., checking order status, querying a database) or side-effect actions that the LLM's static weights cannot resolve internally.

questions.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol), and why was it introduced?
questions.a:
• Model Context Protocol (MCP): An open standard designed to standardize connections between AI applications (LLM hosts) and external tools, databases, and context providers.
  • Why Introduced: Eliminates the fragmentation of writing custom, proprietary API integration wrappers for every distinct tool and model provider by establishing a uniform server-client protocol interface for tool discovery, resource management, and prompt handling.

questions.q: Problem 1: Flaky External LLM APIs & Resilient Retries
questions.a:
Base Question:

How do you write a Python wrapper/decorator to handle intermittent failures when calling external LLM APIs with exponential backoff?

Candidate Approach & Code Solution:

Implement an exponential backoff loop bounded by a maximum retry count to prevent infinite execution loops in production environments.

import time
import random
import logging
from typing import Callable, Any

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

def call_llm_api_stub() -> str:
    """Simulated LLM API call that may fail intermittently."""
    if random.random() < 0.7:
        raise TimeoutError("504 Gateway Timeout: LLM provider unresponsive")
    return "LLM Response: Generation Successful"

def execute_with_exponential_backoff(
    api_func: Callable[[], Any],
    max_retries: int = 3,
    base_delay: float = 1.0,
    backoff_factor: float = 2.0
) -> Any:
    """
    Executes an API call with configurable retry counts and exponential delays.
    """
    delay = base_delay
    for attempt in range(1, max_retries + 1):
        try:
            logging.info(f"Attempt {attempt}/{max_retries}: Calling LLM API...")
            return api_func()
        except Exception as err:
            logging.warning(f"Attempt {attempt} failed: {err}")
            if attempt == max_retries:
                logging.error("Max retries reached. Escalating exception.")
                raise err

            time.sleep(delay)
            delay *= backoff_factor

Follow-Up Questions & Production Hardening

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "What if the API returns a 400 Bad Request or 401 Unauthorized? Will your function retry?"
questions.a: • Candidate Answer: No, non-transient client errors (\(4xx\)) should never be retried. A 400 indicates a malformed payload or invalid prompt parameters, and a 401 indicates authentication failure. Retrying these will yield identical failures, waste compute, and exhaust rate limits. Retries should strictly target transient network faults (\(502, 503, 504\)) and rate limits (\(429\)).

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "How do you make this retry pattern resilient when scaling to thousands of concurrent users?"
questions.a: • Candidate Answer: Apply Full Jitter to the exponential delay. If thousands of worker threads encounter a micro-outage simultaneously, synchronized retries cause a "Thundering Herd" problem, repeatedly overloading the downstream API server at exact interval spikes. Jitter spreads out retry traffic across randomized time windows.

questions.q: Problem 2: Response Caching, Cost Optimization & Cache Invalidation
questions.a:
Base Question:

Frequent identical user queries significantly inflate LLM API billing and increase latency. How do you implement a caching system to mitigate this?

Candidate Approach & Code Solution:

Implement a query-level key-value lookup. Hashing the normalized prompt string generates a cache key to return pre-computed responses instantly.

import hashlib
from typing import Dict, Optional

class SimpleLLMCache:
    def __init__(self):
        self._cache: Dict[str, str] = {}

    def _generate_key(self, query: str) -> str:
        # Normalize whitespace and lower string before hashing
        normalized_query = " ".join(query.strip().lower().split())
        return hashlib.sha256(normalized_query.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()

    def get(self, query: str) -> Optional[str]:
        key = self._generate_key(query)
        return self._cache.get(key)

    def set(self, query: str, response: str) -> None:
        key = self._generate_key(query)
        self._cache[key] = response

Follow-Up Questions & Production Hardening

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "What are the key limitations of relying on an in-memory dictionary cache in production?"
questions.a:
• Candidate Answer:
  • Memory Volatility: In-memory caches clear when the service container restarts or crashes.
  • Instance Isolation: Modern applications deploy across multiple stateless server instances (e.g., Kubernetes pods). In-memory dicts create isolated, inconsistent local caches, resulting in duplicate LLM calls across pods.
  • Fix: Use a centralized distributed cache like Redis, paired with an LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction policy to control memory footprint.

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "Would you blindly cache every LLM response?"
questions.a: • Candidate Answer: No. Caching non-deterministic or real-time context queries (e.g., "What is the current stock price of Apple?", "Generate a personalized greeting for User X") causes stale, invalid outputs.

questions.q: Problem 3: Context Window Constraints & Document Chunking
questions.a:
Base Question:

Large documents often exceed the context window of an LLM. How do you split raw text into chunks, and why is chunk overlap necessary?

Candidate Approach & Code Solution:

Implement a sliding-window text chunker using configurable character limits and overlap intervals to maintain continuity across chunk boundaries.

from typing import List

def chunk_text_with_overlap(text: str, chunk_size: int, chunk_overlap: int) -> List[str]:
    """
    Splits text into overlapping chunks using character-level sliding windows.
    """
    if chunk_overlap >= chunk_size:
        raise ValueError("chunk_overlap must be strictly less than chunk_size")

    chunks = []
    start = 0
    text_length = len(text)

    while start < text_length:
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunk = text[start:end]
        chunks.append(chunk)

        # Advance the window by stride (size - overlap)
        start += (chunk_size - chunk_overlap)

    return chunks

# Test Execution
sample_doc = "Generative AI systems require scalable data pipelines and effective chunking strategies."
chunks = chunk_text_with_overlap(sample_doc, chunk_size=30, chunk_overlap=10)

Follow-Up Questions & Production Hardening

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "Why is chunk overlap critical for retrieval accuracy?"
questions.a: • Candidate Answer: Text chunking creates artificial boundaries. If a critical semantic fact spans across the boundary of Chunk A and Chunk B (e.g., a entity subject in Chunk A and its primary action verb in Chunk B), splitting without overlap fragments the context. Embedding models will lose the core context of both fragments. Overlap preserves semantic continuity across contiguous chunks.

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "Is fixed-character chunking optimal for all document types?"
questions.a:
• Candidate Answer: No. Fixed-character splitting ignores semantic structure, often cutting sentences or code blocks mid-word.
  • Recursive Character Splitting: Hierarchy-aware splitting that attempts to preserve structural boundaries by splitting sequentially on \n\n (paragraphs), \n (lines), (words), and finally "" (characters).
  • Semantic Chunking: Computes similarity between adjacent sentences using embeddings, placing split points only where semantic distance spikes significantly.
import re
from typing import List

def recursive_character_tokenizer_concept(text: str, max_chunk_size: int) -> List[str]:
    """
    Splits content primarily on paragraph delimiters, falling back to lower-level
    separators only when paragraph blocks exceed max_chunk_size.
    """
    paragraphs = text.split("\n\n")
    final_chunks = []
    current_chunk = []
    current_length = 0

    for para in paragraphs:
        if current_length + len(para) <= max_chunk_size:
            current_chunk.append(para)
            current_length += len(para) + 2  # account for delimiter
        else:
            if current_chunk:
                final_chunks.append("\n\n".join(current_chunk))
            current_chunk = [para]
            current_length = len(para)

    if current_chunk:
        final_chunks.append("\n\n".join(current_chunk))

    return final_chunks

questions.q: Problem 4: Retrieval Diversity & Re-Ranking Pipeline
questions.a:
Base Question:

A vector database returns the top 20 candidate documents based on cosine similarity, but you must pass only the 5 most relevant chunks to the LLM context. Write a function to extract top results.

Candidate Code Solution (Initial Sorting):

from typing import List, Dict, Any

def get_top_k_documents(retrieved_docs: List[Dict[str, Any]], top_k: int = 5) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Sorts retrieved vector search results by similarity score and returns top_k.
    """
    sorted_docs = sorted(retrieved_docs, key=lambda x: x.get("score", 0.0), reverse=True)
    return sorted_docs[:top_k]

Follow-Up Questions & Production Hardening

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "What if the top 5 retrieved documents are near-identical copies of each other?"
questions.a: • Candidate Answer: High vector similarity does not guarantee information diversity. If a database contains repeated policy updates or redundant log entries, standard cosine sorting returns \(5\) near-duplicate chunks. This consumes valuable context window space without adding useful information.

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "How do you solve this near-duplicate retrieval issue in production?"
questions.a:
• Candidate Answer: Implement a Two-Stage Retrieval Architecture utilizing Over-Retrieval + Re-Ranking. 1. Stage 1 (High Recall): Retrieve an expanded candidate set (e.g., Top \(K=30\)) from the vector store using fast approximate nearest neighbors (ANN). 2. Stage 2 (High Precision & Diversity): Pass candidates through a Cross-Encoder Re-Ranker (e.g., Cohere Rerank or bge-reranker-large) or run Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to maximize information coverage while penalizing redundant text embeddings.
                    [ User Query ]
                          │
                          ▼
             [ Stage 1: Vector Search ]
              (Fast ANN, High Recall)
                          │
                          ▼
            [ Top 30 Candidate Documents ]
                          │
                          ▼
              [ Stage 2: Cross-Encoder ]
            (Contextual Re-Ranking & MMR)
                          │
                          ▼
         [ Top 5 Diverse & Relevant Chunks ]
                          │
                          ▼
                     [ LLM Context ]

questions.q: Problem 5: LLM Structured Output Parsing, Validation & Guardrails
questions.a:
Base Question:

An downstream service expects the LLM to return valid JSON, but the model occasionally returns malformed JSON, markdown formatting (json ...), or conversational prefix/suffix text. How do you handle this?

Candidate Approach & Code Solution:

Extract the raw JSON string using regex patterns, parse it safely, and validate it against an expected model structure.

import re
import json
from typing import Dict, Any

def sanitize_and_parse_json(raw_llm_output: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Strips conversational text and markdown blocks to parse underlying JSON safely.
    """
    # Pattern to extract content enclosed inside markdown json blocks or raw braces
    json_pattern = r"```(?:json)?\s*(\{.*?\})\s*```|(\{.*\})"
    match = re.search(json_pattern, raw_llm_output, re.DOTALL)

    if match:
        clean_json_str = match.group(1) or match.group(2)
    else:
        clean_json_str = raw_llm_output.strip()

    try:
        return json.loads(clean_json_str)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as err:
        raise ValueError(f"Failed to parse extracted text into valid JSON: {err}")

Follow-Up Questions & Production Hardening

questions.q: Interviewer Question: "What if the model repeatedly generates invalid JSON payloads even after retrying?"
questions.a: • Candidate Answer: 1. Schema Enforcement: Use Pydantic to enforce strict structural and data-type validation beyond basic JSON syntax checks. 2. Self-Correction Retry Loop: Pass the malformed generation and the specific validation error message back to the LLM in a targeted follow-up prompt, requesting a corrected payload. 3. Graceful Fallbacks: If the model fails after \(N\) retry attempts, log the payload for monitoring, fire an alert, and trigger a structured fallback response to maintain upstream service stability.

questions.q: How do you improve document retrieval when user queries diverge significantly from the raw context text?
questions.a:
• Query Rewriting / Expansion: Use a lightweight LLM step to rephrase, expand, or break down messy or ambiguous user queries into well-formed sub-queries before searching the vector index.
  • Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE): Prompt an LLM to generate a hypothetical answer to the user's question, embed that generated answer, and execute vector similarity search against real context chunks.
  • Hybrid Search (Dense + Sparse): Combine Dense Vector Retrieval (capturing semantic intent via embeddings) with Sparse Keyword Retrieval (e.g., BM25 for exact match acronyms, IDs, or medical/legal terminology) using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
  • Cross-Encoder Reranking: Fetch a larger candidate pool (e.g., top-50 chunks) via vector search and pass them through a cross-encoder model (e.g., Cohere Rerank, BGE-Reranker) to output fine-grained relevancy scores for the final top-\(K\) selection.

questions.q: If the retrieved chunks are accurate but the LLM still generates an incorrect or incomplete answer, how do you debug the system?
questions.a:
[ User Query ]
                      │
                      ▼
           [ Vector Index Search ]
                      │
                      ▼
          [ Context Chunks Loaded ]
                      │
     ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
     ▼                                 ▼


[ Context Precision /             [ Context Chunk
Recall Check ]                   Ordering Check ]
(Are key facts missing           (Evaluate "Lost in the
or contaminated?)                  Middle" positioning)
│                                 │
└────────────────┬────────────────┘
│
▼
[ Prompt Template Audit ]
(Check system guardrails, rules,
and delimiter separation)
│
▼
[ Parameter Configuration ]
(Lower Temperature to ~0.0;
adjust Top-P parameters)
│
▼
[ Final Model Isolation ]
(Test with larger LLM context window /
higher-capacity reasoning model)
  1. Isolate Retrieval vs. Generation: Evaluate context precision and recall using metrics (e.g., RAGAS) to confirm whether the necessary facts exist within the retrieved chunks.
  2. Inspect Context Ordering ("Lost in the Middle"): LLMs tend to pay more attention to tokens at the very beginning and end of long prompts. Reorder top chunks so the highest-scoring passages sit at the top or bottom rather than hidden in the middle.
  3. Audit Prompt Template & Delimiters: Ensure clear boundary markers (e.g., <context> ... </context>) separate retrieved passages from system instructions, preventing the model from confusing context with user rules.
  4. Tune Generation Hyperparameters: Reduce the model's temperature (e.g., set to \(0.0\)) and adjust Top-P to enforce deterministic, factual extraction instead of loose creative sampling.

questions.q: What is Prompt Injection, and how do you protect production Gen AI applications against it?
questions.a:
• Definition: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted user input contains malicious instructions designed to bypass system prompts, override safety rules, exfiltrate system instructions, or hijack tool calls.
  • Defense-in-Depth Mitigation Strategy:
  • Input Validation & Sanitization: Strip harmful control tags, enforce strict character/token limits, and run user inputs through dedicated moderation classifiers (e.g., Llama Guard) prior to prompt construction.
  • Strict Structural Separation: Keep system instructions and variable user inputs isolated using clear API structures or prompt boundary tags rather than raw string concatenation.
  • Privilege Restriction on Tools: Enforce least-privilege access on external function/tool integrations (e.g., restrict database tools to read-only views; mandate human confirmation for side-effects).
  • Output Guardrails & Filtering: Inspect generated outputs for sensitive data leaks (PII) or unauthorized system prompt regurgitation before returning responses to users.

questions.q: How do you handle long-term conversation memory in LLMs without exceeding context window limits or inflating token costs?
questions.a:
• Sliding Window Buffer: Retain only the most recent \(N\) message turns (e.g., last 5 interactions) while discarding older messages.
  • Conversation Summarization: Use a background LLM process to periodically condense older conversation turns into a running summary block appended to the system prompt.
  • Vector-Backed Episodic Memory: Store historic user interactions in a vector database. Retrieve relevant past dialogue turns dynamically using semantic similarity search based on the user's active topic.

questions.q: Task 1: Write a Python function that executes an API call with exponential backoff retries when encountering errors.
questions.a:
import time
import requests

def call_api_with_exponential_backoff(url: str, max_retries: int = 5, initial_delay: float = 1.0) -> dict:
    """
    Executes an HTTP GET request with exponential backoff logic.
    Doubles the delay after each failed attempt to prevent service overloading.
    """
    delay = initial_delay

    for attempt in range(1, max_retries + 1):
        try:
            response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
            response.raise_for_status()  # Raises HTTPError for 4xx/5xx codes
            return response.json()
        except (requests.RequestException, Exception) as err:
            print(f"[Attempt {attempt}/{max_retries}] Failed: {err}. Retrying in {delay} seconds...")
            if attempt == max_retries:
                raise RuntimeError(f"API call failed after {max_retries} attempts.") from err

            time.sleep(delay)
            delay *= 2  # Exponential escalation (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...)

# Architectural Explanation provided to Interviewer:
# Exponential backoff prevents "thundering herd" problems during transient API outages or rate limits.
# In production, adding random jitter (e.g., delay + random.uniform(0, 0.5)) prevents synchronized retry spikes.

questions.q: Task 2: Implement an In-Memory Cache for LLM Queries to eliminate duplicate API calls for identical inputs.
questions.a:
import hashlib
from typing import Optional

class LLMQueryCache:
    """
    In-memory caching layer for LLM responses using SHA-256 hashed queries as keys.
    """
    def __init__(self):
        self._cache: dict[str, str] = {}

    def _generate_key(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        # Standardize formatting and hash string to fixed key length
        normalized_prompt = prompt.strip().lower()
        return hashlib.sha256(normalized_prompt.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()

    def get(self, prompt: str) -> Optional[str]:
        key = self._generate_key(prompt)
        return self._cache.get(key)

    def set(self, prompt: str, response: str) -> None:
        key = self._generate_key(prompt)
        self._cache[key] = response

# Example Usage
cache = LLMQueryCache()
user_prompt = "What is the capital of France?"

# First execution (Cache Miss)
cached_res = cache.get(user_prompt)
if cached_res is None:
    # Simulate LLM Call
    llm_output = "The capital of France is Paris."
    cache.set(user_prompt, llm_output)
    print("Fetched from LLM API.")
else:
    print(f"Cache Hit: {cached_res}")

# Second execution (Cache Hit)
cached_res = cache.get(user_prompt)
if cached_res:
    print(f"Cache Hit: {cached_res}")

# Architectural Explanation provided to Interviewer:
# Direct string hashing provides exact-match caching with O(1) lookup time.
# Production Enhancement: Replace exact matching with Semantic Caching (e.g., Redis VL / GPTCache) 
# using embedding similarity thresholds (e.g., cosine distance < 0.05) to catch rephrased queries.

questions.q: What is NLP? Give 3 real-world applications you have seen in production.
questions.a:
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the branch of AI that enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language (text and speech). It combines linguistics, machine learning and deep learning.

Real-world applications:

  • Chatbots and virtual assistants (customer support bots, ChatGPT-style assistants)
  • Sentiment analysis of product reviews / social media
  • Machine translation (Google Translate)
  • Spam and fraud-message detection, email classification
  • Document search, question answering and summarization (RAG systems)

questions.q: What are the stages in the lifecycle of an NLP project (data → deployment → monitoring)?
questions.a:
1. Problem definition – business goal, success metric (accuracy, F1, latency).

2. Data collection – logs, documents, APIs, web scraping, labelled datasets.

3. Data cleaning & preprocessing – remove noise, normalize, tokenize.

4. EDA – word frequencies, class balance, text lengths.

5. Feature engineering / representation – BoW, TF-IDF, embeddings.

6. Modelling – classical ML (Naive Bayes, LR) or deep learning / Transformers / LLMs.

7. Evaluation – precision, recall, F1, BLEU/ROUGE, human evaluation.

8. Deployment – API (FastAPI), batch jobs, containers.

9. Monitoring & maintenance – data drift, model drift, feedback loop, retraining.

questions.q: What are the main challenges in NLP?
questions.a:
• Ambiguity – the same word/sentence can have many meanings.
  • Context and long-range dependencies – meaning depends on earlier text.
  • Sarcasm, irony and idioms – "Great, another Monday!" is negative.
  • Spelling mistakes, slang, emojis, code-mixing (Hinglish).
  • Out-of-vocabulary words and new terminology.
  • Low-resource languages – little labelled data.
  • Domain shift – a model trained on news fails on medical text.
  • Bias in training data, and hallucination in generative models.

questions.q: What is ambiguity in NLP? Explain lexical, syntactic, semantic and pragmatic ambiguity with examples.
questions.a:
Ambiguity means a word, phrase or sentence can be interpreted in more than one way.

  • Lexical ambiguity – a single word has several meanings: "bank" (river bank / money bank).
  • Syntactic (structural) ambiguity – the sentence can be parsed in different ways: "I saw the man with the telescope" (who has the telescope?).
  • Semantic ambiguity – the meaning of the full sentence is unclear even after parsing: "The chicken is ready to eat" (chicken will eat, or chicken will be eaten).
  • Pragmatic ambiguity – meaning depends on context/intent: "Can you pass the salt?" is a request, not a question about ability.
  • (Also anaphoric/referential ambiguity: "John told Mark he won" – who is "he"?)

questions.q: Define corpus, document, vocabulary and token.
questions.a:
• Corpus – a large collection of text documents used for analysis or training (e.g. all Wikipedia articles).
  • Document – a single unit of text in the corpus (one review, one email, one article).
  • Vocabulary – the set of unique tokens/words in the corpus.
  • Token – the smallest unit after tokenization (a word, subword or character).

Example: corpus = 1,000 reviews; each review = document; "good", "bad"... = vocabulary; "I", "love", "it" = tokens.

questions.q: What are the common preprocessing steps in NLP? Which of them should you SKIP when using a Transformer/LLM, and why?
questions.a:
Common steps: lowercasing, removing punctuation/special characters, removing HTML/URLs, tokenization, stopword removal, stemming/lemmatization, handling contractions, spelling correction, removing numbers, handling emojis.

Skip for Transformers/LLMs: stopword removal, stemming/lemmatization, heavy punctuation removal and (often) lowercasing.

Why: Transformers learn from the full context. Words like "not", "no" are stopwords but change meaning ("not good"). Pre-trained models expect natural text with their own tokenizer, so heavy cleaning makes the input look different from the pre-training data and usually reduces accuracy. Only do light cleaning (remove HTML, extra whitespace, PII).

questions.q: What is text normalization? List common normalization methods.
questions.a:
Text normalization converts text into a standard, consistent form so that different variants of the same word are treated alike.

Methods:

  • Lowercasing ("Apple" → "apple")
  • Removing punctuation, special characters, extra whitespace
  • Expanding contractions ("don't" → "do not")
  • Stemming and lemmatization
  • Spelling correction
  • Unicode normalization (removing accents: "café" → "cafe")
  • Converting numbers/dates to a standard format, or replacing them with tokens like <NUM>
  • Handling slang/abbreviations ("u" → "you")

questions.q: What is tokenization? Compare word-level, character-level and subword tokenization.
questions.a:
Tokenization splits text into smaller units called tokens, which are then mapped to IDs for the model.

  • Word-level: "I love NLP" → ["I", "love", "NLP"]. Simple, but huge vocabulary and OOV problem.
  • Character-level: ["I", " ", "l", "o", ...]. Tiny vocabulary, no OOV, but very long sequences and weak meaning per token.
  • Subword-level (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece): "unhappiness" → ["un", "happi", "ness"]. Balanced vocabulary size (30k–200k), rare words are split into known pieces, so no OOV. All modern Transformers/LLMs use subword tokenization.

questions.q: What is stemming and how is it different from lemmatization? When would you prefer each?
questions.a:
Both reduce a word to a base form.

  • Stemming chops suffixes with rules (Porter, Snowball). Fast but crude; output may not be a real word: "studies" → "studi", "running" → "run".
  • Lemmatization uses vocabulary + grammar (POS) to return the dictionary form (lemma): "studies" → "study", "better" → "good" (adjective), "was" → "be".

Prefer stemming for speed on large data (search indexing, simple classifiers). Prefer lemmatization when meaning/readability matters (chatbots, topic modelling, information extraction).

questions.q: Explain over-stemming vs under-stemming with examples.
questions.a:
• Over-stemming: two words with different meanings are reduced to the same stem (false positive). Example: "university" and "universe" → "univers"; "news" → "new".
  • Under-stemming: words with the same meaning are reduced to different stems (false negative). Example: "data" → "dat" but "datum" → "datu"; "alumnus" / "alumni" give different stems.

Lemmatization reduces both problems because it uses a dictionary.

questions.q: Why does WordNetLemmatizer need POS tags? What happens if you don't pass them?
questions.a:
WordNetLemmatizer assumes every word is a noun by default. The lemma depends on the part of speech, so without a POS tag verbs and adjectives are not reduced correctly.

from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer
lem = WordNetLemmatizer()
lem.lemmatize("running")          # 'running'  (treated as noun)
lem.lemmatize("running", pos="v") # 'run'
lem.lemmatize("better", pos="a")  # 'good'

In practice, get POS tags using nltk.pos_tag() and map them to WordNet tags (n, v, a, r).

questions.q: What are contractions (e.g. "don't", "I'm") and how do you handle them?
questions.a:
Contractions are shortened forms of words: "don't" = "do not", "I'm" = "I am", "won't" = "will not".

Why handle them: tokenizers may split them oddly ("don", "'", "t"), and the negation "not" can be lost, which hurts sentiment analysis.

How: expand them using a dictionary or the `contractions` library:

import contractions
contractions.fix("I don't think we'll make it")
# 'I do not think we will make it'

For Transformers, this is usually not required because their tokenizers already handle contractions.

questions.q: How do you handle emojis, URLs, hashtags and HTML tags in text?
questions.a:
• HTML tags: remove with BeautifulSoup `get_text()` or regex `<.*?>`.
  • URLs: remove with regex `https?://\S+` or replace with a token `<URL>`.
  • Hashtags / mentions: remove '#' but keep the word ("#MachineLearning" → "Machine Learning"); replace @user with `<USER>`.
  • Emojis: depends on task – for sentiment, convert to text with `emoji.demojize("ὠ")` → ":grinning_face:" because they carry emotion; otherwise remove them. Modern LLM tokenizers can process emojis directly.
import re, emoji
text = re.sub(r"<.*?>", "", text)
text = re.sub(r"https?://\S+", "<URL>", text)
text = emoji.demojize(text)

questions.q: How do you handle spelling mistakes in user input?
questions.a:
• Spell-check libraries: TextBlob (`TextBlob(t).correct()`), pyspellchecker, SymSpell (very fast, edit-distance based).
  • Edit distance (Levenshtein) to find the closest dictionary word.
  • Context-aware correction using language models (e.g. a T5/BERT-based corrector, or ask an LLM to fix spelling).
  • Use subword tokenization or character-level models (FastText) so misspelled words still get meaningful vectors.
  • For search, use fuzzy matching.

Be careful: do not "correct" domain terms, names or product codes – keep a custom whitelist.

questions.q: What are subword tokenization methods? Explain BPE, WordPiece and SentencePiece briefly.
questions.a:
Subword tokenization splits rare words into frequent smaller units, so the vocabulary stays small and there are no OOV words.

  • BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) – starts with characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent pair of symbols until the vocabulary size is reached. Used by GPT-2/3/4, Llama 3, RoBERTa (byte-level BPE).
  • WordPiece – similar to BPE but merges the pair that maximizes the likelihood of the training data (score = freq(ab) / (freq(a)·freq(b))). Continuation pieces are prefixed with "##". Used by BERT, DistilBERT.
  • SentencePiece – a library that treats text as a raw stream (spaces become "▁"), so it is language-independent and needs no pre-tokenization. Implements BPE or Unigram LM (starts with a big vocabulary and prunes tokens that least reduce likelihood). Used by T5, ALBERT, XLNet, Llama 1/2, Mistral.

questions.q: Explain step by step how the WordPiece tokenizer builds its vocabulary and tokenizes a new word.
questions.a:
Training (building vocabulary):

1. Pre-tokenize text into words (split on whitespace/punctuation).

2. Start with a vocabulary of all single characters; non-initial characters get "##" (e.g. "h", "##u", "##g").

3. For every adjacent pair, compute score = freq(pair) / (freq(first) × freq(second)).

4. Merge the pair with the highest score and add it to the vocabulary.

5. Repeat until the target vocabulary size (e.g. 30,522 for BERT) is reached.

Tokenizing a new word – greedy longest-match-first:

1. Find the longest prefix of the word that is in the vocabulary.

2. Take it as a token, then repeat on the remaining part, looking for "##" pieces.

3. If no piece matches, the whole word becomes [UNK]. Example (bert-base-uncased): "tokenization" → ["token", "##ization"]; "unaffable" → ["una", "##ffa", "##ble"]. The exact split depends on the learned vocabulary.

questions.q: Which tokenizers are used by GPT-family models and by BERT?
questions.a:
• GPT-2 / GPT-3: byte-level BPE (~50k tokens).
  • GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 / GPT-4o: byte-level BPE via OpenAI's tiktoken library (cl100k_base ~100k tokens, o200k_base ~200k tokens).
  • BERT: WordPiece (vocabulary 30,522 for bert-base-uncased).

(For comparison: T5 uses SentencePiece-Unigram; Llama 2 uses SentencePiece-BPE; Llama 3 uses tiktoken-style BPE.)

questions.q: Why does an LLM sometimes struggle to count letters in a word or do arithmetic? (Hint: tokenization.)
questions.a:
LLMs do not see letters or digits – they see tokens. "strawberry" may be one or two tokens, so the model never directly sees the individual letters "r", "r", "r" and must have memorized spelling. Similarly, numbers are split inconsistently ("12345" might be "123" + "45"), so digit-by-digit arithmetic is hard.

Fixes: ask the model to spell the word out first (chain-of-thought), use tools (a Python/calculator tool) for counting and maths, or use models with digit-level tokenization.

questions.q: Write code for word and sentence tokenization (NLTK / spaCy).
questions.a:
import nltk
nltk.download("punkt"); nltk.download("punkt_tab")
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize, sent_tokenize
text = "NLP is fun. Transformers changed everything! Don't you agree?"
print(sent_tokenize(text))
# ['NLP is fun.', 'Transformers changed everything!', "Don't you agree?"]
print(word_tokenize(text))
# ['NLP', 'is', 'fun', '.', 'Transformers', ..., 'Do', "n't", 'you', 'agree', '?']
# spaCy
import spacy
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")      # python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm
doc = nlp(text)
print([t.text for t in doc])
print([s.text for s in doc.sents])
# Subword tokenization (Hugging Face)
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
print(tok.tokenize("Tokenization is unbelievable"))
# ['token', '##ization', 'is', 'unbelievable']

questions.q: Write code for stemming and lemmatization and compare the outputs on the same sentence.
questions.a:
import nltk
nltk.download("wordnet"); nltk.download("averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng")
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer, SnowballStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer
from nltk.corpus import wordnet
from nltk import pos_tag, word_tokenize
text = "The children were running and studies showed better results"
words = word_tokenize(text)
porter = PorterStemmer()
lem = WordNetLemmatizer()
def wn_pos(tag):
    return {"J": wordnet.ADJ, "V": wordnet.VERB, "R": wordnet.ADV}.get(tag[0], wordnet.NOUN)
for w, t in pos_tag(words):
    print(f"{w:10} stem={porter.stem(w):10} lemma={lem.lemmatize(w, wn_pos(t))}")
# children   stem=children   lemma=child
# were       stem=were       lemma=be
# running    stem=run        lemma=run
# studies    stem=studi      lemma=study
# better     stem=better     lemma=good

Observation: the stemmer produces non-words ("studi") and misses irregular forms ("were"), while the lemmatizer returns real dictionary words.

questions.q: Write code for stopword removal. When can removing stopwords hurt a model?
questions.a:
import nltk
nltk.download("stopwords")
from nltk.corpus import stopwords
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize
stop = set(stopwords.words("english"))
text = "This movie is not good and I would not watch it again"
tokens = [w for w in word_tokenize(text.lower()) if w.isalpha() and w not in stop]
print(tokens)   # ['movie', 'good', 'would', 'watch']   <- 'not' was removed!
# Keep negations
stop_custom = stop - {"not", "no", "nor", "never"}
print([w for w in word_tokenize(text.lower()) if w not in stop_custom])
# ['movie', 'not', 'good', 'would', 'not', 'watch']

When removing stopwords hurts: sentiment analysis (negations), question answering ("who", "what"), machine translation, text generation, and any Transformer/LLM, because they rely on full grammatical context.

questions.q: In real-time data users type "Lunch", "lunch" and "LUNCH". Why do we lowercase text, and when should you NOT lowercase?
questions.a:
Why lowercase: so that different surface forms of the same word map to one token/feature. Without it, "Lunch", "lunch" and "LUNCH" become three different vocabulary entries → bigger, sparser vocabulary, fewer examples per word, worse generalization for BoW/TF-IDF/Word2Vec models. Users at inference time type in any case, so training and inference must be normalized the same way.

Do NOT lowercase when case carries meaning:

  • NER: "Apple" (company) vs "apple" (fruit); "US" vs "us".
  • Acronyms, product codes, tickers, IDs ("SBI", "PAN", "IT" department).
  • Sentiment/intent where shouting matters ("I am ANGRY").
  • Transformer/LLM pipelines with cased models – the tokenizer and model were trained on cased text; just pass raw text.

Rule: whatever you do in training, do exactly the same in the inference pipeline.

questions.q: You removed all numeric values from the text. Could numbers contain useful information? How would you handle numbers and punctuation instead?
questions.a:
Yes – numbers often carry the key signal:

  • Prices and amounts ("₹1,999", "20% off"), dates, quantities ("3 days late"), ratings ("5/5"), versions ("iPhone 15"), error codes ("E-4021"), account/transaction amounts in fraud text.

Better approaches than deleting them:

  • Replace with placeholder tokens that keep the type: `<NUM>`, `<PRICE>`, `<DATE>`, `<PERCENT>` (regex or NER).
  • Bucket values ("delay_1_3_days", "amount_high").
  • Extract as structured features (amount, date) for the model alongside the text.
  • Keep them as-is for Transformers/LLMs, which handle numbers in context.

Punctuation: don't blindly drop it – "!!!" signals emotion, "?" signals a question, "not good." vs "not, good" can matter; ":)" is sentiment. Remove only noise for classical models; keep it for Transformers. Decide based on the task and validate with metrics.

questions.q: Users will type stopwords at inference time. If you remove them during training, what happens? When should you remove stopwords and when not? Give practical applications.
questions.a:
Preprocessing must be identical at training and inference – if training removed stopwords, the inference pipeline must remove them too, otherwise the input distribution differs and accuracy drops. The bigger risk is losing meaning: "not", "no", "never", "without" are stopwords in NLTK.

Remove stopwords when: using classical BoW/TF-IDF models for topic-level tasks – document classification by topic, keyword extraction, topic modelling (LDA), search indexing/keyword search – where they add noise and dimensionality.

Keep stopwords when:

  • Sentiment analysis ("not good" ≠ "good").
  • Question answering, chatbots, intent detection ("where", "how", "can I").
  • Machine translation, summarization, text generation, NER.
  • Any Transformer/LLM/RAG pipeline (they need full grammar and context).

Use a custom stopword list that keeps negations if you must remove them.

questions.q: Live-coding: clean this messy real-world review end-to-end and explain why the ORDER of steps matters:
questions.a:
Order matters: remove HTML/URLs/mentions/hashtags before removing punctuation (otherwise "https://..." leaves junk words); expand contractions and slang before removing punctuation (the apostrophe in "it's" is needed); lowercase before dictionary lookups; normalize spaces last.

import re, emoji
SLANG = {"tbh": "to be honest", "plz": "please", "ur": "your", "b4": "before",
         "idk": "i do not know", "btw": "by the way", "gr8": "great", "asap": "as soon as possible"}
CONTRACTIONS = {"it's": "it is", "can't": "cannot", "i'd": "i would", "don't": "do not",
                "i'm": "i am", "won't": "will not"}
def clean(text):
    text = re.sub(r"<.*?>", " ", text)                 # 1. HTML tags
    text = re.sub(r"https?://\S+|www\.\S+", " ", text) # 2. URLs
    text = re.sub(r"[@#]\w+", " ", text)               # 3. mentions + hashtags
    text = emoji.replace_emoji(text, replace=" ")      # 4. emojis
    text = text.lower()                                # 5. lowercase
    for k, v in CONTRACTIONS.items():                  # 6. contractions (needs apostrophe)
        text = text.replace(k, v)
    text = re.sub(r"(\w)\1{2,}", r"\1", text)          # 7. "sooo"->"so", "goodddd"->"good"
    words = [SLANG.get(w, w) for w in text.split()]    # 8. chat slang (before punctuation removal)
    text = " ".join(words)
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z\s]", " ", text)              # 9. punctuation, numbers, symbols
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()           # 10. extra spaces
print(clean(raw))
# hey i just bought this from to be honest it is so good price was rs i got off
# please check your order before buying
print(clean(raw).split())   # tokens

Follow-ups to expect: "goodddd" → "god" if you collapse to one letter blindly (that's why the rule keeps one letter only for 3+ repeats, and some pipelines use a spell-checker afterwards); numbers like "20%" and the price were dropped – mention you would keep them as <PERCENT>/<PRICE> if they matter; for a Transformer you would do only steps 1–4.

questions.q: What is a vector space model in NLP?
questions.a: A vector space model represents every word or document as a numeric vector in a multi-dimensional space. Each dimension is a feature (a vocabulary word, or a learned latent feature). Texts with similar meaning lie close together, so we can measure similarity with cosine similarity or distance, and feed the vectors to ML models. Examples: BoW and TF-IDF (sparse, dimension = vocabulary size) and embeddings (dense, e.g. 300 or 768 dimensions).

questions.q: What is the Bag-of-Words model? What are its limitations?
questions.a:
Bag-of-Words (BoW) represents a document as the count (or presence) of each vocabulary word, ignoring grammar and word order. Example – vocabulary [I, love, NLP, hate]: "I love NLP" → [1, 1, 1, 0].

Limitations:

  • Loses word order: "dog bites man" = "man bites dog".
  • No semantics: "good" and "great" are unrelated dimensions.
  • High-dimensional and sparse (vocab can be 100k+).
  • Cannot handle OOV words.
  • Frequent words dominate unless weighted (→ TF-IDF).

questions.q: What is a Bag of N-grams model? What problem does it solve over plain BoW?
questions.a: A Bag of N-grams counts sequences of N consecutive words instead of single words. Bigrams of "not good movie" → ["not good", "good movie"]. It solves part of BoW's word-order problem: "not good" becomes one feature, so the model can detect negation and short phrases ("New York", "machine learning"). Downside: the vocabulary grows very quickly → even sparser vectors; usually limited to n = 1–3.

questions.q: What is TF-IDF? How do you calculate TF, IDF and TF-IDF? Work out a small example by hand.
questions.a:
TF-IDF weights a word by how important it is to a document relative to the whole corpus.

  • TF(t, d) = (count of t in d) / (total words in d)
  • IDF(t) = log( N / df(t) ), where N = number of documents, df = number of documents containing t
  • TF-IDF = TF × IDF

Worked example (log base 10) – 3 documents: D1 "the cat sat", D2 "the dog sat", D3 "the cat ran".

  • Word "cat" in D1: TF = 1/3; df = 2 → IDF = log(3/2) = 0.176 → TF-IDF = 0.059
  • Word "the" in D1: TF = 1/3; df = 3 → IDF = log(3/3) = 0 → TF-IDF = 0 (common word, no information)
  • Word "ran" in D3: TF = 1/3; df = 1 → IDF = log(3) = 0.477 → TF-IDF = 0.159 (rare word, high weight)

(scikit-learn uses a smoothed version: idf = ln((1+N)/(1+df)) + 1, then L2-normalizes the vector.)

questions.q: What are word embeddings? How are they better than one-hot / BoW vectors?
questions.a:
Word embeddings are dense, low-dimensional vectors (e.g. 100–1024 numbers) learned from data, where words with similar meaning have similar vectors.

Better than one-hot/BoW because:

  • Dense (300 dims vs 100k sparse dims) → less memory, better generalization.
  • Capture semantics: cos(king, queen) is high; famous analogy king − man + woman ≈ queen.
  • Similar words share information, so the model generalizes to words it saw less often.
  • Can be pre-trained on huge corpora and reused (transfer learning).

questions.q: Which algorithms are used to train word embeddings?
questions.a:
• Word2Vec (CBOW and Skip-gram) – Google, 2013
  • GloVe – Stanford, global co-occurrence matrix factorization
  • FastText – Facebook, Word2Vec with character n-grams
  • Doc2Vec – paragraph/document vectors
  • ELMo – contextual embeddings from bi-LSTMs
  • BERT / Transformer-based contextual embeddings
  • Sentence embedding models – Sentence-BERT, OpenAI text-embedding-3, BGE, E5 (used in RAG)

questions.q: Explain Word2Vec and its two architectures (CBOW and Skip-gram). What is the difference?
questions.a:
Word2Vec is a shallow neural network (one hidden layer) that learns word vectors by predicting words from their neighbours within a context window. The learned hidden-layer weights are the embeddings.

  • CBOW (Continuous Bag of Words): predicts the target word from the surrounding context words. Context "the cat __ on the mat" → "sat". Faster, works well for frequent words.
  • Skip-gram: predicts the context words from the target word. "sat" → "the", "cat", "on", "mat". Slower, but better for rare words and small datasets.

Training tricks: negative sampling and hierarchical softmax avoid computing softmax over the whole vocabulary.

questions.q: What are the key hyperparameters of Word2Vec (vector_size, window, min_count, sg, negative) and their role?
questions.a:
• vector_size – embedding dimension (100–300). Larger = more expressive but needs more data.
  • window – max distance between target and context words. Small (2–5) → syntactic similarity; large (5–10) → topical similarity.
  • min_count – ignore words with frequency below this; removes noise/typos.
  • sg – 0 = CBOW, 1 = Skip-gram.
  • negative – number of negative samples (5–20); 0 means use hierarchical softmax (`hs=1`).
  • epochs – passes over the corpus.
  • alpha – learning rate; sample – down-sampling of very frequent words; workers – CPU threads.

questions.q: Compare Word2Vec vs FastText vs GloVe vs Doc2Vec.
questions.a:
• Word2Vec – predictive model using local context windows; one vector per word; cannot handle OOV.
  • GloVe – count-based; factorizes a global word co-occurrence matrix; combines global statistics with local context; also no OOV support.
  • FastText – like Word2Vec but each word = sum of its character n-grams ("where" → "<wh", "whe", "her", "ere", "re>"); handles OOV and misspellings, good for morphologically rich languages.
  • Doc2Vec – extends Word2Vec with a document/paragraph vector (PV-DM and PV-DBOW) to produce a fixed vector for a whole document.

All four are static (one vector per word regardless of context).

questions.q: What is the difference between static embeddings (Word2Vec) and contextual embeddings (BERT)? Give an example with the word "bank".
questions.a:
• Static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) give one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence.
  • Contextual embeddings (ELMo, BERT, GPT) produce a different vector for each occurrence depending on surrounding words.

Example: "I deposited money in the bank " vs "We sat on the river bank ". Word2Vec gives the same vector for both; BERT gives two different vectors – one close to "finance", the other close to "river". This is why contextual models handle ambiguity much better.

questions.q: How do you handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words?
questions.a:
• Subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece) – any word can be built from known pieces; this is the standard solution today.
  • FastText – builds vectors for unknown words from character n-grams.
  • Character-level models.
  • Replace with an <UNK> token (simple but loses information).
  • Spelling correction / lemmatization to map to known words.
  • Use a larger vocabulary or fine-tune on domain data.

questions.q: Explain cosine similarity and why it is important in NLP.
questions.a:
Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors: cos(θ) = (A · B) / (‖A‖ × ‖B‖), ranging from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to 1 (same direction).

Why important in NLP:

  • It measures direction (meaning), not magnitude (length), so a long and a short document on the same topic still score high.
  • Works well for high-dimensional sparse and dense vectors.
  • It is the default metric for semantic search, RAG retrieval, recommendation, duplicate detection and clustering.

questions.q: What similarity / distance metrics are used (cosine, Euclidean, dot product, Jaccard)?
questions.a:
• Cosine similarity – angle between vectors (most common for text).
  • Dot product – cosine × magnitudes; equals cosine for normalized vectors; used by many vector DBs.
  • Euclidean distance (L2) – straight-line distance.
  • Manhattan distance (L1) – sum of absolute differences.
  • Jaccard similarity – |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| for sets of words (good for near-duplicate detection).
  • Levenshtein (edit) distance – for string/spelling similarity.
  • BM25 – ranking function for keyword search.

questions.q: Euclidean distance vs cosine similarity — when would you use which?
questions.a:
• Euclidean distance depends on vector magnitude. A long document has a larger count vector than a short one, so they look far apart even if they are about the same topic.
  • Cosine similarity depends only on the angle (direction), so it ignores length.

Use cosine for text, embeddings, semantic search (most cases). Use Euclidean when magnitude is meaningful (e.g. K-means on normalized numeric features, image features). Note: for L2-normalized vectors, ranking by Euclidean distance and by cosine give the same order.

questions.q: For measuring similarity, why do we use cosine and not sine or tan?
questions.a:
Because cosine behaves exactly like a similarity score should:

  • cos(0°) = 1 → vectors in the same direction = most similar.
  • cos(90°) = 0 → orthogonal = unrelated.
  • cos(180°) = −1 → opposite.

It is monotonically decreasing from 0° to 180°, bounded in [−1, 1], and is cheap to compute from the dot product.

Sine is 0 for both identical (0°) and opposite (180°) vectors, so it cannot distinguish them, and it increases as vectors diverge (a distance-like measure). Tangent is unbounded (infinite at 90°) and undefined there, so it is unusable as a score.

questions.q: How do you check the similarity between two words or two documents?
questions.a:
1. Convert each word/document into a vector – TF-IDF, Word2Vec (average word vectors for a document), or better, a sentence-embedding model.

2. Compute cosine similarity between the vectors.

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
m = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
e = m.encode(["I love machine learning", "I enjoy studying AI", "The weather is hot"])
print(util.cos_sim(e[0], e[1]))   # high  (~0.6)
print(util.cos_sim(e[0], e[2]))   # low   (~0.05)
# Word similarity with Word2Vec
# w2v.wv.similarity("king", "queen")

Other options: Jaccard similarity for word overlap, BM25 for keyword relevance.

questions.q: Create vectors using CountVectorizer (unigrams and bigrams).
questions.a:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
docs = ["I love NLP", "I love deep learning", "NLP is fun"]
# Unigrams
cv1 = CountVectorizer()
X1 = cv1.fit_transform(docs)
print(cv1.get_feature_names_out())
print(X1.toarray())
# Unigrams + bigrams
cv2 = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))
X2 = cv2.fit_transform(docs)
print(cv2.get_feature_names_out())
# ['deep' 'deep learning' 'fun' 'is' 'is fun' 'learning' 'love' 'love deep' 'love nlp' 'nlp' 'nlp
    is']
print(X2.toarray())
# Only bigrams: CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(2, 2))

Note: the default token pattern drops 1-character tokens like "I".

questions.q: Create vectors using TfidfVectorizer and print the top-weighted terms of a document.
questions.a:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
import numpy as np
docs = ["the cat sat on the mat",
        "the dog sat on the log",
        "cats and dogs are great pets"]
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", ngram_range=(1, 2))
X = tfidf.fit_transform(docs)
vocab = tfidf.get_feature_names_out()
# Top-3 weighted terms of document 0
row = X[0].toarray().ravel()
top = np.argsort(row)[::-1][:3]
print([(vocab[i], round(row[i], 3)) for i in top])

Parameters to know: `max_features`, `min_df`, `max_df`, `ngram_range`, `sublinear_tf`, `stop_words`.

questions.q: Train (1) Word2Vec, (2) FastText and (3) Doc2Vec on a small corpus and find similar words.
questions.a:
from gensim.models import Word2Vec, FastText
from gensim.models.doc2vec import Doc2Vec, TaggedDocument
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize
corpus = ["machine learning is fun", "deep learning is a part of machine learning",
          "nlp uses deep learning", "transformers are deep learning models for nlp"]
tokens = [word_tokenize(s.lower()) for s in corpus]
# 1) Word2Vec (sg=1 -> skip-gram)
w2v = Word2Vec(tokens, vector_size=50, window=3, min_count=1, sg=1, epochs=100)
print(w2v.wv.most_similar("learning", topn=3))
# 2) FastText - works for unseen words
ft = FastText(tokens, vector_size=50, window=3, min_count=1, epochs=100)
print(ft.wv.most_similar("learnings", topn=3))     # OOV word still works
# 3) Doc2Vec
tagged = [TaggedDocument(t, [i]) for i, t in enumerate(tokens)]
d2v = Doc2Vec(tagged, vector_size=50, min_count=1, epochs=100)
vec = d2v.infer_vector(word_tokenize("deep learning for nlp"))
print(d2v.dv.most_similar([vec], topn=2))

On a toy corpus the similarities are noisy; use a real corpus (e.g. a few MB of text) for meaningful results.

questions.q: Why can averaging Word2Vec vectors to make a sentence vector lose information? What is better?
questions.a:
Averaging (mean pooling of word vectors) is a simple baseline, but:

  • Word order is lost: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same vector.
  • Negation and composition are lost: "not good" ≈ average of "not" and "good", which stays close to "good".
  • Important words get diluted by many common/filler words in long sentences.
  • Each word has one static vector, so polysemy ("bank") is not resolved.
  • OOV words are simply missing.

Better options: TF-IDF–weighted averaging (down-weights common words), SIF embeddings, Doc2Vec, and today mainly Sentence Transformers / embedding models (SBERT, BGE, E5, OpenAI embeddings) that are trained specifically to produce sentence-level vectors with context and word order.

questions.q: What are Sentence Transformers (SBERT)? Why are they better for semantic search than averaged word vectors or BERT's raw [CLS] vector?
questions.a:
Sentence Transformers (SBERT) are Transformer encoders (BERT/MPNet/MiniLM) fine-tuned with a siamese / bi-encoder setup on sentence pairs (NLI, paraphrase, question–answer pairs) using contrastive losses, so that semantically similar sentences produce embeddings with high cosine similarity.

Why better:

  • Raw BERT [CLS] or mean-pooled BERT vectors were not trained for similarity – their cosine scores are poorly calibrated (often worse than GloVe averages for similarity tasks).
  • Averaged Word2Vec ignores order and context.
  • SBERT encodes the whole sentence in context into one vector that directly supports cosine search, clustering and RAG retrieval; it is fast because documents are encoded once and compared with dot products.
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
q = model.encode("How do I get my money back?")
d = model.encode(["Refund policy: refunds within 7 days", "Office timings are 9 to 6"])
print(util.cos_sim(q, d))   # first document scores much higher

questions.q: Pretrained embeddings vs training embeddings on your own domain data – which would you choose and when?
questions.a:
Use pretrained embeddings (default): small or medium datasets; general language; quick start. Models trained on billions of words capture semantics you cannot learn from a few thousand documents.

Train or fine-tune on domain data when: the domain has its own vocabulary or word meanings (medical, legal, banking codes, internal product names), the pretrained model has many OOV/rare terms, and you have a large domain corpus (millions of tokens) – or fine-tune a pretrained model (continue training / contrastive fine-tuning of a sentence-embedding model on domain query–document pairs).

Best practice: start with a strong pretrained model, measure on your task (e.g. retrieval recall@k), then fine-tune if domain terms are the cause of errors.

questions.q: Explain embeddings to a non-technical person without using the word "vector".
questions.a: An embedding is like giving every word or sentence a position on a giant map of meaning. Things that mean similar things are placed close together – 'refund', 'money back' and 'return payment' sit in the same neighbourhood, while 'office timings' is far away. The computer learns these positions by reading huge amounts of text and noticing which words appear in similar situations. So when a customer asks 'How do I get my money back?', we look up where that question lands on the map and pick the documents placed nearest to it – even if they use completely different words like 'refund policy'. That's how the system finds answers by meaning, not just by matching exact words.

questions.q: How does a neural network work? Explain with a single neuron first.
questions.a:
Single neuron: takes inputs x₁…xₙ, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function: z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ + b, output a = f(z)

Network: neurons are arranged in layers – input layer → hidden layers → output layer. Each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs.

Learning:

1. Forward pass – compute predictions.

2. Loss – compare predictions with true labels.

3. Backpropagation – compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight (chain rule).

4. Update – an optimizer adjusts weights to reduce the loss.

5. Repeat over many batches and epochs until the loss stops decreasing. Non-linear activations let the network learn complex, non-linear patterns.

questions.q: What is the weight update formula in a neural network?
questions.a: Gradient descent update rule: w_new = w_old − η × ∂L/∂w b_new = b_old − η × ∂L/∂b where η is the learning rate and ∂L/∂w is the gradient of the loss with respect to the weight. We move opposite to the gradient because the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.

questions.q: Define: epoch, sample, batch size, iteration, learning rate, weights, biases.
questions.a:
• Epoch – one complete pass of the entire training dataset through the network.
  • Sample – a single data point (one row / one sentence / one image).
  • Batch size – number of samples processed before one weight update (e.g. 32).
  • Iteration (step) – one weight update = one batch. Iterations per epoch = dataset size / batch size. (1,000 samples, batch 100 → 10 iterations per epoch.)
  • Learning rate – step size used when updating weights.
  • Weights – learnable parameters that scale each input; they store what the network has learned.
  • Biases – learnable offsets added to the weighted sum; let a neuron activate even when all inputs are zero (shifts the activation function).

questions.q: What is the difference between a loss function and a cost function?
questions.a:
• Loss function – error for a single training example, e.g. (y − ŷ)².
  • Cost function – average (or sum) of the losses over the whole batch/dataset, possibly plus regularization terms, e.g. MSE = (1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)².

The optimizer minimizes the cost function. In practice the two words are often used interchangeably.

questions.q: Explain the learning rate. What happens if it is too high or too low?
questions.a:
The learning rate (η) controls how big a step the optimizer takes in the direction of the negative gradient.

  • Too high: the updates overshoot the minimum, the loss oscillates or diverges (becomes NaN).
  • Too low: training is very slow, may get stuck in a poor local minimum/plateau, and needs many epochs.
  • Good practice: start with typical values (Adam: 1e-3; fine-tuning Transformers: 1e-5 to 5e-5; LoRA: 1e-4 to 2e-4), use a learning-rate finder, warm-up and schedulers (decay).

questions.q: Explain forward propagation and backpropagation.
questions.a:
Forward propagation: input data passes layer by layer. For each layer, z = W·x + b and a = f(z). The last layer gives the prediction ŷ, and the loss L(y, ŷ) is computed.

Backpropagation: computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight using the chain rule, starting from the output layer and moving backward: ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂a × ∂a/∂z × ∂z/∂w Each layer reuses the gradients already computed for the layer after it, which makes it efficient. The optimizer then uses these gradients to update weights. Frameworks (PyTorch autograd, TensorFlow GradientTape) do this automatically.

questions.q: What is data normalization/standardization and why is it needed for neural networks?
questions.a:
Normalization (min-max scaling): x' = (x − min) / (max − min) → range [0, 1].

Standardization (z-score): x' = (x − μ) / σ → mean 0, std 1.

Why needed:

  • Features on very different scales (age 0–100, salary 0–10,00,000) cause large-scale features to dominate gradients.
  • Gradient descent converges much faster and more stably when features are on similar scales (the loss surface is less elongated).
  • Avoids saturating activation functions (sigmoid/tanh) with very large inputs.

Important: fit the scaler on training data only, then transform validation/test data with it (avoid data leakage).

questions.q: What are the different types of optimizers (SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, Adam, AdamW)?
questions.a:
• SGD – basic gradient descent on mini-batches.
  • SGD with Momentum – adds a velocity term to accelerate and smooth updates.
  • Nesterov Accelerated Gradient – momentum that "looks ahead".
