questions.q: What is a Python REPL tool? What are the security risks of letting an LLM execute code?
questions.a:
REPL = Read–Eval–Print Loop – an interactive environment that reads code, executes it and returns the output (like the Python shell). A Python REPL tool lets the LLM write Python code and run it, then read the result – useful for maths, data analysis (pandas), plotting and file processing.

# pip install langchain-experimental
from langchain_experimental.tools import PythonREPLTool
agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools=[PythonREPLTool()])

Security risks: arbitrary code execution – the model (or a prompt-injected document) could delete files, read secrets/environment variables, exfiltrate data over the network, install malware or consume resources.

Mitigations: run code in an isolated sandbox (Docker container, E2B, gVisor) with no secrets, no or restricted network, read-only file system, CPU/memory/time limits; human approval for risky actions; never run it on production servers.

questions.q: Create one custom tool and one custom agent.
questions.a:
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
ORDERS = {"A101": "Shipped - arriving 14 Oct", "A102": "Processing"}
class OrderInput(BaseModel):
    order_id: str = Field(description="Order ID like A101")
@tool(args_schema=OrderInput)
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    '''Look up the delivery status of a customer order.'''
    return ORDERS.get(order_id.upper(), "Order not found")
@tool
def refund_policy() -> str:
    '''Return the company's refund policy.'''
    return "Refunds within 7 days of delivery for unused items."
system = "You are a polite e-commerce support agent. Use tools; never invent order data."
agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools=[get_order_status, refund_policy], prompt=system)
res = agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Where is my order a101 and can I return it?")]})
print(res["messages"][-1].content)

A fully custom agent can also be built as a LangGraph graph (LLM node + ToolNode + conditional edge) – see the LangGraph answers.

questions.q: What is LangGraph? Why use it instead of a simple agent loop?
questions.a:
LangGraph is a library (from LangChain) for building stateful, controllable agents and multi-step workflows as graphs: nodes are functions/LLM calls, edges define the flow, and a shared state is passed between them.

Why use it instead of a simple agent loop:

  • Explicit control flow – loops, branches, retries, parallel steps; mix deterministic steps with LLM decisions.
  • Persistence/memory via checkpointers – resume conversations, long-running tasks, "time travel" debugging.
  • Human-in-the-loop – pause before sensitive actions for approval/editing.
  • Multi-agent architectures (supervisor, hierarchical).
  • Streaming of tokens and intermediate steps; fault tolerance.
  • Production deployment and observability (LangSmith, LangGraph Platform).

Simple loops break down when you need reliability, state and control; LangGraph makes them explicit.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What is State in LangGraph? How are nodes and edges added? (add_node, add_edge)
questions.a:
State is the shared data structure (usually a `TypedDict` or Pydantic model) that flows through the graph. Every node receives the current state and returns updates to it. Reducers define how updates are merged – e.g. `Annotated[list, add_messages]` appends messages instead of overwriting.

from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]
    category: str
def classify(state: State):
    return {"category": "billing"}           # partial state update
def respond(state: State):
    return {"messages": [("ai", f"Routing you to {state['category']}")]}
graph = StateGraph(State)
graph.add_node("classify", classify)          # add_node(name, function)
graph.add_node("respond", respond)
graph.add_edge(START, "classify")             # add_edge(from, to)
graph.add_edge("classify", "respond")
graph.add_edge("respond", END)
app = graph.compile()
print(app.invoke({"messages": [("user", "I was charged twice")]}))
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: How do you add a conditional edge? What are START and END, set_entry_point and set_finish_point?
questions.a:
Conditional edge – after a node runs, a routing function reads the state and returns the name of the next node:

def route(state: State) -> str:
    return "billing_node" if state["category"] == "billing" else "tech_node"
graph.add_conditional_edges("classify", route,
                            {"billing_node": "billing_node", "tech_node": "tech_node"})
# Typical agent loop: from langgraph.prebuilt import tools_condition
# graph.add_conditional_edges("llm", tools_condition)   # -> "tools" or END
  • START – a special virtual node representing the entry of the graph; `add_edge(START, "x")` makes x the first node.
  • END – a special node meaning the graph finishes; `add_edge("x", END)`.
  • set_entry_point("x") – older equivalent of `add_edge(START, "x")`.
  • set_finish_point("x") – older equivalent of `add_edge("x", END)` – marks x as a node after which the graph stops.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: How does LangGraph support memory/checkpointing and human-in-the-loop?
questions.a:
Memory / checkpointing: compile the graph with a checkpointer; after every step LangGraph saves the full state for a `thread_id`. Calling again with the same thread_id continues the conversation; you can inspect history and "time travel" to earlier states.

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver       # SqliteSaver / PostgresSaver in prod
app = graph.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "customer-42"}}
app.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Hi")]}, cfg)

Human-in-the-loop: pause execution so a human can approve, edit or reject:

app = graph.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver(), interrupt_before=["issue_refund"])
app.invoke(inputs, cfg)               # stops before the refund node
print(app.get_state(cfg).values)      # human reviews the state
app.update_state(cfg, {"approved": True})
app.invoke(None, cfg)                 # resume

(Newer API: call `interrupt(value)` inside a node and resume with `Command(resume=...)`.) The Store API adds long-term memory shared across threads.

questions.q: What is CrewAI? How do you create agents, tasks and run a crew?
questions.a:
CrewAI is a Python framework for building multi-agent systems where several role-playing agents (each with a role, goal and backstory) collaborate on tasks as a crew, like a team of employees.

# pip install crewai crewai-tools
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process
from crewai_tools import SerperDevTool
researcher = Agent(role="Senior Research Analyst",
                   goal="Find the latest developments in {topic}",
                   backstory="Expert at finding and verifying information.",
                   tools=[SerperDevTool()], llm="gpt-4o-mini", verbose=True)
writer = Agent(role="Tech Content Writer",
               goal="Write an engaging blog post on {topic}",
               backstory="Turns complex research into simple articles.", llm="gpt-4o-mini")
research_task = Task(description="Research the top 5 trends in {topic}.",
                     expected_output="Bullet list of 5 trends with sources.", agent=researcher)
write_task = Task(description="Write a 400-word blog post using the research.",
                  expected_output="Markdown blog post.", agent=writer,
                  context=[research_task], output_file="blog.md")
crew = Crew(agents=[researcher, writer], tasks=[research_task, write_task],
            process=Process.sequential, verbose=True)     # or Process.hierarchical
result = crew.kickoff(inputs={"topic": "Agentic AI"})
print(result)

Agent = role, goal, backstory, tools, llm; Task = description, expected_output, agent, context; Crew.kickoff() runs it.

questions.q: Single-agent vs multi-agent systems — when is multi-agent worth the complexity?
questions.a:
Single agent – one LLM with a set of tools. Simpler, cheaper, faster, easier to debug. Good for most use cases (support bot, RAG assistant).

Multi-agent – several specialized agents (researcher, coder, reviewer) coordinated by a supervisor or a workflow.

Worth the complexity when:

  • The task has clearly separable sub-tasks needing different expertise, prompts or tools.
  • There are too many tools for one agent to choose from reliably (> ~10–15).
  • You need parallel work or a reviewer/critic step that checks another agent's output.
  • Different sub-tasks need different models (cheap vs strong) or permissions.

Costs: more LLM calls (cost/latency), coordination failures, harder debugging and evaluation. Start with one agent and split only when you measure a benefit.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol) and what problem does it solve?
questions.a:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard (introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, now widely adopted by OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and IDEs) for connecting AI applications to external tools, data sources and prompts in a uniform way – often described as " USB-C for AI applications ".

Problem it solves: without it, every AI app had to build custom integrations for every tool (M apps × N tools = M×N connectors). With MCP, a tool provider builds one MCP server (e.g. for GitHub, Slack, a database, Google Drive), and any MCP client/host (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, your own LangGraph agent) can use it → M + N.

Architecture: host app → MCP client → MCP server, communicating with JSON-RPC over stdio (local) or HTTP (remote). Servers expose tools (actions), resources (data/files) and prompts (templates). Security: treat third-party servers as untrusted code; review permissions; beware tool poisoning and prompt injection.

questions.q: How do you evaluate and debug agents (traces, LangSmith/Langfuse, step-level metrics)?
questions.a:
• Tracing/observability: log every step – LLM inputs/outputs, tool calls and arguments, tool results, latency, tokens and cost – with LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, or OpenTelemetry. Inspect traces of failed runs.
  • End-to-end metrics: task success rate / goal completion, final-answer correctness (vs reference or LLM-as-judge), user feedback.
  • Step-level (trajectory) metrics: was the correct tool chosen, were arguments valid, number of steps vs optimal, redundant calls, error/retry rate, did it stop correctly.
  • Efficiency: latency, cost per task, tokens.
  • Safety: policy violations, unauthorized actions, prompt-injection resistance (red teaming).
  • Build a test suite of scenarios (including edge cases) and run it on every prompt/model/tool change (regression testing); unit-test tools separately; use deterministic mocks for external APIs.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What are common agent failure modes (infinite loops, wrong tool choice, cost blow-ups) and how do you guard against them?
questions.a:
Common failure modes:

  • Infinite loops / repeated tool calls – the agent keeps searching or retrying.
  • Wrong tool choice or wrong/hallucinated arguments (invented IDs).
  • Cost and latency blow-ups – too many steps or huge contexts.
  • Hallucinated tool results or claiming an action was done when it wasn't.
  • Prompt injection through tool outputs; unsafe or irreversible actions.
  • Losing track of the goal in long tasks; context overflow.

Guards:

  • Max iterations / recursion limit (LangGraph `recursion_limit`), timeouts, and per-task token/cost budgets.
  • Clear tool names, descriptions and Pydantic schemas; validate arguments; fewer, well-designed tools.
  • Error handling in tools that returns helpful messages instead of crashing.
  • Human approval for high-impact actions; least-privilege permissions; sandboxing.
  • Deterministic workflow steps where possible; caching repeated calls.
  • Monitoring, alerts and evaluation suites.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What is Agentic AI, and how is it different from standard Generative AI or a RAG chatbot?
questions.a:
• Generative AI (standard): the model takes an input and produces content in one shot – answer, summary, code. RAG adds a fixed retrieve-then-generate step. The flow is defined by the developer and the model does not act on the world.
  • Agentic AI: the LLM works toward a goal autonomously over multiple steps – it plans, decides which tools/APIs to call, observes results, keeps state/memory, can correct itself, and takes actions (create ticket, query DB, send email), possibly coordinating with other agents.

Example: a RAG bot answers "What is the refund policy?". An agent handles "Refund my last order" – looks up orders, checks eligibility, calls the refund API, asks for confirmation and updates the CRM. Trade-offs: agents are more capable but less predictable, slower, costlier, and need guardrails, permissions and human approval for risky actions.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: Who decides which tool to call? What if the model selects the wrong tool? Why shouldn't an agent have access to every tool?
questions.a:
Who decides: the LLM decides, based on the user request, the conversation and the tool names, descriptions and argument schemas; the application executes the call and can block it.

If it picks the wrong tool:

  • Improve tool descriptions (when to use / when NOT to use), names and schemas; add few-shot examples.
  • Reduce and group tools – fewer, distinct tools; route to a sub-agent with a small toolset.
  • Validate arguments; return clear error messages so the agent can recover.
  • Add deterministic routing for known intents; evaluate tool-selection accuracy in tests.

Why not every tool: more tools → more confusion and wrong selections, bigger prompts (cost/latency), and a larger attack surface – a prompt injection could trigger dangerous tools. Follow least privilege: give each agent only the tools and permissions it needs for its task.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: Your agent has 10 tools. The user asks a simple question, but the agent calls 5 different tools. How do you fix this?
questions.a:
1. Inspect traces – which tools, why (its reasoning), and whether descriptions overlap.

2. Route simple queries first: a classifier/router answers FAQ-type questions directly or with one retrieval call; only complex requests go to the full agent.

3. Tighten tool descriptions and system prompt: "Call a tool only if the answer requires it; prefer answering directly; use the minimum number of tools."

4. Reduce the toolset exposed per request (dynamic tool selection based on intent).

5. Limits: max tool calls / recursion limit, per-request token budget, caching of repeated tool results.

6. Use a cheaper/faster model for routing and a stronger one only when needed.

7. Add tests and metrics for tool-call count and unnecessary calls; regression-test after changes.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: Would you let an LLM perform a sensitive action automatically, like deleting a customer record or making a financial transaction? Should the LLM decide permissions?
questions.a:
No – not without controls. The LLM can propose the action, but:

  • Permissions are enforced by the application/backend, never by the LLM – the tool checks the authenticated user's role, scope and limits in code.
  • Human-in-the-loop approval for destructive, financial or irreversible actions (show a summary, require confirmation/maker-checker approval).
  • Least privilege: read-only tools by default; separate, narrowly scoped write tools; soft-delete instead of hard delete.
  • Validation and limits: business rules in code (amount caps, eligibility), idempotency keys, rate limits.
  • Audit logs of every action; ability to roll back; monitoring and alerts.
  • Protection against prompt injection (an email or document must never be able to trigger a transfer).
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What is the difference between normal function calling and MCP? In MCP, what is the difference between tools and resources?
questions.a:
• Function calling – a model/API feature: you define functions (JSON schemas) inside your application; the model returns a call; your app executes it. Tools are hard-wired into one application and each provider has its own format.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) – an open protocol/standard for how AI applications discover and connect to external capabilities. Tools live in separate MCP servers that any MCP-compatible client (Claude, ChatGPT, IDEs, your agent) can connect to. Under the hood the model still uses function calling – MCP standardizes the integration layer (discovery, schemas, transport, auth), so one server can be reused by many apps.

MCP primitives:

  • Tools – actions the model decides to invoke, which may have side effects (create ticket, run query).
  • Resources – read-only data/context exposed by the server (files, DB records, documents), usually selected by the application/user and loaded into context.
  • Prompts – reusable prompt templates exposed by the server.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: How would you run three independent agents in parallel and make sure one agent's failure doesn't break the others? How do you add retries with backoff?
questions.a:
Parallel execution: run them concurrently with `asyncio.gather` (I/O-bound LLM/API calls) or as parallel branches in LangGraph (fan-out from one node to three nodes, then a join node).

Failure isolation:

  • `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` or wrap each agent in try/except so one exception doesn't cancel the others.
  • Per-agent timeouts (`asyncio.wait_for`), separate error states, and partial results – the aggregator handles missing outputs gracefully.
  • Circuit breakers for repeatedly failing dependencies; bulkheads (separate worker pools/queues) in production.

Retries: retry only transient errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff + jitter and a max attempt count (e.g. `tenacity`), and make actions idempotent.

import asyncio
async def run_agent(name, coro, timeout=30):
    try:
        return name, await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout)
    except Exception as e:
        return name, {"error": repr(e)}          # isolate failure
async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        run_agent("research", research_agent(q)),
        run_agent("sql", sql_agent(q)),
        run_agent("policy", policy_agent(q)))
    return dict(results)
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: LangChain vs LangGraph – when would you use each?
questions.a:
• LangChain – building blocks and integrations (models, prompts, loaders, splitters, vector stores, retrievers, output parsers) and LCEL for linear or simple branching pipelines (prompt → model → parser; standard RAG chain).
  • LangGraph – orchestration for stateful, cyclic, multi-step workflows and agents: loops, conditional routing, retries, persistence (checkpointing), human-in-the-loop, multi-agent coordination, streaming of intermediate steps.

Rule: a straightforward chain or RAG pipeline → LangChain/LCEL; anything with loops, decisions, tools, long-running state or approvals → LangGraph (which uses LangChain components inside its nodes).
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What is the planner–executor architecture? How does it differ from a supervisor (orchestrator) agent?
questions.a:
• Planner–executor (plan-and-execute): a planner LLM first creates a step-by-step plan for the whole task; an executor (agent with tools) carries out each step; the planner can re-plan based on results. Good for long, multi-step tasks; fewer expensive reasoning calls; more predictable.
  • Supervisor / orchestrator agent: a central agent receives the request and delegates sub-tasks to specialized worker agents (research agent, SQL agent, writer agent), routing dynamically at each step and combining their outputs. Focus is on delegation and coordination rather than an upfront plan.

They can be combined: a supervisor whose first step is to create a plan.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: What is agent memory? What are the risks of long-term memory and stale information?
questions.a:
• Short-term memory – the current conversation/thread state (messages, tool results), kept in the context or a checkpointer.
  • Long-term memory – facts persisted across sessions (user preferences, past decisions, summaries), stored in a DB/vector store and retrieved when relevant. Types: semantic (facts), episodic (past interactions), procedural (learned instructions).

Risks:

  • Stale or wrong facts reused confidently (old address, outdated policy).
  • Privacy – storing personal data; consent and right-to-delete.
  • Memory poisoning – injected instructions saved as "memories".
  • Context bloat and cost.

Mitigations: timestamps and TTL/expiry, re-validate against the source system of record for important facts, store facts not instructions, user-visible and deletable memories, PII policies, scoping memory per user/tenant.
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: In a Text-to-SQL agent, how do you prevent the LLM from executing destructive or hallucinated SQL queries?
questions.a:
• Read-only database user (SELECT-only grants) on a read replica; never give DDL/DML rights.
  • SQL validation layer before execution: parse with `sqlglot`/`sqlparse`; allow only SELECT; block DROP/DELETE/UPDATE/INSERT/ALTER, multiple statements and comments; allow-list tables/columns; enforce LIMIT and query timeouts.
  • Schema grounding: give the LLM the exact schema, column descriptions and sample values so it doesn't invent tables/columns; validate identifiers against the real schema.
  • Row-level security / views so users only see permitted data.
  • Dry-run / EXPLAIN to catch errors and expensive queries; self-correction loop with the DB error message (max 2–3 tries).
  • Human approval for any write operation; audit logging of generated SQL.
  • Evaluate on a test set of question→SQL pairs (execution accuracy).
questions.page: Assignment 12: Agents: Tools, LangGraph, CrewAI, MCP

questions.q: When should you fine-tune an LLM and when should you not?
questions.a:
Fine-tune when:

  • You need a consistent style, tone or output format that prompting cannot reliably achieve.
  • A narrow, repetitive task (classification, extraction, routing) where a small fine-tuned model can replace a large expensive one → lower cost and latency.
  • Domain language/jargon the base model handles poorly (medical, legal, internal codes).
  • You have enough good-quality labelled examples (hundreds to thousands).
  • Data must stay on-prem with an open model.

Don't fine-tune when:

  • The problem is missing or changing knowledge → use RAG.
  • Good prompting or few-shot examples already work → start with prompting.
  • You have little/poor data, or no evaluation set.
  • Requirements change often (each change means retraining).

Order to try: prompt engineering → RAG → fine-tuning (or combine).

questions.q: What is Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) and why is it needed?
questions.a:
PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) adapts a large pre-trained model by training only a small number of (new or selected) parameters while keeping most original weights frozen. Methods: LoRA, QLoRA, adapters, prefix tuning, prompt tuning, (IA)³.

Why needed:

  • Full fine-tuning of a 7B+ model needs enormous GPU memory (~16 bytes/parameter with Adam → 100+ GB) and compute.
  • Storing a full copy of the model for every task/customer is expensive; PEFT adapters are only a few MB.
  • Less overfitting and less catastrophic forgetting on small datasets.
  • Makes fine-tuning possible on a single consumer/Colab GPU; often reaches quality close to full fine-tuning.

questions.q: What are the challenges of full fine-tuning and how does LoRA overcome them?
questions.a:
Challenges of full fine-tuning:

  • Memory: gradients and optimizer states for all billions of parameters.
  • Compute/time and cost.
  • Storage: a full model copy (e.g. 14 GB) per fine-tuned task.
  • Catastrophic forgetting and overfitting on small datasets.

How LoRA overcomes them:

  • Freezes the original weights and trains only small low-rank matrices (often < 1% of parameters) → far fewer gradients and optimizer states → much less memory.
  • Faster training; can use bigger batches or smaller GPUs.
  • Adapters are tiny (MBs) – one base model can serve many task-specific adapters, swapped at runtime.
  • Original weights unchanged → less forgetting; after training, adapters can be merged into the weights, so there is no extra inference latency.

questions.q: Explain how LoRA works. How are the weight matrices updated? (W + BA)
questions.a:
Idea: the weight change needed for a new task has a low intrinsic rank, so instead of learning a full update ΔW (d × k), LoRA learns it as the product of two small matrices:

W' = W₀ + ΔW = W₀ + (α / r) · B · A

  • W₀ (d × k) – frozen pre-trained weight.
  • A (r × k) – initialized with small random values; B (d × r) – initialized with zeros, so ΔW = 0 at the start (training begins from the original model).
  • r ≪ min(d, k), e.g. r = 8.

Forward pass: h = W₀x + (α/r)·B(Ax).

Update: during backprop, gradients are computed only for A and B; the optimizer updates them; W₀ never changes.

Parameter saving example: d = k = 4096 → full ΔW = 16.8M parameters; LoRA with r = 8 → 8 × (4096 + 4096) = 65,536 parameters (≈ 0.4%). After training: merge W = W₀ + (α/r)BA for zero inference overhead, or keep adapters separate.

questions.q: What are the 'r' (rank) and 'alpha' parameters in LoRA? Which layers do you apply LoRA to?
questions.a:
• r (rank) – the inner dimension of the LoRA matrices B (d × r) and A (r × k). It controls the capacity of the adapter: larger r = more trainable parameters and expressiveness, more memory, higher overfitting risk. Typical values 4, 8, 16, 32, 64; 8–16 is a common start; bigger for complex tasks/large datasets.
  • lora_alpha – a scaling factor; the update is multiplied by α / r. It controls how strongly the adapter affects the output (similar to a learning-rate multiplier). Common rule: α = r or α = 2r (e.g. r = 16, α = 32).
  • target_modules (which layers) – originally only the attention query and value projections (q_proj, v_proj); today it is common to apply LoRA to all linear layers (q, k, v, o projections + MLP gate/up/down projections), which usually gives better quality.
  • Also: lora_dropout (0.05–0.1), bias.

questions.q: LoRA vs QLoRA — what is the difference and when would you use each?
questions.a:
QLoRA = Quantized base model + LoRA.

  • LoRA: base model loaded in 16-bit (FP16/BF16); LoRA adapters trained on top.
  • QLoRA: base model loaded in 4-bit NF4 (NormalFloat-4) and frozen; LoRA adapters trained in 16-bit. Gradients flow through the de-quantized weights. Extra tricks: double quantization (quantize the quantization constants) and paged optimizers (avoid out-of-memory spikes).

Memory: QLoRA cuts base-model memory by ~4× → a 7B model trains on a single ~16 GB GPU (even free Colab T4), 65–70B on a single 48–80 GB GPU.

When to use:

  • LoRA – enough GPU memory; you want faster training and slightly better quality / no quantization error.
  • QLoRA – limited GPU memory or large models; accept ~20–40% slower training (de-quantization overhead) and a very small quality drop.

questions.q: What is SFT (supervised fine-tuning)? How do you prepare an instruction dataset and chat template?
questions.a:
SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) trains the model on (prompt, ideal response) pairs with next-token prediction loss, usually computed only on the response tokens.

Preparing an instruction dataset:

  • Collect high-quality examples: instruction, optional input/context, desired output (or multi-turn conversations). Quality and diversity matter more than size (1k–10k good examples can be enough).
  • Clean: remove duplicates, PII, wrong answers; balance classes; keep a held-out validation/test split.
  • Store as JSONL in a standard format, e.g. the messages format:
{"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a fraud analyst assistant."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Classify: 'Your KYC expires, click link'"},
              {"role": "assistant", "content": "Phishing"}]}

Chat template: each model expects a specific special-token format for roles. Always use the tokenizer's built-in template so training matches inference:

text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(example["messages"], tokenize=False)

questions.q: How do you format prompts for fine-tuning an open-source chat model (e.g. Llama-style [INST] templates)?
questions.a:
Llama-2-chat style format (Mistral-Instruct uses a similar [INST] format):

<s>[INST] <<SYS>>
You are a helpful assistant.
<</SYS>>
What is LoRA? [/INST] LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method ... </s>
<s>[INST] Next user question [/INST] Next answer </s>

Llama 3 uses a different template with header tokens:

<|begin_of_text|><|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are a helpful assistant.<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What is LoRA?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
LoRA is ...<|eot_id|>

Best practice: don't hand-write these; use `tokenizer.apply_chat_template()` and the same format at inference. For a base model, a simple "### Instruction: ... ### Response: ..." (Alpaca) format also works if used consistently.

questions.q: Which libraries are used to fine-tune LLMs (transformers, PEFT, TRL, bitsandbytes, Unsloth, Axolotl)?
questions.a:
• Hugging Face transformers – models, Trainer.
  • PEFT – LoRA, QLoRA, adapters, prompt tuning.
  • TRL – SFTTrainer, DPOTrainer, PPO/GRPO, reward modelling.
  • bitsandbytes – 8-bit/4-bit quantization (QLoRA).
  • accelerate / DeepSpeed / FSDP – multi-GPU & distributed training, memory optimization (ZeRO).
  • Unsloth – 2× faster, lower-memory LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning.
  • Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, torchtune – config-driven fine-tuning frameworks.
  • datasets (data loading), evaluate, Weights & Biases / MLflow (tracking).
  • Managed: OpenAI fine-tuning API, Azure AI Foundry, AWS SageMaker/Bedrock, Google Vertex AI.

questions.q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you avoid it?
questions.a:
Catastrophic forgetting – when a model is fine-tuned on a new task, it loses previously learned general abilities (e.g. after fine-tuning on legal Q&A it gets worse at general conversation, maths or instruction following), because the weights are overwritten.

How to avoid:

  • Use PEFT/LoRA (original weights frozen) with a modest rank.
  • Lower learning rate and fewer epochs; early stopping.
  • Mix general-purpose data (replay data) with the task data.
  • Regularization toward the original weights (e.g. KL penalty, EWC).
  • Evaluate on general benchmarks as well as the task before and after fine-tuning.
  • Keep separate task adapters instead of one heavily modified model.

questions.q: How do you evaluate a fine-tuned model against the base model?
questions.a:
• Prepare a held-out test set from the same distribution as real use (never used in training), plus some general-ability tests.
  • Task metrics: accuracy/F1 (classification), exact match / field-level accuracy (extraction), ROUGE/BLEU (summarization/translation), pass@k (code).
  • LLM-as-judge pairwise comparison (base vs fine-tuned answers, blind and order-swapped) for open-ended outputs, plus human review of a sample.
  • Compare against strong baselines: base model with a good prompt, few-shot, RAG, and a larger API model.
  • Check format adherence, hallucination rate, latency and cost per request.
  • Check regressions on general benchmarks (MMLU, safety tests) for catastrophic forgetting.
  • Finally, A/B test in production.

questions.q: How do you fine-tune Whisper for speech-to-text?
questions.a:
Whisper (OpenAI) is an encoder–decoder Transformer for speech recognition. Fine-tuning improves accuracy for a specific language, accent or domain vocabulary (e.g. Marathi, Indian English, medical terms).

Steps (Hugging Face):

1. Data: audio + transcript pairs (e.g. Common Voice or your own call recordings); resample audio to 16 kHz.

2. Processor: `WhisperProcessor` = feature extractor (log-Mel spectrogram) + tokenizer; set language and task ("transcribe").

3. Preprocess: compute input_features from audio; tokenize transcripts into labels.

4. Data collator that pads features and labels (labels padding = −100).

5. Load `WhisperForConditionalGeneration` (small/medium for limited GPU; optionally LoRA/8-bit with PEFT).

6. Train with Seq2SeqTrainer / Seq2SeqTrainingArguments (lr ~1e-5, warm-up, fp16, predict_with_generate=True).

7. Evaluate with WER (word error rate) via `evaluate.load("wer")`.

8. Save/push the model and serve with the ASR pipeline.

questions.q: Fine-tune a small model with LoRA on a classification or instruction dataset using PEFT + TRL.
questions.a:
# pip install transformers peft trl datasets bitsandbytes accelerate
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig
model_id = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"               # small model for Colab
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)   # QLoRA (remove for plain LoRA)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
# Dataset in chat "messages" format
ds = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/no_robots", split="train[:2000]")
lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                  target_modules="all-linear")
args = SFTConfig(output_dir="qwen-lora", num_train_epochs=1, per_device_train_batch_size=4,
                 gradient_accumulation_steps=4, learning_rate=2e-4, logging_steps=20,
                 bf16=True, max_length=1024)
trainer = SFTTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=ds,
                     peft_config=lora, processing_class=tokenizer)
trainer.model.print_trainable_parameters()   # e.g. trainable: 0.9% of all params
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("qwen-lora-adapter")      # saves only the adapter (MBs)
# Inference: load base + adapter
from peft import PeftModel
base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
ft = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "qwen-lora-adapter")
# ft = ft.merge_and_unload()   # optional: merge for faster inference

(TRL argument names change between versions – check the installed version's docs.)

questions.q: What are the end-to-end steps to fine-tune an LLM for a business use case?
questions.a:
1. Define the goal and success metric; confirm fine-tuning is needed (prompting/RAG tried first).

2. Collect and prepare data: high-quality input→output examples in chat format; clean, deduplicate, remove PII; split train/validation/test.

3. Choose the base model (size, licence, language, context length) and method – LoRA/QLoRA usually.

4. Set up training: tokenizer + chat template, hyperparameters (LR 1e-4–2e-4 for LoRA, epochs 1–3, rank 8–16, batch size, max length), mixed precision.

5. Train with Hugging Face TRL/PEFT (or a managed service); monitor training/validation loss for overfitting.

6. Evaluate against the base model and baselines on the test set (task metrics, LLM-judge, human review) and check general abilities and safety.

7. Merge/export and optimize (merge adapters, quantize), deploy (vLLM/TGI or managed endpoint).

8. Monitor in production, collect feedback and new data, retrain periodically.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an LLM application? (Offline vs online, reference-based vs reference-free.)
questions.a:
Offline evaluation (before release):

  • Build a test set of realistic inputs with reference answers or grading criteria.
  • Reference-based metrics compare output with a known correct answer: exact match, F1, accuracy, BLEU/ROUGE, semantic similarity, LLM-judge "is it equivalent to the reference?".
  • Reference-free metrics judge the output on its own: faithfulness to retrieved context, relevance, toxicity, format validity, LLM-as-judge rubric scores (helpfulness, correctness, tone).
  • Component-level evaluation: retrieval (recall@k, MRR, context precision/recall) separately from generation.
  • Non-functional: latency, cost per request, robustness, safety/red-team tests.

Online evaluation (in production):

  • User feedback (thumbs up/down, ratings), task completion, escalation rate to humans, conversation length.
  • A/B tests between prompts/models.
  • Sampled LLM-judge scoring of live traffic, monitoring of drift and failures.

Tools: RAGAS, DeepEval, LangSmith, Langfuse, TruLens, promptfoo, OpenAI Evals.

questions.q: What is RAGAS? What metrics evaluate the retriever and the generator?
questions.a:
RAGAS (Retrieval-Augmented Generation Assessment) is an open-source framework for evaluating RAG pipelines, largely reference-free, using LLMs (and embeddings) as judges.

Retriever metrics:

  • Context precision – are the relevant chunks ranked at the top?
  • Context recall – did retrieval find all the information needed for the ground-truth answer?
  • (Context entities recall, noise sensitivity.)

Generator metrics:

  • Faithfulness – is the answer supported by the retrieved context (no hallucination)?
  • Answer relevancy – does the answer address the question?
  • (Answer correctness / factual correctness and answer similarity vs a reference answer.)
from ragas import evaluate
from ragas.metrics import faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"question": qs, "answer": answers,
                          "contexts": contexts, "ground_truth": refs})
print(evaluate(data, metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall]))

(Newer RAGAS versions rename fields to user_input / response / retrieved_contexts / reference.)

questions.q: Explain faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and context recall.
questions.a:
• Faithfulness – measures whether every claim in the answer can be inferred from the retrieved context. An LLM splits the answer into individual statements and checks each against the context. Score = supported claims / total claims (0–1). Low faithfulness = hallucination. Example: context says "refund within 7 days", answer says "refund within 30 days" → unfaithful.
  • Answer relevancy – measures how well the answer addresses the question (not whether it is true). RAGAS asks an LLM to generate possible questions from the answer and computes the average cosine similarity between them and the original question. Incomplete or off-topic/padded answers score low.
  • Context precision – measures whether the relevant retrieved chunks are ranked higher than irrelevant ones (a precision@k averaged over ranks). High = little noise at the top of the results.
  • Context recall – measures whether the retrieved context contains all the information needed to produce the ground-truth answer: each sentence of the reference answer is checked for whether it can be attributed to the context. Needs a reference answer. Low recall = retriever missed information.

questions.q: What is LLM-as-a-judge? What are its biases and how do you reduce them?
questions.a:
LLM-as-a-judge – using a strong LLM to grade outputs of another model/system, with a rubric: score 1–5 for correctness/helpfulness, pass/fail against criteria, or pairwise comparison ("Which answer is better, A or B?"). Scales human-like evaluation cheaply; agrees reasonably well with human raters when well designed.

Biases:

  • Position bias – prefers the first (or second) answer.
  • Verbosity bias – prefers longer answers.
  • Self-preference bias – prefers outputs from its own model family.
  • Inconsistency between runs; weak at checking facts/maths it doesn't know.

Mitigations:

  • Swap A/B order and average (or count only consistent wins).
  • Clear, specific rubrics with examples; ask for reasoning before the score; use binary/low-granularity scales.
  • Use a judge from a different model family, temperature 0.
  • Provide reference answers/context when available.
  • Calibrate against human labels on a sample; use multiple judges.

questions.q: Explain BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR and perplexity. Where is each used?
questions.a:
• BLEU – measures n-gram precision (1–4 grams) of the generated text against reference(s), with a brevity penalty for too-short outputs. 0–1 (or 0–100). Mainly for machine translation.
  • ROUGE – measures n-gram recall/overlap against references: ROUGE-1 (unigrams), ROUGE-2 (bigrams), ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence). Mainly for summarization.
  • METEOR – combines precision and recall (recall weighted higher) and matches stems and synonyms (WordNet), with a penalty for word-order fragmentation. Correlates better with human judgement than BLEU; used for translation/captioning.
  • Perplexity – exp(average negative log-likelihood) of a text under a language model; how "surprised" the model is. Lower = better language modelling/fluency. Used to evaluate LM pre-training and compare models on the same tokenizer/dataset.

Limitation of n-gram metrics: they reward word overlap, not meaning – a correct paraphrase can score low; so for LLM outputs, semantic similarity (BERTScore) and LLM-as-judge are often preferred.

questions.q: What metric is used to evaluate speech-to-text (WER, CER)?
questions.a:
• WER (Word Error Rate) – the standard metric: WER = (S + D + I) / N, where S = substitutions, D = deletions, I = insertions, N = number of words in the reference transcript. Lower is better (0 = perfect; can exceed 1).
  • CER (Character Error Rate) – same formula at character level; better for languages without clear word boundaries (Chinese, Japanese) or for spelling-level accuracy.
import evaluate
wer = evaluate.load("wer")
print(wer.compute(predictions=["i love deep learning"], references=["i love deep learning
    models"]))  # 0.2

Normalize text (case, punctuation) before scoring. Also track latency (real-time factor).

questions.q: How do you build a golden evaluation dataset?
questions.a:
1. Collect real inputs: sample actual user queries/logs (anonymized), plus questions from domain experts covering all important topics.

2. Cover the distribution: easy, hard, multi-hop, ambiguous, out-of-scope ("should say I don't know"), adversarial/prompt-injection, different languages/phrasings.

3. Create reference answers: have domain experts write or verify the ideal answers and the source documents/chunks that contain them. LLMs can draft synthetic Q&A pairs from documents (e.g. RAGAS test-set generator), but humans must review them.

4. Add metadata: category, difficulty, expected source.

5. Size: start with ~50–200 high-quality examples; grow over time.

6. Version it and keep it separate from training data; add every production failure as a new test case.

questions.q: How do you measure hallucination rate in production?
questions.a:
• Automated faithfulness checks on sampled traffic: run an LLM-judge / RAGAS faithfulness or an NLI model to check whether each answer's claims are supported by the retrieved context; hallucination rate = % of answers with unsupported claims.
  • Citation verification: check that quoted/cited sources exist and actually contain the cited text.
  • Detectors: e.g. self-consistency checks (sample several answers, flag disagreement), dedicated hallucination-detection models (e.g. Vectara HHEM, Lynx).
  • User signals: thumbs down, "that's wrong" corrections, escalations to human agents.
  • Human audit: experts review a random sample weekly to calibrate the automated metrics.
  • Track the rate on a dashboard over time, by topic and by model/prompt version, with alerts when it rises.

questions.q: How do you evaluate retrieval quality? Explain Precision@K, Recall@K, MRR (and nDCG).
questions.a:
Need a test set of queries with the known relevant chunks/documents.

  • Precision@K = (relevant chunks in top K) / K – how much of what we retrieved is useful (noise).
  • Recall@K = (relevant chunks in top K) / (all relevant chunks for that query) – did we find everything needed. Most important for RAG (missing context = wrong answer).
  • Hit rate@K – % of queries where at least one relevant chunk is in the top K.
  • MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) = average over queries of 1 / (rank of the first relevant result). Rank 1 → 1.0, rank 2 → 0.5, rank 4 → 0.25.
  • nDCG@K – rewards relevant results at higher ranks, supports graded relevance (highly vs partly relevant).

Example: top-5 results, relevant at positions 2 and 4, total relevant = 3 → Precision@5 = 2/5 = 0.4, Recall@5 = 2/3 = 0.67, reciprocal rank = 1/2 = 0.5. For LLM-based RAG evaluation without labels, use RAGAS context precision/recall.

questions.q: How do you compare two prompt versions, and what are regression testing and shadow testing for LLM apps?
questions.a:
• Comparing prompt versions: run both on the same golden dataset; score with task metrics, format validity, LLM-as-judge (pairwise, order-swapped) and a human sample; compare latency and tokens/cost; inspect disagreements. Then A/B test in production.
  • Regression testing: every change (prompt, model version, retriever, chunking) is automatically re-run against the golden set in CI/CD; the build fails if quality metrics drop below thresholds or previously fixed cases break.
  • Shadow testing: the new version runs in parallel on real production traffic without its output being shown to users; responses are logged and compared with the current version (LLM-judge, metrics) – safe way to validate before rollout.
  • Canary release follows: expose the new version to a small % of users, watch metrics, then expand or roll back.

questions.q: How do you deploy an LLM application to production? Describe the architecture.
questions.a:
Typical production architecture:

  • Frontend – web/mobile chat UI or integration (Slack, WhatsApp, internal portal).
  • API layer – FastAPI/Node service behind an API gateway: authentication, rate limiting, request validation, streaming responses (SSE/WebSockets).
  • Orchestration – LangChain/LangGraph application logic: prompt templates, RAG chain or agent, tools.
  • Guardrails – input checks (PII, prompt injection, topic filters) and output checks (toxicity, PII leakage, format).
  • Model layer – LLM API (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI/Bedrock/Vertex) or self-hosted models on GPUs (vLLM/TGI on Kubernetes), via a model gateway (LiteLLM) for routing, fallbacks and retries.
  • Data layer – vector DB, document ingestion pipeline (scheduled re-indexing), cache (Redis), conversation store (Postgres).
  • Observability – tracing (LangSmith/Langfuse), logs, metrics (latency, tokens, cost), evaluation and feedback.
  • CI/CD – Docker containers, automated eval tests on prompt/model changes, secrets management, versioned prompts/configs.

Start simple (one service + managed APIs) and scale components as needed.

questions.q: How do you reduce latency and cost (caching, smaller models, streaming, batching, prompt compression, routing)?
questions.a:
• Right-size the model: use smaller/cheaper models for simple tasks; route only hard queries to large models (model cascade/router).
  • Caching: exact-match and semantic caching of responses; prompt caching offered by providers for repeated long prefixes (system prompt, documents) – big savings on cost and time-to-first-token.
  • Streaming – show tokens as they arrive (perceived latency drops even if total time is the same).
  • Reduce tokens: shorter prompts, fewer/better retrieved chunks (re-ranking), summarize history, set max_tokens, ask for concise output.
  • Batching – batch offline jobs (Batch APIs are ~50% cheaper); continuous batching for self-hosted models.
  • Parallelize independent calls (retrieval + classification at the same time).
  • Self-hosting optimizations: quantization, vLLM, speculative decoding, GPU right-sizing.
  • Fine-tune a small model to replace a large one for high-volume narrow tasks.
  • Monitor cost per request/feature and set budgets/alerts.

questions.q: What are vLLM, TGI and Ollama? What is continuous batching and PagedAttention?
questions.a:
• vLLM – open-source, high-throughput LLM inference/serving engine (from UC Berkeley). Uses PagedAttention and continuous batching, exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, supports quantization, tensor parallelism, LoRA adapters. Production choice for self-hosted serving.
  • TGI (Text Generation Inference) – Hugging Face's production serving toolkit (Rust/Python) with continuous batching, streaming, quantization, tensor parallelism.
  • Ollama – easy tool to run LLMs locally (laptop/desktop/server) with one command (`ollama run llama3.1`); uses llama.cpp and GGUF quantized models; great for development and small-scale/private use, not for high-throughput serving.
  • Continuous (in-flight) batching – instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish (static batching), the server adds new requests to the batch and removes finished ones at every generation step, so the GPU stays fully utilized → several times higher throughput.
  • PagedAttention – stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks ("pages") that need not be contiguous, like virtual memory in an operating system. Removes memory fragmentation and over-reservation, allows sharing of common prefixes between requests → many more concurrent sequences per GPU.

questions.q: What is Groq / LPU inference and why is its latency so low?
questions.a:
Groq is a company that built a custom AI inference chip called the LPU (Language Processing Unit) and offers a cloud API (GroqCloud) running open models (Llama, Mixtral, Qwen, Whisper) at very high speed (hundreds to over a thousand tokens/second).

Why latency is so low:

  • LLM token generation is memory-bandwidth bound – a GPU must repeatedly read the weights from external HBM. Groq's LPU keeps model weights in large amounts of on-chip SRAM, which is far faster than HBM.
  • Deterministic, compiler-scheduled architecture – the compiler plans every operation and data movement in advance, so there is no runtime scheduling, caches or contention overhead.
  • Many chips are linked with a fast, synchronous interconnect so a model is spread across chips and runs as a pipeline.

Trade-off: needs many chips per model (limited SRAM per chip), supports a selected set of models.

questions.q: What is semantic caching?
questions.a:
Semantic caching stores previous queries and their responses with embeddings. For a new query, compute its embedding and search the cache; if a stored query is semantically similar above a threshold (e.g. cosine > 0.95), return the cached answer instead of calling the LLM. Example: "How do I reset my password?" and "Steps to change my login password" → same cached answer.

Benefits: lower cost and latency for repetitive questions (FAQs, support).

Risks: wrong answers if the threshold is too low (questions that look similar but differ – "credit card limit" vs "debit card limit"); stale answers (set TTL/invalidate when data changes); personalization and access control (don't share user-specific answers across users). Tools: GPTCache, Redis vector cache, LangChain `RedisSemanticCache`.

questions.q: What are guardrails? How do you handle PII, toxic content and jailbreaks?
questions.a:
Guardrails are checks and controls around the LLM that enforce safety, security, compliance and quality rules on inputs and outputs.

  • PII: detect and mask/redact personal data (names, phone numbers, Aadhaar/PAN, card numbers) before sending to the LLM and before logging (Microsoft Presidio, regex, NER); prevent PII leakage in outputs; data retention policies.
  • Toxic/harmful content: moderation models/APIs (OpenAI Moderation, Llama Guard, Azure Content Safety) on input and output.
  • Jailbreaks & prompt injection: classifiers (e.g. Prompt Guard), strong system prompts, separating instructions from data, least-privilege tools, human approval for sensitive actions.
  • Topic and policy rails: keep the bot on allowed topics (NeMo Guardrails), refuse financial/medical advice if required.
  • Output validation: JSON schema validation, grounding/faithfulness checks, citation requirements (Guardrails AI library).
  • Logging, rate limiting and red-team testing.

questions.q: How do you monitor an LLM app in production (latency, tokens, cost, feedback, drift)?
questions.a:
• Operational metrics: request volume, latency (p50/p95/p99, time-to-first-token), error rates, timeouts, rate-limit hits, GPU utilization (if self-hosted).
  • Usage and cost: input/output tokens per request, cost per user/feature/day, cache hit rate.
  • Quality: user feedback (thumbs up/down), LLM-judge scores on sampled traffic, faithfulness/hallucination rate, refusal rate, escalation to humans, task success.
  • Retrieval health: empty or low-score retrievals, top sources used.
  • Drift: changes in query topics/distribution (cluster query embeddings), new unanswered question types, document freshness, provider model version changes.
  • Safety: guardrail triggers, prompt-injection attempts, PII detections.
  • Tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Helicone, Datadog/Grafana + OpenTelemetry; dashboards with alerts; feed failures back into the test set.

questions.q: What is Gradio / Streamlit used for? Build a quick demo UI for your RAG app.
questions.a:
Gradio and Streamlit are Python libraries for building quick web UIs/demos for ML and LLM apps without frontend code. Gradio is especially simple for model demos (and Hugging Face Spaces); Streamlit is better for data apps/dashboards.

# pip install gradio
import gradio as gr
def answer(message, history):
    result = rag_chain.invoke(message)          # the RAG chain built earlier
    sources = ", ".join({d.metadata.get("source", "?") for d in result["docs"]})
    return f"{result['answer']}\n\nSources: {sources}"
demo = gr.ChatInterface(fn=answer, title="Company Policy Assistant",
                        examples=["What is the leave policy?", "How do I claim travel expenses?"])
demo.launch(share=True)          # share=True gives a temporary public link
# Streamlit equivalent (app.py; run: streamlit run app.py)
# import streamlit as st
# q = st.chat_input("Ask a question")
# if q: st.chat_message("assistant").write(rag_chain.invoke(q)["answer"])

questions.q: Which speech-to-text and text-to-speech models have you used?
questions.a:
Answer from your own experience. A good structure: which model, why, what result. Speech-to-text (ASR): OpenAI Whisper (open-source; tiny → large-v3; multilingual incl. Hindi/Marathi; faster-whisper / whisper.cpp for speed), OpenAI gpt-4o-transcribe API, Google Speech-to-Text, Azure AI Speech, AWS Transcribe, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, AI4Bharat IndicConformer (Indian languages).

Text-to-speech (TTS): OpenAI TTS, ElevenLabs, Azure Neural TTS, Google TTS, Amazon Polly; open-source Coqui XTTS, Piper, Bark, Kokoro, AI4Bharat Indic-TTS. Example answer: "I used Whisper-small fine-tuned on call-centre audio to transcribe customer calls, measured with WER (reduced from 28% to 15%), then summarized the transcripts with an LLM." Mention evaluation (WER), latency and handling of accents/noise.

questions.q: What is the difference between a POC and a production-grade GenAI architecture?
questions.a:
POC: proves feasibility fast – a notebook/Streamlit app, one LLM API, local Chroma/FAISS, sample documents, manual testing, no auth, hard-coded prompts.

Production adds:

  • Scalable ingestion pipeline (incremental sync, parsing, OCR, retries, idempotency) and a managed/scalable vector DB.
  • API backend (FastAPI), auth/SSO, RBAC on documents, rate limiting, multi-tenancy.
  • Reliability: timeouts, retries with backoff, fallbacks between models/providers, caching, queues for async work.
  • Security & compliance: guardrails, PII redaction, prompt-injection defences, secrets management, audit logs, data residency.
  • Evaluation & LLMOps: golden dataset, CI regression tests, prompt/model versioning, tracing, monitoring of cost/latency/quality, feedback loop.
  • Infrastructure: containers, Kubernetes/serverless, autoscaling, CI/CD, IaC, cost controls.

Interview tip: the model code is ~10% of a production GenAI system.

questions.q: How would you host an LLM application to keep latency low during high traffic spikes?
questions.a:
• Stateless API layer (FastAPI in containers) behind a load balancer with autoscaling (Kubernetes HPA / Cloud Run) on concurrency/latency.
  • Self-hosted models: vLLM/TGI with continuous batching and PagedAttention, quantized models, GPU autoscaling with warm minimum replicas (cold GPU starts are slow), KV-cache/prefix caching.
  • API models: spread load across regions/deployments and providers; request higher rate limits; fallback model on 429/timeouts.
  • Queue + async processing for non-interactive work; back-pressure and rate limiting per user to protect the system.
  • Caching: semantic cache and prompt caching for frequent queries.
  • Streaming responses for perceived latency; smaller models/routing for easy queries.
  • Load testing (Locust/k6) and monitoring p95/p99 latency, queue depth and error rates.

questions.q: How do you handle flaky LLM APIs – timeouts, rate limits (429) and server errors?
questions.a:
• Timeouts on every call (connect + read) so requests don't hang.
  • Retries only for transient errors (timeouts, 429, 500/502/503) with exponential backoff + jitter and a max number of attempts; respect the `Retry-After` header; never blindly retry non-idempotent actions.
  • Fallbacks: secondary deployment/region or alternative model/provider (LangChain `.with_fallbacks()`, LiteLLM router).
  • Circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling the failing service for a cool-down period and fail fast/fall back.
  • Rate limiting & queuing on your side to stay under provider quotas; token budgeting.
  • Caching to avoid repeated calls; graceful degradation message to users.
  • Monitor error rates and alert. (See the backoff code in Assignment 18.)

questions.q: What is prompt caching, and how is it different from semantic caching? How do you invalidate a cache?
questions.a:
• Prompt caching (provider-side): the LLM provider caches the processed prefix of a prompt (long system prompt, tool definitions, large documents). Later requests with the same prefix reuse it → lower input cost (often 50–90% cheaper on cached tokens) and faster time-to-first-token. The answer is still generated fresh. Put static content first, variable content last.
  • Semantic caching (application-side): you store question → final answer pairs with embeddings; a new question that is semantically similar enough returns the stored answer without calling the LLM.
  • Exact-match caching: hash of the exact prompt/parameters → stored response.

Invalidation: TTL/expiry; invalidate entries when the underlying documents or prompt/model version change (include the doc version and prompt version in the cache key); don't cache personalized or sensitive answers across users; similarity threshold tuning to avoid wrong hits.

questions.q: What is the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications? Explain excessive agency and data exfiltration.
questions.a:
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is a list of the most critical security risks in LLM apps, including: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply-chain risks, data and model poisoning, improper output handling (e.g. executing model output as code/SQL), excessive agency, system-prompt leakage, vector/embedding weaknesses, misinformation (hallucination), and unbounded consumption (cost/DoS).

  • Excessive agency: the LLM/agent has more functionality, permissions or autonomy than needed (e.g. a support bot with delete-account and database-write access, acting without approval). Fix: least privilege, minimal tools, scoped credentials, human approval for high-impact actions.
  • Data exfiltration: sensitive data leaves the system through the AI – e.g. an injected instruction makes the agent send confidential data to an external URL/email, or render a markdown image link with data in the URL. Fix: restrict outbound tools/domains, sanitize outputs, PII/DLP filters, treat retrieved content as untrusted, monitoring.

questions.q: How do you deploy a GenAI change safely, and how do you roll back a bad AI deployment?
questions.a:
• Version everything: prompts, model versions, retriever/chunking configs, embedding model, code – as configuration in Git.
  • Pre-deployment: offline evaluation and regression tests in CI; security tests.
  • Shadow testing on live traffic, then canary release (e.g. 5% of users) with feature flags, watching quality (feedback, judge scores), latency, cost and error metrics.
  • Gradual rollout if healthy.
  • Rollback: switch the feature flag/config back to the previous prompt/model version or redeploy the previous container image (blue-green deployment); keep the previous vector index version available when changing embeddings/chunking (re-indexing is not instant).
  • Post-incident: add the failing cases to the golden dataset.

questions.q: Design a chatbot that answers questions over 10,000 internal company PDFs. Cover ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector DB, retrieval, reranking, LLM choice, evaluation and monitoring.
questions.a:
Clarify first: users and scale (how many employees, queries/day), document types (scanned? tables?), languages, access control (who can see which documents), latency target, data privacy (can data go to an external API?), update frequency.

Ingestion pipeline:

  • Connectors to SharePoint/Drive/S3; scheduled incremental sync (detect new/changed/deleted files).
  • Parsing with layout awareness (Unstructured/Docling/Azure Document Intelligence); OCR for scanned PDFs; tables to Markdown.
  • Chunking: structure-aware recursive chunks, ~500–800 tokens, 10–15% overlap; keep metadata (title, section heading, page, department, access group, date).
  • Embeddings: e.g. text-embedding-3-small or BGE (self-hosted if data is sensitive); batch jobs.
  • Vector DB: 10k PDFs ≈ 0.5–2M chunks → Qdrant/pgvector/Pinecone/OpenSearch with HNSW + metadata filtering for access control.

Query pipeline:

  • Query rewriting with chat history → hybrid search (BM25 + vector) top-30 → cross-encoder re-ranker → top-5 → LLM with a strict grounded prompt and citations (document + page links).
  • Permission filter applied at retrieval time based on the user's groups.
  • LLM choice: a strong mid-size model (GPT-4o-mini/Claude Haiku/Llama-3-70B self-hosted) – benchmark on your test set; route complex questions to a bigger model.
  • Streaming responses, semantic cache for frequent questions.

Evaluation: golden set of ~200 Q&A pairs from domain experts; RAGAS (context recall/precision, faithfulness, answer relevancy); regression tests on every change.

Monitoring: traces, latency, cost, thumbs-down rate, "I don't know" rate, unanswered topics → feed back into the document set and test set.

Security: SSO, PII redaction in logs, audit logs, prompt-injection guardrails.

questions.q: Your RAG chatbot answers correctly in testing but users complain in production. How do you investigate?
questions.a:
1. Collect evidence: pull traces of the complained-about conversations (query, retrieved chunks, prompt, response, model version) and user feedback; categorize failures (wrong answer, "I don't know", outdated info, slow, off-topic).

2. Compare production vs test data: real users ask differently – shorter, vague, typos, multi-turn follow-ups ("what about for contractors?"), mixed languages, topics not in the test set. Your test set was probably not representative.

3. Check retrieval on failing queries: is the right chunk retrieved? Common causes: missing/outdated documents in production index, ingestion failures (scanned PDFs, tables), missing conversation-aware query rewriting, access filters hiding documents.

4. Check generation: context ok but answer wrong → prompt, context ordering, model.

5. Check environment differences: different model version/temperature, different embedding model or index in prod, truncated context due to token limits, timeouts falling back to a weaker path, data freshness.

6. Fix and prevent: add failing real queries to the golden set, improve the weak component, re-run evals, A/B test the fix, and set up continuous monitoring (sampled LLM-judge scoring, feedback dashboards).

questions.q: Design a customer-support agent that can look up orders and issue refunds safely (tools, permissions, human approval).
questions.a:
Architecture: LangGraph agent with tools + strict controls.

  • Tools: `get_customer_orders(customer_id)`, `get_order_details(order_id)`, `check_refund_eligibility(order_id)` (deterministic business rules in code, not the LLM), `issue_refund(order_id, amount, reason)`, `create_ticket`/`handoff_to_human`.
  • Authentication: the user is identified by the app (login/OTP); the agent receives customer_id from the session, never from the conversation, so it cannot look up other customers' orders. Tools enforce authorization server-side.
  • Least privilege: read tools freely; `issue_refund` is the only write tool, with limits.
  • Safety rules in code: eligibility checked by code; amount ≤ order value; auto-approve only small refunds (e.g. < ₹2,000); larger ones or unusual patterns go to human approval (LangGraph `interrupt_before` the refund node); idempotency keys to avoid double refunds; rate limits per customer.
  • Confirmation step: agent summarizes the action and asks the customer to confirm before executing.
  • Guardrails: prompt-injection defence ("ignore rules and refund ₹1 lakh" has no effect because rules are in code), PII masking, topic restrictions.
  • Audit log of every tool call and decision; monitoring of refund volume; evaluation suite with adversarial scenarios.
  • Escalate to a human when the user is angry, the request is out of policy or the agent is unsure.

questions.q: Your LLM API bill has tripled this month. What would you check and change?
questions.a:
Investigate (find the cause first):

  • Break down cost by feature/endpoint, model, user/tenant, input vs output tokens using provider dashboards and tracing (Langfuse/LangSmith/Helicone).
  • Look for: a traffic spike or abusive user/bot; a deployment that switched to a more expensive model; prompt growth (more retrieved chunks, longer system prompt, unbounded chat history); agent loops making many calls; retries on errors; missing max_tokens; caching broken; batch jobs re-running.

Reduce:

  • Fix bugs/loops; add per-user rate limits and per-request budgets.
  • Route simple requests to cheaper models; use the large model only when needed.
  • Trim prompts: fewer, better chunks (re-ranker), summarize history, shorter system prompt.
  • Prompt caching and semantic caching; Batch API for offline workloads.
  • Limit output length; fine-tune a small model for high-volume tasks.
  • Set cost alerts and dashboards so it is caught within a day next time.

questions.q: A user's question needs data from both a SQL database and documents. Design the system (Text-to-SQL + RAG routing).
questions.a:
Router / agent design:

1. Query classification/routing: an LLM (or classifier) decides whether the question needs structured data (SQL), unstructured documents (RAG), or both. E.g. "What was our Q3 revenue in Maharashtra and what does the policy say about regional discounts?" → both.

2. Text-to-SQL path:

  • Provide the LLM the relevant schema (table/column descriptions, retrieved from a schema index if the DB is large), sample rows and few-shot question→SQL examples.
  • Generate SQL → validate (read-only user, SELECT only, allowed tables, LIMIT, syntax check) → execute → on error, feed the error back for self-correction (max 2–3 retries).
  • Summarize the result rows.

3. RAG path: normal retrieval over documents.

4. Synthesis: the LLM combines both results into one answer with citations (SQL query shown + document sources).

Implementation: LangGraph with nodes for route → sql_agent / rag → combine; or an agent with two tools (`run_sql`, `search_docs`).

Safety & quality: read-only DB replica, row-level security, timeouts, evaluate SQL accuracy on a test set (execution accuracy).

questions.q: How would you build a multilingual (e.g. Hindi/Marathi + English) GenAI assistant?
questions.a:
• Model choice: a multilingual LLM that handles Indian languages well (GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude, Llama 3.x/Qwen, or Indic models like Sarvam/Krutrim) – evaluate on real Hindi/Marathi/Hinglish queries first.
  • Language detection of input (including code-mixed and romanized text like "mera balance kitna hai") and reply in the user's language/script.
  • Retrieval: multilingual embeddings (bge-m3, multilingual-e5, Cohere multilingual) so a Marathi query can match English documents (cross-lingual retrieval); or translate the query to English for retrieval and translate the answer back; keep key terms (product names) untranslated.
  • Tokenization cost: Indic scripts use more tokens per word on many tokenizers → higher cost/latency; account for it.
  • Voice: many users prefer voice – ASR (Whisper/IndicConformer) + TTS for Indian languages.
  • Evaluation: native-speaker test sets per language; check fluency, correctness and tone (formal vs informal "aap/tum").
  • Fallback to English or a human agent when confidence is low.

questions.q: Design a document-extraction pipeline that pulls structured fields from invoices/forms with an LLM.
questions.a:
1. Ingest: receive PDFs/images (email, upload, S3).

2. Document understanding: OCR + layout (Azure Document Intelligence, AWS Textract, Docling/PaddleOCR) or a vision-LLM reading page images directly; classify document type (invoice, PAN form, bank statement).

3. Extraction: LLM with structured output (Pydantic schema: invoice_no, date, vendor, GSTIN, line_items[], total, tax) at temperature 0; provide field definitions and few-shot examples.

4. Validation (code, not LLM): schema validation, data types, date formats, GSTIN/PAN regex, line items sum = total, tax calculations, duplicate invoice check, vendor exists in master data.

5. Confidence & human review: low-confidence or failed-validation documents go to a human-in-the-loop review UI; corrections are stored to improve prompts/fine-tuning.

6. Output: push to ERP/database via API; keep an audit trail linking each field to its source page/bounding box.

7. Evaluation: field-level precision/recall/accuracy on a labelled set; straight-through-processing rate; cost and latency per document.

questions.q: How would you handle confidential data when using a third-party LLM API?
questions.a:
• Use enterprise offerings with contractual guarantees: zero data retention, no training on your data, data residency in the required region (e.g. Azure OpenAI in an India region, AWS Bedrock, Vertex AI), private networking (VPC/private endpoints), SOC2/ISO certifications; sign a DPA.
  • Data minimization: send only what is needed (relevant chunks, not whole databases).
  • Redact/mask PII (names, account numbers, Aadhaar/PAN) before sending, re-insert placeholders after (Presidio); tokenization/pseudonymization.
  • Classify data: highly confidential data → self-hosted open models on-prem/VPC; less sensitive → API.
  • Access control: users see only documents they are authorized for; enforce at retrieval.
  • Logging: don't store raw sensitive prompts; encrypt logs; retention limits; audit trails.
  • Comply with regulations (DPDP Act in India, GDPR, RBI/sector guidelines); involve security/legal teams.

questions.q: P95 latency of your assistant is 12 seconds. How do you bring it under 3 seconds?
questions.a:
First measure where the 12 seconds go (tracing per step: query rewrite, embedding, retrieval, re-ranking, LLM time-to-first-token, generation, tool calls, network). Then:

  • Stream the response – users see text within ~1 s (time-to-first-token), which often solves the perceived problem.
  • Reduce output tokens – generation time is roughly proportional to output length; ask for concise answers, set max_tokens.
  • Smaller/faster model for most queries (or a fast provider like Groq), large model only for complex ones; avoid reasoning models where not needed.
  • Shorter prompts – fewer/better chunks via re-ranking; prompt caching of the static prefix.
  • Parallelize independent steps (retrieval from multiple sources, guardrail checks) with asyncio/RunnableParallel.
  • Remove or merge LLM calls – e.g. combine query rewriting + classification into one call, or skip rewriting for first-turn questions; fewer agent steps.
  • Cache frequent answers (semantic cache) and embeddings.
  • Faster infrastructure: vector DB in the same region, HNSW tuning, self-hosted model with vLLM + quantization + speculative decoding.
  • Re-measure p95 after each change.

questions.q: How would you A/B test two prompts or two models in production?
questions.a:
1. Define the success metric up front: thumbs-up rate, task completion, escalation rate, conversion, plus guardrail metrics (latency, cost, hallucination rate).

2. Offline check first: both variants must pass the evaluation suite.

3. Randomly assign users (not individual requests) to A (control) or B (variant) using a feature flag/config, e.g. 90/10 → 50/50; keep the assignment sticky per user.

4. Log the variant ID with every trace.

5. Run long enough for statistical significance (calculate sample size; avoid stopping early; account for weekday effects).

6. Analyze: compare metrics with significance tests/confidence intervals; check segments (languages, query types) and side effects (cost, latency).

7. Roll out the winner gradually; keep the option to roll back. Also consider shadow testing (run B in the background without showing it, then compare with LLM-as-judge) for risky changes.

questions.q: Your production RAG chatbot is confidently hallucinating information that does not exist in the knowledge base, and the client is escalating. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.a:
Immediate containment: acknowledge the issue, collect the failing conversations, add a stricter fallback ("not found in documents") and, if severe, show citations/disclaimers or route high-risk topics to humans.

Diagnose with traces:

1. Was relevant context retrieved? If nothing relevant was retrieved, the model filled the gap from its own knowledge → retrieval/threshold problem.

2. If context was retrieved but the answer adds facts → generation/prompt problem (weak grounding instruction, high temperature, too much noisy context).

3. Check for outdated/conflicting documents, broken parsing, or a recent change in model/prompt version.

Fixes:

  • Strict grounding prompt + "I don't know" behaviour; temperature 0.
  • Relevance threshold, re-ranker, hybrid search; corrective-RAG loop.
  • Mandatory citations + citation validation; a faithfulness check (LLM-judge/NLI) before sending, blocking unsupported answers.
  • Golden dataset with the failing cases; RAGAS faithfulness monitoring in production; report metrics to the client.

questions.q: The knowledge base grew from 10,000 to 5 million documents. Retrieval latency crashed and hosting cost spiked. What do you change?
questions.a:
• Index: move from flat/brute-force search to ANN indexes (HNSW, or IVF-PQ for memory efficiency); tune ef_search/nprobe; use a vector DB built for scale (Milvus, Qdrant, Pinecone, OpenSearch) with sharding and replicas.
  • Reduce vectors and memory: de-duplicate documents, smaller embedding dimensions (Matryoshka truncation, e.g. 3072 → 768), quantization (scalar/binary/PQ), store raw text outside the vector index.
  • Metadata pre-filtering / partitioning by department, tenant, date, document type – search a much smaller subset.
  • Two-stage retrieval: fast cheap first stage (ANN/BM25) → re-rank only top-50.
  • Tiered storage: hot (recent/frequent) vs cold archives; hierarchical retrieval (document summaries first, then chunks).
  • Ingestion at scale: async batch embedding pipeline with queues, incremental updates only for changed docs.
  • Caching of frequent queries; monitor p95 latency and cost per query.

questions.q: A non-technical client insists the chatbot must be "100% accurate and never make a mistake". How do you handle this without jargon?
questions.a:
Be honest, set expectations, and turn it into a risk-managed plan: "No AI system – and no human team – is 100% accurate. What we can promise is a system that is accurate on the questions that matter, transparent, and safe when it's unsure:

  • It answers only from your approved documents and shows the source for every answer, so your staff can check it in one click.
  • When it isn't sure, it says so and hands over to a person instead of guessing.
  • For high-risk topics (payments, legal decisions) a human approves before anything happens.
  • We'll agree on a test set of your real questions and a target (e.g. 95% correct with sources) before go-live, and report accuracy every month while we keep improving it."

Then propose a pilot with measurable acceptance criteria.

questions.q: Production responses suddenly became worse right after a deployment. What do you investigate?
questions.a:
1. What changed? Diff the deployment: prompt version, model/model version (provider auto-upgrade?), temperature/parameters, retriever settings (k, threshold), chunking or embedding model (query and index embeddings must match!), document re-index, guardrail rules, code/libraries.

2. Compare traces before vs after on the same queries – where does it go wrong: retrieval or generation?

3. Run the golden dataset against both versions to quantify the drop.

4. Check data/infra issues: partial re-indexing, ingestion failures, truncated context, timeouts causing fallbacks to a weaker model.

5. Roll back quickly (feature flag/previous version) if impact is high, then fix.

6. Prevent recurrence: CI regression tests, canary/shadow releases, pinned model versions, alerts on quality metrics.

questions.q: A customer wants a multi-agent architecture "because it sounds advanced". What do you recommend?
questions.a: Start from the problem, not the architecture: ask what the system must do, then recommend the simplest design that meets the requirements – often a single agent or even a deterministic workflow/RAG pipeline. Explain trade-offs in business terms: multi-agent systems mean more LLM calls (higher cost and latency), more failure points, harder debugging and testing.
