Recommend multi-agent only when there are clearly separate specialized sub-tasks, too many tools for one agent, need for parallel work or independent review. Offer a path: build the simple version, measure, and add agents where the metrics show a benefit.

questions.q: Design a system that processes and summarizes 10 million documents.
questions.a:
• Ingestion: documents land in object storage (S3/GCS); events/messages go to a queue (Pub/Sub, SQS, Kafka).
  • Workers: autoscaling stateless workers pull jobs → parse/OCR → chunk → summarize (map-reduce for long docs) → store results in a DB/index.
  • Asynchronous & batch: use provider Batch APIs (cheaper) or self-hosted models with vLLM for throughput; rate-limit to stay under quotas.
  • Idempotency: job IDs/content hashes so retries don't duplicate work; skip already-processed documents.
  • Reliability: retries with backoff, dead-letter queue for failed documents, checkpoints, monitoring progress dashboards.
  • Cost: route by document type/length to cheaper models; summarize once and cache; avoid re-processing unchanged files.
  • Quality: sample-based evaluation of summaries (LLM-judge + human), schema validation for structured summaries.
  • Long-running jobs (e.g. 20 min per doc): never block an API request – return a job ID and notify/poll for status.

questions.q: Walk me through a GenAI project you built end-to-end. What was your role and what was the business impact?
questions.a:
How to answer (STAR + architecture, ~3 minutes):

  • Situation/Problem: business context and why it mattered. "Fraud analysts spent ~20 minutes per case searching policy documents and past case notes."
  • Your role: what *you* owned (design, RAG pipeline, evaluation, deployment) and team size.
  • Solution/architecture: walk through data → ingestion/chunking → embeddings → vector DB → retrieval (hybrid + re-ranker) → LLM → guardrails → UI/API → monitoring. Name the tools and why you chose them.
  • Evaluation: how you measured quality (golden set, RAGAS faithfulness, accuracy) and the numbers.
  • Result/impact: quantified – "reduced investigation time from 20 to 6 minutes, used by 150 analysts, 85% answer acceptance".

Tips: prepare one project in depth with a diagram you can draw; be honest about what was a prototype vs production; expect follow-up questions on every component.

questions.q: What was the hardest problem you faced in that project and how did you solve it?
questions.a:
Structure: challenge → why it was hard → options you considered → what you did → measurable result → lesson.

Example answer: "Our RAG bot gave wrong answers for questions about tables in scanned PDFs. Plain text extraction scrambled the rows, so retrieval found the right page but the LLM couldn't read the numbers. I compared three approaches – better OCR, a vision-LLM per page, and a table-aware parser – on 50 table questions. A layout-aware parser that converted tables to Markdown, kept each table as one chunk with an LLM-generated summary for retrieval, raised accuracy on table questions from 41% to 83%. Lesson: evaluate each component separately and fix the data pipeline before changing the model." Pick a genuinely technical problem (data quality, hallucination, latency, cost, evaluation), show your reasoning and trade-offs, and quantify the outcome.

questions.q: How did you evaluate your system and what metrics improved?
questions.a:
Interviewers want to see a disciplined evaluation process, not just "it worked well":

  • Test set: "We built a golden set of 150 real questions with expert-written answers and source documents, including out-of-scope questions."
  • Metrics by component: retrieval – hit rate@5, context recall/precision; generation – faithfulness, answer relevancy/correctness (RAGAS + LLM-as-judge validated against human labels); system – latency p95, cost per query.
  • Baselines and iterations: "Baseline top-5 vector search: 68% hit rate → adding BM25 hybrid: 79% → adding a re-ranker: 88%; faithfulness improved from 0.81 to 0.93 after prompt changes."
  • Online metrics: thumbs-up rate, escalation rate, adoption, time saved.
  • Continuous evaluation: regression tests in CI on every prompt/model change; production failures added to the test set.

questions.q: What would you do differently if you rebuilt it today?
questions.a:
Show reflection and awareness of newer techniques; be honest but positive. Example points:

  • "Build the evaluation set on day one – we added it late and wasted time on changes we couldn't measure."
  • "Use hybrid search and a re-ranker from the start instead of pure vector search."
  • "Invest earlier in document parsing (tables, scanned PDFs), which caused most errors."
  • "Add observability/tracing (Langfuse/LangSmith) before launch."
  • "Use LangGraph for explicit control instead of a loosely controlled agent; add human-in-the-loop for risky actions."
  • "Consider smaller models + routing and prompt caching to reduce cost."
  • "Involve end users earlier to collect realistic queries."

Avoid blaming others; focus on what you learned.

questions.q: How do you keep up with the fast-changing GenAI field?
questions.a:
Give specific, credible habits (and mention something recent you actually learned):

  • Papers & research: arXiv / Hugging Face Daily Papers, Papers with Code; reading key papers (Attention Is All You Need, LoRA, RAG, ReAct, DPO).
  • Official docs and engineering blogs: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, Hugging Face, LangChain/LlamaIndex blogs and release notes.
  • Newsletters/communities: The Batch (DeepLearning.AI), Latent Space, Ahead of AI (Sebastian Raschka), Interconnects, r/LocalLLaMA, X/LinkedIn researchers, local meetups.
  • Courses: DeepLearning.AI short courses, Hugging Face courses.
  • Hands-on: build small projects to test new models/techniques (e.g. tried MCP servers, GraphRAG, a new open model), Kaggle, open-source contributions.
  • Teaching/sharing: writing blog posts or teaching classes forces deep understanding.

questions.q: Explain RAG (or a Transformer) to a non-technical manager in 2 minutes.
questions.a:
RAG explained simply (example): "An AI model like ChatGPT is like a very smart new employee who has read a lot of the internet, but has never seen our company's documents and sometimes guesses confidently when unsure. RAG gives this employee an open-book exam. When someone asks a question, the system first searches our own documents – policies, manuals, past cases – and picks the few most relevant pages. It then gives those pages to the AI and says: 'Answer only using these pages, and tell us which page you used.' Benefits: answers are based on our latest, approved information; every answer shows its source so people can verify it; when a policy changes we just update the documents – no expensive retraining; and sensitive documents can be restricted to the right people.

Limitations: it's only as good as the documents and the search – if the information isn't there, it should say 'I don't know'." Tips: use an analogy, avoid jargon (embeddings, vectors), focus on business value, risks and cost; check for understanding. (Transformer in one line for managers: "a model that reads all words of a sentence at once and learns which words to pay attention to, which is what makes modern AI understand context so well.")

questions.q: Tell me about yourself (for a GenAI Engineer role).
questions.a:
Use a 90-second, present → past → future structure focused on GenAI:

  • Present: current role and the GenAI system you own. "I'm a GenAI engineer at X, where I build RAG and agent-based assistants for fraud and operations teams…"
  • Highlights with numbers: 1–2 projects, your contribution and impact (users, latency, accuracy, cost saved).
  • Skills: LLMs, RAG, LangChain/LangGraph, evaluation, deployment (FastAPI, Docker, cloud), Python; domain expertise (e.g. fraud detection in banking).
  • Past (briefly): how you moved from data science/ML into GenAI.
  • Future/why this role: what you want to build next and why this company.

Keep it conversational, not a resume recital, and end on a hook the interviewer can ask about.

questions.q: Tell me about a failure or production issue in your GenAI project and what you learned.
questions.a:
Use STAR and show ownership:

  • Situation: "After launch, our policy assistant started giving outdated answers to some HR questions."
  • Task: "I owned the RAG pipeline and had to find the cause quickly."
  • Action: "Traces showed old and new versions of the same policy were both indexed; retrieval sometimes picked the old one. I added document versioning and an 'effective date' filter, removed superseded documents during ingestion, added a regression test set for policy-update questions, and an alert on ingestion failures."
  • Result: "Outdated-answer complaints dropped to near zero; we now catch such issues before release."
  • Learning: data lifecycle and evaluation matter as much as the model.

Choose a real failure, don't blame others, and focus on the fix and the prevention.

questions.q: You disagree with a senior architect's technical decision (e.g. which framework or model to use). What do you do?
questions.a:
• Understand first: ask about their reasons and constraints (cost, team skills, compliance, timelines) – they may have context you don't.
  • Make it data-driven, not opinion-driven: propose a small proof-of-concept or benchmark comparing both options on agreed criteria (accuracy on our eval set, latency, cost, maintainability).
  • Discuss privately and respectfully, present results and trade-offs.
  • Disagree and commit: once a decision is made, support it fully, document the risks, and set checkpoints to revisit if metrics show problems.

Example: "We disagreed on fine-tuning vs RAG; I ran a one-week comparison on 100 real questions – RAG matched quality at a fraction of the cost, and the architect agreed to go with it.

questions.q: The client wants the solution in 2 weeks, but you estimate 6 weeks (or your team is lagging behind a deadline). What do you do?
questions.a:
• Don't just say yes or no – understand what the client actually needs by the date (a demo? a pilot? production?).
  • Break the scope down and propose options: an MVP in 2 weeks (core use case, limited documents/users, manual steps) and the full production version in 6 weeks; show what is cut and the risks of skipping (security, evaluation).
  • Be transparent with data (estimates, dependencies) and agree on priorities in writing.
  • If the team is lagging: identify blockers early, re-prioritize must-haves, remove low-value scope, ask for help/resources, communicate status and risks to stakeholders early, not on the deadline day.
  • Never compromise on security/compliance to hit a date.

questions.q: What is the difference between multithreading and multiprocessing in Python? What is the GIL, and how does it affect GenAI backends?
questions.a:
• GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): in CPython, only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time per process. It simplifies memory management but limits CPU parallelism with threads. (Python 3.13+ offers an experimental free-threaded build without the GIL.)
  • Multithreading: multiple threads in one process, shared memory. Because the GIL is released during I/O (network calls, file reads), threads work well for I/O-bound tasks – e.g. calling LLM APIs, vector DB, HTTP requests in parallel. Not useful for CPU-heavy Python code.
  • Multiprocessing: separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL → true parallelism on multiple cores for CPU-bound work – PDF parsing, OCR, chunking, local embedding computation, data processing. Costs: more memory, inter-process communication overhead.

GenAI backend practice: most work is I/O-bound (waiting for LLM/API responses) → use async (asyncio/FastAPI) or threads; push CPU-heavy ingestion to process pools or separate workers; heavy model inference runs in optimized C++/CUDA code (vLLM, PyTorch) which releases the GIL.

questions.q: Concurrency vs parallelism: why use async programming in an AI application? If you must call three independent APIs, would you call them one by one?
questions.a:
• Concurrency – handling many tasks in overlapping time (switching while waiting); one core can do it. Parallelism – tasks literally running at the same time on multiple cores.
  • LLM apps spend most time waiting on network I/O. With async, while one request waits, the event loop serves others → much higher throughput with fewer resources; FastAPI is built on this.
  • Three independent API calls: don't call them sequentially (total = sum of latencies, e.g. 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 s). Run them concurrently (total ≈ slowest call, ~3 s):
import asyncio, httpx
async def fetch(client, url):
    r = await client.get(url, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()
async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        weather, news, stock = await asyncio.gather(
            fetch(client, "https://api.example.com/weather"),
            fetch(client, "https://api.example.com/news"),
            fetch(client, "https://api.example.com/stock"),
            return_exceptions=True)          # one failure doesn't cancel the others
    return weather, news, stock
asyncio.run(main())

Only call sequentially when one call depends on another's result.

questions.q: What are generators and decorators in Python? How do generators relate to streaming LLM responses?
questions.a:
• Generator: a function that uses `yield` to produce values one at a time, lazily, keeping its state between calls – memory-efficient for large/infinite data.
  • Decorator: a function that wraps another function to add behaviour (logging, timing, retries, caching, auth) without changing its code; applied with `@decorator`.
  • Streaming: LLM APIs return tokens as a stream; a generator yields each chunk as it arrives, and a web framework (FastAPI `StreamingResponse`, SSE) sends it to the user immediately → low perceived latency.
import time, functools
def timed(func):                       # decorator
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper
def stream_answer(llm, question):      # generator
    for chunk in llm.stream(question): # LangChain chat model streaming
        yield chunk.content
# FastAPI streaming endpoint
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/chat")
def chat(q: str):
    return StreamingResponse(stream_answer(llm, q), media_type="text/plain")

questions.q: How do you process very large data (e.g. millions of rows or huge files) in Python without Out-Of-Memory errors?
questions.a:
• Stream/iterate instead of loading everything: read files line by line, use generators; `pd.read_csv(..., chunksize=100_000)` and process chunk by chunk.
  • Batch processing for embeddings/LLM calls (e.g. 100 documents per batch) and write results incrementally to disk/DB.
  • Efficient dtypes (category, int32, float32), load only needed columns (`usecols`).
  • Columnar/lazy tools: Polars (lazy mode), DuckDB, PyArrow/Parquet, Dask or Spark for distributed data.
  • Memory-mapped files / NumPy memmap for large arrays; vector DBs instead of in-memory embedding arrays.
  • Free memory (`del`, avoid unnecessary copies), and profile with `memory_profiler`/`tracemalloc`.
  • Scale out with queues and workers rather than one giant process.

questions.q: Write a Python function that calls an LLM API with exponential backoff retries (with jitter) for transient errors.
questions.a:
import random, time
class TransientError(Exception):
    '''Timeouts, HTTP 429 or 5xx errors.'''
def call_with_backoff(fn, *args, max_retries=5, base_delay=1.0, max_delay=30.0, **kwargs):
    for attempt in range(max_retries + 1):
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except TransientError as e:
            if attempt == max_retries:
                raise                                   # give up after last attempt
            delay = min(max_delay, base_delay * (2 ** attempt))   # 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...
            delay = random.uniform(0, delay)            # "full jitter" avoids thundering herd
            print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1} failed ({e}); retrying in {delay:.1f}s")
            time.sleep(delay)
# Usage with the OpenAI SDK
# from openai import OpenAI, RateLimitError, APITimeoutError, InternalServerError
# def ask(prompt):
#     try:
#         return client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-mini",
#                    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], timeout=30)
#     except (RateLimitError, APITimeoutError, InternalServerError) as e:
#         raise TransientError(e)
# call_with_backoff(ask, "Hello")

Key points for the interviewer: retry only transient errors (not 400/401), cap the attempts and the delay, add jitter, respect `Retry-After`, set timeouts, and make the operation idempotent. In production use the `tenacity` library or the SDK's built-in `max_retries`.

questions.q: Implement an in-memory cache (with TTL) for LLM queries so identical requests don't call the API again.
questions.a:
import hashlib, json, time
class LLMCache:
    def __init__(self, ttl_seconds=3600, max_size=10_000):
        self.ttl, self.max_size, self.store = ttl_seconds, max_size, {}
    def _key(self, model, prompt, **params):
        raw = json.dumps({"model": model, "prompt": prompt, **params}, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()
    def get(self, model, prompt, **params):
        k = self._key(model, prompt, **params)
        item = self.store.get(k)
        if item and time.time() - item[1] < self.ttl:
            return item[0]
        self.store.pop(k, None)                  # expired or missing
        return None
    def set(self, model, prompt, response, **params):
        if len(self.store) >= self.max_size:     # simple eviction: drop oldest
            oldest = min(self.store, key=lambda k: self.store[k][1])
            del self.store[oldest]
        self.store[self._key(model, prompt, **params)] = (response, time.time())
cache = LLMCache(ttl_seconds=600)
def cached_llm(prompt, model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0):
    hit = cache.get(model, prompt, temperature=temperature)
    if hit is not None:
        return hit
    response = call_llm(prompt, model=model, temperature=temperature)   # your API call
    cache.set(model, prompt, response, temperature=temperature)
    return response

Notes: the key includes model and parameters; only cache deterministic (temperature 0) requests; in production use Redis (shared across servers, built-in TTL) and consider semantic caching for similar questions. `functools.lru_cache` works for simple cases but has no TTL.

questions.q: Why is FastAPI preferred for GenAI backends, and how does Pydantic fit in?
questions.a:
FastAPI:

  • Async-native (ASGI) → handles many concurrent I/O-bound LLM/API calls efficiently.
  • Easy streaming (StreamingResponse/SSE) for token-by-token output.
  • Automatic validation and OpenAPI/Swagger docs from type hints; very fast; dependency injection for auth, DB sessions, rate limiting.

Pydantic: defines typed data models used for request/response validation (rejects bad input with clear errors), settings management, and – very important in GenAI – validating LLM structured outputs (JSON → Pydantic object, retry if invalid). LangChain `with_structured_output` and tool schemas use Pydantic.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class AskRequest(BaseModel):
    question: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=2000)
    session_id: str
class AskResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    sources: list[str]
app = FastAPI()
@app.post("/ask", response_model=AskResponse)
async def ask(req: AskRequest):
    result = await rag_chain.ainvoke(req.question)
    return AskResponse(answer=result["answer"],
                       sources=[d.metadata["source"] for d in result["docs"]])

questions.q: Quick-fire Python: list vs tuple, shallow vs deep copy, and what is a context manager?
questions.a:
• List vs tuple: list is mutable (append/modify), tuple is immutable, slightly faster and smaller, hashable (usable as dict keys/set elements if its items are hashable). Use tuples for fixed records.
  • Shallow vs deep copy: a shallow copy (`copy.copy`, `list.copy()`, slicing) creates a new outer object but shares the nested objects; a deep copy (`copy.deepcopy`) recursively copies everything.
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3]]
s = copy.copy(a); d = copy.deepcopy(a)
a[0].append(99)
print(s[0], d[0])   # [1, 2, 99] [1, 2]
  • Context manager: an object that sets up and guarantees cleanup of a resource using `with` (implements `__enter__`/`__exit__`, or `@contextlib.contextmanager`). Examples: files, DB connections, locks, `httpx.AsyncClient`, timing blocks. Cleanup runs even if an exception occurs.

questions.q: SQL: find the second-highest salary, and find duplicate records in a table.
questions.a:
-- Second-highest distinct salary
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
-- Using a window function (works for Nth highest; handles ties)
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
      FROM employees) t
WHERE rnk = 2;
-- Duplicate records (same email)
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- Show the full duplicate rows
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT c.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM customers c) t
WHERE rn > 1;

Know the difference: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows; LEFT JOIN returns all rows of the left table with NULLs where there is no match.

questions.q: Precision vs recall vs F1 score – when is recall more important than precision?
questions.a:
• Precision = TP / (TP + FP) – of everything the model flagged, how much was correct. ("When I say fraud, am I right?")
  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN) – of all actual positives, how many did we catch. ("Did I catch all frauds?")
  • F1 = 2 × P × R / (P + R) – harmonic mean; useful for imbalanced data when both matter.

Recall matters more when missing a positive is costly: fraud detection, cancer screening, security threats, RAG retrieval (missing the relevant chunk means a wrong answer).

Precision matters more when false alarms are costly: spam filtering (losing real emails), blocking customer transactions, recommending content. Tune the decision threshold to trade them off; use PR-AUC for imbalanced problems; accuracy is misleading when 99% of transactions are legitimate.

questions.q: What is overfitting, and what is data leakage? How do you prevent each?
questions.a:
• Overfitting: the model memorizes training data (including noise) – great training score, poor validation/test score. Prevent: more data, simpler model, regularization (L1/L2, dropout), early stopping, cross-validation, data augmentation, feature selection.
  • Data leakage: information that would not be available at prediction time leaks into training, giving unrealistically good validation results that collapse in production. Examples: fitting the scaler/TF-IDF on the full dataset before splitting; features computed from the future (e.g. "chargeback flag" when predicting fraud at transaction time); duplicates across train and test; random split on time-series data.

Prevent leakage: split first, then fit preprocessing on train only (sklearn Pipelines); time-based splits for temporal data; group-aware splits (same customer not in both); careful feature review.

  • Cross-validation (k-fold): train/evaluate k times on different splits for a more reliable estimate.

questions.q: How do you handle class imbalance (e.g. 1% fraud vs 99% normal transactions)?
questions.a:
• Right metrics: precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, confusion matrix – not accuracy (99% accuracy by predicting "not fraud" always).
  • Resampling: undersample the majority, oversample the minority, SMOTE (synthetic samples) – only on the training set.
  • Class weights / cost-sensitive learning: `class_weight="balanced"`, `scale_pos_weight` in XGBoost, focal loss for deep learning.
  • Threshold tuning based on business cost of FP vs FN.
  • Better features and anomaly-detection approaches (Isolation Forest, autoencoders).
  • For text: data augmentation (back-translation, LLM paraphrasing), more labelled minority examples.
  • Use stratified splits so each fold has minority examples.

questions.q: How do you detect and handle outliers before feeding data into ML or embedding models?
questions.a:
Detect:

  • Statistical: IQR rule (below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR), z-score > 3.
  • Visual: box plots, histograms, scatter plots.
  • Model-based: Isolation Forest, LOF, DBSCAN; for text/embeddings – points far from cluster centroids, unusually long/short documents, wrong language, garbage OCR text.

Handle (depends on cause):

  • Data errors → fix or remove.
  • Genuine extreme values → cap/winsorize, log-transform, or use robust models/scalers (RobustScaler, tree models).
  • In fraud, outliers are often the signal – don't remove them; model them.

For RAG ingestion: filter empty/boilerplate chunks, duplicated pages and corrupted OCR before embedding.

questions.q: Why are traditional ML concepts (classification vs regression, loss functions, metrics) still asked in GenAI interviews?
questions.a:
Because GenAI systems are built on and around them:

  • LLMs are trained by minimizing a loss function (cross-entropy on next-token prediction); fine-tuning, RLHF/DPO and embedding training all rely on losses and optimization.
  • Many GenAI products still contain classical ML tasks: intent classification, routing, re-ranking, fraud scoring, anomaly detection, evaluation classifiers.
  • Evaluation needs ML thinking: precision/recall for retrieval and guardrails, train/test splits, overfitting, leakage, statistical significance in A/B tests.
  • Production issues (drift, imbalance, bias, monitoring) are classic MLOps topics.

It shows the candidate understands *why* models behave as they do, not just how to call an API.

Quick definitions: classification predicts a category (fraud / not fraud, uses cross-entropy); regression predicts a number (transaction amount, uses MSE/MAE).

questions.q: What is data drift vs model (concept) drift vs training–serving skew? Batch vs online inference?
questions.a:
• Data drift: the input distribution changes over time (new product names, new customer segment, users start asking about a new policy) while the relationship may stay the same.
  • Concept/model drift: the relationship between inputs and the target changes (fraudsters change tactics, so old patterns no longer indicate fraud) → model accuracy decays.
  • Training–serving skew: features/preprocessing at serving time differ from training (different tokenization, missing feature, different scaler) – a bug, not a change in the world.

Detect/handle: monitor input statistics (PSI, KS test, embedding-distribution shift), prediction distributions and live metrics; retrain or update the knowledge base; share one feature/preprocessing pipeline between training and serving.

  • Batch inference: predictions for many records on a schedule (nightly scoring, bulk document summarization) – cheap, high throughput, not real-time.
  • Online (real-time) inference: prediction per request with low latency (chatbot, transaction fraud check at payment time) – needs always-on serving and scaling.

questions.q: What is NLP? Give 3 real-world applications you have seen in production.
questions.a:
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the branch of AI that enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language (text and speech). It combines linguistics, machine learning and deep learning.

Real-world applications:

  • Chatbots and virtual assistants (customer support bots, ChatGPT-style assistants)
  • Sentiment analysis of product reviews / social media
  • Machine translation (Google Translate)
  • Spam and fraud-message detection, email classification
  • Document search, question answering and summarization (RAG systems)

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q1

questions.q: What are the main challenges in NLP?
questions.a:
• Ambiguity – the same word/sentence can have many meanings.
  • Context and long-range dependencies – meaning depends on earlier text.
  • Sarcasm, irony and idioms – "Great, another Monday!" is negative.
  • Spelling mistakes, slang, emojis, code-mixing (Hinglish).
  • Out-of-vocabulary words and new terminology.
  • Low-resource languages – little labelled data.
  • Domain shift – a model trained on news fails on medical text.
  • Bias in training data, and hallucination in generative models.

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q3

questions.q: What is tokenization? Compare word-level, character-level and subword tokenization.
questions.a:
Tokenization splits text into smaller units called tokens, which are then mapped to IDs for the model.

  • Word-level: "I love NLP" → ["I", "love", "NLP"]. Simple, but huge vocabulary and OOV problem.
  • Character-level: ["I", " ", "l", "o", ...]. Tiny vocabulary, no OOV, but very long sequences and weak meaning per token.
  • Subword-level (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece): "unhappiness" → ["un", "happi", "ness"]. Balanced vocabulary size (30k–200k), rare words are split into known pieces, so no OOV. All modern Transformers/LLMs use subword tokenization.

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q8

questions.q: What is stemming and how is it different from lemmatization? When would you prefer each?
questions.a:
Both reduce a word to a base form.

  • Stemming chops suffixes with rules (Porter, Snowball). Fast but crude; output may not be a real word: "studies" → "studi", "running" → "run".
  • Lemmatization uses vocabulary + grammar (POS) to return the dictionary form (lemma): "studies" → "study", "better" → "good" (adjective), "was" → "be".

Prefer stemming for speed on large data (search indexing, simple classifiers). Prefer lemmatization when meaning/readability matters (chatbots, topic modelling, information extraction).

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q9

questions.q: What are subword tokenization methods? Explain BPE, WordPiece and SentencePiece briefly.
questions.a:
Subword tokenization splits rare words into frequent smaller units, so the vocabulary stays small and there are no OOV words.

  • BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) – starts with characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent pair of symbols until the vocabulary size is reached. Used by GPT-2/3/4, Llama 3, RoBERTa (byte-level BPE).
  • WordPiece – similar to BPE but merges the pair that maximizes the likelihood of the training data (score = freq(ab) / (freq(a)·freq(b))). Continuation pieces are prefixed with "##". Used by BERT, DistilBERT.
  • SentencePiece – a library that treats text as a raw stream (spaces become "▁"), so it is language-independent and needs no pre-tokenization. Implements BPE or Unigram LM (starts with a big vocabulary and prunes tokens that least reduce likelihood). Used by T5, ALBERT, XLNet, Llama 1/2, Mistral.

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q15

questions.q: Which tokenizers are used by GPT-family models and by BERT?
questions.a:
• GPT-2 / GPT-3: byte-level BPE (~50k tokens).
  • GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 / GPT-4o: byte-level BPE via OpenAI's tiktoken library (cl100k_base ~100k tokens, o200k_base ~200k tokens).
  • BERT: WordPiece (vocabulary 30,522 for bert-base-uncased).

(For comparison: T5 uses SentencePiece-Unigram; Llama 2 uses SentencePiece-BPE; Llama 3 uses tiktoken-style BPE.)

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q17

questions.q: In real-time data users type "Lunch", "lunch" and "LUNCH". Why do we lowercase text, and when should you NOT lowercase?
questions.a:
Why lowercase: so that different surface forms of the same word map to one token/feature. Without it, "Lunch", "lunch" and "LUNCH" become three different vocabulary entries → bigger, sparser vocabulary, fewer examples per word, worse generalization for BoW/TF-IDF/Word2Vec models. Users at inference time type in any case, so training and inference must be normalized the same way.

Do NOT lowercase when case carries meaning:

  • NER: "Apple" (company) vs "apple" (fruit); "US" vs "us".
  • Acronyms, product codes, tickers, IDs ("SBI", "PAN", "IT" department).
  • Sentiment/intent where shouting matters ("I am ANGRY").
  • Transformer/LLM pipelines with cased models – the tokenizer and model were trained on cased text; just pass raw text.

Rule: whatever you do in training, do exactly the same in the inference pipeline.

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q22

questions.q: Users will type stopwords at inference time. If you remove them during training, what happens? When should you remove stopwords and when not? Give practical applications.
questions.a:
Preprocessing must be identical at training and inference – if training removed stopwords, the inference pipeline must remove them too, otherwise the input distribution differs and accuracy drops. The bigger risk is losing meaning: "not", "no", "never", "without" are stopwords in NLTK.

Remove stopwords when: using classical BoW/TF-IDF models for topic-level tasks – document classification by topic, keyword extraction, topic modelling (LDA), search indexing/keyword search – where they add noise and dimensionality.

Keep stopwords when:

  • Sentiment analysis ("not good" ≠ "good").
  • Question answering, chatbots, intent detection ("where", "how", "can I").
  • Machine translation, summarization, text generation, NER.
  • Any Transformer/LLM/RAG pipeline (they need full grammar and context).

Use a custom stopword list that keeps negations if you must remove them.

📌 From Assignment 1 · Q24

questions.q: What is the Bag-of-Words model? What are its limitations?
questions.a:
Bag-of-Words (BoW) represents a document as the count (or presence) of each vocabulary word, ignoring grammar and word order. Example – vocabulary [I, love, NLP, hate]: "I love NLP" → [1, 1, 1, 0].

Limitations:

  • Loses word order: "dog bites man" = "man bites dog".
  • No semantics: "good" and "great" are unrelated dimensions.
  • High-dimensional and sparse (vocab can be 100k+).
  • Cannot handle OOV words.
  • Frequent words dominate unless weighted (→ TF-IDF).

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q2

questions.q: What is TF-IDF? How do you calculate TF, IDF and TF-IDF? Work out a small example by hand.
questions.a:
TF-IDF weights a word by how important it is to a document relative to the whole corpus.

  • TF(t, d) = (count of t in d) / (total words in d)
  • IDF(t) = log( N / df(t) ), where N = number of documents, df = number of documents containing t
  • TF-IDF = TF × IDF

Worked example (log base 10) – 3 documents: D1 "the cat sat", D2 "the dog sat", D3 "the cat ran".

  • Word "cat" in D1: TF = 1/3; df = 2 → IDF = log(3/2) = 0.176 → TF-IDF = 0.059
  • Word "the" in D1: TF = 1/3; df = 3 → IDF = log(3/3) = 0 → TF-IDF = 0 (common word, no information)
  • Word "ran" in D3: TF = 1/3; df = 1 → IDF = log(3) = 0.477 → TF-IDF = 0.159 (rare word, high weight)

(scikit-learn uses a smoothed version: idf = ln((1+N)/(1+df)) + 1, then L2-normalizes the vector.)

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q4

questions.q: What are word embeddings? How are they better than one-hot / BoW vectors?
questions.a:
Word embeddings are dense, low-dimensional vectors (e.g. 100–1024 numbers) learned from data, where words with similar meaning have similar vectors.

Better than one-hot/BoW because:

  • Dense (300 dims vs 100k sparse dims) → less memory, better generalization.
  • Capture semantics: cos(king, queen) is high; famous analogy king − man + woman ≈ queen.
  • Similar words share information, so the model generalizes to words it saw less often.
  • Can be pre-trained on huge corpora and reused (transfer learning).

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q5

questions.q: Explain Word2Vec and its two architectures (CBOW and Skip-gram). What is the difference?
questions.a:
Word2Vec is a shallow neural network (one hidden layer) that learns word vectors by predicting words from their neighbours within a context window. The learned hidden-layer weights are the embeddings.

  • CBOW (Continuous Bag of Words): predicts the target word from the surrounding context words. Context "the cat __ on the mat" → "sat". Faster, works well for frequent words.
  • Skip-gram: predicts the context words from the target word. "sat" → "the", "cat", "on", "mat". Slower, but better for rare words and small datasets.

Training tricks: negative sampling and hierarchical softmax avoid computing softmax over the whole vocabulary.

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q7

questions.q: How do you handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words?
questions.a:
• Subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece) – any word can be built from known pieces; this is the standard solution today.
  • FastText – builds vectors for unknown words from character n-grams.
  • Character-level models.
  • Replace with an <UNK> token (simple but loses information).
  • Spelling correction / lemmatization to map to known words.
  • Use a larger vocabulary or fine-tune on domain data.

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q11

questions.q: Explain cosine similarity and why it is important in NLP.
questions.a:
Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors: cos(θ) = (A · B) / (‖A‖ × ‖B‖), ranging from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to 1 (same direction).

Why important in NLP:

  • It measures direction (meaning), not magnitude (length), so a long and a short document on the same topic still score high.
  • Works well for high-dimensional sparse and dense vectors.
  • It is the default metric for semantic search, RAG retrieval, recommendation, duplicate detection and clustering.

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q12

questions.q: Euclidean distance vs cosine similarity — when would you use which?
questions.a:
• Euclidean distance depends on vector magnitude. A long document has a larger count vector than a short one, so they look far apart even if they are about the same topic.
  • Cosine similarity depends only on the angle (direction), so it ignores length.

Use cosine for text, embeddings, semantic search (most cases). Use Euclidean when magnitude is meaningful (e.g. K-means on normalized numeric features, image features). Note: for L2-normalized vectors, ranking by Euclidean distance and by cosine give the same order.

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q14

questions.q: Why can averaging Word2Vec vectors to make a sentence vector lose information? What is better?
questions.a:
Averaging (mean pooling of word vectors) is a simple baseline, but:

  • Word order is lost: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same vector.
  • Negation and composition are lost: "not good" ≈ average of "not" and "good", which stays close to "good".
  • Important words get diluted by many common/filler words in long sentences.
  • Each word has one static vector, so polysemy ("bank") is not resolved.
  • OOV words are simply missing.

Better options: TF-IDF–weighted averaging (down-weights common words), SIF embeddings, Doc2Vec, and today mainly Sentence Transformers / embedding models (SBERT, BGE, E5, OpenAI embeddings) that are trained specifically to produce sentence-level vectors with context and word order.

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q20

questions.q: What are Sentence Transformers (SBERT)? Why are they better for semantic search than averaged word vectors or BERT's raw [CLS] vector?
questions.a:
Sentence Transformers (SBERT) are Transformer encoders (BERT/MPNet/MiniLM) fine-tuned with a siamese / bi-encoder setup on sentence pairs (NLI, paraphrase, question–answer pairs) using contrastive losses, so that semantically similar sentences produce embeddings with high cosine similarity.

Why better:

  • Raw BERT [CLS] or mean-pooled BERT vectors were not trained for similarity – their cosine scores are poorly calibrated (often worse than GloVe averages for similarity tasks).
  • Averaged Word2Vec ignores order and context.
  • SBERT encodes the whole sentence in context into one vector that directly supports cosine search, clustering and RAG retrieval; it is fast because documents are encoded once and compared with dot products.
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
q = model.encode("How do I get my money back?")
d = model.encode(["Refund policy: refunds within 7 days", "Office timings are 9 to 6"])
print(util.cos_sim(q, d))   # first document scores much higher

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q21

questions.q: Explain embeddings to a non-technical person without using the word "vector".
questions.a:
An embedding is like giving every word or sentence a position on a giant map of meaning. Things that mean similar things are placed close together – 'refund', 'money back' and 'return payment' sit in the same neighbourhood, while 'office timings' is far away. The computer learns these positions by reading huge amounts of text and noticing which words appear in similar situations. So when a customer asks 'How do I get my money back?', we look up where that question lands on the map and pick the documents placed nearest to it – even if they use completely different words like 'refund policy'. That's how the system finds answers by meaning, not just by matching exact words.

📌 From Assignment 2 · Q23

questions.q: How does a neural network work? Explain with a single neuron first.
questions.a:
Single neuron: takes inputs x₁…xₙ, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function: z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ + b, output a = f(z)

Network: neurons are arranged in layers – input layer → hidden layers → output layer. Each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs.

Learning:

1. Forward pass – compute predictions.

2. Loss – compare predictions with true labels.

3. Backpropagation – compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight (chain rule).

4. Update – an optimizer adjusts weights to reduce the loss.

5. Repeat over many batches and epochs until the loss stops decreasing. Non-linear activations let the network learn complex, non-linear patterns.

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q1

questions.q: Explain the learning rate. What happens if it is too high or too low?
questions.a:
The learning rate (η) controls how big a step the optimizer takes in the direction of the negative gradient.

  • Too high: the updates overshoot the minimum, the loss oscillates or diverges (becomes NaN).
  • Too low: training is very slow, may get stuck in a poor local minimum/plateau, and needs many epochs.
  • Good practice: start with typical values (Adam: 1e-3; fine-tuning Transformers: 1e-5 to 5e-5; LoRA: 1e-4 to 2e-4), use a learning-rate finder, warm-up and schedulers (decay).

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q5

questions.q: Explain forward propagation and backpropagation.
questions.a:
Forward propagation: input data passes layer by layer. For each layer, z = W·x + b and a = f(z). The last layer gives the prediction ŷ, and the loss L(y, ŷ) is computed.

Backpropagation: computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight using the chain rule, starting from the output layer and moving backward: ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂a × ∂a/∂z × ∂z/∂w Each layer reuses the gradients already computed for the layer after it, which makes it efficient. The optimizer then uses these gradients to update weights. Frameworks (PyTorch autograd, TensorFlow GradientTape) do this automatically.

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q6

questions.q: What are the different types of optimizers (SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, Adam, AdamW)?
questions.a:
• SGD – basic gradient descent on mini-batches.
  • SGD with Momentum – adds a velocity term to accelerate and smooth updates.
  • Nesterov Accelerated Gradient – momentum that "looks ahead".
  • AdaGrad – per-parameter learning rate, decays with accumulated squared gradients (good for sparse data, but LR shrinks too much).
  • RMSProp – fixes AdaGrad using an exponential moving average of squared gradients.
  • Adam – Momentum + RMSProp (first and second moment estimates with bias correction). Default choice for most problems.
  • AdamW – Adam with decoupled weight decay; standard for Transformers/LLMs.
  • Others: Adadelta, Nadam, Lion, Adafactor (memory-efficient for large models).

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q8

questions.q: What is the use of an activation function? What happens without one?
questions.a:
An activation function adds non-linearity, so the network can learn complex patterns. It also controls the output range (e.g. probabilities with sigmoid/softmax).

Without activation functions, every layer is a linear transformation, and a stack of linear layers collapses into one linear layer – a 100-layer network would be no more powerful than linear/logistic regression and could not learn non-linear patterns like XOR.

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q13

questions.q: Which loss function should be used for regression, binary classification, multi-class and multi-label problems?
questions.a:
• Regression: MSE (penalizes large errors), MAE (robust to outliers), Huber (mix of both). Output: linear.
  • Binary classification: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE). Output: 1 neuron + sigmoid.
  • Multi-class (one label per sample): Categorical Cross-Entropy (one-hot labels) or Sparse Categorical Cross-Entropy (integer labels). Output: N neurons + softmax.
  • Multi-label (several labels per sample): Binary Cross-Entropy per class. Output: N neurons + sigmoid.
  • Others: Hinge loss (SVM-style), KL divergence (distillation), contrastive / triplet loss (embeddings), Focal loss (heavy class imbalance, e.g. fraud detection).
  • LLM pre-training = cross-entropy on next-token prediction.

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q16

questions.q: What are vanishing and exploding gradients? Why do they occur and how do you fix them?
questions.a:
• Vanishing gradients: gradients become extremely small as they are propagated back through many layers (or time steps), so early layers learn very slowly or not at all.
  • Exploding gradients: gradients become extremely large, causing huge weight updates, unstable training and NaN loss.

Why they occur: backprop multiplies many derivatives together (chain rule). If they are < 1 (sigmoid/tanh derivatives, small weights) the product shrinks exponentially; if > 1 (large weights) it grows exponentially. Very deep networks and RNNs over long sequences are most affected.

Fixes:

  • ReLU-family activations instead of sigmoid/tanh.
  • Proper weight initialization (He/Xavier).
  • Batch Normalization / Layer Normalization.
  • Residual (skip) connections (ResNet, Transformers).
  • LSTM/GRU instead of vanilla RNN.
  • Gradient clipping (for exploding gradients).
  • Lower learning rate.

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q17

questions.q: If the previous layer has 8 neurons and the current Dense layer has 512 neurons, how many parameters does the current layer have? (Show the calculation.)
questions.a:
For a Dense (fully connected) layer: parameters = (inputs × neurons) + biases = (8 × 512) + 512 = 4,096 + 512 = 4,608 parameters. Each of the 512 neurons has 8 weights (one per input) plus 1 bias.

📌 From Assignment 3 · Q22

questions.q: What is the difference between an RNN and an ANN?
questions.a:
• ANN (feed-forward) – input flows in one direction; each input is processed independently; fixed input size; no memory.
  • RNN – has a loop: the hidden state from the previous time step is fed back with the current input, h_t = f(W_xh·x_t + W_hh·h_(t−1) + b). It has memory, processes sequences of any length, and shares the same weights across time steps.

Use ANN for tabular data; RNN for sequential data (text, speech, time series).

📌 From Assignment 4 · Q1

questions.q: Why do RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients and how can it be solved?
questions.a:
During BPTT, the gradient for early time steps is a product of many terms involving W_hh and the derivative of tanh (≤ 1). Over long sequences this product shrinks exponentially, so the gradient from words far back becomes ~0. Result: the RNN cannot learn long-term dependencies ("The man who lived in the house that ... was tall").

Solutions:

  • LSTM / GRU – gated architectures with an additive memory path.
  • ReLU activations + identity/orthogonal initialization.
  • Gradient clipping (for exploding gradients).
  • Skip connections, layer normalization.
  • Ultimately attention / Transformers, which connect every position directly.

📌 From Assignment 4 · Q6

questions.q: Explain the LSTM cell: cell state, hidden state and the three gates (forget, input, output).
questions.a:
An LSTM cell has two states and three gates:

  • Cell state (C_t) – the long-term memory "conveyor belt"; information flows along it with only small, controlled changes.
  • Hidden state (h_t) – short-term memory / output at the current step.
  • Forget gate f_t – decides what to remove from the cell state (sigmoid: 0 = forget, 1 = keep).
  • Input gate i_t – decides what new information to add, together with the candidate values C̃_t (tanh).
  • Output gate o_t – decides what part of the cell state is output as the hidden state.

Gates use sigmoid (values 0–1) to act like soft switches.

📌 From Assignment 4 · Q7

questions.q: How does LSTM address vanishing gradients and long-term dependencies?
questions.a:
The key is the additive cell-state update: C_t = f_t ⊙ C_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ C̃_t.

  • The gradient flowing back through the cell state is multiplied by the forget gate f_t, not by repeated weight matrices and tanh derivatives.
  • When f_t ≈ 1, the gradient passes almost unchanged across many time steps (the "constant error carousel"), so it does not vanish.
  • The gates learn what to keep for a long time (e.g. the subject of a sentence) and what to forget, so important information can be carried across long sequences.

LSTMs reduce, but do not completely eliminate, the problem for very long sequences (hundreds+ of steps).

📌 From Assignment 4 · Q9

questions.q: What is a GRU? Explain its gates (update, reset). How does it differ from LSTM?
questions.a:
A GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) is a simplified LSTM with two gates and only one state (hidden state, no separate cell state).

  • Update gate z_t – how much of the past to keep vs how much new information to add (combines LSTM's forget + input gates).
  • Reset gate r_t – how much of the previous hidden state to use when computing the new candidate.

Equations: z_t = σ(W_z·[h_(t−1), x_t]); r_t = σ(W_r·[h_(t−1), x_t]); h̃_t = tanh(W·[r_t ⊙ h_(t−1), x_t]); h_t = (1 − z_t) ⊙ h_(t−1) + z_t ⊙ h̃_t Differences from LSTM: 2 gates vs 3, no cell state, ~25% fewer parameters, faster to train, often similar accuracy.

📌 From Assignment 4 · Q11

questions.q: Why did Transformers replace RNNs/LSTMs for most NLP tasks?
questions.a:
• Parallelization: RNNs process tokens one by one; Transformers process the whole sequence at once → much faster training on GPUs.
  • Long-range dependencies: self-attention connects any two tokens directly (path length 1), whereas RNNs must pass information through many steps.
  • No vanishing gradient through time.
  • Scalability: Transformers scale to billions of parameters and huge datasets; this enabled pre-training (BERT, GPT) and transfer learning.
  • Better results on almost every NLP benchmark.

(RNNs are still used in small/edge or streaming settings, and new recurrent-style models like Mamba/state-space models are being explored for long contexts.)

📌 From Assignment 4 · Q14

questions.q: What is attention and why was it needed (the bottleneck problem)?
questions.a:
Attention lets the model, while producing each output, look at all input positions and focus on the most relevant ones by computing a weighted sum of their representations, where the weights are learned relevance scores.

Why it was needed – the bottleneck problem: in RNN seq2seq the whole input sentence had to be squeezed into one fixed-size vector. Long sentences lost information, and translation quality dropped sharply with length. With attention (Bahdanau 2014), the decoder gets a different context vector at every step, built directly from all encoder states. It also handles alignment (which source word matches which target word) and gives some interpretability (attention maps).

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q3

questions.q: What is self-attention? Explain Query, Key and Value with an intuitive example.
questions.a:
Self-attention lets every token in a sequence look at every other token in the same sequence and build a context-aware representation of itself. Each token embedding x is projected into three vectors with learned matrices: Q = xW_Q, K = xW_K, V = xW_V.

  • Query – "what am I looking for?"
  • Key – "what do I contain / what can I be matched on?"
  • Value – "the information I give if selected."

Intuition (library search): your query is the search text, keys are the book titles, values are the book contents. You compare the query with all keys, and read a weighted mix of the matching contents.

Example: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired." The query for "it" matches strongly with the key of "animal", so the new vector for "it" contains information from "animal".

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q5

questions.q: What is Scaled Dot-Product Attention? Write the formula. Why do we divide by √dₖ?
questions.a:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √dₖ ) · V Steps: (1) dot product of each query with all keys = similarity scores; (2) divide by √dₖ; (3) (optional mask); (4) softmax → attention weights that sum to 1; (5) weighted sum of value vectors.

Why divide by √dₖ: for vectors with dₖ dimensions (unit-variance entries), the dot product has variance dₖ, so with dₖ = 64 the scores become large. Large values push softmax into regions where one weight ≈ 1 and others ≈ 0, making gradients extremely small. Scaling by √dₖ keeps the variance ≈ 1 and keeps training stable.

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q6

questions.q: What is multi-head attention and why is it better than a single head?
questions.a:
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations ("heads") in parallel, each with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V projecting to a smaller dimension (d_model / h). Outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected with W_O: MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head₁, …, head_h)·W_O (BERT-base: 12 heads × 64 dims = 768.)

Why better than one head: each head can learn a different type of relationship – one head for syntax (subject–verb), one for coreference ("it" → "animal"), one for nearby words, etc. A single head would average all of these into one distribution. Total compute is about the same as one full-size head.

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q7

questions.q: How do Transformers account for word order? Explain positional encoding using sine and cosine.
questions.a:
Self-attention is permutation-invariant – without extra information, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical. So Transformers add a positional encoding vector to each token embedding before the first layer.

Sinusoidal formula (original Transformer): PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 10000^(2i/d_model) ) PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i/d_model) ) Even dimensions use sine, odd use cosine; each dimension pair has a different wavelength (from 2π to 10000·2π), like the hands of a clock running at different speeds.

Why sine/cosine: unique encoding for every position; values bounded in [−1, 1]; PE(pos + k) is a linear function of PE(pos), so the model can easily learn relative positions; no parameters; can extrapolate to longer sequences than seen in training.

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q9

questions.q: What is masked (causal) attention and why is it used in the decoder?
questions.a:
Masked (causal) self-attention prevents a position from attending to future positions. Before softmax, scores for future tokens are set to −∞ using an upper-triangular mask, so their attention weights become 0.

Why: the decoder generates text left-to-right. During training we feed the whole target sentence at once (for parallelism), so without the mask the model could "cheat" by looking at the next word it is supposed to predict. The mask makes training match inference, where future tokens do not exist yet. All GPT-style decoder-only LLMs use causal masking. (A separate padding mask hides [PAD] tokens.)

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q14

questions.q: Explain the complete Transformer architecture end-to-end (draw it).
questions.a:
Encoder (N = 6 identical layers):

1. Input tokens → token embeddings (× √d_model) + positional encodings.

2. Each layer: multi-head self-attention → Add & LayerNorm → feed-forward network → Add & LayerNorm.

3. Output: a contextual vector for every input token.

Decoder (N = 6 layers):

1. Shifted-right target tokens → embeddings + positional encodings.

2. Each layer: masked multi-head self-attention → Add & Norm → cross-attention (Q from decoder, K/V from encoder output) → Add & Norm → FFN → Add & Norm.

Output head: Linear → Softmax over vocabulary → next-token probabilities. Original base model: d_model = 512, 8 heads, d_ff = 2048, dropout 0.1, Adam with warm-up. Training uses teacher forcing; inference is autoregressive (generate one token, append, repeat). (Draw it: two stacks side by side, encoder output arrows feeding into every decoder layer's cross-attention.)

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q17

questions.q: What is the time and memory complexity of self-attention with respect to sequence length?
questions.a:
For sequence length n and model dimension d:

  • Time: O(n² · d) – every token computes a score with every other token (the n × n attention matrix).
  • Memory: O(n²) for the attention matrix (per head, per layer), plus O(n·d) activations.

Doubling the context length makes attention 4× more expensive. This is why long-context models use Flash Attention (reduces memory to O(n) by not storing the full matrix), sliding-window/sparse attention, and KV caching during generation. (RNNs are O(n·d²) but sequential.)

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q18

questions.q: How do LLMs understand words with multiple meanings, e.g. "bank" of a river vs a financial "bank"?
questions.a:
Through contextual embeddings built by self-attention:

1. The token "bank" starts with the same input embedding in both sentences.

2. In every Transformer layer, self-attention lets "bank" attend to the surrounding words – "river", "water", "sat" in one sentence; "deposit", "loan", "money" in the other.

3. The weighted mix of those context vectors is added to the "bank" representation layer after layer, so by the upper layers the two "bank" vectors are completely different – one close to finance concepts, the other close to geography.

4. Multi-head attention lets different heads capture different cues (nearby words, syntax, topic). This is the key advantage over static embeddings like Word2Vec, which give "bank" one fixed vector.

📌 From Assignment 5 · Q21

questions.q: Give examples of encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder–decoder models. Which tasks suit each?
questions.a:
• Encoder-only: BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ALBERT, DeBERTa, ELECTRA; embedding models (BGE, E5). Best for understanding tasks – classification, NER, extractive QA, embeddings/semantic search.
  • Decoder-only: GPT-2/3/4, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, Falcon, Claude. Best for generation – chat, completion, code, reasoning; also any task framed as text generation.
  • Encoder–decoder: T5, Flan-T5, BART, mBART, Pegasus, Whisper. Best for input → output transformation – translation, summarization, speech-to-text.

📌 From Assignment 6 · Q1

questions.q: Explain Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA).
questions.a:
• MHA (Multi-Head Attention): every head has its own Q, K and V projections. Highest quality, but at inference the KV cache stores K and V for every head → large memory.
  • MQA (Multi-Query Attention): all heads have their own Q, but share a single K and a single V head. KV cache shrinks by the number of heads (e.g. 32×) → much faster decoding, but some quality loss and training instability. (PaLM, Falcon.)
  • GQA (Grouped-Query Attention): a middle ground – query heads are split into G groups; each group shares one K/V head. E.g. 32 query heads, 8 KV heads → 4× smaller KV cache with quality close to MHA. Used in Llama 2-70B, Llama 3, Mistral. GQA with G = 1 is MQA; G = number of heads is MHA.

📌 From Assignment 6 · Q3

questions.q: What is the KV cache and why is it needed? How does it affect memory at long context lengths?
questions.a:
KV cache: during autoregressive generation, each new token must attend to all previous tokens. Without caching, the model would recompute keys and values for the entire prefix at every step (quadratic waste). The KV cache stores the K and V tensors of all previous tokens for every layer, so at each step only the new token's Q, K, V are computed and the new K, V are appended.

Benefit: generation becomes much faster (linear work per new token instead of reprocessing everything).

Memory cost: KV cache size = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head_dim × sequence length × batch size × bytes per value. Example: Llama-2-7B (32 layers, 32 heads × 128 dim, FP16) ≈ 0.5 MB per token → a 4,096-token context needs ~2 GB per sequence. At long contexts the KV cache can be larger than the model weights; solutions are GQA/MQA, KV-cache quantization, PagedAttention (vLLM), sliding windows.

📌 From Assignment 6 · Q5

questions.q: What are the types of positional embeddings (absolute, learned, relative, RoPE, ALiBi)? Absolute vs relative?
questions.a:
• Absolute sinusoidal (original Transformer) – fixed sine/cosine vectors added to embeddings.
  • Absolute learned (BERT, GPT-2) – a trainable embedding per position; cannot go beyond max length (512/1024).
  • Relative position (Transformer-XL, T5 relative bias) – encode the distance between tokens (i − j) inside attention instead of absolute positions.
  • RoPE – Rotary Position Embedding (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, GPT-NeoX) – rotates Q and K vectors by an angle proportional to their position, so the dot product depends only on relative distance.
  • ALiBi (BLOOM, MPT) – adds a linear penalty to attention scores proportional to distance; good length extrapolation.

Absolute vs relative: absolute embeddings encode "I am at position 5"; relative embeddings encode "this token is 3 positions before me". Relative methods generalize better to longer sequences and capture what really matters (distance between words), while absolute learned embeddings are limited to the trained length.

📌 From Assignment 6 · Q8

questions.q: What is BERT? How is it bidirectional?
questions.a:
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) – Google, 2018 – is a stack of Transformer encoder layers pre-trained on large text (Wikipedia + BooksCorpus) and then fine-tuned for downstream tasks. BERT-base: 12 layers, 768 hidden, 12 heads, 110M parameters; BERT-large: 24 layers, 1024 hidden, 16 heads, 340M.

How it is bidirectional: it uses un-masked self-attention, so every token attends to all tokens on both left and right at every layer at the same time. This is possible because it is trained with Masked Language Modelling – the word to predict is hidden, so seeing both sides is not cheating. (Unlike ELMo, which just concatenated separate left-to-right and right-to-left LSTMs, BERT is "deeply" bidirectional.)

📌 From Assignment 6 · Q13

questions.q: Which tasks are used for BERT pre-training (MLM and NSP)? Why did RoBERTa drop NSP?
questions.a:
1. Masked Language Modelling (MLM): 15% of tokens are selected; of these, 80% are replaced with [MASK], 10% with a random token, 10% left unchanged; the model predicts the original tokens. (The 80/10/10 split reduces the mismatch because [MASK] never appears during fine-tuning.)

2. Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): given sentence A and B, predict whether B actually follows A (50% real, 50% random) using the [CLS] output. Intended to help tasks like QA and NLI.

Why RoBERTa dropped NSP: experiments showed NSP did not help and sometimes hurt performance – the task was too easy (random sentences usually differ in topic) and it forced training on short segment pairs. RoBERTa instead trained only with MLM on full-length contiguous text, with dynamic masking, bigger batches, more data and longer training, and outperformed BERT.

📌 From Assignment 6 · Q14

questions.q: What is a Large Language Model? How is it trained (pre-training → instruction tuning → alignment)?
questions.a:
A Large Language Model (LLM) is a very large (billions of parameters) Transformer, usually decoder-only, trained to predict the next token on massive text data. Through this it learns grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and coding ability, and can perform many tasks through prompting.

Training stages:

1. Pre-training – self-supervised next-token prediction on trillions of tokens (web, books, code). Produces a base model that completes text. Most expensive stage (thousands of GPUs, weeks/months).

2. Instruction tuning / SFT – supervised fine-tuning on (instruction, response) pairs and multi-turn chats, so the model follows instructions and adopts a chat format.

3. Alignment / preference tuning – RLHF (reward model + PPO), DPO or similar methods using human (or AI) preference data, to make responses more helpful, honest and harmless. Recent models add reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks (maths, code) to improve reasoning.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q1

questions.q: What is the difference between a base model and an instruct/chat model?
questions.a:
• Base model – only pre-trained; it continues text. Ask "What is the capital of France?" and it may continue with more questions instead of answering. Useful as a starting point for your own fine-tuning, or with few-shot prompting.
  • Instruct / chat model – base model + SFT + alignment. It follows instructions, answers questions, uses a chat template (system/user/assistant roles), refuses unsafe requests. Use this for applications.

Example names: Llama-3-8B (base) vs Llama-3-8B-Instruct.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q2

questions.q: What is RLHF? Explain the reward model and PPO. What is DPO and why is it simpler?
questions.a:
RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback):

1. SFT – fine-tune the base model on good demonstrations.

2. Reward model – humans compare pairs of responses to the same prompt (A better than B). Train a model to output a scalar score that predicts human preference.

3. PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) – the LLM (policy) generates responses, the reward model scores them, and PPO updates the LLM to maximize reward, with a KL penalty that keeps it close to the SFT model (prevents "reward hacking" and gibberish). PPO clips updates for stability.

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): skips the separate reward model and RL loop. It uses the preference pairs directly with a simple classification-style loss that increases the probability of the chosen response and decreases the rejected one, relative to a frozen reference model.

Why DPO is simpler: only two models (policy + reference) instead of four (policy, reference, reward, value), no sampling during training, stable like ordinary fine-tuning, fewer hyperparameters, cheaper. Variants: IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q3

questions.q: What is a context window? What problems appear with very long contexts ("lost in the middle", cost, latency)?
questions.a:
The context window is the maximum number of tokens (prompt + generated output) the model can process at once – e.g. 8k, 128k, 200k or 1M+ tokens.

Problems with very long contexts:

  • "Lost in the middle" – models use information at the beginning and end of the context better than information buried in the middle.
  • Cost – API pricing is per token; huge prompts are expensive.
  • Latency – time-to-first-token grows with prompt length (attention is O(n²), plus KV-cache memory).
  • Distraction – irrelevant content can reduce accuracy; effective context is often shorter than the advertised limit.

Mitigations: RAG (send only relevant chunks), put key instructions at the start/end, summarization, prompt caching, re-ranking.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q5

questions.q: Explain decoding strategies: greedy, beam search, top-k, top-p (nucleus) and temperature.
questions.a:
• Greedy decoding – always pick the highest-probability token. Fast, deterministic, but repetitive and can miss better sequences.
  • Beam search – keep the top-B partial sequences at each step and return the best overall. Good for translation/summarization; tends to be generic and repetitive for open-ended chat.
  • Temperature – divides logits by T before softmax. T < 1 → sharper, more deterministic; T > 1 → flatter, more random/creative; T → 0 ≈ greedy.
  • Top-k sampling – sample only from the k most likely tokens.
  • Top-p (nucleus) sampling – sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p (e.g. 0.9); adapts the candidate set size to the model's confidence.

Other controls: repetition / frequency / presence penalties, min-p, max_new_tokens, stop sequences.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q6

questions.q: What is quantization (INT8, 4-bit, GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF)? What do you trade off?
questions.a:
Quantization stores model weights (and sometimes activations/KV cache) in lower precision – FP32 (4 bytes) → FP16/BF16 (2) → INT8 (1) → 4-bit (0.5 byte) – to reduce memory and speed up inference.

  • INT8 (LLM.int8()) – 8-bit with outlier handling; near-lossless.
  • 4-bit NF4 (bitsandbytes) – used by QLoRA for training on consumer GPUs.
  • GPTQ – post-training quantization that minimizes layer-wise error using second-order information; fast GPU inference.
  • AWQ – activation-aware; protects the ~1% most important weights; good quality at 4-bit.
  • GGUF – file format used by llama.cpp / Ollama for CPU and Apple-silicon inference, with many quant levels (Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0).

Trade-off: less memory, lower cost and faster inference vs some loss in accuracy (small at 8-bit, noticeable at 3-bit and below, especially on maths/reasoning), plus calibration effort and hardware/kernel support.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q7

questions.q: What is hallucination in an LLM? What causes it and how do you reduce it?
questions.a:
Hallucination – the model generates content that is fluent and confident but factually wrong, unsupported or made up (fake citations, wrong numbers, non-existent APIs).

Causes: LLMs are trained to produce *plausible* next tokens, not verified facts; gaps or errors in training data; knowledge cut-off; ambiguous prompts; sampling randomness; training that rewards answering over saying "I don't know".

How to reduce:

  • RAG – ground answers in retrieved documents and instruct "answer only from the context; say 'I don't know' otherwise".
  • Ask for citations/quotes from sources and verify them.
  • Lower temperature for factual tasks.
  • Clear, specific prompts; chain-of-thought or self-verification steps.
  • Tools (search, calculator, database) for facts and maths.
  • Fine-tuning on domain data; better/larger models.
  • Evaluation and guardrails: faithfulness checks (RAGAS), LLM-as-judge, human review for high-risk outputs.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q12

questions.q: What is multimodality? Name a few multimodal models and explain how images are fed to them.
questions.a:
Multimodality – a model that can take in and/or generate more than one type of data: text, images, audio, video.

Examples: GPT-4o, Gemini (1.5/2.x), Claude 3+/4 family (vision), Llama 3.2 Vision, Qwen-VL, LLaVA, Pixtral; Whisper (audio → text); DALL·E, Stable Diffusion (text → image).

How images are fed: a vision encoder (ViT/CLIP-style) splits the image into patches (e.g. 14×14 pixels) and turns them into embeddings; a projection layer/adapter maps these into the LLM's token embedding space; the resulting "image tokens" are placed in the sequence alongside text tokens and the LLM attends to both. In code, you send the image as base64 or a URL inside the message content:

from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
msg = HumanMessage(content=[
    {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this chart"},
    {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{b64}"}}])
llm.invoke([msg])

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q15

questions.q: What is a token? Roughly how many tokens is a word or a page, and why does token count matter?
questions.a:
A token is the unit an LLM reads and writes – a word, part of a word, punctuation or space, produced by the model's tokenizer (BPE etc.).

Rule of thumb (English): 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 words → 100 tokens ≈ 75 words; one A4 page of text ≈ 500–700 tokens. Hindi/Marathi and other non-Latin scripts often need more tokens per word.

Why it matters:

  • Cost – APIs charge per input and output token.
  • Latency – generation time grows with output tokens; prompt processing with input tokens.
  • Context window limits – prompt + history + retrieved chunks + answer must fit.
  • Chunk sizes for RAG are usually defined in tokens.

Count with the model's tokenizer (e.g. `tiktoken` for OpenAI).

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q19

questions.q: Can hallucinations be completely eliminated from a GenAI application?
questions.a:
No. LLMs generate text by predicting likely tokens, so there is always some probability of a fluent but wrong statement. They can be reduced to an acceptable level and managed, not eliminated:

  • Ground answers with RAG and instruct "answer only from context, otherwise say I don't know".
  • Low temperature, clear prompts, structured outputs.
  • Citations so users can verify; tools for facts and calculations.
  • Validation layers: faithfulness checks, rules/regex for numbers and IDs, LLM-as-judge.
  • Human-in-the-loop for high-risk outputs; confidence thresholds and fallbacks.
  • Continuous evaluation and monitoring of hallucination rate.

The right answer in interviews: be honest about the limitation and explain the risk-based controls you put around it.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q20

questions.q: How would you choose an LLM for a production application, and how do you compare two LLMs?
questions.a:
Selection criteria:

  • Quality on YOUR task – build an evaluation set and test candidates; public benchmarks are only a first filter.
  • Latency (time-to-first-token, tokens/sec) and cost per request at expected volume.
  • Context window, multimodal needs, tool calling and structured-output support, languages.
  • Data privacy/compliance – data residency, retention, on-prem need → open-weight vs API.
  • Reliability/rate limits, vendor support, licence, fine-tuning options.

Comparing two LLMs: run both on the same golden dataset with the same prompts; score with task metrics + LLM-as-judge (pairwise, order-swapped) + human review of a sample; compare latency and cost; check failure cases (hallucination, format errors, refusals); then A/B or shadow test in production. Often the answer is a router: a cheap model for easy queries and a strong model for hard ones.

📌 From Assignment 7 · Q22

questions.q: Explain the Trainer and TrainingArguments classes.
questions.a:
• TrainingArguments – a configuration object with all training hyperparameters and settings: output_dir, learning_rate, num_train_epochs, per_device_train_batch_size, weight_decay, eval_strategy, save_strategy, logging_steps, fp16/bf16, gradient_accumulation_steps, load_best_model_at_end, report_to, etc.
  • Trainer – a high-level class that runs the full training loop for you: batching, forward/backward pass, optimizer (AdamW) and LR scheduler, mixed precision, multi-GPU/distributed training, evaluation, checkpointing, logging and early stopping (callbacks).
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments
args = TrainingArguments(output_dir="out", learning_rate=2e-5, num_train_epochs=3,
                         per_device_train_batch_size=16, eval_strategy="epoch",
                         save_strategy="epoch", load_best_model_at_end=True)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_ds,
                  eval_dataset=val_ds, compute_metrics=compute_metrics)
trainer.train(); trainer.evaluate()

📌 From Assignment 8 · Q11

questions.q: What are autoregressive models?
questions.a:
Autoregressive models generate a sequence one token at a time, where each new token is predicted from all previously generated tokens: P(x) = Π P(x_t | x_1 … x_(t−1)). The generated token is appended to the input and the process repeats until an end token or max length. Examples: GPT family, Llama, Mistral (decoder-only LLMs); the decoder of T5/BART is also autoregressive. They use causal masking during training. Contrast: BERT (masked/non-autoregressive) cannot generate text naturally.

📌 From Assignment 8 · Q12

questions.q: What are system, user and assistant messages? (SystemMessage, HumanMessage, AIMessage)
questions.a:
• System message (SystemMessage) – sets the model's behaviour, role and rules for the whole conversation: "You are a helpful banking assistant. Answer only from the provided context." Usually first, given high priority.
  • User / Human message (HumanMessage) – the end user's input/question.
  • Assistant / AI message (AIMessage) – the model's responses; previous ones are included in the history so the model remembers the conversation. Can also contain tool calls.
  • ( ToolMessage – the result of a tool call sent back to the model.)
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage, AIMessage
messages = [SystemMessage(content="You are a concise Python tutor."),
            HumanMessage(content="What is a list?"),
            AIMessage(content="An ordered, mutable collection."),
            HumanMessage(content="And a tuple?")]
llm.invoke(messages)

📌 From Assignment 9 · Q2

questions.q: Explain zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot (N-shot) prompting.
questions.a:
• Zero-shot – only the instruction, no examples: "Classify the sentiment of: 'The food was cold.'"
  • One-shot – one example of input → output before the real input.
  • Few-shot (N-shot) – N examples (typically 2–10) that demonstrate the task and format:
Review: "Amazing camera!" -> Positive
Review: "Battery died in 2 hours." -> Negative
Review: "Delivery was quick and packaging good." ->

Few-shot improves accuracy and format consistency for tasks with a specific style or labels. Choose diverse, representative examples, and watch out for label bias (balance the classes) and order effects.

📌 From Assignment 9 · Q3

questions.q: What is Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting? When does it help?
questions.a:
Chain-of-Thought prompting asks the model to show intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer – either with few-shot examples that include reasoning, or simply by adding "Let's think step by step" (zero-shot CoT). Example: "A shop has 23 apples, sells 20 and buys 6 more. How many? Let's think step by step." → "23 − 20 = 3; 3 + 6 = 9. Answer: 9." Helps with: arithmetic, multi-step logic, word problems, planning, complex classification decisions. It works best with large models. It adds tokens (cost/latency), and is less needed with built-in reasoning models. For production, you can ask for reasoning first and then the final answer in a separate field so you can parse it.

📌 From Assignment 9 · Q4

questions.q: How do temperature, top_p and top_k affect generation? Which settings would you use for a factual Q&A bot vs creative writing?
questions.a:
• Temperature – scales randomness. Low (0–0.3) → focused, deterministic, repeatable; high (0.8–1.2) → diverse, creative, more errors.
  • top_k – sample only from the k most probable tokens (e.g. k = 40).
